The principle that media and propaganda work must be led by the Communist Party and serve its line.

t: Report on the 2025 symposium on the development of the discipline of scientific atheism
zh: 2025年科学无神论学科发展研讨会综述
paras: This is a report on a symposium on the development of the discipline of scientific atheism, held in Beijing on 30 November 2024 to plan work for 2025. It was organised by the CASS Centre for Science and Atheism and the China Atheism Society, with the journal Science and Atheism as co-organiser. The report notes that the discipline is a 'special discipline' funded under the CASS 'Pinnacle Strategy'. Over thirty scholars and students attended, in person and online.

Participants came from the Central Party School, the Central Institute of Socialism, the China Tibetology Research Center, several universities and several CASS institutes. The report is organised in three parts: ten priority research themes for 2025, key tasks in building the discipline, and proposals for the discipline's platforms. It ends with a summing-up by He Xinyuan, head of the special discipline, after remarks by Luo Wendong, Party secretary of the Academy of Marxism, and others.

On research, speakers called for systematic study of the classic writers on atheism, for work on the four systems (disciplinary, academic, discourse and textbook) of Marxist atheism, and for criticism of theology. They also urged work on science popularisation, on the Sinicisation of religion, on atheist education, Party building and the Two Integrations, and on countering cults and religious extremism. Li Shen argued that atheism is the soul of Marxist religious studies and that the spread of theism is linked to non-Marxist religious studies. Peng Ruihua listed new channels of religious infiltration in universities, including online games, big-data targeting and shared-bike QR codes. Several speakers proposed atheist education in Xinjiang, for cadres and in Party schools.

On building the discipline, Zhu Xiaoming proposed a 'four-piece set': an anthology of the classics' writings on atheism, interpretive studies, a textbook on Marxist atheism and an atheism dictionary. Others urged making atheism a compulsory subject for cadres and young students, and a stable university discipline, starting with a second-level discipline within Marxist theory. On platforms, speakers urged the China Atheism Society to recruit young scholars and the journal to seek CSSCI listing. Some also urged the research centre to work as a think tank. He Xinyuan pledged to consolidate the four platforms, start textbook writing and press for inclusion in cadre training. Read the original if you want a detailed record of how Chinese specialists plan the institutional growth and priorities of scientific atheism as an academic field.
quoteEn: Atheism is the soul of Marxist religious studies.
quoteZh: 无神论是马克思主义宗教学的灵魂

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-Leninist approach to atheism, which treats religion as a social and historical phenomenon and promotes atheist education. In China it is a field of research and propaganda under the Marxist theory discipline.
A CASS programme that funds selected disciplines, including 'special' and endangered ones, to raise their standing.

Official policy that religions in China should adapt to Chinese society and socialism under Party leadership. The Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) called for advancing it systematically.
Xi Jinping's formula for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
The study of religion from a Marxist standpoint, which participants distinguish from Western and non-Marxist religious studies.

t: A study of the spread of "micro-superstition" among young people
zh: 青少年群体“微迷信”行为蔓延态势研究
paras: Zhuo Mingliang and Yuan Tao examine "micro-superstition" (wei mixin), a term they use for lightly held, everyday beliefs and practices that lack scientific basis but are widely followed, such as praying for exam luck or consulting online fortune-telling. The authors argue that, although these practices involve a lower degree of belief than traditional superstition, they remain superstitious in nature. In their view, if left unchecked among young people, they erode scientific outlook, the spirit of striving and collectivism, and pose an ideological security risk.

The article opens with a short history of the modern, anti-scientific meaning of "superstition" in China. It then proceeds in four parts: five main manifestations, four potential harms, four causes, and four policy recommendations. The manifestations include temple incense-burning, worship of statues on school campuses before exams, online divination such as "cyber merit" and "AI Buddha", imported practices such as tarot, astrology and Japanese shrine charms, and a market in superstition-themed products. The authors cite figures on temple ticket bookings, social media topics and the fees charged by tarot bloggers.

On harms, the authors claim that micro-superstition damages young people's inner world, invites fraud, spreads negative values, and opens a channel for Western ideological infiltration. They also warn that shared group identities could serve political mobilisation, citing the "Arab Spring" as an analogy. On causes, they stress anxiety arising from developmental pressures (the sense of being unable to "lie flat" yet unable to win the "rat race"), the spread of individualism, utilitarianism and pan-entertainment trends online, venture capital that has turned fortune-telling into a profitable industry, and weakened anti-superstition education that leaves young people tolerant of it.

The authors propose that youth organisations and government departments study and respond to young people's real difficulties, especially in employment and marriage. They also call for stricter supervision of self-media, with sensitive-word databases, penalties and blocking of overseas sites, tighter regulation and investment screening of the cultural and entertainment market, and stronger education in scientific atheism and Marxist materialism through schools, the Communist Youth League and central media. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese academics frame youth folk-belief practices as an ideological and governance issue, with concrete survey-style examples and policy proposals.
quoteEn: "Micro-superstition" is in essence still a superstitious mentality, and may to some extent affect individual decisions and actions.
quoteZh: “微迷信”本质上仍属于迷信心理，可能会在某种程度上影响个人决策与行动。

glossary.explanation: The authors' term for light, everyday superstitious behaviours that give psychological comfort without amounting to full devotion. Examples include praying for exam luck or online fortune-telling.
A Marxist-materialist framework for rejecting religious and supernatural beliefs, taught in Chinese Party and academic settings. The article proposes it as the fundamental remedy for superstition.
A popular term for young people's choice to withdraw from intense competition and live with minimal effort. The authors pair it with the "rat race" (neijuan) to describe a no-win situation.
An official concept holding that the Party-state must protect the dominant socialist ideology from competing or foreign ideas, especially among the young.

t: Accelerating the construction of a self-reliant Chinese atheism knowledge system
st: An interview with Tian Xinming of the Higher Education Science Research Development Centre, Ministry of Education
zh: 《马克思主义研究》记者：加快建构中国自主无神论知识体系
zhSub: 访教育部高等学校科学研究发展中心田心铭研究员
source: Marxist Studies (马克思主义研究), 2024 no. 7
paras: This is an interview, conducted by a reporter for the journal Marxist Studies (issue 7, 2024), with Tian Xinming, a researcher formerly at the Ministry of Education's higher-education social science research centre. It asks how atheism, described as an indispensable but weak discipline within philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, can be built up under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Tian answers that, following Xi's remark that the task is ultimately to build a self-reliant Chinese knowledge system, the discipline should now build a self-reliant atheism knowledge system.

The interview has three parts: why, what kind of system, and how. Tian first defines "knowledge system" as the umbrella term for the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems, then reviews the discipline's history. He then sets out four dimensions of "Chinese self-reliance": guiding ideology, object of study, academic resources, and subjectivity and originality. The last part proposes a structure and method, and closes on the Two Integrations.

Tian argues that the discipline started late and developed slowly, producing the saying "atheism has no one to speak for it, theism does". He nonetheless sees enough accumulated work since the 18th Party Congress (2012) to allow "integration" and "final assembly". For Tian, the guiding ideology must be Marxism as a whole, not isolated quotations. The object of study is the contradiction between a godless material world and the presence of belief in gods in social consciousness, together with the opposition of atheism and theism. Marxism serves both as guide and as primary academic resource, whereas traditional Chinese culture and foreign scholarship are resources only. Tian calls for a unified, theoretically grounded ("systematic and学理") discipline cluster covering theory, history and practice. An introductory textbook on atheism would condense the whole system around three questions: whether gods exist, what role atheism and theism play, and how to uphold atheism and treat religion in practice.

Tian concludes that the Two Integrations are the fundamental route to building the system, and that Marxist guidance, blending of resources, subjectivity and originality, and systematisation all apply them. In practice, he says, the work must support the Party's religious policy, which combines firm atheism as a worldview with unity between believers and non-believers. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-academic blueprint for establishing atheism as a discipline, including its proposed structure and its link to religious policy.
quoteEn: The guiding ideology is singular, while academic resources are diverse. The guiding ideology cannot be pluralised, and academic resources cannot be made uniform.
quoteZh: 指导思想是唯一的，学术资源是多样的。指导思想不能多元化，学术资源不能单一化。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's current official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
The principle of combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, affirmed at the 20th Party Congress (2022).
In Xi Jinping's 2022 formulation, the task of Chinese social science is to build a self-reliant knowledge system. Tian uses the term to cover disciplinary, academic and discourse systems.

t: Practical explorations in special-topic education on the Marxist view of religion in universities
st: The case of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
zh: 高校马克思主义宗教观专题教育的实践探索
zhSub: 以中国科学院大学为例
paras: Yang Tianjiao and Chen Tianjia ask how the Marxist view of religion, together with the Party's religious policy, can be taught more effectively in Chinese universities. They note that university ideological and political courses lack a dedicated chapter on the subject, so it is usually taught as scattered points of knowledge. Drawing on the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (UCAS), the authors argue that a stand-alone special topic is feasible and welcomed by students, but that it needs better content, discourse and institutional support.

The article has three parts. It first describes the design and practice of a religion topic that UCAS has run since 2019 within a compulsory postgraduate course on Chinese Marxism and the contemporary world. It then evaluates the results through a questionnaire and interviews covering 1,365 master's and doctoral student responses. Finally it offers strategies and recommendations for strengthening such education.

On design, the authors describe a topic organised around the Marxist view of religion, drawing also on philosophy, sociology, psychology and brain science. It starts from students' own questions, such as why Party members may not hold religious beliefs, and links religion to the holistic national security outlook through cases of alleged foreign religious infiltration, cults and spiritual pyramid schemes. According to the survey, 93.7% of respondents were satisfied with the teaching, and 65.71% had vague understandings of the Marxist view of religion. Nearly half had encountered alien-themed cult or spiritual-practice content online. Only 23.22% correctly answered a question on the principles of religious affairs management. The authors conclude that students want systematic knowledge but find classical formulations abstract and know the policy background poorly.

The authors recommend understanding the regularities of teaching this subject, with an atheist foundation and interdisciplinary rigour. They call for an educational discourse that is authentic, sincere and appropriate, avoiding command and preaching. They also propose stronger Party leadership in universities, academic support, training for ideological and political teachers to compensate for a shortage of specialist scholars, and a dedicated national textbook. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese example of how religion is taught in university ideological courses, including the survey data and the authors' own assessment of weaknesses.
quoteEn: The religious question is one of the major issues in governing the country, and it takes extremely diverse and complex forms worldwide.
quoteZh: 宗教问题是治国理政的重大问题之一，在全球范围内呈现出极为多元复杂的表现。

glossary.explanation: The official theoretical framework on the origin, nature and social role of religion, based on Marx, Engels and later Party statements. It underpins China's religious policy and the Party's promotion of scientific atheism.
A concept introduced by Xi Jinping in 2014 that treats security broadly, covering political, cultural, social and other domains. The article applies it to religious infiltration and cults.
Compulsory courses in Chinese schools and universities that teach Marxism, Party theory and official policy.

keywords: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

t: The origins, spread and social role of religion in Southeast Asia: an analysis
zh: 东南亚宗教的起源、传播及其社会作用探析
paras: Wang Xiaofeng asks how religion in Southeast Asia arose, spread and functioned socially, and answers from the Marxist view of religion and historical materialism. The article argues that religious consciousness must be explained from material production and the level of the productive forces, not from ideas alone. It presents this as a theoretical and practical research task, since Southeast Asian politics, culture and diplomacy cannot be understood without religion.

The article has five parts. It first traces the origins of primitive religion, then the spread of Buddhism and Islam through trade. It then examines how colonial powers used religion, and how religious figures took part in anti-colonial struggles. A closing section looks ahead. Cases include Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia and the Philippines, supported by many quotations from Marx and Engels and by studies from Southeast Asian and Chinese scholars.

Wang makes three main moves. First, early peoples with weak productive forces were subjugated by nature, so they personified natural forces. Wang cites sun worship in Indonesia and Vietnam, bird totems in Vietnam, ancestor worship and Malay animism. Second, Buddhism and Islam travelled along trade routes: Indian merchants and monks brought Buddhism, and Arab merchants brought Islam, with Malacca as a centre. Third, citing Marx's 'opium of the people', Wang contends that French colonizers used Buddhism in Vietnam, and Spanish and later American rulers used Catholicism in the Philippines, to pacify the population. In Wang's account the Philippine church held wide political and economic powers. Yet Wang also reports that monks and Muslim leaders led or joined resistance in Vietnam, Malaya and the Philippines, with religious and national conflicts becoming intertwined.

Wang concludes that religion will persist in Southeast Asia and keep shaping politics, because it is embedded in mainstream and popular culture and in a plural society. Malaysia is the main example. There, Wang says, Islamism and Malay nationalism are merging, religious bureaucracy is expanding, and religious identity is deepening social division. Wang warns of future 'religious risks' and calls for specialist study of Southeast Asian religion guided by the Marxist view. Read the original if you want a Marxist-framed account of Southeast Asian religious history, or a sample of how Chinese atheism-studies scholarship treats the region.
quoteEn: Under conditions of low-level productive forces, the ancient peoples of Southeast Asia gave a distorted and inverted reflection of many natural phenomena and deified them, and primitive religion thereby arose.
quoteZh: 在低水平生产力的条件下，东南亚的古人对许多自然现象作出歪曲和颠倒的反映，把自然现象神化，从而产生了原始宗教。

glossary.explanation: The body of Marxist theory on the nature, origins and social functions of religion and its relation to politics and culture. Chinese scholarship in religious and atheism studies uses it as its official guiding framework.
The Marxist theory that material production and social relations of production ultimately determine social life and consciousness.

t: The global significance of upholding the direction of the sinicization of religion in China
zh: 坚持我国宗教中国化方向的全球主义意涵
paras: Since 2015, Xi Jinping has called for upholding the direction of the sinicization of religion in China as part of guiding religion to adapt to socialist society. Li and Yin respond to foreign scholarship that, in their account, presents the policy as a uniquely Chinese measure to secularise, Hanify, control or eliminate religion, contrary to global trends and to religious freedom. They argue that the policy has a local, Chinese orientation but also carries rich "globalist" implications, and that the two are not in contradiction.

The article, published in Science and Atheism in 2024, first notes that overseas research includes an edited volume distinguishing "top-down" from "bottom-up" sinicization. It then examines the policy from seven angles: its fit with the objective laws of religious development, its engagement with global religious realities, its consistency with religious freedom, its alignment with religious modernism, its respect for fine traditional culture, its value for global religious governance, and a closing synthesis.

The authors' central move is to ground the policy in Marxist religious studies: religion is superstructure, shaped by economic base and society, so religions necessarily become localised and adapt to their times. Refusing this, they say, produces conflict, extremism and terrorism. They argue that sinicization is therefore a response to global religious conflict, which they say has reached China through extremism and "de-sinicization" currents. They hold that the policy is a form of guidance consistent with freedom of belief and with UN counter-terrorism resolutions. They also contend that it follows the global path of religious modernism and respects both Chinese and religious traditions. Finally, they cite France's burqa ban and US church-state separation as examples of other states steering religions to fit national values.

Li and Yin conclude that the policy is "both Chinese and the world's" and offers a reference for global religious governance. They attribute foreign criticism to anti-China forces that, in their view, fear the policy's success will challenge their own governance models. They urge confidence in China's path, theory, system and culture, and continued application of the Party's theory of religious work in the new era. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars rebut foreign critiques of religious policy and frame it in terms of global trends and Marxist religious theory.
quoteEn: The policy of guiding the sinicization of religion is both China's own and the world's.
quoteZh: 引导宗教中国化政策,既是中国的,也是世界的

glossary.explanation: Official policy line, stated by Xi Jinping in 2015 and 2016, that religions in China should adapt to Chinese culture and society. Critics abroad often read it as forced assimilation, while Chinese officials present it as guidance.

glossary.zh: 积极引导宗教与社会主义社会相适应
glossary.pinyin: jījí yǐndǎo zōngjiào yǔ shèhuì zhǔyì shèhuì xiāng shìyìng
glossary.en: guiding religion to adapt to socialist society
glossary.explanation: Long-standing Party policy line that religions should be actively guided to fit socialist society. The article treats sinicization as its concrete form.
The article's term for how states and the international community manage religious affairs, extremism and church–state relations.

t: Religion does not play a prominent role in the shared spiritual home of the Chinese nation
zh: 中华民族共有精神家园中宗教角色并不突出
paras: Wang Qichang asks what makes up the shared spiritual home of the Chinese nation and what part religion plays in it. The short piece argues that, compared with the West, religion's role in building this home is not prominent. It opens by defining the shared spiritual home as the historically formed cultural and spiritual system of a unified multi-ethnic China, to which every self-identifying Chinese person is emotionally attached.

Wang cites Xi Jinping's 2021 Central Conference on Ethnic Work, which listed building the shared spiritual home among its "twelve musts". The article then divides the concept into three levels: ideas, culture and everyday life. At each level it sets Chinese examples beside Western ones, including Plato, Thomas More, Hegel on Greece and Heidegger's "poetic dwelling".

At the level of ideas, Wang points to the ideal of "great harmony under heaven" (datong) from the Book of Rites, later taken up by Kang Youwei and Sun Yat-sen. At the cultural level, the home is the continuous history and rich culture of China, including Confucian culture, the arts, the written script and classical poetry, whose popularity on television shows is offered as evidence. At the level of life, it is the unity of heaven and humanity and a love of nature, shown in Tao Yuanming's pastoral poetry and, in Wang's example, the popularity of the video creator Li Ziqi.

Wang concludes that Daoist ideas of the unity of heaven and humanity and Buddhist compassion may have contributed to the shared spiritual home and may help in building it. Even so, the article holds that religion's role here is not prominent in comparison with the West. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese scholar of atheism frames the nation's spiritual home in cultural rather than religious terms.
quoteEn: But compared with the West, religion's role in the process of building the Chinese nation's shared spiritual home is not prominent.
quoteZh: 但相对于西方，宗教在中华民族共有精神家园的构筑过程中作用并不突出。

glossary.zh: 中华民族共有精神家园
glossary.en: shared spiritual home of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A concept in official ethnic-affairs discourse for the common cultural and spiritual attachment of all ethnic groups in China. Xi Jinping listed building it among the "twelve musts" at the 2021 Central Conference on Ethnic Work.
An ideal of a just and harmonious world, described in the Book of Rites (Liji). Later thinkers such as Kang Youwei and Sun Yat-sen drew on it.
A traditional Chinese idea, associated with Daoist and other thought, of harmony between humans and the natural order.

t: Grasping the relationship between religion and culture within the "Five-Sphere Integrated Plan"
zh: 在“五位一体”总体布局中把握宗教与文化的关系
paras: Qiu Shi, writing in the journal Science and Atheism, takes up how religion and culture should be related in Chinese theory and practice. The piece is an excerpted contribution to a seminar on traditional Chinese religion and traditional Chinese culture, held in Beijing on 21 April (2024) by the China Atheism Society and the CASS Centre for Science and Atheism. Qiu argues that, within the Five-Sphere Integrated Plan, religion is a political matter and not a cultural one, and that the "religion-as-culture" thesis has complicated the question.

The article first clarifies the two terms, both of which Qiu calls elastic. It then examines Party congress reports and the Party's theory of religious work, and ends with a critique of Western religious studies.

Qiu holds that "culture" in the Five-Sphere Integrated Plan means the spiritual-cultural sphere alongside the economy, politics, society and ecology, and that the discussion should be confined to this sense. Religion belongs to the political sphere as part of united front work. According to Qiu, the 19th and 20th Party Congress reports (2017, 2022) never mention religion in their cultural sections, and of the "nine musts" only the requirement of the sinicization of religion concerns culture. In that framework Chinese culture guides and permeates religion. Religion is culture, Qiu concedes, but a special kind that must be guided by fine traditional culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture.

Qiu calls two Western claims fallacies: that primitive culture was religious culture, and that religion is the essence and soul of a culture. In Qiu's account, these inflate religion and set ancient superstition against modern scientific culture. Qiu calls for stronger critical analysis of Western religious studies to defend the scientific character of the Party's religious theory. Read the original if you want a short statement of the official Chinese argument for treating religion as a political rather than cultural question.
quoteEn: In the Party's theory, guidelines and policies on religious work in the new era, religion is a political question and not a cultural one, and religious work is political work and not cultural work.
quoteZh: 在新时代党的宗教工作理论和方针政策中，宗教属于政治问题而不是文化问题，宗教工作属于政治工作而不是文化工作。

glossary.explanation: The Party's framework for national development across the economy, politics, culture, society and ecological civilisation, formalised at the 18th Party Congress (2012).
The policy of adapting religions in China to Chinese society, culture and socialism under Party leadership.
The Party's work of building alliances with and managing non-Party groups, including religious communities.
A view, criticised here as Western in origin, that treats religion as a form or the essence of culture.

t: The position and role of traditional Chinese religion in traditional Chinese culture
st: Centred on the debates among Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism
zh: 中国传统宗教在中国传统文化中的地位和作用
zhSub: 以儒释道三教论争为中心
paras: Lü Jianfu asks what place and function traditional religion held within traditional Chinese culture. The piece is an edited set of remarks from an April 2024 symposium in Beijing on 'traditional Chinese religion and traditional Chinese culture'. The symposium was organised by the Chinese Atheism Society, the CASS Research Centre for Science and Atheism and the journal Science and Atheism, to carry out Xi Jinping's speech on cultural inheritance and development and to examine how traditional culture bears on the sinicization of religion. Lü's thesis is that religion was essentially subordinate to a Confucian-centred culture, with its role limited to faith and philosophical thought.

The article first sketches religion's development from primitive nature worship through the Xia, Shang and Zhou periods to the shift towards a humanistic culture in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. It then traces how the Three Teachings came to be paired: Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism from the Han–Wei period onwards. A third section compares the three teachings' character, and a fourth assesses their influence on Chinese life, philosophy and art.

Lü argues that describing Chinese culture as made up of the 'Three Teachings' is a modern idea. In Lü's account it stems from the historical comparison and debate among the three, from the use of Christianity as a template for classifying national cultures, and from later efforts to set tradition against the West. Lü contends that it overstates religion and blurs the line between religious and secular culture. On this view, the Han-era 'sole honouring of Confucianism' and the Six Arts created a complete cultural system, and Confucianism, as state ideology, stayed dominant. Its religious element lay in venerating Heaven and ancestors, while Buddhism and Daoism were religions proper. The author maintains that they never became coequal, and that when religion intruded into politics, as in the 'Three Wu persecutions of Buddhism', it was suppressed.

Lü credits Buddhism with raising the level of Chinese dialectical thinking, with Sui–Tang Buddhist philosophy as a peak, though its idealism also influenced Neo-Confucianism. Lü also notes Buddhism's artistic legacy, such as the Dunhuang grottoes. Lü cites the saying 'Confucianism governs the world, Daoism the body, Buddhism the mind', and concludes that Confucian belief was universal while Buddhist and Daoist faith was a partial choice. Lü adds that this philosophical heritage helped China accept Marxist dialectical materialism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese scholar of religion, writing in an atheism-studies journal, positions religion as subordinate within traditional culture.
quoteEn: Overall, then, traditional Chinese religion occupied an essentially subordinate position in traditional Chinese culture, its role confined to spiritual spheres such as religious belief and philosophical thought.
quoteZh: 故总体而言，中国传统宗教在中国传统文化中基本上处于附属地位，其作用限定在宗教信仰以及哲学思想等精神领域。

glossary.explanation: A policy slogan calling for religions in China to adapt to Chinese culture and socialist society, promoted by the Party leadership in recent years.

The traditional pairing of Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism as China's main intellectual and religious traditions. The author also notes an older sense referring to the Xia, Shang and Zhou cultural traditions.
The Han dynasty policy, associated with Emperor Wu, of making Confucian learning the state ideology.
The six Confucian classics (Changes, Odes, Documents, Rites, Music, Spring and Autumn Annals), which the author treats as the base of a full cultural system.
The traditional belief of reverence for Heaven and imitation of the ancestors, which the author treats as Confucianism's religious element.

t: Plekhanov's critique of the "religious quest" and his exposition of Marxist atheism
zh: 普列汉诺夫对“宗教探寻”的批判和马克思主义无神论的阐释
paras: Zhang Jiansong examines Georgi Plekhanov's long essay "On the So-Called Religious Quests in Russia", written after the defeat of the 1905 revolution and under Stolypin's reaction. In that climate, Zhang explains, bourgeois scholars read the defeat as divine punishment, and a "God-building" current even arose inside Social Democracy. The article argues that Plekhanov used historical materialism to clear away this fog, defend Marxist atheism and steady revolutionary morale, and that the work still has practical value for religious theory and religious work today.

The article follows the three finished parts of the essay, found in volume three of Plekhanov's selected philosophical works. Part one, "On Religion", sets out the basic theory; part two, "More on Religion", criticises Tolstoy, Lunacharsky and Gorky; part three attacks the Decadents, chiefly Merezhkovsky and Minsky. A planned fourth part on the Vekhi group was never written. A short closing section draws lessons for present-day China.

Zhang reports that Plekhanov defines religion as a system of ideas, emotions and activities (myth, religious feeling and ritual). Drawing on ethnology, Plekhanov traces animism, totemism and the idea of gods to hunting life and low productive forces, which Zhang takes as confirmation that social being determines social consciousness. Using this framework, Plekhanov argues that every religion contains supernatural spirits, so "atheist religions" such as Tolstoy's, Lunacharsky's "fifth religion" and Gorky's deification of humanity are illusory. He treats them as consolation sought by disillusioned intellectuals. He also argues that the Decadents scorned workers' economic struggles as vulgar while pursuing individualist, bourgeois comfort and mystical escape.

In the closing section Zhang draws two lessons: remain firm Marxists, and fight wrong ideological currents boldly. Zhang contrasts Soviet collapse after Gorbachev abandoned Marxism's guiding role with the Chinese Communist Party's adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Zhang also lists historical nihilism, constitutional democracy, "universal values" and neoliberalism as currents to be confronted, together with abnormal religious phenomena in some regions. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Plekhanov's religious theory, or want to see how it is applied to current ideological and religious work in China.
quoteEn: Plekhanov's readiness to draw the sword and fight when faced with erroneous currents of thought deserves our emulation.
quoteZh: 普列汉诺夫面对错误思潮的亮剑精神、斗争精神，值得我们学习。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: Official formula for the Party's project of fitting Marxist theory to China's conditions and to contemporary developments.
In Party usage, a label for views that question or negate the official account of the Party's and socialism's history.

t: Zhang Zai's reworking of the "naturalist" view of ghosts and spirits inherited from the Qin–Han period
zh: 论张载对秦汉以来“自然主义”鬼神观的改造
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2024 no. 2
paras: Zhang Zai's (Song-dynasty Confucian) account of ghosts and spirits has often been treated as a representative of ancient Chinese materialism and atheism. Wang argues that a purely naturalist reading cannot capture it, because in Song–Ming Neo-Confucianism ghosts and spirits concern the substance of the Way. In Wang's view, Zhang Zai deliberately turned away from the naturalist view that had prevailed since the Qin and Han, and moved atheism from a narrow to a broader sense.

The article has five parts. It first sets out the naturalist view and its limits, taking in the Guanzi, the Book of Rites, the Appended Remarks of the Book of Changes, Wang Chong and Fan Zhen. It then examines Zhang Zai's concept of "spirit" (shen) as substance and its link to the Great Void, and his reading of "ghosts and spirits" as function. The last sections turn to ritual sacrifice, the idea of "establishing teaching through the Way of spirits", and his rejection of belief in monstrous and malignant beings, before a brief conclusion.

Wang says the naturalist view treated ghosts and spirits as refined qi and as the expanding and contracting of yin and yang. It denied that the dead survive as ghosts, culminating in Fan Zhen's thesis that the spirit perishes with the body. Wang judges this a narrow atheism: it attacks only concrete consciousness, strips Confucianism of its transcendent dimension, and fails to answer Buddhist objections, such as those of Zongmi. Zhang Zai, by contrast, separates finite perception from "spirit" as unlimited, constant and the substance of heaven. Ghosts and spirits are the "innate capacity" of the two qi: they are not qi itself, yet not apart from it. This avoids both naturalism and the Buddhist split between substance and function. In sacrifice, Zhang Zai rejects personified mountain-and-river deities and fixed ritual hierarchies, holding that sacrifice communes with the shared Void nature of ancestors and Heaven. He refutes tales of malignant beings by appeal to what all can see, as against private visions.

Wang concludes that Zhang Zai kept the naturalist element, starting from the phenomenal world, but restored the transcendent dimension without becoming a thoroughgoing atheist. His view is not a deviation in the history of atheism but a "candid friend" (zhengyou) to it, and Wang Fuzhi later built on it. Read the original if you study Song–Ming Neo-Confucianism, Chinese debates on atheism, or Confucian responses to Buddhism and want a close reading of Zhang Zai's texts.
quoteEn: Zhang Zai's reworking of the naturalist view of ghosts and spirits since the Qin and Han also pushed the development of atheism from a narrow sense towards a broad one.
quoteZh: 张载对秦汉以来自然主义鬼神观的改造，也促使无神论的发展从狭义走向广义。

glossary.explanation: The basic stuff of the cosmos in much Chinese philosophy, which condenses into things and disperses at their dissolution.
Zhang Zai's term for the formless original state of qi and for the substance of Heaven, empty but not nothing.

glossary.en: establishing teaching through the Way of spirits
glossary.literal: setting up instruction by the Way of spirits
glossary.explanation: A phrase from the Book of Changes, meaning that sages use reverence for the spiritual to educate and transform the people.
A paired category in Chinese philosophy: the underlying reality (ti) and its operation or manifestation (yong).

glossary.en: thesis that the spirit perishes with the body
glossary.literal: theory of the extinction of spirit
glossary.explanation: Fan Zhen's fifth-to-sixth-century argument against the Buddhist doctrine of an immortal soul.
A term from Mencius for what people can do without learning; Zhang Zai makes it a feature of Heaven's own nature.

t: Atheist propaganda and education in rural areas of China's southwestern border: current situation and countermeasures
zh: 西南边境农村地区无神论宣传教育现状与对策
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2024 no. 2
paras: Yue Zongfeng asks how well Marxist atheist propaganda and education is working in rural areas along China's southwestern border, and what should be done to improve it. Writing in the context of central documents that call for strengthening atheist education in the countryside (the 2018 No. 1 Document on rural revitalization and a 2021 opinion on ideological and political work), the author treats the border as a weak point of ideological work. The article's thesis is that the overall situation is good, but that several problems, above all foreign religious infiltration and illegal religious activity, require a systematic set of countermeasures.

The study is based on fieldwork on the China–Myanmar border in six prefectures and cities of Yunnan (Nujiang, Dehong, Baoshan, Lincang, Pu'er and Xishuangbanna), carried out in three rounds between December 2019 and November 2023. It draws on 812 valid questionnaires out of 1,000 distributed, plus 68 semi-structured and in-depth interviews. The article has three parts: the current situation, four problems that merit attention, and five groups of countermeasures.

On the situation, Yue reports that 62.8 per cent of respondents held communist (atheist) belief and 22.4 per cent were religious believers. In the author's reading this shows that atheism remains dominant, although religious belief is still well above the level in inland China. Yue also cites low rates of superstitious practice, with 94 per cent reporting none, and high satisfaction with grassroots government work on atheist education. The problems identified are the inertia of ethnic religious tradition, foreign religious infiltration alongside illegal religious activity, inaction and even belief in spirits among some grassroots cadres and Party members, and spiritual emptiness linked to the hollowing out of villages next to the border. Yue argues that these conditions leave room for religious groups to compete with the Party for rural leadership.

The proposed countermeasures are to promote border prosperity and agricultural modernization, since the author follows Marx in treating poverty as the soil of religion. They also include investment in education and culture, a joint early-warning and management system against infiltration, stronger Party leadership with accountability for cadres and atheism as a criterion for Party admission, and a drive to spread Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era together with local ethnic cultural activities. Read the original if you want survey figures on religion and atheist education in Yunnan's border villages, or an example of how Party scholars frame religious infiltration and policy responses in border regions.
quoteEn: Although religious belief is widespread in the rural areas of the southwestern border because of ethnic tradition and historical and geographical factors, Marxist atheism still holds the dominant position in the people's thinking.
quoteZh: 西南边境农村地区虽然基于民族传统和历史地理因素的影响，宗教信仰盛行，但马克思主义无神论仍在人民群众思想中占主导地位。

glossary.explanation: A national strategy announced in 2017 and set out in the 2018 No. 1 Document, aimed at developing the rural economy, culture and governance.

glossary.literal: revitalise the border, enrich the people
glossary.explanation: A state policy to develop border regions and raise the incomes of residents there.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official name for Xi Jinping's body of theory, written into the Party constitution in 2017 as a guide to action.
In the article's definition, religious activity that violates the constitution, laws, regulations and policies, including unauthorised gatherings and temple building.

t: An analysis of Yan Yuan's atheist thought
zh: 颜元的无神论思想探析
paras: Yan Yuan, a thinker of the late Ming and early Qing, is often described as an Enlightenment figure, but Xu Jiulin argues that scholarship has misread his atheism. Earlier studies, Xu says, focus on his attacks on Buddhism and Daoism and treat his atheism as theoretically unoriginal. Xu's thesis is that Yan's atheism is aimed chiefly at the religionised Confucianism of Cheng–Zhu Neo-Confucianism, which Yan believed had absorbed Buddhist and Daoist ideas, and that it can only be understood through his materialist theory of qi and his practical learning.

The article has four parts. It first examines Yan's qi-based ontology and his epistemology, then his practice-oriented thought summed up as getting one's hands on the matter and doing it. A third section assesses the significance and limits of his atheism, and a short conclusion follows. Xu draws on Yan's own writings and, at points, on Marx and Engels as comparison.

Xu argues that Yan reversed the Cheng–Zhu priority of principle (li) over qi, holding that li exists only within qi. On this basis Yan rejected a pure, transcendent world of li, the claim that qi is the source of evil, and the Buddhist and Daoist views of the world as empty and still. His epistemology of seeing principle in affairs likewise denies that ghosts, reincarnation, hell or immortals can be known. Yan's practical doctrine affirms the body and its desires. It rejects quiet-sitting, the Cheng–Zhu maxim of preserving heavenly principle and eliminating human desires, and fatalism, and it widens practice to include military, agricultural and economic matters. Xu reads all this as a critique of religious alienation.

Xu concludes that Yan helped Confucianism shed Buddhist and Daoist influence and move from speculative learning towards practical learning, and that this makes his thought significant for the Enlightenment. Xu also notes limits: Yan prayed to a supreme deity at night, his qi theory kept some idealist and agnostic traces, and he sought liberation from religion through moral cultivation rather than through the growth of productive forces. Read the original if you study Chinese materialism, Neo-Confucianism's religious dimension, or how Chinese scholars read Confucian thinkers alongside Marxist critiques of religion.
quoteEn: Yan Yuan's critique of Cheng–Zhu Neo-Confucianism and of Buddhist and Daoist religious thought was ultimately meant to free people from theological bondage and to pull their attention back from heaven to the human world.
quoteZh: 颜元对程朱理学和佛道宗教思想的批判终究是要将人从神学束缚中解放出来，并将人的关注点从天上拉回到了人间

glossary.literal: theory of qi as the root
glossary.explanation: The view that qi, the material-energetic stuff of the cosmos, is the origin of all things. Chinese Marxist scholars often present it as a materialist strand in Chinese philosophy opposed to the primacy of li (principle).
The school of Song-dynasty Confucianism associated with Cheng Yi, Cheng Hao and Zhu Xi, which treats li (principle) as the ultimate reality. It became state orthodoxy in later imperial China.

glossary.en: getting one's hands on the matter and doing it
glossary.literal: to lay hands on it and actually do the thing
glossary.explanation: Yan Yuan's slogan for learning through direct, practical engagement. He used it to reinterpret 'investigating things' (gewu) in the Great Learning as hands-on practice.

glossary.en: preserving heavenly principle and eliminating human desires
glossary.explanation: A Neo-Confucian maxim urging moral cultivation by keeping to cosmic principle and suppressing selfish desires. Yan Yuan and later critics attacked it as denying real human needs.

t: Key issues in further advancing the sinicization of religion in China
zh: 深入推进我国宗教中国化的几个关键问题
paras: How can the Party more effectively advance the "sinicization of religion" (zongjiao zhongguohua), which Xi Jinping stressed in 2021 and which the 20th Party Congress report (2022) again set as a task? He Xinyuan, a researcher at the Academy of Marxism, argues that, beyond supporting religious circles in interpreting doctrines in line with contemporary China and fine traditional Chinese culture, three things must be grasped. These are the core socialist values as the "greatest common divisor", Marxist atheism, and the Party's leadership.

The article is organised in three sections matching these points. It begins from the premise that religion must adapt to its society and will long exist in socialist China. It cites the 2018 white paper figure of nearly 200 million believers and over 380,000 clergy. It draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin and later Party leaders, and on Xi Jinping's speeches, including the 2021 National Conference on Religious Work.

In the first section, He argues that unity among believers and non-believers should be sought at the level of shared values. Their fundamental political and economic interests are said to coincide, and the core socialist values are presented as the value consensus all can accept. Using them to guide religion does not mean asking believers to abandon faith, but a "political bottom line" must hold: upholding Party leadership, patriotism and socialism with Chinese characteristics. In the second, He holds that Marxist atheism is a "major principle". Unchecked spread of theism is said to threaten the Party's guiding ideology and governing position. Atheist education is described as aiming neither to eliminate religion nor to set believers against non-believers, but to help people view religion scientifically. Patriotism, collectivism and socialism education in religious circles, including the "four histories", is proposed as the practical route. In the third, He argues that religion is never a private matter for a Marxist party, citing Marx, Engels, Lenin and successive Chinese leaders. Party leadership is said to work through political leadership, ideological guidance and guidance of interests, and through the Party's cultural leadership, with ideological work at its core.

He concludes that guidance by the core socialist values, adherence to Marxist atheism and atheist education, and strengthened Party leadership are essential to advancing sinicization. In his view, this brings out religion's positive role, respects the laws of religion's survival, and addresses prominent problems in the religious field. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a Party-affiliated scholar of atheism frames religious policy in the Xi Jinping era.
quoteEn: Religion is a special kind of social ideology, which means that much of religious work is closely tied to ideological questions.
quoteZh: 宗教是一种特殊社会意识形态，这决定了宗教工作的许多内容都同意识形态问题密切相关。

glossary.explanation: A policy formulation stressed by Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress, requiring religions in China to adapt to Chinese culture and socialist society and to accept Party leadership.
A mathematical metaphor used by Xi Jinping for the widest shared ground among different social groups, used especially in united front work.
A set of twelve values promoted by the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012), at national, social and individual levels, such as prosperity, democracy, equality and patriotism.
The Party's official worldview position on religion, under which Party members must be atheists and atheist education is promoted while freedom of religious belief is formally maintained.
A term Xi Jinping used explicitly in June 2023, referring to the Party's leadership over ideology and culture; the Chinese term also corresponds to Gramscian cultural hegemony.
Education covering the history of the Party, of the People's Republic, of reform and opening up, and of socialist development.

t: Innovative mechanisms for universities to prevent and defuse the risk of online religious infiltration
zh: 高校防范和化解网络宗教渗透风险的创新机制研究
paras: Zhang Aihui and Gao Jianjun take up the question of how Chinese universities can more effectively guard against what they call online religious infiltration by hostile Western forces. They argue that the internet has made online religion a new form of religious life and that infiltration through it threatens ideological security on campus. Their answer is a five-part "innovative mechanism" combining Marxist religion education, reformed ideological and political education, campus culture, legal regulation and a dedicated anti-infiltration team.

The article first sets out why the task matters: in the authors' account it answers Western ideological "containment", supports students' healthy development, and raises the effectiveness of ideological and political education. It then reports a questionnaire survey of 1,080 valid responses at three universities in northern Jiangsu, plus 20 case interviews, to describe how online religion reaches students. A section on causes precedes the proposed mechanisms.

The survey finds that 44.71% of students learn about religion mainly through online platforms, that most are curious but ambivalent about religion, and that 85.32% see online religious propagation as having both benefits and drawbacks. Students are fairly cautious about online information but, the authors say, underestimate the danger of deliberate infiltration. The authors attribute infiltration to the reach of converged media, students' weak critical judgement, shortcomings in ideological and political education (no student named a politics teacher as a first source of help, and few universities teach Marxist views of religion as a dedicated subject), and some universities' limited awareness of the risk. The proposed remedies include strengthening Marxist religion education and scientific atheism, teaching the "four histories", integrating ideological content into all courses, using local and red culture, student societies against cults, campus network rules based on the 2018 Regulations on Religious Affairs and the 2021 measures on internet religious information services, and a team ranging from teachers and counsellors to parents, IT staff and student Party members.

The authors conclude that universities should combine education, humane care for students, cultural influence, legal supervision and coordinated staffing to build a long-term defence, and they call for regular training for the anti-infiltration team. The text relies on Xi Jinping's statements at the 2015 and 2016 work conferences to frame the policy. Read the original if you want survey data on Chinese students' attitudes to online religion, or an example of how Party-aligned scholarship frames religion, ideological security and university governance.
quoteEn: To prevent, resist and defuse the risk of online religious infiltration, universities must see the situation clearly, proceed from their own circumstances, act on several fronts, guide flexibly and build jointly, creating a long-term mechanism against online religious infiltration.
quoteZh: 高校要防范、抵御和化解网络宗教渗透风险就要认清形势，结合高校实际，多方发力，灵活疏导，协同共建，创造出防范和抵御网络宗教渗透的长效机制。

glossary.explanation: The article's term for the use of the internet by overseas religious organisations and individuals to spread religious content in China, which it presents as aimed at interfering in internal affairs and undermining the political system.
The system of political and moral instruction in Chinese schools and universities, including compulsory ideological and political theory courses.
The Party's official theoretical stance on religion, which treats it as a distorted reflection of the world. The article wants it taught as a dedicated subject.

glossary.en: integrating ideological content into all courses
glossary.explanation: A reform requiring teachers of all subjects, not only politics teachers, to build value guidance into their teaching.

t: An analysis of Qu Qiubai's scientific atheism
zh: 瞿秋白科学无神论思想探析
paras: Xiao Kaiqiang examines how Qu Qiubai (1899–1935), an early leader of the Chinese Communist Party, developed a fairly systematic scientific atheism. The article argues that Qu applied dialectical and historical materialism to criticise religious theology and popular superstition, and in doing so advanced the spread of early Marxist atheism in China. Xiao presents this as relevant to research and propaganda on Marxist atheism in the new era.

The article has four parts. It first traces the theoretical and practical roots of Qu's thought, from his early exposure to Daoism, Buddhism and Tolstoy's ethics of love, to his turn to Marxism after 1920, including his years as a journalist in Soviet Russia. It then sets out the content of his atheism under four headings. A third part assesses his historical contribution, and a short conclusion follows.

Xiao argues that Qu's thought arose from two sources: a deliberate choice of Marxist atheism, and the need to fight imperialism and feudalism in a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society, where missionaries and the doctrine of the divine right of kings were used to dull resistance. On content, Qu held that religion is a product of social labour and changes with social development. He judged its role dialectically, as once useful in primitive society but later a tool of class rule that confined thought and obstructed science. He treated religious theism and idealism as kin, differing in form but not in essence. To free the masses from religion, Qu proposed advancing science, popular education and a cultural revolution against superstition.

Xiao concludes that Qu was a pioneer of Marxist atheism in China. He cites Qu's translations of works such as Gorev's on materialist philosophy, which Mao Zedong praised in 1943, and his drafting of a 1923 programme calling for the separation of education from religion. Xiao also credits Qu's practical proposals for propaganda and for handling religious questions. In Xiao's view, theistic ideas now spread in more hidden ways, which gives Qu's work contemporary significance. Read the original if you want a detailed account of early Chinese Communist views on religion and superstition, drawn largely from Qu's own writings.
quoteEn: Religion is a product of social labour.
quoteZh: 宗教是社会劳动的产物

t: Domestic research on Lenin's view of religion since reform and opening up: a review and outlook
zh: 改革开放以来国内列宁宗教观研究：综述与展望
paras: This article, published in Science and Atheism in 2024, reviews how Chinese scholars have studied Lenin's view of religion since reform and opening up. The authors say the topic matters because religious work occupies an important place in Chinese modernization, and Lenin's outlook is presented as a living application of the Marxist view of religion in Russia. They conclude that the field has produced solid results but is now thin, repetitive and in need of renewal.

The review is organised around four clusters of work: the theoretical sources of Lenin's view; its periodisation and the grounds for it; its content and distinctive features; and assessments of its theoretical significance and present-day value. A fifth section evaluates the field as a whole and sets out five directions for future study.

On sources, Zhang and Gao report broad agreement that Marx and Engels were the most direct influence, with additional influences from Plekhanov and Dietzgen, Russian revolutionary democrats such as Herzen and Chernyshevsky, and the French materialists. On periodisation, most scholars treat the October Revolution of 1917 as the dividing line between a stage of theory and a stage of practice. Others propose three-stage schemes with different dates, such as those of Liu Yaqiong, Li Jie and Ma Yingjie, Guo Ruike and Li Danyang. On assessment, the review distinguishes studies of single components, such as religious freedom or atheist propaganda, from wholly affirmative evaluations and from dialectical ones. Chen Rongfu, Li Jie and Ma Yingjie note historical and regional limits, and Lü Daji later concluded that parts of Lenin's approach leaned 'Left'.

The authors identify five gaps. These are the weak study of contemporary relevance, which they say has cooled in recent years; the reliance on three main texts; the lack of an agreed periodisation standard; the scarcity of systematic monographs; and the absence of detailed comparison with later Soviet leaders and with practice in China and other socialist states. They call for Lenin's view to be studied further so that it can inform Party religious work, the sinicisation of religion and the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a map of Chinese-language scholarship on Lenin and religion, with names and works to follow up.
quoteEn: Research interest in Lenin's view of religion has been declining in recent years, and high-quality theoretical work is relatively limited.
quoteZh: 列宁宗教观的研究热度近年来呈现减退态势，高质量的理论研究成果较为有限

glossary.explanation: Official Party term for China's own path of modernization, promoted especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
Official policy line that religions in China should adapt to Chinese culture and to socialist society under Party leadership.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978.

t: The theoretical connotations, value implications and practical requirements of "not believing in evil, not fearing ghosts, not fearing pressure"
zh: “不信邪、不怕鬼、不怕压”的理论内涵、价值意蕴及实践要求
source: Science and Atheism (《科学与无神论》), 2024 no. 2
paras: Duan Ganghui takes up the formula "not believing in evil, not fearing ghosts, not fearing pressure", which Xi Jinping set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) as part of the call to strengthen the Party's fighting spirit. The article argues that the formula is a coherent theoretical system rather than a slogan. In Duan's account it runs through the Party's spiritual lineage, and it equips the Party to face the "two great global and domestic situations" of the current era.

The article has three parts. The first traces each of the three phrases through statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Xi. The second sets out the formula's value for great-power rivalry, for Chinese modernization and for the Party's "unique problems". The third lists practical requirements for Party members.

In Duan's reading, each phrase corresponds to one quality. "Not believing in evil" means upholding truth and independence and is tied to aspiration (zhiqi). "Not fearing ghosts" means revolutionary momentum plus tactical skill and is tied to backbone (guqi). "Not fearing pressure" means a sense of hardship and bottom-line thinking and is tied to confidence (diqi). Duan treats them as a logical sequence concerning direction, overcoming difficulty and long-term rule, answering questions about the path, national rejuvenation and strengthening the Party. The article says the formula gives the Party initiative in the contest with the United States and the West in ideological, material and strategic terms. It describes the formula as a spiritual force behind Chinese modernization and as the key to the Party's "unique problems", which it says include loss of fighting spirit among some cadres, a "skills panic" and weakening of moral and disciplinary bottom lines.

For practice, Duan calls for firm belief built on scientific theory, Party history, current achievements and Chinese civilization. Duan also calls for preserving revolutionary momentum while using the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to fight flexibly, holding firm on principle and adapting on tactics. In addition, Duan urges cadres to build "inner skills" through study and "outer skills" through investigation and research, so as to anticipate internal and external risks. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how the Party's current discourse on struggle is organised and justified, with references to Mao, Deng, Jiang and Xi.
quoteEn: "Not believing in evil" concerns the question of direction, "raising the banner and setting the course", and is the logical starting point of this thought. "Not fearing ghosts" concerns the question of development, "tackling hard problems", and is its logical intermediary. "Not fearing pressure" concerns the question of security in "long-term governance", and is its logical end point.
quoteZh: “不信邪”涉及“举旗定向”的方向问题，是这一思想的逻辑起点；“不怕鬼”涉及“攻坚克难”的发展问题，是这一思想的逻辑中介；“不怕压”涉及“长期执政”的安全问题，是这一思想的逻辑终点。

glossary.pinyin: bù xìn xié, bù pà guǐ, bù pà yā
glossary.en: not believing in evil, not fearing ghosts, not fearing pressure
glossary.explanation: A formula expressing the Party's fighting spirit. Mao Zedong used "not believing in evil" and "not fearing ghosts", and Xi Jinping added "not fearing pressure" in the 20th Party Congress report (2022).
A method Xi Jinping promotes of preparing for the worst case while striving for the best outcome. It involves setting red lines that must not be crossed.

glossary.en: the two great global and domestic situations
glossary.explanation: Official shorthand for the strategic overall situation of national rejuvenation and for the world undergoing changes unseen in a century. It is used to frame the current period.
The official term for China's own path of modernization, presented as distinct from the Western model.

t: Strengthening Party building requires adherence to Marxist atheism
zh: 加强党的建设必须坚持马克思主义无神论
paras: Wang Lili and Dai Lixing argue that Marxist atheism is a requirement of Party building, not a private matter for Party members. Taking as their starting point the National Conference on Religious Work (April 2016), which called Marxist atheism a great principle, they contend that the Communist Party of China, as a Marxist governing party, must apply it to its own construction.

The article is organised in three parts. The first links atheism to the Party's vanguard character and purity; the second to the mass base of the Party's rule; the third to the Party's self-reform. The authors draw on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Chen Yun and Xi Jinping, as well as on the December 2023 revised Regulations on Disciplinary Actions of the Communist Party of China.

In the first part, the authors reason that the Party's nature, goals and discipline all require members to be thoroughgoing atheists. They argue that allowing members to hold religious beliefs would let idealism and materialism coexist inside the Party and split it ideologically. They read the cases of corrupt officials who consulted fortune-tellers or worshipped Buddha as evidence of a flawed worldview. In the second part, they set "people-centred" thinking against "god-centred" thinking and say the Party must work wholly for and rely on the people, not on deities. They hold that this is compatible with respecting religious freedom and uniting believers, but that atheist education must continue. They also present religion as a channel for foreign infiltration, which they describe as a political problem. In the third part, they link atheism to a fighting spirit, citing Mao's remarks on "ghosts" and Lenin's "militant materialism", and to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform.

The authors conclude that atheist propaganda and education must be sustained to protect the Party's ideological security and its leading position. They also hold that it should secure the initiative in the ideological field and win over the masses and the younger generation, while uniting believers around the Party. They present this as part of the effort to advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated atheism journal justifies the ban on Party members holding religious belief and ties it to Xi Jinping's discourse on ideals, the people and self-reform.
quoteEn: For Communist Party members to be firm Marxist atheists is a concrete embodiment of preserving the Party's vanguard character and purity, and a basic requirement of being a qualified Party member.
quoteZh: 共产党员做坚定的马克思主义无神论者，是保持共产党的先进性和纯洁性的具体体现，是做一名合格的党员的基本要求。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It covers discipline, anti-corruption and ideological education within the Party.
The idea that the Party can correct itself and remove its own problems through criticism, discipline and anti-corruption. It is emphasised in Xi Jinping's discourse.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The official long-term national goal, associated with the Chinese Dream and stressed under Xi Jinping.
A phrase from Lenin's 1922 article "On the Significance of Militant Materialism", which called for a materialist and atheist struggle against idealist worldviews.

t: The "Second Integration" and the emergence of Marxist atheism in modern China
st: A study centred on the critique of "spiritualism" in New Youth, 1918–1919
zh: “第二个结合”与马克思主义无神论在近代中国的出场
zhSub: 以1918—1919年《新青年》灵学批判为中心考察
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2024 no. 1
paras: How did Marxist atheism come to appear in modern China? Liu and Hu argue that the answer lies partly in the campaign waged in the journal New Youth in 1918–1919 against "spiritualism" (lingxue), a current that used the name of science to promote belief in ghosts and spirits. In their account, the victory of Chen Duxiu and other New Culture advocates was a self-directed choice of advanced intellectual weapons. It also displayed traits of excellent traditional Chinese culture that, the authors say, fit the people-centred, scientific and open character of Marxist atheism and so prepared the ground for its spread.

The article has three main parts. The first describes the spread of Western psychical research into China, where it merged with native soul-beliefs and planchette divination (fuji), and the activities of the Shanghai Spiritualist Society (Shanghai Lingxue Hui). It then narrates three concentrated rounds of criticism in New Youth between May 1918 and April 1919, involving Chen Duxiu, Liu Bannong, Chen Daqi, Liu Shuya, Wang Xinggong and others. The second part treats the campaign as cultural soil for Marxist atheism. The third matches its features to Marxist atheism, and a short conclusion follows.

Liu and Hu's central move is to identify three inherited traits in the campaign: patriotism, continuity with the ancient struggle between atheism and theism, and an inclusive attitude to foreign ideas. They read the campaign as anti-imperialist and anti-feudal, since spiritualism was said to serve foreign cultural control and the restorationist forces of the Beiyang government. They also point to the critics' use of Wang Chong's thought alongside Darwinian evolution and material monism. The authors then pair four features with Marxist atheism. The critics' emphasis on human beings over gods matches its people-centred stance, and their monist materialism matches its theoretical basis. Their exposure of pseudo-science matches its scientific character, and their inclusiveness matches its openness. The authors concede that the critics' atheism was still pragmatic, mechanical and short of dialectical materialism.

The authors conclude that the campaign was a landmark in Chinese atheist history and, in their phrase, announced Marxist atheism before it arrived. They say the Marxist introductions in New Youth then displaced Enlightenment-style atheism, followed by the 1922 anti-Christian movement and the 1923–1924 debate on science and metaphysics. They add that, today, only adherence to scientific atheism can realise freedom of religious belief and bring out the strengths of Chinese traditional culture, and they call this a task of the new era. Read the original if you study the early history of Chinese atheism, the New Culture Movement, or how Chinese scholars link the Two Integrations to Marxist atheism.
quoteEn: The exposure in New Youth in 1918–1919 of superstitious practices such as planchette divination and "soul photography" shows points of fit with the scientific character of Marxist atheism.
quoteZh: 1918—1919年《新青年》灵学批判对“扶乩”“灵魂摄影”等迷信行为的揭露表现出与马克思主义无神论科学特质的相契合之处。

glossary.explanation: A formula associated with Xi Jinping: the first integration joins Marxism with Chinese reality, and the second joins Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture. The article treats the early meeting of Marxist atheism and Chinese culture as a case of the second.

The Chinese name for psychical research and spirit-communication in the early 20th century. It combined Western ideas with native practices such as planchette divination, and the article treats it as pseudo-science.

A traditional Chinese practice in which participants hold a stick or planchette that writes characters said to be messages from spirits. Spiritualist societies used it as supposed experimental proof of souls.
The journal founded by Chen Duxiu in 1915 that became the main platform of the New Culture Movement. It later carried the first major introductions of Marxism in China.
The official term for the parts of China's cultural heritage that Party discourse regards as worth inheriting. It is distinguished from feudal elements said to be obsolete.

The atheist outlook grounded in dialectical and historical materialism, which treats religion as an ideology determined by the economic base. In Chinese academic usage it is closely tied to "scientific atheism".

t: Lessons from atheist propaganda and education since reform and opening up
zh: 改革开放以来无神论宣传教育的经验启示
paras: Su Bin takes up the record of atheist propaganda and education in China since reform and opening up (1978 onwards) and asks what experience can be drawn from it. The article describes a path from a brief revival in the early period, through decline and a situation in which 'theism has its speakers, atheism has none', to a turnaround around the turn of the century and a new phase since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Su argues that success rests on four mutually supporting conditions: the Central Committee's commitment, scholars' responsibility, implementation by localities and departments, and the mobilisation of the masses.

The article is organised in five parts: one section for each of the four conditions, followed by a conclusion. It draws on statements and documents of successive Party leaders from Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping, on the careers of scholars such as Ren Jiyu and Du Jiwen, and on regional cases. These include Gansu and Henan on schools, Zhejiang and Wenzhou on Party members who hold religious belief, Shanxi on rural superstition, and Xinjiang and Ningxia on de-extremification.

In Su's account, the Central Committee has consistently kept Marxist atheism within the mainstream ideology, held that Party members may not believe in religion and must propagate atheism, and ruled that atheist education does not conflict with freedom of religious belief. The article presents the 2003 instruction from Hu Jintao as having settled the scholarly dispute on this point. Scholars supply the political conviction, scholarly integrity, policy advice and early action, as in the 1995 'Two Sciences Alliance' campaign against superstition. Localities and departments turn directives into practice in schools, in Party organisation and discipline work, in publicity and online governance, and in ethnic regions.

Su holds that atheist education is in essence mass work. In Xinjiang, Su describes the campaign against religious extremism as combining it with outreach to specific groups. The author also notes mobilising ordinary people to monitor violations through new media and through community watch networks. Su cautions against treating religious difference as political opposition or linking extremism to particular ethnic groups. The conclusion calls for atheist ideas to be woven into scientific and cultural knowledge, 'like salt dissolved in food', and for unity among all actors so that Marxist atheism remains dominant in people's thinking. Read the original if you want a Party-aligned account of how atheism work is organised across Party, academia, local government and mass campaigns, with concrete regional cases.
quoteEn: Religious work is in essence mass work, and atheist propaganda and education is in essence mass work as well.
quoteZh: 宗教工作本质上是群众工作，无神论宣传教育本质上也是群众工作。

glossary.explanation: The Party-state's term for efforts to spread Marxist atheism and a scientific worldview through schools, media, Party training and campaigns against superstition. 'Propaganda' (xuānchuán) is the standard neutral term in Chinese official usage.
The official policy guaranteeing citizens' religious belief within legal limits. The article argues it does not conflict with promoting atheism, while Party members are barred from religious belief.
Official term for policies in Xinjiang aimed at countering religious extremism. The article describes them as combining education, legal measures and mass work.

t: From reason to culture
st: A study of Jack David Eller's atheist thought
zh: 从理性走向文化
zhSub: 大卫·艾勒的无神论思想研究
paras: This article studies the atheist thought of Jack David Eller, an American anthropologist and prominent atheist writer. Ping and Chen ask how Eller moves from rational refutation of theism towards a broader cultural struggle. They argue that his thought is marked by rationalism, an anthropological perspective, a combative spirit and a commitment to developing atheism further, and that it is valuable for studying atheism across cultures despite certain limits.

The article draws mainly on Eller's Natural Atheism and Atheism Advanced, together with his articles defending atheism. It is organised in four parts: atheism grounded in rationalism; atheism seen through anthropology (tolerance, morality, language and everyday life); atheism as struggle; and atheism as a developing, evolving position. A closing section sets out the authors' assessment of its shortcomings.

In Ping and Chen's account, Eller first treats atheism as identical with reason. He places the burden of proof on theists, rebuts the cosmological, ontological and teleological arguments plus experiential and social ones in twelve steps, and defends a "presumption of atheism". In Atheism Advanced he then judges this insufficient, because religion succeeds by controlling people, not persuading them. Drawing on anthropology, he treats religion as one cultural creation among many. He denies that tolerance and morality derive from religion, locating them in culture, nature and reason. He urges atheists to stop speaking Christian language, to see how Christianity colonises time, space, art and habits, and to build their own vocabulary, organisations and education.

Ping and Chen conclude that Eller's thought is theoretically innovative and practically suggestive, and that his anthropological approach widens the paths of atheist critique. They also identify limits. In their view he loads atheism with tasks it cannot bear, since it is not a complete worldview. He also remains tied to rationalism and Western-centrism. His doubts about atheist collective action, and his choice of Henry VIII's England over the Soviet and Chinese cases, are cited as examples. Read the original if you study Western atheism, the American atheist movement, or how Chinese scholars of atheism assess foreign thinkers.
quoteEn: Eller sets higher demands for atheists and also offers a new path for the development of atheism.
quoteZh: 艾勒向无神论者提出了更高的要求，也为无神论的发展提供了一个新的路线。

t: A scientific-atheist interpretation of Engels's contradiction between the "expected" and the "unexpected"
zh: 恩格斯“预期与非预期”矛盾的科学无神论诠释
paras: Engels observed late in life that the purposes of human action are anticipated, while the results the action actually produces are not. Li Wen asks why history, made by purposeful people, so often yields outcomes nobody intended, and why theistic readings cannot answer this. The article argues that Engels's treatment of the "expected and unexpected" contradiction starts from real people and their practice, and therefore refutes every theistic interpretation. In this way it shows the force of Marxist scientific atheism.

The article has four parts. It first sets out theistic readings, tracing them from traditional theology through Vico to Kant's "Nature" and Hegel's "cunning of reason". It then argues that the "unexpected" is not the work of divine will, and that the "expected" has nothing to do with deities. A short conclusion draws out theoretical and practical implications.

Li's central move is that Vico's providence, Kant's plan of nature and Hegel's absolute reason are, in the article's reading, new gods replacing old ones, and so are refined forms of theism. Behind them lies a mystified expression of objective historical law, together with hidden human purposes. Engels, in Li's account, strips this veil away. For Engels, historical necessity is determined by the conditions of real life, and people are the authors of their own history. The unexpected arises from two sources: the tension between historical law and human purposes, and the clash of individual wills, whose resultant is something nobody willed. For the "expected", Li cites Engels's view that gods are humanity's own projections and reflections of alienation. Realising expectations therefore depends on practice moving from conflict to agreement between conformity to law and conformity to purpose.
