Li concludes that Marxist scientific atheism is a mature atheism that rejects both traditional and rationalist theism. The contradiction, a "Gordian knot", can only be cut by humanity itself. Li adds that theism is sometimes used by states and interest groups for political and economic gain, and that removing it frees people's initiative to change the world. The article claims relevance for deeper study of the contradiction, for people's pursuit of real happiness, and for the Party's religious work and atheist education in the new era. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese scholars of scientific atheism apply Engels's late historical writings to Western philosophy of history and to religion.
quoteEn: Following the line of practical materialism, Engels discusses the "expected and unexpected" contradiction starting from real people and their practice.
quoteZh: 恩格斯循着实践唯物主义的思路，从现实的人及其实践出发去言说“预期与非预期”矛盾。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist form of atheism, presented in Chinese scholarship as grounded in materialism and social science rather than mere denial of God. It is taught as part of Party ideology and religious-affairs work.

Chinese shorthand for Engels's point, in his late letters on historical materialism, that actions have intended aims while their actual results are unintended. Chinese scholars treat it as a contradiction within history.
Hegel's idea that absolute reason works through individuals' passions to realise ends they did not intend.
In Marxist usage, the objective regularities governing social development, grounded in the production and reproduction of real life.

t: Xi Jinping's original contributions to Marxist atheism: a study
zh: 习近平总书记关于马克思主义无神论的原创性成果研究
paras: Zhu Xiaoming takes up Xi Jinping's statements on upholding and propagating Marxist atheism, drawn mainly from the national religious work conferences of 2016 and 2021 and from Xi's speeches on organisational and propaganda work. Following Xi's call (June 2023) to study the original theoretical results of the Party's new concepts, Zhu argues that four of these statements are original: neither the classics nor earlier Party leaders made them. In Zhu's account they continue earlier thought while adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

The article takes the four statements in turn: upholding Marxist atheism is a "major principle"; Marxist atheism must always remain the mainstream ideology and hold the leading place in people's thinking; the relationship between freedom of religious belief and ideological struggle must be handled correctly; and atheist propaganda must be strengthened in a targeted way so that atheism "takes root in people's hearts". A closing section sets out how the four fit together.

For the first statement Zhu gives four reasons. The Party's dialectical and historical materialism is itself thoroughly atheist. Atheism, unlike religious freedom, which Zhu says applies to religious work, covers all areas of Party and state work. The author reads the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as showing that atheism disappeared and religion and ethno-religious separatism returned. And rising spiritual needs in China pose new ideological challenges. On the second and third, Zhu argues that inclusiveness towards believers must not weaken atheism's leading role, and that religion is both an ideology and a social entity, so policy must address both. On the fourth, Zhu stresses party schools, universities and schools as venues, and engaging with scientific unknowns.

Zhu concludes that the four statements form a framework running from principle to leading position, key relationship and practical requirement, and that they guide new research and propaganda work on atheism. Zhu also holds that this work is a long-term foundation for preventing religious risks, not a campaign. Read the original if you want a Party-aligned account of how Xi's atheism statements are being systematised in Chinese religious and ideological policy discourse.
quoteEn: Atheist propaganda and education is not a campaign to be finished in one stroke; it must win encounters under specific conditions while holding to its direction, persevering and applying steady effort over the long term.
quoteZh: 无神论宣传教育不是“毕其功于一役”的运动，既要打好特定条件下的遭遇战，又要铆定方向，坚持不懈，绵绵用力，久久为功。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: An official formula for developing Marxist theory in light of Chinese conditions and contemporary circumstances. Party documents use it to describe the creation of new theoretical results.
A basic policy in China's constitution and religious work. The article says it includes the freedom to believe, not to believe, and to propagate atheism.
A high-level Party meeting that sets policy on religion. Conferences were held in 2016 and 2021 under Xi Jinping.

t: A study of the religious beliefs of American youth
zh: 美国青年的宗教信仰状况研究
source: World Religious Cultures (Shijie zongjiao wenhua), 2020 no. 1
paras: This is a literature review of nearly a century of American research on the religious beliefs of young people, from the early twentieth century to the late 2010s. Han Qi argues that the field mirrors both social and religious change in the United States. In Han's account, the research traces secularisation and privatisation of religion, and offers lessons for studying religious belief among Chinese youth.

The review divides the field into three stages, using 1960 and the start of the twenty-first century as dividing lines. Before the 1960s, studies were mainly descriptive quantitative surveys of college students' attitudes. From the 1960s to the end of the century, work moved to the science–religion relationship, the measurement of religiosity and long-term tracking, notably Hoge's studies. Since 2000, studies of 'emerging adults' and spirituality have dominated, with qualitative and mixed methods.

Han stresses two main moves. First, Hoge's longitudinal work showed declining commitment and church participation to the mid-1970s, then a conservative turn described as a 'return of the 1950s'. Han treats this as an episode within a continuing secularising trend. Second, drawing on Christian Smith's National Study of Youth and Religion and Souls in Transition, Han reports that only about 15 per cent of emerging adults are spiritually open. Most see religion as a private matter, and parents' religious practice remains a strong influence. Han presents therapeutic individualism as the cultural background to spiritual seeking, and follows Smith in holding that claims of a youth turn to 'spiritual but not religious' are exaggerated and do not yet threaten the traditional religious structure.

Han concludes that the research has advanced through better methods and richer perspectives, and that its findings are rooted in American culture and cannot simply be transferred elsewhere. For China, Han calls for Marxist theory of religion as the basis of study, and for uniting believing and non-believing youth around the core socialist values. Han also proposes more rigorous questionnaire design and sampling, longitudinal analysis of existing surveys, and research perspectives of Chinese origin. Read the original if you want a guide to the main American studies of youth religion and to how a Chinese Marxist researcher draws lessons from them.
quoteEn: The trend of religious secularisation has not reached its end as first predicted, but has found a suitable place within privatisation.
quoteZh: 宗教的世俗化趋势并没像它最开始被预测的那样走到终点，而是在私人化中找到了一个合适的位置。

glossary.explanation: The body of Marxist thought on religion that Chinese official scholarship treats as the basic framework for understanding religious questions in a socialist state.
A set of twenty-four characters in twelve values, promoted officially since the 18th Party Congress (2012) at national, social and individual levels.

t: The atheistic implications of Song-dynasty Neo-Confucianism
zh: 论宋代理学的无神论意蕴
paras: Zhou Yun and Wang Minmin ask how Song-dynasty Neo-Confucianism (lixue), a movement whose thinkers firmly believed in ritual sacrifice and spirits, nevertheless advanced atheism. Their thesis is that the Neo-Confucians introduced philosophy in order to explain spirits and human–spirit communication more clearly, but in doing so disenchanted nature and dissolved the spirits' independence. The authors stress that this effect was unintended and that no complete atheism existed in Chinese history; it is atheistic only in terms of a developmental process.

The article has three parts. The first documents the Neo-Confucians' devotion to sacrifice and spirits, citing Zhou Dunyi, Cheng Yi, Zhang Zai and Zhu Xi on ritual, Zhu Xi's ancestral halls, divination, and Yang Jian's mystical experiences. The second examines their rational critique of popular belief and their theoretical reworking of the spirits. The third draws out the atheistic implications in two respects.

The authors argue that Zhang Zai, the Cheng brothers, Zhu Xi, Zhang Shi and Chen Chun attacked 'strange beings and wicked spirits' and opposed idol-making, partly in a Song scientific climate. They then recast Heaven and spirits through principle (li) and qi, so that Heaven becomes principle and spirits become traces of natural transformation. Zhou and Wang read the diagram of the Supreme Ultimate as a philosophical account of the generation of things that removes a willing Heaven or Lord on High. The emphasis on sincerity (cheng) also made spirits dependent on the worshipper's subjective effort, which Chen Chun carried toward treating sincerity as the spirits' ontological basis.

The authors also find internal contradictions that, in their account, exposed the vanity of belief in spirits: Zhang Zai and Zhang Shi treated ritual or divination as tools of governing yet defended them as classical doctrine, and Chen Chun criticised spirit-writing while conceding that spirits act through people. They conclude that Neo-Confucianism reached the peak of contemporary rational thought and dealt superstition a heavy blow, while only unintentionally advancing atheism; such contradictions drive further theoretical development. Read the original if you want a close textual study, with Song sources, of how religious and rationalist elements coexisted in Neo-Confucian thought and how Chinese scholars frame this as a stage in the history of atheism.
quoteEn: Song-dynasty Neo-Confucianism was not thoroughgoing atheism; like all ancient schools, it was only an intermediate link in the development of atheism.
quoteZh: 宋代理学不是彻底的无神论，和所有古代学派一样，理学只是无神论发展的一个中间环节。

glossary.explanation: The Song–Ming philosophical revival of Confucianism, associated with Zhou Dunyi, the Cheng brothers, Zhang Zai and Zhu Xi, which explained the world through principle (li) and qi.
In Neo-Confucianism, the underlying order or pattern of things, often identified with the Way of Heaven.
The material-energetic stuff of which things are formed; Neo-Confucians used its gathering and dispersal to explain natural phenomena and spirits.
A Confucian virtue of inner authenticity, which Neo-Confucians turned into the principle by which humans and spirits respond to each other.
Popular belief in perceptible, supernatural apparitions, which Neo-Confucians such as Zhang Zai distinguished from the 'spirits' they themselves accepted.

t: The atheist thought in Mao Zedong's Xunwu Investigation and its lessons for today
zh: 《寻乌调查》中的无神论思想及其启示
paras: Liu and Zhang examine the atheist thought contained in Mao Zedong's Xunwu Investigation, the social survey of Xunwu county that Mao carried out in May 1930 during the Agrarian Revolutionary War. They argue that chapters three to five of the report deal in depth with theistic questions and embody Marxist standpoint and method. In their view this thought is an important milestone in the Sinicization of Marxist atheism and still offers guidance for research on religion and atheist education today.

The article has four parts. It first sets out why religious organisations, believers and ideas had to be handled correctly in the revolutionary base areas. It then reconstructs four sets of views in the report: on religion, folk belief, feudal superstition and secret societies, the last chiefly the Tongshan Society. A third part assesses the historical standing of this thought, and a fourth draws present-day lessons.

Liu and Zhang argue that Mao analysed each form of belief by class position and economic exploitation, not by belief alone. They cite his category of 'deity landlords' (temples, monasteries, shrines and altars), his breakdown of the social composition of believers and his reading of motives for joining churches. On superstition, Mao found geographical, psychological and economic roots: peasants' reluctance to move house when land was divided reflected real material loss, not merely outdated thinking. The authors trace how these findings fed Soviet-period policy on clerics' land and voting rights, the treatment of clan and communal land, and freedom of religious belief. They also see in the report the three bases of Mao Zedong Thought: seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence.

For the present, the authors propose that research on theism be guided by the 'six musts' of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and that Marxist atheism be adapted to the Chinese context through the Two Integrations, including linkage to traditional Chinese atheistic ideas. Atheist education should go deep into reality, daily life and the masses, in the primary stage of socialism. They also call for implementing the policy of religious freedom fully while resisting infiltration by foreign religious currents and cults. Read the original if you study the history of Chinese Communist policy on religion, Mao's survey method, or how current Party writing on atheism draws on early revolutionary sources.
quoteEn: In the Xunwu Investigation Mao Zedong analysed the concrete forms of theism, such as religion, folk belief, feudal superstition and the Tongshan Society, upholding the basic theory of Marxist atheism and applying the Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method throughout.
quoteZh: 毛泽东在《寻乌调查》中分析了宗教、民间信仰、封建迷信、同善社等有神论的具体形态，坚持了马克思主义无神论基本理论，贯穿了马克思主义的立场观点方法

glossary.explanation: Formula in Party theory: combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. Here it is applied to Marxist atheism.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology since 2017, written into the Party and state constitutions. It includes the 'six musts' (people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, innovation, problem orientation, systematic thinking, a global vision) cited as method.
Official judgement that China remains at an early, long-lasting stage of socialist development. The authors use it to explain why theism will persist for a long time.

glossary.literal: landlords of the way of the gods
glossary.explanation: Mao's term in the Xunwu Investigation for temples, monasteries, shrines and altars that owned land and collected rents. He classed them among 'public landlords'.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义无神论中国化
glossary.explanation: The process of applying and adapting Marxist atheism to Chinese conditions, as part of the wider adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context.

t: Defining the concept of extremism under the rule of law: rules and definition
zh: 极端主义概念法治化界定研究:规则与定义
paras: Chinese statutes such as the Criminal Law, the Counter-Terrorism Law and the Regulations on Religious Affairs use the term "extremism" without giving it a clear legal definition. Wang and Zhuang ask how China should define the concept within a rule-of-law framework, as a basis for a future dedicated counter-extremism or de-extremification law. They argue that the concept should be defined as a "composite" whose content is exclusion or "sole existence", and that the definition must follow five rules.

The article is a combined philosophical, legal and criminological study. It first surveys scholarly views on the genus concept (the broader category) of extremism, with five positions: statement and conduct, conduct, theory or statement and conduct, ideology and belief, and leaving it blank. It also surveys views on the differentia (the feature separating extremism from related concepts), which range from one element to four. It then classifies legal texts from Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, China and a draft Russian federal law into five types: evasive, blank, transferred, differentia-specified and fully determined.

The authors argue that the disagreements stem mainly from different rankings of two values: individual cultural-spiritual freedom and the public interest of state and society. They hold that composite genus concepts breach the logical rule that a genus must be one level above the defined term. They also hold that existing definitions cover only part of extremism's extension and rely on vague evaluative vocabulary. Their five rules are: the genus must be the next-higher concept; the definition's extension must equal that of extremism, with exemptions for legitimate self-protection, necessity and consent; the law's purpose and title must be consistent; linguistic vagueness must be reduced; and both values must be balanced. Drawing on the traditional Chinese idea of "zhongyong" (the mean) and "coexistence", they propose that extremism's essential features are exclusionary means, aims contrary to coexistence, and expression through theories, conduct, social systems or statements. They favour "counter-extremism" over "counter-extremist activity" or "de-extremification" as the legislative aim.

Wang and Zhuang conclude that defining extremism is unavoidable for counter-extremism legislation touching national security. They say the definition must rest on China's traditional culture and national conditions, align with international practice and follow rule-of-law rules. They call for supporting instruments, such as concrete criteria for identifying extremism and a dynamic catalogue of extremist materials, and propose after-the-fact punishment and indirect intervention as safeguards. Read the original if you work on Chinese counter-extremism legislation, comparative Central Asian anti-extremism laws, or the legal theory of defining contested concepts.
quoteEn: The genus concept of extremism is a \"composite\", comprising theories, systems of thought and doctrine, conduct or style of action, social systems, and statements.
quoteZh: 极端主义属概念是“复合体”，包括理论、思想及学说体系、行为或作风、社会制度、主张

glossary.explanation: A policy and legal term for curbing and eliminating the process of becoming radicalised, used for example in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region's regulations. The article treats it as one possible legislative aim alongside counter-extremism.
In classical definition theory, the higher-level category to which a defined term belongs. The article debates whether extremism belongs to conduct, ideology, belief or something else.
The essential feature that distinguishes a concept from other concepts under the same genus. The article analyses which elements, such as aim and means, serve as extremism's differentia.
A Confucian ideal of balance, neither excess nor deficiency. The authors cite it to read "extremism" as contrary to the idea of coexistence.

t: Guidelines and policies of the Chinese Communist Party on religious work during the War of Liberation
zh: 解放战争时期中国共产党宗教工作的方针政策探析
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2023 no. 6
paras: Zhou Wei examines how the Chinese Communist Party handled religion in the liberated areas during the War of Liberation (1945–1949), when several religions and competing religious forces coexisted. The article argues that, guided by Marxism, the Party framed practical policies that implemented freedom of religious belief, advanced democratic reform of religion and won over religious figures and believers, building consensus and strength for founding the new China. Zhou holds that studying this record enriches the Party's theory of religious work in the new era.

The article is a historical-policy study built on Party documents, newspaper reports and local cases from North, Northeast, Inner Mongolia, Suiyuan and other areas. It has four main parts: forming a people's democratic united front with religious circles; gradually deepening democratic reform of the old religious system; implementing freedom of religious belief; and resolutely striking at illegal and reactionary religious forces. A short conclusion draws out lessons for today.

On the united front, Zhou describes the Party condemning Nationalist persecution of religious communities, admitting believers to trade unions and peasant associations, guaranteeing their voting rights, and mobilising them against civil war. On reform, the Party is said to have abolished clerical exploitation, adjusted religious landholding while leaving religious bodies enough land to support themselves, separated religion from education, and protected religious property and relief. Freedom of belief covered lawful missionaries, ethnic minority customs and atheist propaganda. The Party is also described as treating religion differentially, prosecuting missionaries accused of espionage and banning reactionary secret societies (huidaomen) while protecting law-abiding believers.

Zhou concludes that, following Marx, the Party understood religion would eventually die out only after a very long process, so administrative force should neither ban nor promote any religion. In the author's account, the period raised the Party's prestige among religious circles, advanced the legalisation and democratisation of religious work, and furthered the adaptation of Marxist views of religion to China. Zhou calls for fully implementing religious freedom, governing online religion, deepening Marxist atheist education and improving religious laws so religion can adapt to socialist society. Read the original if you want a source-rich account of early Communist religious policy and its framing in current Party discourse.
quoteEn: Administrative force can be used neither to ban any religion nor to promote any religion.
quoteZh: 既不能用行政的力量去禁止某种宗教，也不能用行政的力量去推行某种宗教。

glossary.explanation: The broad alliance of classes and groups, including religious circles, that the Party sought to organise against the Nationalists and imperialism in the late 1940s.
The Chinese Communist designation for the 1945–1949 civil war with the Nationalist government, ending with the founding of the People's Republic.
The official policy that citizens may believe or not believe in religion; the article traces its wartime statements and its inclusion in the 1949 Common Program.
A collective term for folk sects and secret societies such as the Yiguandao, which the Party classed as reactionary and banned.

t: The formation of Marx's historical-materialist view of religion and its critique of capitalist fetishism
zh: 马克思历史唯物主义宗教观的形成及其对资本主义拜物教的批判
paras: Gu Jianhong asks how Marx's view of religion took shape and how it was applied to capitalist society. Starting from the claim that capitalism's advance has produced a spiritual crisis and that religious questions are increasingly prominent, Gu argues that Marx's historical-materialist view of religion supplies the intellectual basis and guiding principles for handling such questions today. The article holds that this view emerged through a move from theism to atheism and through struggle with idealism and old materialism, grounded in Marx's practical engagement with social life.

The article has four parts. It first traces Marx's shift from the rationalist Jewish faith of his youth to atheism, then follows the formation of his historical-materialist position through the Rheinische Zeitung, Feuerbach, the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question, the 1844 Manuscripts and the Theses on Feuerbach. It then turns to Marx's critique of fetishism, from early uses of the word to Capital, and ends with brief conclusions on contemporary relevance.

Gu's central move is to distinguish stages. Under Enlightenment rationalism and Bruno Bauer's influence, Marx's atheism still moved within speculative criticism of religion's 'content', which Gu calls illusory. Journalism on Moselle peasants and wood theft, followed by Feuerbach's materialism, redirected him to earth rather than heaven. Gu argues that the Theses on Feuerbach then went beyond Feuerbach's abstract humanism, so that religious alienation is traced to social alienation. The second move is that Marx carried this stance into political economy. Fetishism, Gu says, moves from a matter of social consciousness to one of social being: commodity, money and capital hide relations between people behind relations between things, and the 'economic trinity' in Capital completes this inversion.

Gu concludes that religion is rooted in real social life and that any religious view detached from social reality is unreliable. Marx's analysis of fetishism, in this account, shows the stance at work and points toward the free and all-round development of the human being. Gu calls for upholding this view in building socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, so that religion's relations with the economy, politics and culture are handled correctly and Chinese modernization has a spiritual foundation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey of the textual sources of Marx's religion critique, linked to fetishism and to contemporary religious policy.
quoteEn: Religion is rooted in real human social life and is a transcendent expression of it; solving religious problems requires starting from that real social life, and any transcendent view of religion detached from social reality is unreliable.
quoteZh: 宗教根源于人类现实的社会生活，是对人类现实社会生活的超验性表达，解决宗教问题需要从人类现实的社会生活出发，任何离开社会现实的超验性宗教观都是不可靠的。

glossary.explanation: Official Party term for China's own path of modernization, prominent in Party discourse since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
Marx's term for the way, under commodity production, social relations between people appear as relations between things, which then seem to rule over people.

t: Atheist thought in Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State
zh: 恩格斯《家庭、私有制和国家的起源》无神论思想的探讨
paras: Ding Qiang and Mou Degang ask what Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State contributes to the Marxist atheist view of religion. The book gives little space to religion as such, and the authors note that existing studies approach it through women's emancipation, marriage and the state. They argue that it applies scientific atheism to primitive society and shows religion to be a historical category, shaped by the economic base and changing as society moves from gentile to class order.

The article first situates the book in the development of Marx's and Engels's views of religion. It names two leaps: the move to a historical-materialist view around The German Ideology, and a later clarification of primitive society through their anthropological studies. It then works through three themes: that religion must be verified within historical processes, that its function must be sought in social life, and that its character differs between the barbarian and civilised eras. The evidence is mainly Engels's discussion of the Iroquois, Greeks, Romans and Germans, drawing on Morgan and Marx's notes.

On the first theme, the authors argue that for Engels the gens created its gods, not the reverse. Ancestor worship, they say, shifted from a female to a male ancestor with the move from matriarchal to patriarchal clans, and some practices, such as cannibalism, persisted as ritual as productive forces advanced. They contrast this with Bachofen's view of religion as a decisive lever of history, which Engels said leads to mysticism. On the second theme, they argue that early religion regulated conflicts within the clan and between the clan and nature, as in Iroquois initiation rites and agricultural festivals. On the third, they say that with private property and the state, Engels's "spontaneous" religion became "artificial" religion: religious powers were stripped away, sacred customs such as temple prostitution were degraded, and religion's purpose served the ruling class.

The authors conclude that where Engels's earlier works treated religion in broad historical or epistemological terms, the Origin approaches it from material production and social organisation. This, they say, completes the case that religion is a historical category and shows its shift from a force binding the clan against nature to a tool of minority rule. They acknowledge that the book does not discuss the features of artificial religion in civilised society or religion's final fate, but argue that it underlies Engels's account of religion's emergence, development and eventual disappearance in Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy. Read the original if you study Marxist theories of religion, Engels's late anthropological work, or how Chinese scholarship on scientific atheism reads the classics.
quoteEn: The objects of worship, religious ideas and ritual activities of primitive religion originate in the socio-economic conditions of primitive society, and are not the product of any god, of reason, or of human nature.
quoteZh: 原始宗教的崇拜对象、宗教观念和宗教祭祀活动，源于原始社会的社会经济状况，而不是什么神的、理性的或人的本性的产物。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-materialist approach to atheism, which explains religion by its social and historical roots. It is institutionalised in Chinese academia, including in the journal Science and Atheism, where this article appeared.

t: Ai Siqi's atheist thought and its lessons
st: A textual study based on Popular Philosophy (Dazhong zhexue)
zh: 艾思奇的无神论思想及其启示
zhSub: 基于《大众哲学》的文本考察
source: Science and Atheism (Kexue yu wushenlun), 2023 no. 6
paras: Guo Zuquan and Huang Xiaodan examine the atheist thought in Ai Siqi's Popular Philosophy, the popular exposition of Marxist philosophy that began as lectures in 1934 and was serialised in the journal Dushu shenghuo. They argue that the book does more than popularise Marxism: it analyses theism and atheism in philosophy and proposes ways of combating theism. From this the authors draw lessons for atheist work today.

The article has three parts. The first traces the sources of Ai's atheism: the spread of modern scientific knowledge, his study of Marxist classics in Japanese and German during two stays in Japan, and his family background, including a childhood experiment that tested a nun's superstition. The second sets out the book's content: Ai's critique of theism, his atheist positions, and his use of materialist dialectics as a "weapon of struggle". The third derives three contemporary lessons.

On the core argument, the authors report that Ai finds theism concealed in several philosophical positions, among them idealism, fatalism, pseudo-materialism, pragmatism and mechanism. For Ai, idealism is "a bridge" to religion, and theistic ideas are often used to control the masses. Against these he sets practice, the objectivity and self-motion of matter, and the laws of dialectics: contradiction, the transformation of quantity into quality, and the negation of the negation. Ai explains change by internal contradiction rather than a "magician", and uses the collapse of the Leifeng Pagoda as an example. The authors' lessons are that Marxist atheism should be integrated with the Party's purpose and essential character, that it should hold the ideological high ground, and that it should be popularised.

The authors conclude that Party members must be firm Marxist atheists, citing Xi Jinping's 2016 remarks, and that atheism education should be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They call for religious studies with Chinese characteristics to rest on atheism, and for ideological and political education to be oriented by it. They also propose popularising atheism among cadres and the public, using new media, and building atheism as a university discipline with accessible textbooks and student lecture teams. Read the original if you want to see how Ai Siqi's 1930s philosophical popularisation is used to support current Party-line arguments for atheist education.
quoteEn: Ai Siqi's idea of popularising philosophy still has important reference value and lessons to offer today.
quoteZh: 艾思奇的哲学大众化思想在今天仍然具有重要的参考意义和借鉴价值。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018. The article treats it as the guiding framework for atheism education.
Ai Siqi's widely read introduction to Marxist philosophy. It began as lectures titled Philosophical Talks (Zhéxué jiǎnghuà) and was renamed in 1936 to avoid Nationalist censorship.
The materialist rejection of belief in gods and spirits that Chinese Party theory treats as part of Marxism. The Party requires its members to be atheists.
Ai Siqi's term for philosophical idealism (wéixīnzhǔyì), contrasted with materialism. In his account it contains theistic elements.

t: Cultural enlightenment and the shaping of belief: the formation of atheist knowledge in New Youth
zh: 文化启蒙与信念塑造：《新青年》无神论知识的生成
source: Science and Atheism (Kexue yu wushenlun), 2023 no. 6
paras: Yang Lan examines how atheist knowledge took shape in the journal New Youth (Xin qingnian) and how its orientation shifted from cultural enlightenment to revolutionary mobilisation. Earlier scholarship, the article says, has mostly traced the journal's themes, circulation and impact, or the atheist thought of Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao. Yang instead takes the interaction of knowledge and practice as a lens. The thesis is that atheism in the journal moved from a critique of old religion in support of the republic to a scientific atheism tied to proletarian liberation and, ultimately, to the activities of the Chinese Communist Party.

The article follows New Youth from 1915 to the mid-1920s in three stages. The first covers the attack on Confucianism as a state religion and on spiritualist ghost-belief, in the political setting of Yuan Shikai's sacrificial ceremonies and attempted restoration. The second covers the 'replace religion with science' project, and the third the turn to the 'sacredness of labour' and to Marxism. Yang draws on pieces by Chen Duxiu, Yi Baisha, Wang Xinggong, Gao Xian, Qu Qiubai, Li Dazhao and others, as well as translations.

Yang argues that in the first stage contributors such as Chen Duxiu, Liu Bannong, Qian Xuantong and Chen Daqi used Western precedents and modern science to criticise the 'Confucian religion', the Spiritualist Society and religion's social role. They then tried to build positive content: they mined Chinese philosophers for atheist ideas, wrote the history of religion and life, and introduced scientific method and a 'scientific' outlook on life. After 1919, Yang contends, atheism was linked to socialism and the labour movement. Qu Qiubai's 1923 'new manifesto' extended science to social science, and Comintern texts connected atheist education to proletarian culture. The use of historical materialism to explain human origins and social development turned a plain atheism into scientific atheism.

Yang concludes that atheism ran through the journal's whole life and registered changes in its enlightenment aims. Cultural enlightenment drew on modern science to defend the republic and attack feudal autocracy and superstition. Labour enlightenment stressed proletarian culture and class liberation, and after 1920 the increase in Soviet-Russian sources changed the journal's Euro-American models. Yang presents the shift to scientific atheism as a distinctive course in the transformation of Chinese revolutionary thought, and says the Party's popularisation of these ideas among students and workers made them an ideological weapon. Read the original if you study the early history of Marxism, atheism and science propaganda in China, or want a detailed list of New Youth articles on the subject.
quoteEn: New Youth's discussion of atheism ran through the whole life of the journal, and the process by which atheist knowledge took shape shows the changes in the journal's enlightenment orientation.
quoteZh: 《新青年》对于无神论的讨论，贯穿了其办刊始终，而无神论知识的生成过程，呈现了刊物启蒙定位的变化。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist form of atheism that grounds the rejection of religion in historical materialism and the analysis of social development, in contrast to a 'plain' atheism based on criticising ghosts and gods. In Chinese academic usage it is an established field of study.
The Marxist theory that material production and the relations of production shape social change and consciousness. The article treats it as the tool that turned atheism into a scientific doctrine.
A slogan from a November 1918 speech by Cai Yuanpei, which became a current of thought in the May Fourth era valuing workers and labour.
A journal founded by Chen Duxiu in 1915 (first titled Youth Magazine) that became the main platform of the New Culture Movement and later of early Chinese communists.
The early Republican proposal, backed by Kang Youwei and others, to make Confucianism a state religion or write it into the constitution. New Youth contributors opposed it.

t: Understanding the standpoint, viewpoint and method of Xi Jinping's important statements on religious work through the "Six Musts"
zh: 从“六个必须坚持”认识和把握习近平总书记关于宗教工作的重要论述的立场观点方法
paras: This short essay, one of three written contributions to a journal feature on studying Xi Jinping's statements on religious work, asks how the Party's religious work in the new era should be understood through the "Six Musts" (liu ge bixu jianchi) set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Zuo Peng argues that Xi's statements on religious work are the religious-work chapter of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and that each of the six principles supplies a standpoint, viewpoint or method for that work. An editors' note places the piece after a June 2023 symposium on the statements, addressed by Wang Huning.

The article is organised in six numbered sections, one for each principle: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, adhering to fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systematic thinking, and a global vision. Each section opens with the principle's general meaning and then applies it to religion, quoting Xi and the Party congress report. The author cites 2018 figures of nearly 200 million religious citizens and over 380,000 clergy.

Zuo's central moves are as follows. First, religious work is treated as mass work and united-front work: the author says that respecting believers' faith while protecting their practical interests will draw them around the Party and strengthen its social base. Second, the Sinicization of religion is presented as Xi's theoretical and practical innovation, grounded in the historical Sinicization of imported religions. Zuo pairs it with "fundamental principles" (upholding the Marxist view of religion) and "breaking new ground" (adapting that view to new conditions). Third, the problem-oriented section lists the issues Zuo sees: growing numbers of believers, foreign infiltration, commercialisation, illegal proselytising and Party members taking part in religious activity. The remedy is Marxist atheism as the mainstream ideology, stronger rule of law and firm atheism among Communists. The systematic-thinking section stresses "guidance" (dao) through education, culture, policy, administration and law.

Zuo concludes that the global-vision principle requires telling China's religious story abroad. The author says that Chinese religious policy handles religious questions effectively and offers "Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach" to problems such as safeguarding freedom of belief and curbing religious extremism. The author describes foreign criticism of Chinese religious policy as hostile distortion, and this characterisation is the author's own. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Party theorists map religious policy onto the Six Musts.
quoteEn: Adhering to fundamental principles while breaking new ground means unwaveringly upholding the Marxist view of religion, continually enriching and developing the theory of religion of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and promoting the continued development of religious work in practice.
quoteZh: 坚持守正创新，就是要毫不动摇坚持马克思主义宗教观，不断丰富和发展中国特色社会主义宗教理论，推动我国宗教工作实践不断发展。

glossary.literal: six things that must be adhered to
glossary.explanation: A summary in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) of the worldview, methodology and standpoint of Xi Jinping Thought. The six are: put the people first, be self-confident and self-reliant, uphold fundamental principles and break new ground, be problem-oriented, apply systematic thinking, and have a global vision.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
The official policy of requiring religions in China to adapt to Chinese culture and socialist society. It was given prominence under Xi Jinping.

t: Guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, strengthening cultural confidence in the practice of the Sinicization of religion
zh: 以习近平文化思想为指导，在宗教中国化实践中增强文化自信
paras: This short commentary, one of three written reflections solicited by the journal Science and Atheism, asks how Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, first formally proposed at the national conference on propaganda, ideological and cultural work in October 2023, should guide the work of making religion Chinese. Zhang argues that the 'Second Integration' of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture is the key criterion and path for the Sinicization of religion, and that this process shows the reach of Xi's cultural thought beyond propaganda work into religious affairs.

An editors' note places the piece after a June 2023 symposium on Xi's important expositions on religious work. Zhang first locates the 'Second Integration' within Xi's 2023 speech on cultural inheritance and development. The author then turns to the 'five identifications' (with the motherland, the Chinese nation, Chinese culture, the Communist Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics) and reviews the religions one by one: Buddhism, Daoism, Tibetan and Theravada Buddhism, then Catholicism, Protestantism and Islam. The closing section sets out cautions.

Zhang reads the five identifications as political and, above all, cultural identification, which Xi calls the deepest level of identification. The main path is to immerse each religion in fine traditional culture, gradually and by category. In the author's account, Han Buddhism and Daoism, already well Sinicized, face a task of 're-Sinicization'. Catholicism, Protestantism and Islam, by contrast, are said not yet to be fully 'religions of China', and the author cites Western 'ideological infiltration' and 'Arabization' tendencies as challenges. Zhang also contrasts China's utilitarian polytheistic tradition with Western monotheism's 'alienated' theocentrism, and suggests that reassessing polytheism would strengthen cultural confidence.

Zhang warns against idealising a religion's historical Sinicization, against treating minority religious forms as models without change, and against using the slogan to expand proselytising. Sinicization is not meant to attract more believers. It is described as gradual and practical, 'more a matter of doing than of saying', and not to be reduced to slogans or showpiece projects. Zhang calls on academics, as the 'third team' in religious work, to do field research and study the history, experience, rationale and paths of Sinicization. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholars link Xi Jinping Thought on Culture to religious policy and to the Sinicization of specific religions.
quoteEn: Adhering to the direction of the Sinicization of religion is a gradual process, and it is more a matter of doing than of saying.
quoteZh: 坚持宗教中国化方向是一个渐进的过程，更多的是一个做的事情，而不是一个说的事情。

glossary.explanation: A body of ideas on culture presented as the cultural part of Xi Jinping Thought, first explicitly put forward at the national conference on propaganda, ideological and cultural work in October 2023.
The second of the 'Two Integrations': combining the basic tenets of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. The first is combining Marxism with China's concrete realities.
A policy since the 18th Party Congress (2012) that calls on religions in China to adapt to Chinese culture, socialist values and Party leadership.
A formula calling on religious believers to identify with the motherland, the Chinese nation, Chinese culture, the Communist Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics.
The official name for China's path and system under Party leadership since the reform era.

t: The scientific positioning, rich content and worldview and methodology of General Secretary Xi Jinping's important expositions on religious work
zh: 习近平总书记关于宗教工作的重要论述的科学定位､丰富内涵和世界观､方法论
paras: Zhu Xiaoming asks how Xi Jinping's important expositions on religious work should be placed within the Party's theory, what they contain, and how they should be studied and applied. The article argues that they form part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the third major theoretical achievement of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. It also holds that they supply a basis for building Marxist religious studies as an academic discipline.

The article has four sections. The first locates the expositions historically, tracing religious-work theory from Mao Zedong Thought through the reform-era theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics to the present. The second sets out their content in "three levels". The third turns to the worldview and methodology behind them, and the fourth to the implications for the discipline of Marxist religious studies.

Zhu's central move is to organise the "Nine Musts" from Xi's 2021 national conference on religious work into three levels. The first three concern how religion is understood: the importance of religious work, strong leadership mechanisms, and developing socialist religious theory with Chinese characteristics. The next three concern how religious issues are handled: the Party's basic principles, the Sinicization of religion, and uniting believers around the Party and government. The last three concern methods: positive and healthy religious relations, support for religious bodies' self-building, and rule of law. Zhu then links the "Six Musts" (putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, staying true to fundamental principles while innovating, problem orientation, systems thinking, and a global outlook) to the worldview and methodology of the 20th Party Congress (2022). Applying them together with the Two Integrations, Zhu says, yields scientific understanding and keeps the theory current.

Zhu calls on scholars to treat Marxist religious studies and Marxist atheism as priority disciplines. They should interpret Xi's expositions accurately, study the new concepts and judgements as principled theoretical results, and pursue integrated innovation. The aim is to make the discipline more systematic and academically grounded, drawing on Xi's 2023 remarks on systematising theory. Zhu also urges continuing the tradition of Marxist religious studies begun by Ren Jiyu. Read the original if you want a compact Party-orthodox account of how religious-work theory is periodised and structured, and how it is linked to disciplinary development.
quoteEn: The "Nine Musts" are a logically rigorous and internally unified organic whole, constituting the general outline guiding the Party's religious work in the new era.
quoteZh: “九个必须”是逻辑严密､内在统一的有机整体,建构了指导新时代党的宗教工作的总纲要｡

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018. It is presented as the latest stage of adapting Marxism to China.
The formula of combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
Nine requirements for religious work set out by Xi Jinping at the 2021 national conference on religious work. They are presented as the core of the Party's new-era religious-work theory.

glossary.literal: six things that must be adhered to
glossary.explanation: Six requirements for studying and applying Xi's expositions on religious work. They parallel the worldview and methodology set out at the 20th Party Congress.
Official policy direction that religions in China should adapt to Chinese society and culture and to socialism, under Party leadership.

t: Marxist atheism and two questions in building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation
zh: 马克思主义无神论与中华民族现代文明建设的两个问题
paras: In June 2023 Xi Jinping called, at a symposium on cultural inheritance and development, for building a \"modern civilization of the Chinese nation\". Tian Xinming takes up two questions: what this concept means, and how upholding Marxist atheism relates to building such a civilization. Tian argues that the concept is equivalent to a new form of human civilization and to Chinese modernization, and that Marxist atheism supports both the unity and the inclusiveness of that civilization.

The article has two parts. The first clarifies the concept by linking it to Xi's other formulations, in line with Xi's call to make theory more systematic and academically grounded. The second takes two of the five \"outstanding characteristics\" of Chinese civilization that Xi has described, unity and inclusiveness, and asks how atheism bears on each and on their relationship. Tian draws on Xi's speeches, the Constitution and Lenin and Mao Zedong.

In the first part, Tian reads the modern civilization of the Chinese nation, a new form of human civilization and Chinese modernization as one object seen from three angles. In Tian's account, it is civilization of the Chinese nation, socialist in character, and modern, formed through the Two Integrations under Party leadership. In the second part, Tian argues that unity now rests on Marxism as the guiding ideology. Marxism is a thoroughly materialist and atheist worldview, and the Party's mission and ultimate goal rest on it. Tian warns that if theism spread and religious believers multiplied, it would erode the ideological base, weaken unity and affect the Party's governing foundation. Inclusiveness, by contrast, appears in constitutional provisions on freedom of religious belief. Tian holds that unity and inclusiveness are inseparable and that atheist propaganda is consistent with religious freedom.

Tian concludes that atheist work must be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and must balance ideological struggle against religious freedom. Propaganda should target the masses, especially young people, and keep Marxist atheism dominant in mainstream ideology. It should also stay within ideological limits: no administrative measures, no propaganda in places of worship or aimed specifically at believers, no priority over the Party's central tasks, and no equating of criticism of theism with rejecting all religious culture. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist atheism scholar links official civilizational concepts to policy on religion and ideological work.")
quoteEn: The fundamental nature of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation is that it is both a civilization of the Chinese nation and a socialist civilization, a unity of socialism and Chinese civilization.
quoteZh: 中华民族现代文明的根本性质在于，它是中华民族的文明，又是社会主义的文明，是社会主义和中华文明的统一体。

glossary.en: modern civilization of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping introduced in June 2023 at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development. Tian reads it as the civilizational form of Chinese modernization.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: A phrase Xi Jinping used in 2021 at the Party centenary, describing what the Party says it has created through socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization.
The official name for China's path of modernization under Party leadership, presented as distinct from Western models.
The Party's formula of integrating Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
The atheist component of the materialist Marxist worldview, which Party members are expected to uphold. Official policy pairs it with constitutional freedom of religious belief.
The official designation of China's system and path since the reform era.

keywords: modern civilization of the Chinese nation

t: The background, atheist content and contemporary relevance of "Stories of Not Fearing Ghosts"
zh: 《不怕鬼的故事》的编写背景、无神论蕴含及其现实镜鉴
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2023 no. 5
paras: Ren Baolong and Chong Juan examine Stories of Not Fearing Ghosts (《不怕鬼的故事》), a collection of folk tales from classical Chinese notebook fiction that Mao Zedong personally decided to compile and helped edit in the early 1960s. They argue that understanding how the book came about and what atheist ideas it carries is useful for atheist propaganda and education in the new era, and for consolidating Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere.

The article has three parts. It first sets out the domestic and international situation of the late 1950s and early 1960s and the book's editing and publication. It then reads the stories as atheist texts. It finally draws four practical lessons for present-day atheist education.

On background, the authors describe Sino-Soviet disagreement, Western pressure and the persistence of feudal superstition at home. Mao took 'ghosts' as a metaphor for enemies and difficulties, and from 1959 told ghost stories on several occasions. The Institute of Literature of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, under He Qifang, compiled the book, and Mao followed the selection and the preface closely. It was published in 1961 with 70 items, and a revised edition with 66 followed that October. On content, the authors identify three themes: 'there are no ghosts in the world'; 'the more one fears ghosts, the more ghosts there are'; and contempt for ghosts strategically but respect for them tactically. They illustrate each with specific tales, such as Wang Jia, Song Dingbo and Chen Zaiheng.

For the present, the authors call for four things. Atheist propaganda should be openly and boldly Marxist, and general Marxist education should not replace it. It should focus on Party cadres and young people. It should draw on atheist resources in traditional Chinese culture. Its language should be renewed through stories, short videos, memes and plain or online speech. They also call for flexible tactics that combine courage in strategy with care in each concrete case. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how this Mao-era text is now read as a model for atheist education, with plot summaries of the tales and a list of recommended methods.
quoteEn: Despising ghosts strategically is a form of courage that shows fearlessness; taking them seriously tactically is a skill that shows great wisdom.
quoteZh: 战略上藐视鬼是一种勇气，体现大无畏；战术上重视鬼是一种本领，彰显大智慧。

glossary.explanation: The Party's term for the promotion of Marxist atheism among Party members and the public. It is carried out through publications, teaching and media.

t: Two decades of Japanese reflection on the Aum Shinrikyo affair
zh: 二十余年来日本社会对奥姆真理教事件的反思
paras: Huang surveys how Japanese society has reflected on the Aum Shinrikyo affair over more than twenty years. The cult carried out the March 1995 sarin attack on the Tokyo subway, which, according to the article, killed 14 people and injured about 6,300. Its founder Asahara Shoko and twelve others were executed in July 2018. Huang's thesis is that the affair resulted from several interacting factors, that Japan's lack of religious regulation was the fundamental one, and that Japan's experience offers lessons for China's work against cults.

The article is a review of scholarship, journalism, memoirs by former members and court reporting. Authors cited include Shimazono Susumu, Shimada Hiromi, Ota Toshihiro, Egawa Shoko, Murakami Haruki and the former member Hayashi Ikuo. It is organised in three parts: the cult's defining features, the causes of its rise, and proposed countermeasures. A concluding section draws implications for China.

Huang reports that the literature identifies three features: a doctrine pieced together from existing religions and bent to justify crime, a hierarchy with personal worship and mind control, and a pursuit of money and political power. Scholars dispute the "mind control" thesis. The article groups the proposed causes into five: Japan's social system, lax religious oversight, a social current seeking spirituality, sensationalist media coverage, and scholars' mistaken endorsements. In Huang's own ranking, the first and fourth are environmental, media and scholarly errors are incidental, and absent regulation is the fundamental cause. The 1951 Religious Corporations Act limited oversight. Revisions after 1995 and the 2022 assassination of Abe Shinzo, in Huang's account, show that governance remains weak.

On countermeasures, Huang describes individual vigilance, critical thinking, neutral media, university education, and exit counselling by the Japanese association for leaving cults. Huang judges these efforts useful but limited, since individuals bear the risks of religious freedom and civic groups lack unified leadership. For China, the author calls for deeper study of online cults, vigilance against commercialised "mind-body-spirit" courses, mobilising social forces, and above all strong regulation. Huang says Japan's experience confirms the correctness of China's anti-cult work. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-by-source guide to Japanese Aum scholarship and to how Chinese anti-cult research draws on it.
quoteEn: The absence of religious regulation can be regarded as the fundamental factor behind the Aum affair, which allowed Aum to grow and left its unlawful activities unchecked for a long time.
quoteZh: 而宗教监管的缺位则可以被视为奥姆事件发生的根本因素，纵容了奥姆的发展壮大并长时间放任奥姆的不法活动。

t: The internal logic of atheistic thought in the Laozi
zh: 论《老子》无神思想的内在逻辑
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), posted on marxism.cass.cn 29 December 2023
paras: Is the Laozi (Daodejing) a theistic or an atheistic text? Qi Xiangyang and Zhang Rui note that modern scholarship has split into three camps: those who read the Dao as idealist and therefore theistic, those who read it as materialist and therefore atheistic, and those who accept the Dao's materiality while conceding that the text still affirms ghosts and spirits. The authors argue that the first two camps apply a Western idealism-versus-materialism test that does not fit the text. They propose that the lower (empirical) and upper (metaphysical) realms must be read together, and that the text's dialectical outlook produces a systematic, if not absolute, atheism.

The article is built in four parts. It first examines the lawlike character of the Laozi's dialectical outlook, then its removal of divine agency from the empirical world, then the atheisation of the realm of origins, and finally the text's place in the history of Chinese atheistic thought. Evidence comes from close readings of chapters of the received text, the Guodian bamboo slips and the Mawangdui silk manuscripts. It also draws on commentators from Wang Bi to Feng Youlan, Xu Fuguan and Guo Qiyong.

The authors' central move is to argue that the Laozi's doctrine that the myriad things 'carry yin and embrace yang' is a cognition of objective regularity, even if it lacks the conditions and laws of modern dialectics. Because society is itself a unity of contradictions, rulers should practise non-action (wuwei) rather than rely on Heaven's mandate or spirits. The Laozi also explains natural phenomena, such as rain, through the union of heaven and earth. Ghosts and spirits survive only as marginal symbols without power over human affairs. The second move is that the Dao was abstracted from critical observation of the empirical world, from the bottom up. Unlike the traditional Heaven, with its will and personality, the Dao has no purpose, will or values, acts only through non-action, and is closer to a law. The authors judge it materialist in Marxist terms, while citing Liu Xiaogang's warning against retrospective reading.

The authors conclude that earlier figures such as Zichan and Yan Ying produced only scattered atheistic remarks and kept Heaven as the supreme ground. The Laozi, they argue, replaced Heaven with the Dao and offered the most systematic atheistic worldview of the Spring and Autumn period. They add that later cosmogonies, including Taiyi Sheng Shui, the Huangdi Sijing and the Huainanzi, place spirits in a subordinate position within the generative sequence. Read the original if you study early Chinese philosophy, the history of Chinese atheism, or how Chinese scholars apply Marxist categories to classical texts.
quoteEn: The Dao was put forward on the premise of a critique of the empirical world; it is a bottom-up philosophical abstraction.
quoteZh: “道”的提出是以对经验世界的批判为前提，是一种自下而上式的哲学抽象。

glossary.explanation: The central concept of the Laozi, the ultimate source and pattern of all things. Scholars dispute whether it is spiritual, material or a principle of regularity.
The Laozi's ideal of governing without coercive, wilful interference, letting things follow their own nature. It is not simple inaction.
The authors' term for the Laozi's recognition that opposites transform into and unite with each other. They distinguish it from dialectics as a worked-out method.
In early Chinese thought, a supreme power or realm that could confer rule and send blessings or disasters. It could also mean nature or moral order.

t: A reader's guide to Heine's On the History of Religion and Philosophy in Germany
zh: 《论德国宗教和哲学的历史》导读
source: Studies of Classic Marxist Works (马克思主义经典著作研究), posted 2023-12-29
paras: This is a reader's guide, published in the series on classic Marxist works, to Heinrich Heine's On the History of Religion and Philosophy in Germany (1834). Qin Ming starts from Engels's remark in Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy that Heine was the first to see the revolutionary content of Hegel's philosophy. Qin argues that the book helps readers understand Engels, and Marx's 1843 claim that the critique of religion is the premise of all critique.

Qin notes that Heine wrote the book to explain German religion and philosophy to a French audience, so that they could read German literature. Qin calls it a short and simply organised work, a recognised entry point to Marxist theory, and a prime example of Heine's polemical writing, in which poetic language carries deep philosophical thought. The guide follows Heine's three parts in turn. The first covers Christianity, Catholicism, Luther's Reformation and the emergence of German philosophy. The second is a transitional survey of the philosophers from Descartes to Lessing. The third covers Kant through Hegel.

Qin's central line is that, in Heine's account, philosophy emerged from the Reformation, freed itself from religion and became a revolutionary force. Qin reads Heine's Luther as the figure who gave reason the right to interpret scripture and so opened intellectual freedom. The second part is organised around the dispute between sensualism (materialism) and spiritualism (idealism), seen in Locke against Leibniz, Plato against Aristotle, and Spinoza's synthesis. In the third part Kant's Critique of Pure Reason is the blade that cut off the head of deism, and Fichte, Schelling and Hegel complete the line. Qin also sets Heine's thesis beside Engels: thought precedes action, and Germany's philosophical revolution will precede a political one, which when it comes will shock the world.

Qin concludes that reading Heine clarifies how philosophy separated from religion and gained revolutionary force. In Qin's view it also illuminates the prehistory of Marxism and its historical continuity with earlier thought. Qin adds comments of their own, for example that Kant's obscure style in the first Critique may have been a defence against religious persecution. Read the original if you want a concise guide to Heine's text and to how Chinese Marxist scholarship links it to Engels and early Marx.
quoteEn: Reading Heine helps us understand not only the relation between religion and philosophy in Germany, and how philosophy broke free from religion to become independent and release a world-shaking revolutionary force, but also the prehistory of the birth of Marxism and its historical continuity.
quoteZh: 读海涅不仅有助于了解德国宗教与哲学的关系，以及哲学如何摆脱宗教走向独立，并爆发出惊世的革命性力量，而且有助于理解马克思主义诞生的前史，以及马克思主义的历史传承性。

t: Out of monotheistic religion, not yet out of monotheistic thinking
st: Zhao Tingyang and Alain Le Pichon on the monotheistic mode of thought
zh: 走得出一神教，未走出一神论
zhSub: 赵汀阳与阿兰·乐比雄对一神论思维的讨论
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2023 no. 5
paras: This is a review essay on The Shadow of Monotheism: Correspondence between a Philosopher and an Anthropologist, a book of letters exchanged over about three years between the Chinese philosopher Zhao Tingyang and the French anthropologist Alain Le Pichon. Xiao and Liu present it as an experimental transcultural dialogue rather than a conventional exchange of ideas. They argue that the book's central insight is that the world has largely left monotheistic religion behind but has not left monotheism as a way of thinking, which persists in modern secular forms.

The review first sets out the two correspondents' concerns: Le Pichon asks about China's place and role in the world, while Zhao asks how the world can escape the clash of civilizations and ideological conflict. It then covers three themes. The first is the contrast between China's direct relation of heaven and humanity and the European need for mediators between God and humans. The second is the shift from religious monotheism to modern monotheism built on absolute subjectivity. The third is the ontological problems this creates, ending with resources from Chinese thought for reordering the world.

In the reviewers' account of Zhao's argument, modern Western thought replaced God with the sovereign, rational individual, whose self-justification mirrors Trinitarian theology and amounts to a "pseudo-religion" (the human rights doctrine is cited as an example). Combined with universalism, this mode of thinking is said to produce clashes of civilizations and ideological struggles. Its logical extension is the self-made human, gene editing and superintelligent AI, which could judge humans as worthless and create a "qualitative inequality" in the right to life. Against this Zhao proposes a relational ontology of co-existence, drawing on Confucian ren and a "New Tianxia System", and replaces innate human rights with "prepaid human rights", which are conditional on fulfilling one's duties to others.

The reviewers conclude that monotheistic thinking is spreading through global language, law, markets, technical standards and popular culture. They note that Le Pichon's optimism about China's cultural influence is judged premature, and that Zhao's more sober view is closer to the facts. They add that transcultural exchange can break the "spell" of monotheism, but that belief runs deeper than reason, and that the ten letters amount to groundwork for mutual learning among civilizations. Read the original if you want a detailed guide to Zhao Tingyang's critique of Western subjectivity and monotheistic thinking, and to how Chinese scholars present the exchange with Le Pichon.
quoteEn: Stepping out of monotheistic religion may take only a little time, but there is no way to predict when we will step out of monotheism as a mode of thought.
quoteZh: 步出一神教或只需稍加时日,步出一神论却难有预期。

glossary.explanation: A traditional Chinese notion that the cosmic order (tian) and human life are continuous. The review follows Zhao in treating this relation as direct, needing no mediator.
Zhao Tingyang's proposal for a world order, adapting the ancient concept of tianxia. It is based on relational rationality and aims to minimise conflict rather than maximise interest.
The central Confucian virtue. Zhao reads it as the basic ethical relation between any two persons.
Zhao's proposed alternative to the doctrine of innate human rights. Rights are enjoyed only by those who fulfil their obligations to others and respect others' rights.

glossary.literal: monotheism (as doctrine or mode of thought)
glossary.explanation: In the review, a term for an exclusive and dogmatic habit of thought derived from monotheistic religion (yishenjiao). It is said to survive in secular political and cultural forms.

t: A critical analysis of Messianic Marxism
zh: 对弥赛亚式马克思主义的批判性分析
paras: Jia Jinyue examines "Messianic Marxism", the strand of thought that joins Marxism to messianic motifs and reads socialist revolution and communism as a quasi-religious story of redemption. The author argues that this reading misrepresents Marx. In Jia's account it is a variant of religious teleology that strips Marxism of its class character, its critical edge and its scientific standing. Only historical materialism, Jia holds, can show what the school is and why it fails.

The article has three parts. The first sets out how Messianic Marxism arose in response to the crisis of postmodernity and what it claims. It draws on Karl Löwith, Walter Benjamin, Jacques Derrida and Wilhelm Dilthey, and the author also names Fredric Jameson and Arnold Toynbee as representatives. The second part tests the school's claims against Marx's early texts and its method of reading. The third part reinterprets the school from the standpoint of historical materialism and considers what this means for understanding Chinese modernization.

Jia presents the school's claims as follows: Marx's "prehistory" and future history echo a Judaeo-Christian scheme, exploitation is treated as a moral "original sin", and the proletariat becomes a chosen people. The rebuttal rests on two moves. First, Marx's study of the Book of Isaiah under Bruno Bauer in 1839 took place in the heyday of biblical criticism, so Jia reads it as critical reflection rather than reception. Jia adds that Marx later attacked Christian-tinged socialism in The Eighteenth Brumaire and Moses Hess's messianic tendencies in The German Ideology. Second, the school is said to cut Marx's texts apart, treat materialism as speculation and ignore its scientific character. Jia concludes that it is religious teleology, lacks revolutionary practice, is detached from the people and material interests, and remains Eurocentric.

Jia concludes that the school's ambiguous critique of capitalism amounts at most to a despairing struggle on the way back to Christian theology. Real solutions to the dilemmas of modernity lie in changing relations of production, not in waiting for redemption. The author adds that China's path differs because it has kept to the materialist conception of history instead of turning Marxism into religion, and that this offers another angle on Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Benjamin, Löwith and Derrida's theological readings of Marx, or if you are interested in how Chinese scholarship frames Marxism and religion.
quoteEn: Messianic Marxism is in essence a variant of \"religious teleology\".
quoteZh: 弥赛亚式马克思主义本质是“宗教目的论”的变种。

glossary.explanation: The official Party-state term for China's own path to modernization, prominent in official discourse since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.

Marx and Engels's theory that history is shaped by material production and class relations, with consciousness arising from social being. Chinese texts often use the term 'materialist conception of history' interchangeably.
A label for readings that combine Marxism with Jewish-Christian messianic and eschatological themes, associated here with Benjamin, Derrida and others. The article uses it as an object of critique.

t: Raising the level of rule of law in the administration of internet religious affairs
zh: 提高互联网宗教事务管理法治化水平研究
paras: Zhang Xiaochen asks how the administration of religious affairs on the internet can be placed more firmly on a legal footing. The article argues that such administration bears directly on national security and social stability. In the author's account, China has built a policy framework and a growing body of law, but faces real gaps that call for a more complete legal system.

The article has four parts. It first defines internet religious affairs administration as government administration of individuals and organisations engaged in online religious activity, and links it to political, ideological and social security. It then traces developments from the late 1990s, when the first temple-run website appeared, to the present. Next it sets out three challenges. Finally it offers proposals.

Zhang's core move is to present policy and law as a "two-wheel drive". The policy side is a four-way framework of Party leadership, government administration, social coordination and religious self-discipline. The legal side runs from the National Security Law and Cybersecurity Law to the 2017 Regulations on Religious Affairs and the 2021 Measures for the Administration of Internet Religious Information Services. Zhang identifies three problems. Few laws address the topic: three laws, one administrative regulation and one departmental rule. Enforcement is harder because of low entry barriers for proselytising, algorithmic push and closed online groups. Public legal education is weak, so some platforms stay out of the matter and some believers misread the rules. Zhang proposes a dedicated regulation on internet religious affairs and rules on religious apps and algorithmic recommendation. Zhang also proposes provisions for foreigners' online religious activity, local regulations, and stronger enforcement, judicial and legal-education mechanisms.

Zhang concludes that stronger rule of law is part of carrying out the Party's and state's major decisions on religious work, with Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee. The article adds that this guarantee needs trained legal personnel and technology such as big data and artificial intelligence. It acknowledges that further work could examine legal supervision and Party regulations. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic frames internet religion as a security and legal-governance issue, with concrete examples of regulations and local measures.
quoteEn: The administration of internet religious affairs is an important task in safeguarding national security and stability.
quoteZh: 互联网宗教事务管理是维护国家安全稳定的一项重要工作。

glossary.explanation: Government administration of individuals and organisations involved in religious activity online. The author treats it as part of religious work and of national security work.
The expectation that religious bodies manage and restrain themselves in line with law and Party policy. It is one of the four elements of the framework the author describes.
The author's image of policy framework and legal construction advancing together to raise administrative capacity.

glossary.zh: 互联网宗教信息服务管理办法
glossary.pinyin: hùliánwǎng zōngjiào xìnxī fúwù guǎnlǐ bànfǎ
glossary.en: Measures for the Administration of Internet Religious Information Services
glossary.explanation: A departmental rule issued jointly by several agencies in 2021. It sets licensing requirements and content boundaries for online religious information.

t: The relationship between the Anti-Christian Movement and the founding of the Chinese Socialist Youth League
zh: 非基督教运动与中国社会主义青年团成立的关系探析
paras: The article asks how the Anti-Christian Movement of 1922 related to the founding of the Chinese Socialist Youth League. Scholars disagree: some hold that the League initiated and led the movement, others that members took part only as individuals, and others that the Comintern reports on Party leadership are unreliable. Peng and Chen argue that local League branches deliberately launched the movement, and that it in turn consolidated those branches and prepared the League's national founding in May 1922. They also argue that the League never achieved unified leadership of the movement.

Drawing mainly on contemporary newspaper reports and participants' memoirs, the authors first trace the movement's background: the 1920 religion debate of the Young China Association, and the spread of Lenin's theory of imperialism, especially through the Congress of the Toilers of the Far East in early 1922. They then examine the League branches in Shanghai, Beijing and Guangdong, and the First National Congress in Guangzhou. A short conclusion assesses the movement's end and legacy, including its return in 1924 as the campaign to recover educational rights.

Peng and Chen argue that the three branches played different roles. Shanghai launched the movement in March 1922 and framed Christianity as a vanguard of capitalist and imperialist aggression. In Beijing the League's call produced a larger but Enlightenment-style anti-religion alliance, whose mixed membership put it beyond Communist and League control, so it never turned decisively anti-imperialist. In Guangdong the League led through the press and by organising student and anti-religion alliances. The authors note that a Comintern representative's claim that the movement had wrecked the Christian conference is inaccurate. They cite the First Congress's resolution on relations with other organisations, which called for both struggle against and use of the YMCA, and for efforts to win leadership of non-Christian groups.

The authors conclude that the movement gave the League its practical setting, spread Marxism-Leninism, enlarged its influence among students and trained early members. The League's plan to expand its leadership after the congress was frustrated by the Zhili–Fengtian war, political change in Beijing, the shift of attention to the labour movement and the students' summer departure.
