Read the original if you study the early history of the Communist Party and the Youth League, or the debate over Comintern sources and who actually led the Anti-Christian Movement.
quoteEn: The Anti-Christian Movement was the real-world setting for the founding of the Chinese Socialist Youth League and carries important historical significance.
quoteZh: 非基运动是中国社会主义青年团成立的现实背景，具有重要的历史意义。

t: The development, main content and historical assessment of Yun Daiying's atheist thought
zh: 恽代英无神论思想的发展脉络、主要内涵及历史评价
paras: This article examines the atheist thought of Yun Daiying (1895–1931), an early leader of the Chinese Communist Party and a pioneer in spreading atheism in modern China. Zhou argues that Yun applied Marxist atheism to criticise religious theology and feudal superstition, and in doing so built a relatively complete atheist outlook of his own. The article sets out its origins, content and value, and also names its limits.

The piece has three parts. The first traces the development of Yun's atheism: its theoretical foundations in materialism and the doctrine of knowability, the late Qing and Republican climate of rampant superstition, and his move from youthful atheism to a Marxist position after he joined the Party in 1921. The second sets out five areas of content: the basic questions about religion, religious freedom, faith versus scientific belief, theism and science, and methods of dealing with theism. The third assesses his contribution and shortcomings.

Zhou's central claim is that Yun's thought matured when he left behind his early ambivalence, including admiration for Jesus's personality, and began to explain religion through political and economic systems, imperialism and feudal exploitation. In Zhou's account, Yun held that religion is a human creation with six psychological and historical sources, that its positive functions will fade until it dies out, and that it should not be forcibly suppressed, though illegal activity must be punished. He saw scientific belief as open to doubt while religious belief is exclusive, and he saw theism as obstructing science and reason. His remedies were guiding religion to adapt to society, including church self-government, atheist education, popularising science, and breaking superstition through cultural and political revolution.

Zhou credits Yun with exposing religious mysticism, spreading scientific knowledge and advancing the adaptation of Marxist atheism to the Chinese context. Zhou also finds two weaknesses: theoretical inconsistency, with traces of Daoist and Confucian ideas and statements that leave room for belief in gods, and an emotional, one-sided view of Christianity as a tool of imperialism, as in his remark that every Christian is a 'foreign slave'. Zhou says he should not be judged by present-day standards and that studying him can inform research on Marxist atheism and the handling of religious questions and superstition today. Read the original if you study the early Chinese Marxist treatment of religion, or the history of atheist propaganda in the Republican era.
quoteEn: Yun Daiying held that religious belief and scientific belief differ clearly in essence and must not be equated.
quoteZh: 恽代英认为，宗教信仰和科学信仰有着明显的本质的区别，不能把宗教信仰与科学信仰等同。

t: The artistic critique in the construction of Marx's scientific atheism
zh: 马克思科学无神论思想的艺术批判建构
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论)
paras: Marx's atheism is usually read through his philosophical critique of religion and theology. Jiang Xuebin asks whether it also has an artistic dimension, and argues that it does. In Jiang's account, Marx built a distinct 'artistic critique' of divinity, which adds a further strand to the development of his scientific atheism.

The article follows Marx's thinking in three steps, running from his early creative writing to his mature theory. It begins with the poems, the novel Scorpion and Felix and other youthful literary work. It then turns to Marx's statements on the nature of art, and finally to his writings on 'artistic production'. Jiang contrasts Marx throughout with the idealist aesthetics of Schelling, in which art is bound up with God.

Jiang's central claim is that each stage removes divinity from art in a different way. In the early poems, gods, stars and spirits are said to be projections of nature and of human limits, while inspiration comes from real love and real life. Marx's mature view of art rests on materialism, practice and social need, so that art is a conscious human activity and not a divine emanation. Under the heading of artistic production, Marx treats art and religion as particular modes of production. Art then becomes a lens for criticising capitalism, in which the writer is a wage-labourer and artistic work turns into a commodity. Jiang holds that these problems come from capitalist contradictions, which gods cannot solve and only human practice and emancipation can.

Jiang concludes that Marx's artistic critique traces a line from poetic intuition, through the theoretical grounding of art in philosophy, practice and society, to a practical critique of artistic production under capitalism. On this reading, art is a human practice and a mode of production, and is neither a vehicle of the divine nor a tool for manipulating people in God's name. The article presents this as showing how Marx's atheism matured and as opening a literary and artistic path for contemporary research on scientific atheism. Read the original if you are interested in Marx's aesthetics, his early poetry, or how Chinese scholars of atheism link literature and the theory of artistic production to the critique of religion.
quoteEn: Marx's construction of an artistic critique, based on literary creation, the disclosure of the essence of art and the theory of artistic production, reflects the theoretical path along which his atheism gradually matured.
quoteZh: 马克思基于文学创作、艺术本质揭示和艺术生产理论进行的艺术批判构建，反映出马克思无神论思想逐步走向成熟的理论脉络

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese Marxist scholarship for atheism grounded in materialism and the sciences, as distinct from earlier speculative or purely polemical forms. It has its own research field and journals in China, including Science and Atheism.

Marx's term, used in the Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy, for art as a branch of spiritual production under capitalism. Chinese aesthetics treats it as a core concept linking art to political economy.

t: Historical experience and lessons from the Communist Party's handling of religious issues in southern Xinjiang in the 1950s
zh: 20世纪50年代中国共产党处理南疆地区宗教问题的历史经验与启示
paras: Yan Shaohua asks how the Chinese Communist Party dealt with religion in southern Xinjiang in the 1950s, and what that record offers for religious work today. The article argues that the Party's approach was cautious, steady, flexible and gradual. In Yan's account it achieved its aims without major social upheaval, and it gave local people real freedom both to believe and not to believe. Yan says this had no precedent in the region's history and that it still instructs the handling of religion in Xinjiang.

The article first reviews four strands of 1950s practice, drawing on speeches by Wang Enmao, Party directives and local gazetteers. They are publicising the policy of freedom of religious belief; carrying out the democratic reform of religious institutions; building an anti-feudal united front with religious figures; and, last, lessons for the present. It uses Kashgar, Aksu, Hotan and Zepu as examples.

Yan's core claim is that policy was tied to the Party's central task of each period. Early on, the Party stressed freedom to believe in order to counter the Nationalist rumour that communists would abolish religion. Atheist education and the freedom not to believe were promoted fully only from 1958. Yan argues that separating religion from administration, justice, marriage and education, and then abolishing religious feudal privileges, waqf land and religious levies, rested on gradualism. The Party distinguished clerics from landlords and brought religious figures into land-reform committees and study classes. Yan says this narrowed the target of struggle and widened unity.

Yan draws three lessons for the new era. Religious work must serve the Party's central task, now stability and long-term security in Xinjiang. The separation of religion and state must be upheld, so that religion is a private matter and is not tied to ethnicity; Yan states that there is no such thing as a "Muslim nation". The Sinicization of Islam in Xinjiang, Yan argues, requires Party leadership and the principle of the "state's presence". Yan calls for Party and government bodies to guide scriptural interpretation and the governance of religion. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Xinjiang religious policy of the 1950s is framed as a model for current policy, with extensive local sources.
quoteEn: Religion must not be bound up with ethnicity; there is no such thing as a so-called "Muslim nation".
quoteZh: 宗教不得与民族捆绑，没有所谓的“穆斯林民族”。

glossary.explanation: A Party strategy of building alliances with non-Party groups and social forces to pursue its goals. Here it refers to cooperation with religious figures against feudal landlords.
The principle that religion should not interfere in administration, law, education or marriage. In the Party's usage it treats religion as a citizen's private matter within limits set by state law.
Land endowed to Islamic institutions under the waqf system. The article describes it as a feudal exploitation system run by religious elites, which was redistributed and then collectivised.
An official policy of guiding religions to adapt to Chinese culture and socialist society under Party leadership. It is applied to Islam in Xinjiang.
The campaigns of the early 1950s that abolished landlord and feudal privileges in minority areas. They included rent reduction, land reform and, later, reform of religious institutions.

t: Some reflections on atheism and the sinicization of religion from the perspective of the "Second Integration"
zh: “第二个结合”视角下对于无神论与宗教中国化问题的几点认知
paras: This text is a summary of a speech by Zhang Xinying, delivered on 9 July 2023 at a symposium on "the Second Integration and atheism" organised by the editors of the journal Science and Atheism. It responds to Xi Jinping's remarks of 2 June 2023 describing the "Second Integration" (combining Marxism with China's fine traditional culture) as a fresh emancipation of thought. Zhang asks whether traditional culture contains religious elements, what role its atheistic factors play, and whether its beliefs can serve the sinicization of religion. The answer is that traditional culture does contain such elements, and that they can support religious sinicization.

Zhang says each question could fill a long study and offers three fragmentary observations. The first concerns the historical sources of the "fine traditional culture" that Xi repeatedly cites. The second takes up the claim that Chinese culture is humanist rather than god-centred. The third applies both points to the direction of sinicizing religion, including foreign religions such as monotheistic faiths.

Zhang argues that the core values of fine traditional culture were largely fixed by Confucian-led pre-Qin thinkers in the "Axial Age", before Buddhism and Daoism existed as complete religions. The "three pillars" description of Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism is therefore conditional, and Zhang warns against equating tradition with the backward features of late feudal society. In Zhang's reading, the early Chinese view of the gods dissolved the boundary between gods and humans and made religion serve worldly life. Zhang calls this an original humanist undertone, quite unlike the "god-centred" monotheism of other cultures. Zhang adds that it made Marxism easier to embrace in China. Zhang cites Paul Tillich's 1957 remark that Confucianism was a positive condition for the success of communist faith.

Zhang concludes that traditional beliefs can supply useful resources for the sinicization of religion. Traditional religions should open a new chapter, while foreign monotheistic religions should learn from Chinese culture how to coexist with mainstream politics and ideology. They should also link up with the core socialist values and play their social role within Chinese modernization. Zhang presents this as a goal of the Second Integration and as a way of joining Marxist religious studies with Marxist atheist education. Read the original if you want to see how a senior scholar of religion links the Second Integration to official policy on religion and atheism.
quoteEn: This is the most practically valuable fine tradition of Chinese religion within the system of traditional Chinese culture.
quoteZh: 这是中国宗教在中华传统文化体系内最富有现实价值的优秀传统。

glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formulation, first stated in 2021, of combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture. It is the second of the Two Integrations, the first being integration with China's concrete realities.
Official policy requiring religions in China to adapt to Chinese society, culture and socialist politics. Since 2015 it has been promoted as a guiding direction for religious work.
The official term for the parts of Chinese tradition regarded as worth inheriting and developing, as distinct from what is called its dross.
The official name for the Party's path of modernization with Chinese characteristics, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
A set of 24 characters of values promoted officially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), at the national, social and individual levels.

t: Traditional Chinese culture and atheism
zh: 中国传统文化与无神论
source: Science and Atheism (public account), symposium of 9 July 2023
paras: This is the record of a speech by Li Shen at a symposium on "the Second Integration and atheism", organised on 9 July 2023 by the editorial office of the journal Science and Atheism. The symposium followed Xi Jinping's 2 June 2023 talk on cultural inheritance and development, in which he called the "second integration" (of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture) a further liberation of thought. Li's theme is how traditional Chinese culture relates to atheism. Li holds that Chinese tradition combined near-universal belief in gods with a long, continuous line of thinkers who rejected crude sorcery and superstition.

Li first sketches the development of Chinese culture from the legendary Yellow Emperor and Flame Emperor era through the Shang and Zhou, the Qin unification and the Han decision to honour Confucianism alone. He then follows Confucian thought through Wang Bi, Kong Yingda, the Song Neo-Confucians and the Four Books, noting parallel changes in Buddhism and Daoism. The second half is a chronological survey of atheist thinkers from Confucius and Xunzi to Wang Chong, Fan Zhen, Han Yu, Liu Zongyuan, Liu Yuxi, Ouyang Xiu, Cao Duan and Xiong Bolong.

Li argues that Confucianism gave the ancient state stability and cultural continuity, making Chinese culture the only one uninterrupted for five thousand years, and that unity was treated as normal and division as abnormal. In his account, Chinese rulers and people alike believed in gods, and the deities of the state faith were regarded as protectors of the state, which fostered tolerance. He contrasts this with world religions centred on individual salvation, which, he says, treated other peoples' gods as idols to be removed and, with capitalist expansion, nearly destroyed the cultures of tolerance and peace. Within this setting, thinkers from Confucius onwards corrected sorcery and excessive worship. Examples include Xunzi on unusual celestial events, Wang Chong's rejection of the correspondence between heaven and humanity, Fan Zhen's analogy of the blade and its sharpness, and Ouyang Xiu's refusal to record supposed omens.

Li concludes that these ideas form a sequence within fine traditional culture and supply valuable material for present-day atheism. He adds that ancient atheism spread with difficulty and its proponents suffered hardship. Scientific, thoroughgoing atheism, he says, can flourish only in a socialist society guided by Marxism. Confucianism, by his account, was good at preserving order but could not cope with modern imperialist aggression, so the Qing abolished its ruling status before the 1911 Revolution and the founding of the People's Republic gave tradition new life. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese atheism scholars link the "Second Integration" to the history of Chinese irreligious thought.
quoteEn: But from Confucius at the latest, thinkers in every age kept correcting and discarding crude sorcery and unrestrained superstition about ghosts and spirits, and this formed the long-standing atheist tradition in our traditional culture.
quoteZh: 但是，至少从孔子开始，历代都有思想家不断纠正和抛弃低级、粗陋的巫术和滥渎无度的鬼神迷信，这就构成了我国传统文化中历史悠久的无神论传统。

glossary.explanation: Refers to the Han dynasty's decision to make Confucianism the orthodox guiding ideology of the state, traditionally associated with Emperor Wu and Dong Zhongshu.
A Han Confucian doctrine, developed by Dong Zhongshu, that Heaven responds to human conduct with omens and disasters, rewarding or punishing rulers.
Ritual offerings beyond those prescribed by the state; from the Han onward they were treated as illegitimate and were targeted by officials and thinkers.

t: Chen Liang's atheism and his critique of Confucianism as a religion
zh: 陈亮无神论思想及其对儒教的批判
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2023 no. 3
paras: Chen Liang, a Southern Song utilitarian thinker long regarded in Chinese scholarship as a representative of ancient materialism, is the subject of this article. Liu asks what his atheism amounted to within Confucian thought. Liu argues that it was an attack on the religious-theological elements of Confucianism (rujiao, 'Confucian religion') and a defence of human value, and that it helped keep Confucian learning (ruxue) from turning into a full religion.

Prior scholarship, Liu notes, has mostly studied Chen's atheism through the 'relation of Heaven and man' and views on ghosts and spirits, without stating clearly that it criticised Confucianism as a religion. Liu builds on Ren Jiyu's thesis that Confucianism is a religion, and on Hou Wailu's reading of Chen's debate with Zhu Xi as 'militant atheism'. The article has three parts: Chen's rejection of Confucianism's mystical elements; his affirmation of human value and agency; and an assessment of his place in Confucianism's self-correction, with a short conclusion.

In the first part, Liu argues that Chen's materialist epistemology held that the boundary between Heaven and man is 'plainly knowable'. On that basis Chen denied the sacredness of sages and classics, and reinterpreted the 'Way' (dao) as something inseparable from concrete things and everyday affairs. He also attacked the Neo-Confucian 'Heavenly principle' (tianli) as a disguised theism that suppresses human desires. In the second part, Liu presents Chen's slogan that the Way's survival depends on people as an answer to Zhu Xi. Chen stressed human agency, defended legitimate desire, criticised the introspective doctrines of mind and nature, and valued heroes and human planning over fate. Liu cites Marx and Engels to frame this as negating the divine in order to affirm the human.

Liu concludes that Confucian learning is a 'study of the human' rather than a religion. The author holds that Confucianism was repeatedly corrected from within, and that Chen played this role against the Song-Ming Neo-Confucians, whose system Ren Jiyu called the completion of the Confucian 'god-making movement'. Liu concedes that Chen's atheism was incomplete: he still showed some reverence for Heaven's mandate and wrote prayers for rain. Liu still judges the flaws minor. In the context of promoting excellent traditional Chinese culture today, the author calls for removing the religious-theological elements of Confucianism and drawing on its positive components. Read the original if you want a Marxist-atheist reading of the Chen Liang–Zhu Xi debate, with extensive quotations from Chen's writings and letters.
quoteEn: Chen Liang opposed the absolute authority of 'Heavenly principle' and stressed the legitimacy of 'human desires', which in effect highlighted the human being's position as subject at the level of practice.
quoteZh: 陈亮反对“天理”的绝对权威，强调“人欲”的合理性，实际上突出了人在实践哲层面中的主体地位

t: The two-way interaction between Chinese philosophy and Marxist atheism and its significance
st: Han-dynasty philosophy in Ren Jiyu's history of philosophy
zh: 中国哲学与马克思主义无神论的双向互动及其意义
zhSub: 以任继愈哲学史视域下的汉代哲学诠释为中心
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2023 no. 3
paras: Wang Shiliang asks how the work of Ren Jiyu (1916–2009), a leading Marxist historian of Chinese philosophy and religion, linked the study of Chinese philosophy with Marxist atheism. The article argues that Ren fused two approaches: a Marxist history of philosophy and his thesis that Confucianism is a religion. In Wang's reading, this fusion produced a two-way interaction between Chinese philosophy and Marxist atheism, and it still carries methodological meaning for atheism research and education today.

The article opens with Ren's 'three histories' of Chinese philosophy (the four-volume History of Chinese Philosophy, the Concise History, and the History of the Development of Chinese Philosophy) and his work on the 'three teachings' of Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism. It then traces Ren's conception of the history of philosophy, including a shift in emphasis between the early textbook and the later multi-volume history. The central case study is Ren's interpretation of Han-dynasty philosophy: Dong Zhongshu, the Baihu tong, Wang Chong, and the relation between philosophy and natural science.

Wang shows that Ren first defined philosophy's history as a history of struggle between materialism and idealism, shaped by Zhdanov's definition and class analysis. Later Ren gave greater weight to the history of human cognition and described Chinese philosophy as advancing through struggle with religion. In the Han case, Ren reads Dong Zhongshu's doctrine of heaven–human correspondence as a theology serving centralised autocracy, and the Baihu tong as completing a 'state religion of feudal society'. Wang Chong appears as a 'militant atheist' whose empiricism hit at the core of Confucian doctrine, although Ren also notes contradictions, such as fatalism, that stopped him from being a thoroughgoing atheist. Han medicine and agriculture, Ren argues, show the practical knowledge that undercuts theology.

Wang concludes that Ren applied Marxist principles to the concrete course of Chinese philosophy and deepened understanding of its cognitive history. Wang adds that Ren carried out Mao Zedong's call to criticise theology and so widened the 'ideological front' of Marxist atheism. For the present, Wang suggests that atheism research and education should link up with the new liberal arts, ideological and political courses, and textbook systems. Read the original if you want a detailed account of Ren Jiyu's reading of Dong Zhongshu, the Baihu tong and Wang Chong, or of how Chinese Marxist scholarship treats religion and Confucianism.
quoteEn: Ren Jiyu insisted on 'revealing the regularities of the process by which human cognition broke free from religion', carried through in his study of Chinese philosophy the scholarly aim of uniting philosophical research with the critique of theology, and thereby extended the 'ideological front' of Marxist atheism.
quoteZh: 任继愈坚持“把人类认识挣脱宗教的过程的规律性揭示出来”，在中国哲学研究中贯彻了哲学研究与批判神学相统一的学术宗旨，扩展了马克思主义无神论的“思想阵地”

glossary.en: the thesis that Confucianism is a religion
glossary.literal: the theory that Confucianism is a religion
glossary.explanation: Ren Jiyu's view, put forward in the early 1980s, that Confucianism developed into a religion with a distinctive form suited to feudal China. It was debated widely in Chinese scholarship.

glossary.literal: mutual response of heaven and humans
glossary.explanation: Dong Zhongshu's Han-dynasty doctrine that heaven and human affairs, especially the ruler's conduct, respond to one another. Ren reads it as a theological system.

glossary.literal: Comprehensive discussions in the White Tiger Hall
glossary.explanation: A Han text recording the Confucian classical debates held at the White Tiger Hall under Emperor Zhang in 79 CE. Ren treats it as completing a state religion.
A common Party-Marxist term for the domain of ideas to be held and expanded against rival worldviews. Here it refers to the reach of Marxist atheism.

t: The impact of Christian missions on the sense of community of the Chinese nation, and how to respond
st: The case of Christian missions in the China–Burma border region in the 1930s
zh: 基督教传播对中华民族共同体意识的影响及应对
zhSub: 以20世纪30年代基督教在中缅边境地区的传播为例
paras: Gao Tietai takes up the question of how Christian missions weakened the national identity of ethnic groups on the China–Burma border in the 1930s, and what lessons that history holds today. The article, published in the journal Science and Atheism (2023, no. 3), uses 'Christianity' in the broad sense of Catholicism and Protestantism. Its thesis is that missionary activity diluted local attachment to the motherland and to Chinese culture, and that contemporary efforts to forge a stronger sense of community of the Chinese nation, together with the 'Sinicisation' of Christianity, can draw on the responses of that period.

The article has four parts. It first describes confused national identity among border peoples during the boundary disputes of the early twentieth century, citing the 1933 Banhong incident and the Sino-British boundary survey commissions of 1935–37. It then sets out three channels of missionary influence. A third part reviews how officials, scholars and the public understood the problem and responded. A final part draws implications for Yunnan today.

Gao argues that missionaries gained great appeal among converts, whom the author says 'knew only the pastor, not the government'. They ran church schools with texts in missionary-created scripts or in English and Burmese, and the author says some lessons were hostile to Han Chinese. They also recast historical memory, for instance by presenting Jesus as the brother of Zhuge Liang, whom many local peoples revered. Contemporary Chinese commentators, in Gao's account, did not interfere directly with belief. They promoted border education, the national language, textbooks on shared history and the thesis that the Chinese nation is one. They also favoured localised churches and political propaganda carried by itinerant teaching teams.

Gao concludes that the 1930s measures partly resisted missionary division and prompted early thinking about Christianity's 'Chinese-isation'. For the present, the author calls for the Sinicisation of Christianity in border areas, wider use of the standard national language and script, and stronger historical memory of the Chinese nation. The stated aim is to resist overseas religious infiltration and to consolidate the sense of community of the Chinese nation as the main line of ethnic work. Read the original if you study Party ethnic and religious policy, Christianity in Yunnan, or how Republican-era frontier history is used in current Chinese policy discourse.
quoteEn: Missionaries first equated Jesus with Zhuge Liang and then replaced Zhuge Liang with Jesus, thereby altering the historical memory of the southwestern peoples, creating a new mental map and weakening the common culture of the Chinese nation.
quoteZh: 传教士先以耶稣等同孔明，再用耶稣代替孔明，从而改变西南族群的历史记忆，形成了新的心理构图，淡化中华民族的共同文化。

glossary.zh: 铸牢中华民族共同体意识
glossary.en: sense of community of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: forging a firm consciousness of the Chinese nation as a community
glossary.explanation: A slogan made the main line of the Party's ethnic work at the Central Conference on Ethnic Work (2021). It stresses a shared national identity across the country's ethnic groups.
A policy line that religions in China should identify with the political system, adapt to socialist society and express themselves through Chinese culture. Here it is applied to Christianity.

glossary.literal: state common spoken and written language
glossary.explanation: The official term for standard Mandarin and the Chinese characters. Its promotion in minority areas is a stated policy priority.
A thesis debated in the 1930s, associated with Gu Jiegang, that China's peoples form a single nation. Gao treats it as a response to frontier crisis.

t: Questions to be answered in upholding the direction of the sinicization of religion in China
zh: 坚持我国宗教中国化方向需要回答的几个问题
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2023 no. 3
paras: Dong Xiaoqin takes up misunderstandings that, according to the author's fieldwork, have arisen at the grassroots as the Party promotes the sinicization of religion. Believers ask what sinicization means, why it is needed and what will happen to their religion afterwards. Dong argues that these questions come from missing or one-sided understandings, and that the policy's meaning is clarified by answering three questions: whether it aims to "transform away" religion, whether it politicises religion, and whether it develops religion. The answer to each is no.

The article has three main sections and a short conclusion. It draws on speeches by Xi Jinping, Mao Zedong's 1945 report On Coalition Government, early constitutional documents and the 1954 Constitution. It also uses the historical cases of Buddhism and Islam in China, and statistics on believers and religious venues cited by the author.

On the first question, Dong holds that sinicization leaves "basic beliefs, core doctrines and ritual systems" intact. What changes is how doctrine is interpreted so that it fits socialist society and traditional Chinese culture, as Buddhism and Islam did historically. Dong proposes an official platform for interpreting scriptures, run under Party and government leadership, whose representatives must be politically reliable, learned, law-abiding and trusted by believers. The author presents this as protecting religious discourse power and security against what is described as hostile Western infiltration and religious extremism. On the second, Dong traces the Party's record on religious freedom and says sinicization is not "Party-run religion" or control. The author adds that freedom of belief is bounded by law. On the third, Dong says the aim is to guide religion to adapt to socialism, not to promote it. The Party's stance is that administrative force should neither develop nor abolish religion, and religion is cast as a "harmony" voice in China's plural culture. Dong ties this to the "one guidance, five identifications, three loves and four histories" education.

Dong concludes that sinicization is a gradual strategic task to be pursued under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It should be led by the Party, with religious circles as the main actors and scholars as support. The goal is a religious system of thought, institutions and governance with Chinese characteristics, and the author also calls for a stronger academic discourse system. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of atheism answers, in official terms, the grassroots and foreign objections to the sinicization of religion.
quoteEn: The sinicization of religion is not meant to develop religion, but to guide religion to adapt better to China's socialist society.
quoteZh: 宗教中国化不是为了发展宗教，而是为了引导宗教更好地适应中国社会主义社会。

glossary.explanation: A policy stressed since around 2015 that asks religions in China to adapt to socialist society and Chinese culture. Official texts present it as a direction for religious doctrine, institutions and practice.

glossary.zh: 一引领五认同三爱四史教育
glossary.pinyin: yī yǐnlǐng wǔ rèntóng sān ài sì shǐ jiàoyù
glossary.en: one guidance, five identifications, three loves and four histories
glossary.explanation: A summary of Xi Jinping's 2021 directives on religious work. Religious circles are to be guided by socialist core values, identify with the country, nation, culture, Party and socialism, and study patriotism, collectivism and socialism along with the history of the Party, New China, reform and opening up, and socialism.

t: Experience and prospects of Marxist atheism propaganda and education in the new era
st: Report on the 10th Scientific Atheism Forum and the 2022 annual conference of the China Atheism Society
zh: 新时代马克思主义无神论宣传教育的经验与展望
zhSub: 第十届科学无神论论坛暨中国无神论学会2022年学术年会综述
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2023 no. 2
paras: This is a report on the 10th Scientific Atheism Forum of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, held together with the 2022 annual conference of the China Atheism Society. The meeting took place online on 27 November 2022 under the theme "Marxist atheism propaganda and education in the new era: experience and prospects". It was convened to put into practice Xi Jinping's speeches at the 20th Party Congress (2022) and at the national religious work conferences of 2016 and 2021. It was organised by the CASS Academy of Marxism, Heilongjiang University and the Society, with more than 130 scholars and officials attending.

After the opening and closing addresses, the report sorts the papers into six themes. These are the history and experience of atheism education; basic theory, including early Party leaders' atheist thought; practical experiments with different audiences (students, peasants, cadres, border regions); the relationship between Marxist atheism and Marxist religious studies; building Marxist religious studies as a discipline; and the Party's religious work, including the "sinicization of religion". Each section summarises individual speakers in a sentence or a short paragraph.

Several threads recur. Historical overviews divide the new era into stages and argue that atheism work lapsed after 1987, so that research must be rebuilt before propaganda can succeed. Zhang Ge's own paper identifies five teaching models, from fragmentary inclusion in ideological courses to independent systematic courses. On the discipline, speakers such as Li Shen, Zhang Xinying, Xi Wuyi and Jia Runguo describe atheism as the "hard core" of Marxist religious studies. Lü Jianfu and Zuo Peng warn of Western religious studies, "de-ideologisation" and overstating religion's positive cultural functions. Tian Xinming treats ideological struggle and freedom of religious belief as a unity that contains opposition, and says atheist education should target society at large, not believers specifically.

The closing summary by Jia Runguo judges the conference a success and says the atheism cause is developing well since the 2021 conference called for strengthening Marxist religious studies. It adds that the work is long and demanding, and that the "Three Musts" from the 20th Party Congress apply to it. Practical proposals include wider teaching of atheism courses, more teachers, and a clearer leadership system, with Party organisation, propaganda and education departments leading the work among cadres and young people. Read the original if you want a detailed map of the speakers, institutions and positions in current Chinese official debates on Marxist atheism, religious studies and religious policy.
quoteEn: The key to advancing the building of Marxist religious studies in the new era is to uphold Marxist atheism.
quoteZh: 新时代推进马克思主义宗教学建设，关键就是要坚持马克思主义无神论。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-Leninist form of atheism, presented as grounded in materialism and a critique of religion. In China it is promoted by the China Atheism Society and CASS research centres.

The Marxist approach to studying religion, which the 2021 national religious work conference called on China to strengthen as a discipline. Speakers here describe it as closely tied to scientific atheism.
An official policy direction under which religions in China are to adapt to socialist society and Chinese conditions. Speakers at the forum discuss its stages and history.
A high-level Party and government meeting on religious policy; those of 2016 and 2021 are cited as setting the direction for atheism education.
A formula in the 20th Party Congress report (2022) calling on the Party to stay modest and prudent, to keep up hard struggle, and to keep a spirit of striving.

t: The atheist thought of Marx's doctoral dissertation and its significance in the new era
zh: 马克思博士论文的无神论思想及其在新时代的意义
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2023 no. 3
paras: Wang Xiang asks what Marx's doctoral dissertation, The Difference Between the Democritean and Epicurean Philosophy of Nature (written 1839–41), contributes to the history of Marxist scientific atheism. The article argues that, despite its debt to Hegelian idealism and Bruno Bauer's philosophy of self-consciousness, the dissertation is the true opening work of Marx's critique of religion. In Wang's reading it is the logical starting point of scientific atheism and a first decisive step towards it.

The article has three parts. The first traces the atheist motives behind the choice of topic, from Marx's Rhineland upbringing and two school essays to his time in Berlin among the Young Hegelians. The second sets out three strands of atheist thought in the dissertation. The third draws four lessons for atheist theory and education in the new era, with reference to the 20th Party Congress (2022).

Wang's core argument is that the dissertation does three things. First, by defending Epicurus' doctrine of the atomic swerve through "self-consciousness", Marx sets out an ontological atheist principle and places philosophy above religion. Second, Marx applies an early theory of alienation to nature worship, treating religion as alienated self-consciousness. Wang presents this as the first stage of a path from religious to political, labour and money alienation, and as giving atheism a practical, combative character. Third, Marx's rebuttal of Plutarch on the immortality of the soul grounds an atheist humanism that is a precursor of communist thought. Wang concedes the idealist limits of this stage but argues they were products of their time.

Wang draws four requirements for the new era. Scientific atheism must keep its thoroughgoing critical spirit and confront theism, including hostile religious influence from inside and outside China, in order to protect ideological security. Its development must be viewed historically and dialectically, and dismissing the dissertation for its idealism is called mistaken. The doctrine must be pursued in a spirit of truth, avoiding decontextualised misreadings of the classics. Atheism must also keep its philosophical concern with ultimate values, aimed at communism and the free, all-round development of the person. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academy account of how Marx's early writings are used to ground scientific atheism and current policy on religion.
quoteEn: In essence, Marxist scientific atheism is critical, and this critical character is rooted in its practicality and its relation to its times.
quoteZh: 从本质上来说，马克思主义科学无神论是批判性的，这种批判性根源于实践性和时代性

glossary.explanation: The Marxist form of atheism, treated in Chinese scholarship as grounded in historical materialism and the critique of religion rather than in earlier Enlightenment atheism. It is a recognised research and teaching field in China.
A group of German philosophers, including Bruno Bauer and David Strauss, who used Hegel's philosophy to criticise religion and the state. Marx belonged to their circle in the late 1830s.
A central concept of Hegel and of Bruno Bauer's philosophy. Wang says the young Marx used it to defend Epicurus' atomic swerve and to place reason above religion.

The process by which humans' own creations come to stand over them as foreign powers. Wang traces Marx's theory from religious alienation in the dissertation to political, labour and money alienation.
The Communist Party of China's national congress held in October 2022. The article cites its report to support its arguments about theory and problem-orientation.

t: The content, characteristics and methods of Sinicized Marxist psychology of religion
zh: 中国化马克思主义宗教心理学的内容、特点及方法
paras: Zhou Puyuan and Li Ping take up the question of how the psychology of religion should be built in China. They argue that, since Wundt founded experimental psychology, work on the mind has split into a philosophical tradition and a quantitative natural-science tradition that do not meet. In their account, a psychology of religion adapted to Chinese conditions and guided by Marxism ("Sinicized Marxist psychology of religion") can bridge the two. It does so by joining quantitative and qualitative work, and rational and non-rational factors, in practice.

The article has three parts: the field's content, its characteristics and its methods. On content, the authors sketch the field's origins in the introduction of Western psychology of religion into China, which they divide into beginning, stagnation and start-up periods. They then discuss the field as both psychology and religious studies, and offer a definition. The second part lists seven characteristics. The third sets out research methods, ending with the "new liberal arts" agenda.

The core argument places the field within social psychology and treats religion through Lü Daji's four elements: ideas, feelings, behaviour and institutions. Religious consciousness is described as a distorted reflection of reality, religious feeling as a bond of identity, and religion as a special ideology. The authors give the seven characteristics as clear guiding ideology, critical spirit, interdisciplinarity, atheism, usefulness to policy-making, practice and guidance. They describe the field as scientific atheism in worldview and method. In their view it criticises Western theistic currents, such as Freud's reduction of religion to neurosis, and offers theoretical support to the Party and government in religious affairs.

On method, the authors call for dialectical logic, which they break down into the contradiction-as-motive-force approach, statistics (fieldwork data) and classification. They also call for historical materialism as the overarching guide, and for a wide range of discipline-specific methods, from history to anthropology and theology. They conclude that this diversity, though it complicates theory, gives the field greater inclusiveness than other disciplines. They also hold that it should help build an autonomous Chinese knowledge system and guide believers towards compatibility with socialist society. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars of scientific atheism define and justify a Marxist psychology of religion and its policy role.
quoteEn: Sinicized Marxist psychology of religion is in essence a scientific-atheist worldview and methodology, and correctly explaining the world's \"ontology\" and \"theory of reflection\" is its fundamental task.
quoteZh: 中国化马克思主义宗教心理学在本质上是科学无神论的世界观和方法论，正确阐明世界的“本体论”和“反映论”是中国化马克思主义宗教心理学研究的根本任务。

glossary.zh: 中国化马克思主义宗教心理学
glossary.explanation: The authors' term for a psychology of religion guided by Marxism and adapted to Chinese conditions. They present it as a distinct field within Chinese scholarship on religion and scientific atheism.
The Marxist-materialist denial of gods and the supernatural, taught and researched in China as a discipline. It is distinct from mere unbelief and is tied to Party ideology work.
An official Chinese education initiative from about 2018. It encourages crossing disciplinary boundaries within the humanities and social sciences, and between them and the sciences.
The Marxist view that social being, above all material production, determines social consciousness. The authors treat it as the overarching method for studying religion.

t: The logic, features and paths of intelligent algorithms empowering Marxist atheist propaganda
zh: 智能算法赋能马克思主义无神论宣传的逻辑、特征与路径
paras: Luo Guoqing asks how intelligent algorithms, which now steer online information input, processing and distribution, can be used to strengthen Marxist atheist propaganda and education. Writing in 2023 and citing Party documents since the 18th Party Congress (2012) that call for strengthening atheist education, Luo argues that combining the two is theoretically necessary, practically required and technically feasible. The article presents algorithms as a new form of power with an ideological function that Marxist atheism must learn to steer.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the internal logic of the combination. The second identifies three features of algorithm-enabled atheist propaganda. The third proposes four practical paths. Examples come from Chinese social media, including Sina Weibo accounts that promote science and oppose superstition and cults, and the WeChat account of the journal Science and Atheism.

Luo's core argument is that algorithms are double-edged. In the article's account, online religious propagation, cults and hostile overseas forces exploit recommendation systems, "information cocoons" and the Matthew effect to push fortune-telling and theistic content and to draw users toward religious belief. Atheist propaganda should therefore be built into the algorithmic system, following Xi Jinping's call to "master algorithms with mainstream values". Luo describes the technical route as tagging atheist content, profiling users and matching the two, and as creating immersive "simulated environments" and "smart fields" for data analysis and prediction. The resulting propaganda is said to shift from one-way output to multi-party interaction, from mass broadcasting to personalised delivery, and from grand narrative to concrete, everyday and emotional storytelling.

Luo proposes four paths. The first is upgrading algorithms: raising the weight of atheist content, filtering sensitive terms and adding reverse-push programmes that show atheist material to users who browse theistic content. The second is innovating content and discourse, including short-video accounts, while keeping the scientific rigour of the theory. The third is raising the atheist theoretical competence of algorithm designers, content moderators and audiences. The fourth is strengthening regulation under the rules on internet religious information services and algorithmic recommendation, with responsibilities assigned to government departments and platforms. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar links algorithmic governance, online religion and ideological security, with concrete platform examples.
quoteEn: Combining Marxist atheist propaganda with intelligent algorithms, and conducting algorithmic communication of Marxist atheism, helps absorb the strong propaganda energy of algorithmic media platforms and form an all-round communication matrix for Marxist atheism.
quoteZh: 把马克思主义无神论宣传与智能算法结合起来，进行马克思主义无神论算法化传播，有利于吸收各算法媒介平台的强大宣传能量，形成全方位的马克思主义无神论传播矩阵。

glossary.explanation: The official ideological position on religion in China, which holds that religion arises from social conditions and will eventually wither away. Party documents call for atheist education, especially among Party members and young people.

A term for the narrowing of a user's information environment when algorithms repeatedly push similar content. Chinese commentators use it to describe how recommendation systems may reinforce existing preferences and beliefs.
The idea that the dominance of mainstream Marxist ideology must be protected against hostile or foreign ideas. It is often applied to online spaces, religion and information flows.
A term from communication studies (Lippmann's "pseudo-environment") for a media-constructed picture of reality. Here it means immersive online settings built to deliver atheist messages.

t: A study of Xi Jinping's important statements on religious work in Xinjiang in the new era
zh: 习近平总书记关于做好新时代新疆宗教工作重要论述研究
paras: Jia and Pu set out to systematise what Xi Jinping has said about religious work in Xinjiang since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They argue that these statements form part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and of the Party's strategy for governing Xinjiang. In their account, the statements offer a complete framework for religious work in the region and guidance for the whole country.

The article, published in Science and Atheism in 2023, has three parts. The first sets out five strands of Xi's statements: Party leadership of religious work; the Sinicization of Islam in Xinjiang; governing Xinjiang according to law; building 'three contingents' of personnel; and combating religious extremism. The second identifies five modes of thinking in the statements: political, innovative, strategic, dialectical and systems thinking. The third assesses their theoretical and practical value.

On Sinicization, the authors argue that Islam in Xinjiang has been well localised but is less Sinicized than in inner China, because its Chinese outlook and standpoint are not firmly grounded. They present Xi's remedy as strengthening identification with Chinese culture, guiding religious figures towards interpretations suited to the times, and resolving whether Xinjiang looks 'east or west'. On law, they stress the principle of protecting what is legal, stopping what is illegal, curbing extremism, resisting infiltration and cracking down on crime. They also stress meeting believers' normal religious needs. They define religious extremism as a political struggle, not an ethnic or religious question, and cite a 2016 Kashgar survey of clergy to show how weak the clergy's education is.

The authors conclude that Xi's statements opened a new level of understanding of Xinjiang religious work and set out its direction and methods. They also credit the statements with strengthening Party leadership and with guiding the handling of incidents involving religion. They cite the regional government's 2022 report of five consecutive years without violent terrorist cases as evidence of results. They also argue that formulations first devised for Xinjiang, such as the 'five identifications' and forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, now guide ethnic and religious work nationwide. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars present the policy rationale for religious governance in Xinjiang.
quoteEn: Treating the winning of hearts and minds as the greatest politics is the core meaning of General Secretary Xi Jinping's political thinking.
quoteZh: 把争取人心作为最大政治，是习近平总书记政治思维的核心要义

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018. Authors treat Xi's statements on specific policy areas as components of it.
The official policy of making Islam adapt to Chinese culture, society and socialism. The article treats it as the core issue of religious work in Xinjiang.
Xi's 2021 formulation naming three groups of personnel for religious work: Party and government cadres, religious representatives, and researchers on religion.
A formula calling for identification with the motherland, the Chinese nation, Chinese culture, the Communist Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics.

glossary.zh: 铸牢中华民族共同体意识
glossary.en: forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A Party slogan from the Xi era on consolidating a shared national identity above ethnic and religious identities.

t: Annual development planning meeting of the CASS Research Centre for Science and Atheism and the journal Science and Atheism: a summary
zh: 中国社会科学院科学与无神论研究中心和《科学与无神论》年度发展规划会综述
paras: This is a report on the annual development planning meeting of the Research Centre for Science and Atheism at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) and its journal Science and Atheism, held on 4 February 2023 at the Academy of Marxism. Gong Yun, deputy director of the Academy and director of the Centre, chaired. He set two agenda items: the Centre's main work for the year and the building of the journal. Both were treated as platforms for strengthening the discipline of scientific atheism.

About thirty scholars attended, from CASS bodies (the Party committee, the Institute of Contemporary China Studies, the Institute of World Religions, the Academy of Marxism), the China Research Institute for Science Popularization, Shanghai Normal University, the Central Institute of Socialism, the United Front Work Department, Tsinghua University, Renmin University and the People's Public Security University. Huang Yanhong first reviewed 2022: publication of Principles of Scientific Atheism, a draft reader on atheist education for rural areas, courses for united front cadres and for a Marxism school in the north-west, and the tenth scientific atheism forum. She also gave journal figures: 62 papers, a composite impact factor of 0.521 and a comprehensive one of 0.244, with page counts to rise further in 2023.

Participants then made proposals on the Centre. Zhu Xiaoming argued that atheism underpins the Party's guiding ideology and should not be treated as optional. He distinguished the struggle between theism and atheism, which he assigned to the propaganda, education and organisation departments, from the struggle with extreme or separatist ideas inside religious circles, which he assigned to the united front department. He attributed a 'rebound' of religious fervour to the pandemic and economic fluctuations. Li Shen held that Marxist religious studies is in essence Marxist atheism, and proposed a research society under the China Atheism Society. Others proposed an introduction to Marxist atheism, an atheism dictionary and library, 'atheism lecture halls' at universities, more work in Xinjiang and Tibet, and closer ties with science popularization bodies and the anti-cult association.

On the journal, speakers asked for new columns on scientific spirit and method, more translations of foreign atheists, and topics such as religion among students, rural religion, religious infiltration and the science-fiction work The Three-Body Problem. Several urged entry into core-journal indexes (CSSCI, AMI, Peking University core list) and wider circulation, and Zhang Xinying cautioned that scientific atheism remains a marginal discipline with manuscript-supply problems. Speakers also asked for more publicity, a website and joint conferences. Read the original if you want a detailed record of how Chinese atheism researchers set their institutional priorities in 2023.
quoteEn: He holds that both science popularization research and atheism research should make their own voices heard.
quoteZh: 他认为，科普研究和无神论研究都应当发出自己的声音。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist-based academic discipline in China that studies atheism and religion and promotes atheist education. The meeting discussed building it as a discipline.
The study of religion from a Marxist standpoint. Li Shen at the meeting identified it in essence with Marxist atheism.
A Chinese Communist Party central department that handles relations with religious, ethnic and other non-Party groups, including religious affairs.

t: The significance of Engels's late-life research on religion
zh: 论恩格斯晚年宗教研究意蕴
paras: Why did Engels, after Marx's death in 1883 and while completing Capital, devote so much effort to religion? Wang and Jing treat this research as a significant side-strand of his late work and ask what it was for. They argue that it served three purposes: the needs of the revolutionary struggle, the defence and development of historical materialism, and the resolution of Engels's own lifelong engagement with the Bible.

The article is organised in four parts: the practical needs of the international workers' movement; the defence of historical materialism; Engels's personal "Bible complex"; and a conclusion. It draws on Engels's letters, Anti-Dühring, his writings on early Christianity and his remarks on Bruno Bauer. It also traces Engels's early religious development through his letters to the Graeber brothers and his engagement with German biblical criticism.

On the first purpose, the authors say Engels rejected two errors: radical atheism and forced abolition of religion (Bismarck's Kulturkampf, the Blanquists, the Bakuninists, Dühring), and Christian socialism, which blurred the line between religious faith and communist ideals. For the second, they argue that Engels used the idea of "intermediate links" between economic base and ideology to answer economic determinism. They also read his warning against treating the materialist method as a ready-made formula, aimed at the Party's "Young Ones", as a call to study history in depth. On the third, they hold that his 1894 essay on early Christianity resolved an interest begun in 1841. In it Engels reassessed Tübingen School and Bauer's criticism, crediting Bauer but correcting what he saw as Bauer's idealist errors.

The authors conclude that Engels's critical stance towards religion was consistent, and that critique means sublation rather than simple negation. They claim that he moved from criticising heaven to criticising its worldly basis, so no "mild turn" occurred in his late years. They also reject the view that late Engels diverged from Marx, since he worked throughout from historical materialism. In their view, his late writings enriched Marxist religious theory and hold an unshakeable place in it. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of Engels's late writings on religion and early Christianity, and of the debates about continuity between Engels and Marx.
quoteEn: Engels's attitude towards religion in his later years did not undergo a mild shift.
quoteZh: 恩格斯晚年对待宗教的态度并没有发生温和的转变。

glossary.explanation: The rendering of Hegel's Aufhebung: to negate while preserving and elevating. The authors use it to say that critique of religion is not mere denial.
Engels's idea that legal and political ideologies mediate between the economic base and more distant ideologies such as philosophy and religion.
A current that combines Christian ethics with socialist aims and favours reform by peaceful, legal means. The authors present it as a source of confusion in the workers' movement.

t: Marx's critique of religion and the formation of the materialist conception of history
st: An analysis centred on Marx's early writings
zh: 马克思的宗教批判与唯物史观的形成
zhSub: 以马克思青年时期论著为中心的分析
paras: Huang Jinhui and Min Li take up the relationship between Marx's critique of religion and the emergence of the materialist conception of history. They argue that the materialist conception of history was formed in the course of criticising religion and the Prussian state that religion defended, so the two stand in an "endogenous" relation. In their view this link is a key to understanding how Marx's thought developed, yet it has not received due attention among Chinese scholars.

The article first reads Marx's early writings in three stages. The first is the doctoral dissertation period (1836–1841). The second covers the Rheinische Zeitung and the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher (1842–1844), including "On the Jewish Question" and the "Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right: Introduction". The third runs from 1844 to 1846, with the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The Holy Family, the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. It then assesses the role of the religion critique in forming the theory, and ends with what the study means today.

The authors contend that Marx's explanation of religion moved from ideas (lack of reason or self-consciousness), to politics (the state and its interests), to the economy (alienated labour, money, material production and exchange). His method moved correspondingly from speculative philosophy, through Feuerbach's humanist materialism, to historical materialism. In the authors' reading, criticising Feuerbach and the Young Hegelians for explaining religion without material production and social relations pushed Marx to the "practice" category and to the view that the human essence is the ensemble of social relations. They add that the aim shifted from theoretical critique to changing the world. The German Ideology is presented as the first systematic statement of the theory and of a Marxist view of religion: religion disappears only when the real social relations that produce it are overthrown.

Huang and Min conclude that the religion critique was both the entry point and a driving force for the theory. They say it also led Marx on to the study of capitalist production and surplus value, and so to political economy and scientific socialism. They argue that neglecting this link produces misunderstandings. They also draw a policy lesson. On their account, Marx's view implies that religious work in China should avoid both "left" and right errors and should build laws guiding religion to adapt to socialism with Chinese characteristics. They add that raising education and science, improving income distribution and advancing common prosperity would gradually remove the conditions on which religion rests. Read the original if you study the development of Marx's early thought, or the theoretical basis of Chinese religious policy.
quoteEn: Marx's critique of religion played an indispensable role in the germination, emergence and formation of the materialist conception of history; it was the critique of religion that drove Marx to complete a revolutionary turn in theory and method.
quoteZh: 马克思的宗教批判在唯物史观的孕育、萌发与形成过程中，发挥了不可或缺的作用，正是宗教批判推动马克思完成了理论与方法的革命性转向。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese term for historical materialism, Marx and Engels's theory that material production and forms of exchange determine social, political and ideological life. Chinese scholarship usually dates its formation to The German Ideology.
A long-standing Chinese socialist goal of shared wealth, given new prominence in official discourse under Xi Jinping. It is used here to mean narrowing wealth gaps.
The official name for China's current system and path, associated with reform and opening up. Party policy requires religions to "adapt" to it.

t: Religion and politics in the perspective of Marx and Engels
zh: 马克思恩格斯视域中的宗教与政治
paras: Tang Zixiang asks how Marx and Engels understood the relationship between religion and politics, a question the author sets against the persistence of religion in contemporary politics (the Iranian revolution, 11 September 2001, Hindu nationalism). Tang notes that primordialists such as Huntington treat religion as a cause of conflict, while instrumentalists treat it as a tool of material forces. The article argues that Marx and Engels resolve this by tracing religious questions back to their social and economic roots, so that religion has both a positive and a negative political face, and its final resolution lies in human emancipation.

The article is built in three parts. The first treats religion as the sacred cloak of mass resistance, drawing mainly on Engels's The Peasant War in Germany and his essay on Ludwig Feuerbach. The second treats religion as an instrument of class oppression and aggressive expansion, using Marx on the Eastern Question and Engels on Russia, Spain and England. The third reconstructs the path from criticism of religion to political emancipation to human emancipation, drawing on Marx's On the Jewish Question and the introduction to his critique of Hegel's philosophy of right.

Tang argues that, in medieval Europe, theology absorbed all ideology, so peasant and plebeian movements, such as Thomas Müntzer's, had to take religious form. The author reads Engels as comparing early Christianity with the modern workers' movement. The cloak is dropped, Tang says, in the French bourgeois revolution, and socialism seeks salvation in this world. On the negative side, Tang holds that rulers use religion to deceive their own people and to justify wars, but that religious wars are at root class struggles over material interest, not caused by ideas. Tang also reads Marx as saying that political emancipation does not require abolishing religion. The modern state can separate from religion while religion flourishes in civil society, as in the North American states, but this emancipation remains partial and abstract.

Tang concludes that criticism of religion is the premise of all criticism, and that the problem is solved only by overcoming alienation and restoring to people their own world and relations. In this account the proletariat, armed with philosophy, is the agent of universal human emancipation. With high productive forces and the disappearance of classes, the state and religion would leave the historical stage. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based account of how Marx and Engels linked religion, class struggle and the state, written for a Chinese journal on science and atheism.
quoteEn: The roots behind the marriage of religion with politics and war lie not in heaven but on earth.
quoteZh: 宗教与政治、战争联姻背后的根源不是在天上，而是在人间

t: An outline of the atheist thought in the Guanzi chapter "Neiye"
zh: 《管子˙内业》无神论思想举要
paras: Lu Minglun asks what atheist thinking can be found in "Neiye" (Inward Training), a chapter of the ancient Chinese compendium Guanzi. Lu argues that the chapter, a representative work of the Daoist current of the Jixia Academy in the Warring States period, built a fairly systematic outlook whose account of matter and of life carries a distinct atheist consciousness and is an early and original contribution.

The article has four parts. The first examines how the chapter denies that ghosts and spirits have a ruling will. The second looks at how it affirms human subjectivity, in knowledge and in personal growth. The third turns to its exploration of the mechanisms of life, including health and longevity. A short conclusion assesses the chapter's place in the history of Chinese thought. Lu sets the discussion against Shang-dynasty belief in a personified Lord on High and the Zhou sense of a heavenly mandate.

Lu's central claim is that "Neiye" takes refined qi (jingqi) as the origin of all things, including human beings, so that "ghosts and spirits" are only a mode of circulation of this qi. On this reading, insight comes from concentrated qi and not from spirits, and divination is dispensable. Statecraft depends on rulers' sound decisions and agriculture on the natural seasons, so the "heaven of will" becomes a "natural heaven". Lu then argues that the chapter makes sagehood the result of cultivating body and mind, with a calm heart and upright posture, and not a divine endowment. The same logic governs health: longevity follows from preserving qi, from controlling emotions and from relaxed, undistracted practice, so life span lies with the person and not with the gods. Lu cites Marx's remark that atheism affirms human existence through the negation of God.

Lu concludes that "Neiye" elevates the human and lowers the divine, and had an enlightening effect. Lu concedes that it was a product of its age, that its theory is not fully consistent (it does not clearly separate matter from mental activity) and that its ideas on life-nurturing remain partly idealised. Lu calls on contemporary philosophers to mine such ancient texts for atheist ideas and develop them creatively for the needs of the new era, in service of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you are interested in early Chinese materialist and atheist thought, or in how Chinese scholars present classical Daoist texts in an atheist framework.
quoteEn: "Neiye" lowers the divine and raises the human, strives to free people from superstitious thinking and urges them to exercise their subjective initiative and pursue their own worth, and in this it has the merit of being a pioneer.
quoteZh: 《内业》抑神仰人，努力把人们从迷信的思想里解放出来，倡导人积极主动地发挥主观能动性，追求自身价值，这一点是具有先发之功的。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central slogan of Chinese Communist Party discourse, prominent since the 18th Party Congress (2012), referring to restoring China's national strength and international standing.
A slogan introduced by Xi Jinping in 2012, equated with the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
In the Guanzi, a fine, subtle form of qi regarded as the origin of all things and the basis of life and intelligence.
An academy in the state of Qi in the Warring States period that gathered scholars of many schools and is associated with the "hundred schools of thought" debates.

t: The formation and development of Marx and Engels's critique of religion and its scientific transcendence of the bourgeois view of religion
zh: 马克思恩格斯宗教批判思想的形成发展及其对资产阶级宗教观的科学超越
paras: Meng Fei and Yuan Xiaomin ask how Marx and Engels's critique of religion took shape and why it should count as a scientific advance over bourgeois views of religion. They argue that the critique grew out of the founding of dialectical and historical materialism, takes the material conditions of life as the basis for understanding religion, and supplies a method for practical religious work in different countries.

The article has three main parts. The first traces Marx and Engels's path from theism to atheism, from humanist to social psychology, and from economic reality to historical materialism. The second turns to Engels's later years, covering Anti-Dühring and Dialectics of Nature. The third sets out three ways in which the critique goes beyond bourgeois thinking about religion, and a short conclusion follows.

In the authors' account, Marx moved from Hegel through Bruno Bauer and Feuerbach, breaking with Bauer in On the Jewish Question and with Feuerbach in the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. Feuerbach, they say, traced religion to alienated human nature but treated the human being as abstract and isolated, whereas Marx and Engels start from economic relations and class society. The authors argue that this yields three claims. Religion is an alienated fantasy and a special form of ideology. Its social roots lie in conditions human beings cannot master, and religious struggles are in essence struggles for political power between classes. It will wither away as science advances and as private ownership of the means of production is abolished and production is planned. They credit Engels with linking religion to the natural sciences, criticising pseudo-science and rejecting Dühring's call to ban religion in a future society.

The authors conclude that the critique was an indispensable step in making the Marxist view of religion scientific. They draw a practical lesson from Engels: religion should be guided appropriately rather than prohibited, and freedom of religious belief is defended. They call for Marxist religious studies in the new era to draw on this body of thought and, in light of China's national conditions and the specific realities of religion in China, to build a sinicised Marxist study of religion. Read the original if you want a compact survey, from a Chinese Marxist perspective, of how Marx and Engels's views on religion developed and how they are applied to religious work in China today.
quoteEn: Marx and Engels's critique of religion is a scientific understanding of religion: it explores the truth of "this world" on the basis of historical materialism and seeks, from a realistic standpoint, a real path to human emancipation.
quoteZh: 马克思恩格斯宗教批判思想是对宗教的科学认识，是立足唯物史观探索“此岸世界”的真理，是从现实角度寻求人类解放现实的道路

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory that material production and social relations determine historical development and forms of consciousness, including religion.
The term used in China for the Party and state's management of and policy towards religious affairs and believers.
The body of Marxist views on the nature, origins, functions and eventual disappearance of religion, which Chinese scholarship treats as a component of Marxism.

glossary.zh: 中国化的马克思主义宗教学
glossary.explanation: A call to develop the Marxist study of religion in a form adapted to Chinese conditions, in line with the broader project of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context.

t: On the theoretical construction of Marxist religious studies
zh: 关于马克思主义宗教学理论建设的有关问题
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论)
paras: Responding to Xi Jinping's call at the 2021 National Conference on Religious Work to "strengthen the disciplinary construction of Marxist religious studies", Lü asks what that discipline is and how it relates to the "Marxist view of religion". The author argues that the two concepts share the same content and differ only in register. Marxist religious studies is, in Lü's view, a scientific and fully formed discipline, and efforts to deny it or fold it into Western religious studies are misguided.

The article has three parts. The first defends the scientific status of Marxist religious studies, drawing on Ren Jiyu's 1979 definition and on the debates in two textbooks, the General Theory of Religious Studies and its New Edition. The second traces how the "Marxist view of religion" became an ideological concept in the 1990s, in the context of Xinjiang. The third examines the discipline system and proposes a structure for it.

Lü rejects the textbooks' claim that Marx and Engels offered only a "view" of religion, not a "study". In Lü's account, their criteria of independence and systematicness are flawed: a discipline is defined by the quality of its principles, methods and objective laws, not by quantity. Marxist religious studies, following Ren, is a science of the laws of religion's emergence, development and eventual disappearance, grounded in dialectical and historical materialism and in scientific atheism. Lü holds that the "Marxist view of religion" arose from 1990s propaganda and education work after the 1990 Baren unrest and was later stretched to absorb Western religious studies and the "religious culture" theory. Lü further argues that Western religious studies has no general discipline and no real sub-disciplines. Comparative religion, the philosophy of religion and the sociology of religion are described as theology repackaged or as branches of other fields. The author reads the proliferation of such sub-disciplines, including "Marxist" versions of them, as religious infiltration of philosophy and the social sciences.

Lü proposes building on the discipline that has actually taken shape over 60 years and dropping "general religious research" as a separate field. Three areas would be strengthened: Marxist religious theory, scientific atheism, and the theory and policy of proletarian parties' religious work, each with a detailed list of sub-topics. Read the original if you want a detailed, polemical statement of one position in Chinese debates over Marxist religious studies, including its account of the 1990s background and its proposed disciplinary framework.
quoteEn: Marxist religious studies belongs to Marxism by nature, but belongs to religious studies in disciplinary classification.
quoteZh: 马克思主义宗教学性质上属于马克思主义，但学科分类上属于宗教学。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist classics' basic stance on religion, used mainly in Party-cadre and ideological education. The article argues it became an ideologically loaded concept in the 1990s.
The academic discipline studying religion from a Marxist standpoint. In China it is associated with Ren Jiyu and Mao Zedong's 1963 directive to strengthen religious research.
A Marxist atheist worldview grounded in historical and dialectical materialism, taught and researched as a field in China.
A view in Chinese scholarship that treats religion as a cultural phenomenon. The author criticises it as a non-Marxist doctrine.
A periodic high-level Party meeting setting policy on religious affairs. The 2021 meeting called for strengthening Marxist religious studies.

t: The threefold basis for the principle that religious activities must not interfere in social life, and how to put it into practice
zh: 宗教活动不得干涉社会生活的三重依据及践行理路
source: Science and Atheism (《科学与无神论》)
paras: Yang and Qian take up a line from Xi Jinping's speech at the National Conference on Religious Work (December 2021): "religious activities must not interfere in education, the judiciary, administrative functions and social life." They note that religion's willingness to engage in society has grown in recent years, with more frequent conflicts and group incidents involving religious demands. Their thesis is that the principle rests on a theoretical basis, an institutional basis and a practical basis, and that it needs further institutional and social measures to be carried out.

The article has four parts. It first derives the principle from Marxist theory, then from Party policy documents and state law since reform and opening up. The third part draws on the authors' own collection of public-opinion cases, gathered with monitoring software using Buddhism, Islam and Christianity as keywords. The last part sets out three practical routes.

On theory, the authors argue that Marxist views of religion clash with the nature of modern social life in three ways: the illusory nature of religion against the practical character of social life, the private nature of faith against the public nature of social life, and religious mysticism against modern rationality. They hold that religion must therefore stay in the private sphere. On practice, they describe three problems: religious infiltration of politics, education, culture and daily life; the disorderly expansion of house churches, which they say disrupts rural kinship ties and campus life; and the entanglement of ethnic and religious issues. In their account this entanglement produces biased law enforcement in civil disputes and lets extremist, terrorist and separatist forces use religion, citing the 2009 and 2014 violent incidents in Urumqi.

For implementation, Yang and Qian call for the principle to be written consistently into Party documents and laws, with new departmental rules such as norms for managing house churches, an early-warning and response system for religion-related public opinion, and revision of religious doctrines and regulations. They also propose greater practical care for the people, tailored to why people turn to religion, so that Party and government care comes before religious care. They further want the governance pattern of Party leadership, government management, social coordination and religious self-discipline strengthened, with interdisciplinary research and better-trained officials. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholarly journal on science and atheism justifies limits on religious activity in public life, with examples of the cases it cites.
quoteEn: Therefore, religious activities must be confined to the sphere of private life and must not be allowed to permeate and interfere in public social life.
quoteZh: 因此，必须将宗教活动限制在私人生活领域，不能任其渗透和干涉社会公共生活。

glossary.explanation: A periodic high-level Party meeting that sets the direction of religious policy. Xi Jinping spoke at the 2016 and 2021 sessions.
Protestant congregations that meet outside the officially registered "Three-Self" churches. The authors treat their unregistered status as a governance problem.
