glossary.explanation: The Chinese rendering of the Western term "cult", used in Chinese scholarship for groups regarded as harmful or deviant. It is closely tied in Chinese usage to the category of "evil cults" (xiéjiào).
A neutral scholarly label in the sociology of religion for recently emerged religious groups, used as an alternative to the term "cult".
A phrase from William James's 1902 definition of religious life, which sociologists of religion use to analyse new religions without judging their truth or harmfulness.
Non-religious groups, such as ICSA, that warn the public about cults and help people harmed by them, as distinct from evangelical Christian counter-cult groups.

t: The basic pattern and development trends of research on "cults" in graduate training
st: A bibliometric analysis of doctoral and master's theses, 1990–2020
zh: 研究生培养中对邪教问题研究的基本格局和发展趋势
zhSub: 基于博硕士学位论文的计量分析（1990—2020年）
paras: Cheng and Li ask how research on xiejiao (rendered "cults" in official English usage) has been distributed within China's graduate education between 1990 and 2020, and where it is heading. Using bibliometric and text analysis, they argue that the field is geographically concentrated, institutionally scattered, thinly staffed and shaped by political events. They frame the study as a response to Xi Jinping's call at the 2021 national religious work conference to build a research force in Marxist religious studies.

The sample is 205 doctoral and master's theses (32 doctoral, 121 academic master's, 52 professional master's) drawn from the CNKI and Wanfang databases. The authors analyse them by region, institution, discipline, supervisors and teacher–student lineages, and by five research perspectives: the history of secret sects and "hui dao men"; specific groups; law and policy on prevention and punishment; theoretical study of cults; and the relation to overseas new religions. They also trace changes by decade and degree type.

The authors report that Beijing produced 28% of theses, nearly three times Shanghai's share. Output surged after the 1999 Falun Gong incident and the founding of the China Anti-Cult Association (2000), then declined, which they read as academic research responding quickly to current events and public opinion. Only about 3.5% of institutions sustained a research team, and 92% of supervisors guided just one thesis. Lineages rarely go beyond two generations, mainly because graduates move into other work. The authors also find that the leading institution has shifted from Renmin University and Shandong University to the People's Public Security University of China, and that law is becoming the dominant discipline, partly because of the expansion of professional degrees.

Cheng and Li conclude that the field lacks a stable team and a developed academic lineage, which they say hinders its institutionalisation. They propose treating the topic as a priority, with special state-funded graduate quotas and international exchange. They also call for stronger supervisor training, policy and funding support for universities and institutes, and a multidisciplinary collaboration network with common core courses. Read the original if you want detailed data on how Chinese universities have trained researchers on this topic, or on how state priorities shape that research.
quoteEn: If teacher–student lineages are simple, it is hard for a school of thought to form, and the discipline's development can hardly continue.
quoteZh: 师承关系简单则难成某一学派，学科的发展很难延续。

glossary.explanation: The official Chinese term for religious or quasi-religious groups the state deems illegal and harmful. It is applied to groups such as Falun Gong and Almighty God, and its scope is contested outside China.
A term for folk secret societies and sects, used in the early People's Republic to describe what is now called xiejiao.

t: Problems in the study of American atheism and proposed remedies
zh: 陈发扬：美国无神论研究存在的问题及对策
paras: Chen Fayang asks why China needs to study atheism in the United States and what is wrong with the existing research. The article argues that sharpening ideological struggle between China and the United States makes systematic study of American atheism necessary, and that current work is too thin in researchers, content, methods and output. Chen presents the study of American atheism as a way to "know oneself and know the enemy" in that struggle.

The article has four parts. It first sets out the rationale, citing recent US legislation on Uyghurs, Tibet and Hong Kong, which Chen describes as ideological interference in China's internal affairs. It then surveys Chinese and foreign scholarship on the origins, definitions and classifications of atheism, on modern figures such as Einstein, and on contemporary American atheists' experiences. It then lists four weaknesses and ends with four matching recommendations.

Chen reads American atheists' position as evidence about US ideology. The article cites estimates that atheists are 2% to 14% of the population, and a 2007 Gallup poll in which 53% of respondents would not vote for an atheist president. From this Chen concludes that American claims about freedom and democracy do not hold for atheists. The surveyed studies include work on stigma, marginalisation and the psychological strain of atheists, including atheists of colour. Chen finds few Chinese specialists, many of whom only translate. Chen also doubts that foreign researchers are objective and notes that the research gives little attention to atheism's history since the founding of the US or to the influence of American Marxists. It relies on texts rather than surveys or interviews, and it has produced no monographs.

Chen calls for specialised conferences and graduate and postdoctoral research directions to draw in more scholars. The article also asks for work on the historical development of American atheism and its schools, and on its relations with American Marxists. It proposes field interviews and questionnaires among workers, farmers, business owners and students, plus theories borrowed from American researchers, such as minority stress theory. Chen also wants analysis of atheists' difficulties, forecasts of trends, and monographs and reports. Read the original if you want a Chinese view of how American atheism is studied, with many cited authors, and of why it is tied to ideological security.
quoteEn: In sum, the increasingly fierce ideological struggle between China and the United States requires us to strengthen research on American atheism.
quoteZh: 总之，中美日益激烈的意识形态斗争要求我们加强对美国无神论的研究。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Chinese Party-state discourse for protecting the dominance of Marxism and Party-led ideas against hostile ideological influence, especially from abroad.

t: Causes, results, value: a three-dimensional reading of Engels's late study of Christianity
zh: 起因·成果·价值：恩格斯晚年基督教研究的三维解读
paras: Why did Engels, in his last years, turn to early Christianity, and what did the turn yield? Writing in Science and Atheism in 2022, Yan Yu argues that the decisive cause was the practical needs of the socialist movement, which runs as a single thread through the whole enterprise. The article places this argument within the National Conference on Religious Work of December 2021 and the call for the sinicization of religion.

The article is organised in three parts: causes, results and value. On causes, it discusses Engels's earlier critique of religion, the death of Bruno Bauer in 1882, and the struggles of the 1890s within the labour movement. On results, it examines three works, Bruno Bauer and Early Christianity, The Book of Revelation and On the History of Early Christianity, under three headings: early Christianity compared with socialism, the nature and conditions of religious prophecy, and the formation of a world religion. The value of this work is then assessed for content, method and practice.

Yan holds that Engels's comparison of early Christianity with socialism served to defend scientific socialism against Fabianism, reformism, the abuse of 'materialism' as a slogan by the Social Democratic 'Young' faction, and religious-style deception inside socialist currents. Both movements, in Yan's account, arose among the oppressed, but Christian deliverance lies in a beyond, while socialism changes the material world through practice. Engels is also read as tracing prophecy to pseudonymous authorship and the authority of its real authors, and as explaining Christianity's rise through the Roman Empire's dissolution of national religions, the doctrine of redemption through Christ's sacrifice and simplified ritual. Methodologically, Yan credits Engels with moving from religion in general to specific religions and stages, grounded in historical sources.

Yan concludes that Engels's late work completed Marxist theory of religion in both thought and practice. The article connects this to present policy: it calls for using Marxist theory of religion to guide religious work, to keep the sinicization of religion and the adaptation of religion to socialist society, and to guard against Western use of religion to divide China. Read the original if you study Marxist theory of religion, Engels's late writings, or how Chinese scholars link classical texts to current religious policy.
quoteEn: Specific, stage-by-stage study and critique of particular religions under the guidance of the materialist conception of history is the innovative method of Engels's late study of Christianity.
quoteZh: 在唯物史观指导下对具体宗教分阶段进行具体的研究和批判是恩格斯晚年基督教研究的创新方法。

glossary.explanation: A policy line stressing that religions in China should adapt to Chinese culture and conditions and be led by Chinese institutions. It has been emphasised in Party religious policy under Xi Jinping.
A high-level Party and state meeting setting policy on religious affairs. The one cited here was held in December 2021, with a speech by Xi Jinping.
The body of Marxist writing and doctrine on religion's origins, nature and decline, treated in China as an official component of Marxism and a basis for religious policy.

t: A struggle of nation and class hidden beneath religious appearances
st: Marx's critique of Bauer on the Jewish question
zh: 隐藏在宗教表象下的民族与阶级之争
zhSub: 马克思对鲍威尔关于犹太人问题的批判
paras: This article, published in the journal Science and Atheism (2022, no. 2), re-reads Marx's "On the Jewish Question" (1844) as a reply to Bruno Bauer's 1842 essays. Wang argues that the dispute only appears to be about Judaism versus Christianity. In Wang's reading it is really a dispute over whether nation or class offers the "way out" for human beings, and Marx's critique "substitutes" a class perspective for nationalism.

The author sets the debate in 1840s Germany, where nationalism and anti-Semitism were growing. The article has three parts: Bauer's view that "privilege" is the key to the Jewish question; Marx's view that the "Jewish spirit" is the key; and a comparison of the national and class solutions. Wang also draws on theories of the origins of the modern nation, including Benedict Anderson's Imagined Communities, and notes that some foreign scholars cite the text to portray the young Marx as anti-Semitic.

According to Wang, Bauer treats Jewish exclusiveness, rooted in religious law, as a "religious privilege" and a "civil privilege" (above all moneylending). Bauer concludes that Jews must give up their religion and national particularity and merge into the new nation-state. Marx replies that after political emancipation religion is a private matter in civil society, so Jews need not abandon their faith to become citizens. The real source of oppression is the worldly "Jewish spirit", meaning practical need, egoism and the worship of money, which Marx finds to be the principle of civil society as a whole. Wang argues that Jews were therefore not opposed to the nation-state but helped drive its formation, and that political emancipation, resting on bourgeois egoism, cannot emancipate them.

Wang concludes that, for Marx, the Jewish question can be resolved only by abolishing private property through the proletariat's class struggle, with philosophy and the proletariat joined together. The article then turns to the present. Wang says that because China remains in the primary stage of socialism, the Party must take religious questions seriously. Wang calls for vigilance against foreign forces that invoke religious freedom and narrow nationalism, and for linking the proletariat's historical mission to the Chinese Dream and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, on the basis of the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese journal on religion and atheism interprets Marx's early writings on nationalism, religion and class, and applies them to contemporary policy.
quoteEn: Therefore, Marx's critique of Bauer is in essence a replacement of nationalism by the concept of class.
quoteZh: 因此，马克思对鲍威尔的批判，实质上是用阶级观念取代民族主义。

glossary.explanation: The official Party thesis that China is still at an early, long-lasting stage of building socialism, with underdeveloped productive forces. It is used to justify the country's current policies and priorities.
A slogan, associated with Xi Jinping, calling for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
A slogan promoted by Xi Jinping from 2012, presenting national rejuvenation, prosperity and strength as a shared goal.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's long-term goal of restoring China to national strength and international standing, closely tied to the Chinese Dream.

t: Marxist research should treat the study of religion as a discipline equal in importance to philosophy
zh: 马克思主义研究应把宗教学作为和哲学 同等重要的学科
paras: Li Shen asks why Marxist research should give the Marxist study of religion (Marxist religious studies) the same standing as Marxist philosophy. The article, published in the journal Science and Atheism in 2022, argues that the two are not separate fields. Marxist philosophy grew directly out of German classical philosophy, which Li describes as in effect Germany's religious studies of the day, so that Marxist philosophy is also Marxist religious studies.

The article proceeds in four parts. It first examines German classical philosophy as a critique of religion, taking in Kant, Hegel, Strauss, Bauer and Feuerbach. It then turns to Marx's critique of Hegel and the Young Hegelians, and to Marx and Engels's critique of Feuerbach, drawing on texts such as the Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right: Introduction, The German Ideology, the Theses on Feuerbach and Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy. A final part draws out the relation between Marxist philosophy and Marxist religious studies.

Li contends that many of the best-known philosophical statements by Marx and Engels were first statements about religion. Examples are "man makes religion", religion as "the opium of the people", and Engels's basic question of the relation of thinking to being, which Li reads as first of all a question about religion, since it arises from ideas of soul and the creation of the world. In Li's account, German classical philosophy still kept "a religious tail", with Kant's moral God, Hegel's absolute idea and Feuerbach's religion of love. Marx and Engels therefore had to criticise it, moving from criticising heaven to criticising earth. They also criticised Feuerbach for neglecting revolutionary practice and for treating the human essence as an abstraction rather than the ensemble of social relations. Li holds that historical and dialectical materialism were thus achievements in religious studies as well as in philosophy.

Li concludes that Marxist philosophy and Marxist religious studies share one root and one theoretical foundation, and that understanding the former requires studying religion in depth. He cites Ren Jiyu's view that Marx's founders made religious studies a science. Li says Marxist religious studies has long been absorbed into philosophy or not recognised, and so has been underdeveloped in China. He notes that the national religious work conference of December 2021 called for strengthening the discipline, and calls on Marxist research to give it equal weight with philosophy. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese specialist in Marxist religious studies makes the case for the discipline's standing, through a reading of Marx and Engels's texts on religion.
quoteEn: Therefore, to understand Marxist philosophy in depth, one must understand Marxist religious studies in depth, and grasp Marx and Engels's study and critique of religion.
quoteZh: 因此，要深入理解马克思主义的哲学，就必须深入理解马克思主义的宗教学，理解马克思恩格斯对宗教的研究和批判。

glossary.explanation: The study of religion on the basis of dialectical and historical materialism, a field with an established place in Chinese academia. Ren Jiyu is regarded as one of its founders in China.
The tradition of Kant, Fichte, Schelling, Hegel and Feuerbach, which Marxist theory names as one of the direct sources of Marxism.
A group of Hegel's followers, including Strauss, Bauer and Stirner, who stressed his dialectic and criticised religion and the state. Marx and Engels belonged to it early on before breaking with it.

t: Fully implementing the Party's theory of religious work in the new era
zh: 全面贯彻新时代党的宗教工作理论
paras: This article, published in Studies on Marxism in late 2021, responds to the National Conference on Religious Work of December 2021, which formally put forward the "Party's theory of religious work in the new era". Zhu Xiaoming argues that scholars must study and apply this theory in full, grasping its core meaning, its spirit and its practical demands, and use it to strengthen the discipline of Marxist religious studies.

The article has three parts. The first places the theory in relation to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, to the Party's earlier theory of religion, and to the Marxist view of religion. The second sets out the "nine musts" and eight issues that Zhu says need correct handling. The third reviews the history and present state of Marxist religious studies in China, from Ren Jiyu's work in the 1980s to recent textbooks and seminars.

Zhu's central claim is that the theory combines individual freedom of religious belief with the Party and government's social-level education, management and guidance. "Fully" means guarding against loosening the latter or neglecting the former. Zhu distinguishes the essence of religion (illusory) from the essence of religious work (mass work), and holds that neither claim cancels the other. Zhu also separates religion's individual character, a private choice, from its social character as organised groups subject to law. Calls to "let go" of religion are said to rest on ignoring the second. Zhu presents sinicisation of religion and rule-of-law management as paired levers, and describes foreign religious infiltration and Western use of the "religion card" as risks. The article also treats atheism and theism as a contest in the ideological sphere. It asks Party members to uphold and actively propagate Marxist atheism, answers three objections to such propaganda, and says it should not target religious believers or take place in religious venues.

Zhu concludes that Marxist religious studies must be built on theory, drawing on Ren Jiyu's tradition. The author notes a drift towards theologisation and Westernisation in the 1990s and says recent conferences, textbooks and courses show renewal. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how a Party-affiliated scholar of atheism interprets the 2021 religious work line, including its treatment of atheist propaganda and Marxist religious studies.
quoteEn: The core meaning and spirit of the Party's theory of religious work in the new era is to combine freedom of religious belief at the individual level, that is, respecting and protecting every citizen's freedom to believe, not to believe and to propagate atheism, with education, management and guidance by the Party and government at the social level, which hold the direction and safeguard the overall situation.
quoteZh: 新时代党的宗教工作理论的核心要义和精神实质，是个人层面上的宗教信仰自由，即尊重和保护每一个公民都有信教、不信教和宣传无神论的自由，与社会层面上党和政府把握方向、维护大局的教育、管理、引导相结合。

glossary.explanation: A summary of the Party's religious work principles set out by Xi Jinping at the December 2021 National Conference on Religious Work. It covers leadership, theory, basic policy, sinicisation of religion, unity of believers, rule of law and related points.
Official policy direction that religions in China should adapt to Chinese society and culture and be guided by socialist core values.
The atheist position grounded in dialectical and historical materialism. Party members are required to uphold it, and the article argues for its active propagation.

t: A study of the Anti-Christian Movement of the 1920s
zh: 1920年代非基督教运动研究
paras: Sun Qian examines the Anti-Christian Movement that broke out in 1922 and argues that it was, in essence, a patriotic anti-imperialist mass movement launched and led by the early Chinese Communist Party. In the author's account, Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao, Yun Daiying and other early Communists led the anti-Christian, anti-religion and education-rights movements. The article holds that this leadership prepared the Party, in theory and in practice, for handling religious questions later.

The article has two parts. The first sets out why the movement should be read as Party-led: how the Party organised young people through the Socialist Youth League, how the movement served the Party's anti-imperialist and anti-feudal aims, and how Marxism served as its intellectual weapon. The second part draws lessons for the present, on Party leadership of youth, on religious work in relation to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and on developing a religious theory with Chinese characteristics. Sun draws on Party congress resolutions, League documents and writings by early Communist leaders.

Sun argues that the target was never Christianity alone. Citing the Party's second and third congresses (1922, 1923), Sun shows that the Party treated the churches as a pioneer of imperialist economic, political and spiritual aggression, and used the campaign to mobilise patriotic youth. Early Communists also applied a historical-materialist view of religion, tracing its social roots and its dependence on the economic base. They judged its social role dialectically and rejected its promotion. They also developed ideas of freedom of belief, which includes freedom not to believe, separation of religion and education, and self-run Chinese churches. Sun concedes that excessive sharpness and a failure to distinguish ordinary believers from reactionary clergy initially narrowed the movement, but says the Party soon corrected this and sought a united front that would seek common ground on anti-imperialism while setting aside differences of belief.

Sun concludes that the movement still offers guidance under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The author calls for strengthening Party leadership over youth and for arming students with Marxist religious theory in university courses. Religious work, Sun says, should serve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, national security and ideological security. The author also proposes upholding and developing socialist religious theory with Chinese characteristics, including the "five characteristics" of religious questions. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated journal in 2022 presents the 1920s anti-Christian campaign as a precedent for current religious policy.
quoteEn: The aim of the Anti-Christian Movement was not simply to oppose Christianity, but to use it as a way of broad anti-imperialist revolutionary mobilisation, uniting patriotic youth to accomplish the historic task of opposing imperialism and feudalism.
quoteZh: 非基督教运动的目的不是单纯反基督教，而是通过这种方式进行广泛的反帝国主义革命动员，团结广大爱国青年共同完成反帝反封建的历史任务。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal, closely associated with Xi Jinping's slogan of the Chinese Dream. It denotes restoring China's national strength and international standing.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义宗教理论
glossary.pinyin: Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì zōngjiào lǐlùn
glossary.en: socialist religious theory with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: The Party's official body of thought on religion. It rests on freedom of religious belief, independent self-run religious bodies, and guiding religion to adapt to socialist society.
A Party strategy of building alliances with non-Party groups, here with religious circles, to pursue shared political aims.
The Communist youth organisation founded in 1920–22, a predecessor of the Communist Youth League. The article calls it the Party's reserve force and preparatory school.

t: In defence of atheism
st: From the perspective of Kai Nielsen
zh: 为无神论辩护
zhSub: 基于凯·尼尔森的视角
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2022 no. 1
paras: Yang Lei presents the case for atheism made by Kai Nielsen (1926–2021), a Canadian Marxist philosopher and contemporary advocate of atheism. The article asks how Nielsen defends atheism in a secularising but still religiously confused culture. Yang's answer is that Nielsen offers a coherent philosophical case: the concept of God is incoherent, morality does not rest on belief in God, and religion works as an ideology that should be shaken off.

The article opens with Nielsen's biography (a vague Protestant upbringing, conversion to Catholicism, later study of anthropology and philosophy) and his main works on religion. These include Contemporary Critiques of Religion, An Introduction to the Philosophy of Religion, Atheism & Philosophy and God and the Grounding of Morality. It then draws mainly on the essay collection Atheism & Philosophy and is organised in three sections, followed by a short closing discussion. The sections cover the falsity of the concept of God, the claim that morality cannot be built on faith in God, and escape from the spell of religious ideology.

In the first section Yang reports Nielsen's argument that statements such as 'the world has an infinite, eternal creator' can be neither verified nor falsified, so they are not factual statements and the core of theistic religion is incoherent. Yang adds that, for Nielsen, revelation and religious experience are unreliable. Nielsen also asks why one authority should be accepted rather than another, and he rejects agnosticism as well as theism. In the second section, the good must be understood independently of God. Power and creative ability do not show goodness, and cruelty remains wrong even if God commands it. Morality exists to adjudicate fairly between human interests and needs. The third section treats religion as an ideology that, in Nielsen's view, fosters submission and defers hope to heaven. Yang links this to Marx's critique of religion and to d'Holbach, and cites Nielsen's remark that the richer our concept of God, the poorer our concept of man.

Yang concludes that, for Nielsen, morality is independent of religion and people can find meaning in love, friendship, knowledge and self-respect without God. Yang concedes that parts of the collection sound somewhat positivist and empiricist. Even so, Yang holds that Nielsen's philosophical scrutiny of religious belief deepens understanding of atheism and of the nature of faith. Yang ends by arguing that only the scientific atheism of Marxism can dispel religious superstition and reveal the world's materiality and objective laws. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-academic introduction to Nielsen's philosophy of religion and to how his arguments are used to support scientific atheism.
quoteEn: Nielsen maintains that morality is independent of religion and cannot be founded on religion.
quoteZh: 尼尔森主张道德独立于宗教，道德不能以宗教为基础。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist approach to atheism taught and researched in China. It treats religion as a social and historical phenomenon and bases the rejection of religious belief on a materialist worldview.

t: "Explaining religion through history": Ren Jiyu's understanding of historical materialism and its use in the study of religion
zh: “用历史说明宗教”
zhSub: 任继愈对唯物史观的理解及其在宗教研究中的运用
paras: Kong Fanxi examines how the philosopher and religion scholar Ren Jiyu (1916–2009) understood historical materialism and applied it to religion. The article argues that Ren's guiding principle, "explaining religion through history" rather than history through religion, grew out of his turn to Marxism after 1949. Kong holds that this principle laid the foundation for a Marxist study of religion in China.

The article begins with Ren's intellectual path: his study of the classics, his part in thought reform and land reform, and his 1956 break with Confucianism. It then looks at three fields of Ren's work: Buddhism (the Collected Essays on Han–Tang Buddhist Thought and the three-volume History of Chinese Buddhism), Daoism, with Ren's changing readings of Laozi, and Confucianism, which Ren treated as a religion. A short conclusion pulls these together.

On Buddhism, Kong reports that Ren set three principles: religious questions must be placed on a real social footing, ideas must not be treated in isolation, and individual figures must not be overstated against the whole historical process. Applying the base–superstructure relationship, Ren read Buddhism's fortunes as tracking Chinese feudal society. Doctrines that suited the economic base, such as Chan and Tiantai, thrived, while the Faxiang school, transplanted unaltered from India, withered. His Laozi research shows the difficulty of applying the theory. Ren moved from calling Laozi materialist to calling him idealist, and then rejected both labels as imposed later. He drew the lesson that historical materialism means concrete analysis, faithful to what ancients left unclear, and attentive to regional culture such as that of Chu. On Confucianism, Ren derived its religious character from the features of Chinese feudal society. He held that Confucian thought was reworked twice, under the Han and the Song–Ming. He also held that Neo-Confucianism matched the "essence" of religion, the relation between humans and the divine, as well as its outward forms, which he said included Confucius as founder and the doctrine of "heaven, earth, ruler, parents, teacher".

Kong concludes that Ren's understanding deepened through concrete research. Kong presents it as a model for combining Marxism's basic principles with fine traditional Chinese culture and for advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context. It also points the way, Kong says, toward a Marxist discipline of religious studies with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a detailed account of Ren Jiyu's Marxist methods in Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian studies, or of how Chinese scholars assess the origins of Marxist religious studies.
quoteEn: We do not use religion to explain history; we use history to explain religion.
quoteZh: 我们不是用宗教说明历史，而是用历史说明宗教。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist concept in which the economic base of society determines its political and ideological superstructure, which in turn acts back on the base. Ren used it to explain how religions develop.

t: Engels's critique and transcendence of Feuerbach's view of religion
zh: 恩格斯对费尔巴哈宗教观的批判与超越
paras: Zhao Gaiping and Wang Fan ask how Engels, in criticising Feuerbach, developed a historical-materialist view of religion. They argue that Engels's critique set out the nature, origin, development and eventual disappearance of religion from the standpoint of historical materialism. In their account, this sublated and went beyond Feuerbach and marked the maturity of Marxist religious theory.

The article follows Engels's moves in four sections, drawing mainly on Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, Anti-Dühring and The German Ideology. It first credits Feuerbach with turning religion's "inverted world outlook" from God-centred to human-centred. It then treats Engels's critique of Feuerbach's "new religion of love", of the claim that religious change determines history, and of Feuerbach's inability to find a way to remove religion. A short conclusion draws implications for religious work in China today.

The authors argue that Engels praised Feuerbach for showing that God is a projection of alienated human essence, but called him a materialist "below" and an idealist "above". Feuerbach's "abstract man" and religion of love, they say, ignore class society and the social relations of production. Engels replaced this with real individuals acting in history. He also reversed Feuerbach's claim that religious change drives history: using the histories of religion in general and of Christianity in particular, the authors show religion shifting with social conditions and class struggle. Criticism of heaven must therefore become criticism of earth, and theology must give way to politics.

On the disappearance of religion, the authors hold that it will fade only when real social relations stop confronting people as alien forces. They list three conditions drawn from Engels: public ownership of the means of production, a great development of productive forces, and a higher ideological and cultural level among the masses. It cannot be abolished by administrative order. They add that China is in the primary stage of socialism, so religion will long persist. They call for developing the economy, raising cultural levels, managing religion by law, guarding against illegal religious activity and pursuing the sinicization of religion. Read the original if you want a close Chinese reading of Engels's texts on Feuerbach and religion, and the policy conclusions drawn from them.
quoteEn: The facts show that it is not changes in religion that determine social history; on the contrary, it is social history that determines changes in religion.
quoteZh: 事实证明，并不是宗教的变迁决定社会历史，而恰恰是社会历史决定宗教变迁。

glossary.explanation: The official Chinese Communist Party characterisation of China's present development stage, formalised in the 1980s. It is said to last a long time and to shape policy in areas including religion.
An official policy direction that religions in China should adapt to Chinese culture and to socialist society, under Party guidance.
The Chinese rendering of Hegel's Aufhebung: to negate something while preserving and raising its valid elements.

t: Several issues in building Marxist religious studies
zh: 马克思主义宗教学建设若干问题
paras: This text is a speech by Jia Runguo, published in Science and Atheism (2022, no. 1), given at a seminar co-hosted by the Institute of World Religions, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, and the Chinese Society for the Study of Religion. Jia presents the seminar as a sign of a high degree of theoretical awareness about advancing Marxist religious studies in the new era, and offers five basic reflections on how the field should be built.

The speech moves through five headings: the essence of Marxist religious studies, its distinctive character, its foundations, the key to building it, and the way to complete it. Jia draws on Marx's 1844 introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, on the history of religious studies in the People's Republic, and on Xi Jinping's 2016 symposium on philosophy and social sciences.

Jia argues that Marxist religious studies is the disciplinary form of the Marxist view of religion, which Jia summarises as five components (religion's essence, origins, forms, functions and policy) and characterises as scientific atheism. Its distinctive character, in Jia's account, is that of a socialist political science of religion, since Marx and Engels' critique of religion led into their critique of politics and economics. Religious studies should therefore observe religion politically and correct what Jia calls tendencies towards theologisation and Westernisation. Jia holds that its basis is the principles of religious studies together with histories of the major religions, and that the two representative current textbooks on the principles of religious studies have diluted the Marxist view of religion, while the Buddhism, Christianity and Islam histories from the early reform era are outdated.

Jia concludes that textbooks are the key lever for building the discipline, academic and discourse systems, because nearly three decades of research progress have not been matched in teaching materials. Jia proposes a nationally organised, centrally funded five-tier textbook system: Marxist views of religion, Marxist atheism and principles; histories of the major religions and of atheism; critiques of Chinese and foreign theology and Western religious theory; general histories of Chinese and world religion; and religious anthropology, sociology, psychology and politics. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Chinese scholar sets out the political and pedagogical agenda for Marxist religious studies in the new era.
quoteEn: Marxist religious studies means turning the ideas of the Marxist view of religion into systematic scholarship and an academic discipline.
quoteZh: 马克思主义宗教学就是把马克思主义宗教观的思想内容学理化、学科化

glossary.explanation: The set of Marxist propositions on religion's essence, origins, forms, social functions and policy, which official Chinese scholarship treats as the basis of Party religious policy.
The Marxist-materialist form of atheism taught and promoted in China. Jia treats it as the essence of the Marxist view of religion.

glossary.zh: 学科体系、学术体系、话语体系
glossary.pinyin: xuékē tǐxì, xuéshù tǐxì, huàyǔ tǐxì
glossary.literal: discipline system, academic system, discourse system
glossary.explanation: A formula Xi Jinping stressed in 2016 for building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. It covers the disciplinary structure, research and the ways of speaking in a field.

t: The Communist Party of China's experience in guiding religion to adapt to socialist society
zh: 中国共产党引导宗教与社会主义社会相适应的经验研究
paras: Tian Wei and Yang Ping ask how the Communist Party of China has approached its policy of guiding religion to adapt to socialist society, and what lessons can be drawn for religious work in the new era. They argue that this policy reflects a creative application of the Marxist view of religion and a distinctly Chinese method of religious work. The experience, in their account, answers four questions: why religion should be guided, on what requirements, under whose leadership, and by what means.

The article is organised in four parts, each matching one of these questions. It first treats the ideological basis, then the requirements that govern guidance, then Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee, and finally the methods used. The authors support their points with statements by Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping and Jiang Zemin, and with Party documents. These include Central Document No. 19 of 1982 and the 1992 United Front Work Department outline that first stated the formula in full.

The authors argue that the Party's scientific understanding of religion has three elements: its illusory nature and social roots, its eventual withering away as a long process, and its dual social role. From this they conclude that guidance is necessary, that administrative coercion is ruled out, and that guidance is feasible because religion can play a positive role. They say the requirements have been enriched over time. The target of adaptation stresses social progress, the means of guidance ("dao") has gained weight in the new era, and the direction is the sinicisation of religion. Leadership, they write, is secured by attention to religious work, coordinated mechanisms (Party committee leadership, United Front coordination, legal administration by religious affairs departments) and cadre training. Guidance is carried out through political, legal and cultural means. Political means centre on uniting religious figures and believers. Legal means centre on administering religious affairs according to law, which the authors illustrate with a count of regulations and with cases such as extremism, the over-extension of the "halal" concept and the commercialisation of Buddhism and Daoism. Cultural means centre on integrating religious doctrine with Chinese culture and core socialist values.

The authors conclude that guiding religion is a long process of exploration and that the resulting experience is a valuable asset of the Party. They call for continued summing-up of this experience, linked to practice, in order to enrich socialist religious theory with Chinese characteristics and promote high-quality development of religious work. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-line account of how Chinese scholars present the history, rationale and instruments of official religious policy, with dated sources from 1938 to the new era.
quoteEn: Guiding religion to adapt to socialist society is a long process of exploration, and the experience formed in it is a valuable asset of our Party.
quoteZh: 引导宗教与社会主义社会相适应是一个长期探索的过程，在这个过程中形成的相关经验是我们党的宝贵财富

glossary.zh: 引导宗教与社会主义社会相适应
glossary.pinyin: yǐndǎo zōngjiào yǔ shèhuì zhǔyì shèhuì xiāng shìyìng
glossary.en: guiding religion to adapt to socialist society
glossary.explanation: A core principle of Party religious policy, stated in full in a 1992 central document. It was later written into the Party Constitution (2007) and treated as the basic direction of religious work.
The official policy that religions in China should align with Chinese culture, society and Party leadership. It is presented as the direction of guidance in the new era.
The 1982 Party document on the basic viewpoint and policy on religious questions in China's socialist period. It remains a key reference for Party religious policy.
The Party's policy and set of institutions for building alliances with non-Party groups, including religious circles. The United Front Work Department coordinates religious work.
An official slogan for development that stresses quality and efficiency over speed. Here it is applied to religious work.

t: On the atheist character of the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists
zh: 论中国共产党人精神谱系的无神论特色
paras: Written in the year of the Communist Party of China's centenary (2021), this article asks how Marxist atheism shapes what official discourse calls the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists, the series of revolutionary "spirits" that trace back to the founding spirit of the Party. Ding Yu argues that Marxist atheism is the indispensable moral and intellectual ground of this genealogy and the foundation of the Party's mainstream ideology. Understanding this, the author holds, helps keep atheism dominant in the people's thinking.

The article opens with Xi Jinping's centenary speech and the Party's century-long struggle for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It then proceeds through four sections, each linking one feature of the genealogy to atheism: ideals and convictions, the people-centred standpoint, the seeking of truth from facts, and the spirit of struggle. Evidence comes from Xi Jinping's speeches, Mao Zedong's writings and the early revolutionary and Yan'an periods.

Ding contends that firm ideals rest on a thoroughly materialist worldview. In this account, belief in the inevitable victory of socialism is scientific, and a Party member who does not hold to atheism cannot be a consistent materialist and will waver in conviction. Devotion to the people is distinguished from religious devotion: believers dedicate themselves to God, while Communists dedicate themselves to the people. Ding also presents seeking truth from facts as an atheist way of thinking, citing the Party's campaigns against fatalism and superstition and Mao's break with dogmatic deference to superiors, the Comintern and books.

On struggle, Ding reads atheism broadly as a refusal to fear "ghosts", citing Mao's 1960s Stories of Not Fearing Ghosts. The article proposes three tasks: keep the ban on Party members holding religious belief, directing struggle at separatist, religious-extremist and terrorist forces while uniting believers around the Party, and renew methods of struggle. The last includes resisting Western ideological infiltration, strengthening the Party's voice abroad and reforming atheist education so it wins over the next generation. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-affiliated scholarship ties atheism to the Party's founding spirit, its mass line and its policy on religion.
quoteEn: Upholding Marxist atheism is the spiritual pillar the Communist Party has had from birth.
quoteZh: 坚持马克思主义无神论，是共产党与生俱来的精神支柱。

glossary.zh: 中国共产党人精神谱系
glossary.explanation: An official term for the series of named "spirits" (for example the Jinggangshan spirit and the Yan'an spirit) formed in the Party's history. Xi Jinping presents the founding spirit as their source.

A formulation Xi Jinping gave in his 2021 centenary speech, summarising the Party's founding ethos as upholding truth and ideals, practising the original mission, and being unafraid of sacrifice and loyal to the people.
A principle associated with Mao Zedong and later with Deng Xiaoping, adopted as the Party's ideological line. It requires basing policy on actual conditions rather than doctrine or authority.
The atheist position grounded in dialectical and historical materialism. The Party presents it as the basis of its worldview and as the reason Party members may not hold religious belief.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The official goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, presented as the single theme of the Party's work over a century.

t: Advancing the discipline, academic and discourse systems of contemporary Chinese atheism
st: Studying Xi Jinping's speech at the Symposium on Philosophy and Social Sciences
zh: 推进当代中国无神论学科体系、学术体系、话语体系建设
zhSub: 学习习近平《在哲学社会科学工作座谈会上的讲话》
paras: How should atheism be built as a scholarly discipline in China today? Tian Xinming answers by reading Xi Jinping's speech of 17 May 2016 to the Symposium on Philosophy and Social Sciences, which the article treats as the guiding document for the field. Tian argues that contemporary Chinese atheism must be Marxist atheism, and that its discipline system, academic system and discourse system must be built together under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The piece appeared in the journal Science and Atheism.

The article has three parts. The first defines the fundamental mark of the discipline, namely adherence to Marxism as guiding thought. The second sets out what the construction task involves: a discipline system, an academic system and a discourse system. The third gives the routes to follow, which are integrating three kinds of resources and pursuing problem-oriented theoretical innovation. Tian draws throughout on Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong's On Practice and Xi's speech.

Tian first distinguishes stages of atheism: ancient naive atheism, modern atheism based on natural science, and Marxist atheism. Marxist atheism is called scientific in a stricter sense because it rests on a scientific worldview and view of history. Second, Tian proposes that the discipline system cover historical, theoretical and practical research, plus study of Marxist atheist thought itself. The last is a guide to the discipline but must not replace research on its real object, an argument backed by Engels's warning against using historical materialism as a pretext for not studying history. The academic system is the theory, and the discourse system is the concepts that express it. Tian suggests compiling a general introduction (Gailun) that gathers and assembles existing terms and results. Third, Tian says Marxism is both guiding thought and the primary resource, alongside traditional Chinese culture and foreign scholarship. Tian also takes up questions such as whether Party members may hold religious belief, whether atheist propaganda may reach the general public, and how to counter religious influence.

Tian concludes that atheism is a weak discipline that needs to be strengthened. The author proposes that existing results, including the Chinese Atheism Society's recent publications, be integrated into a unified system, and counts this integration as a form of innovation in itself. Tian links the work to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, religious work and the modernization of national governance. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of Marxist atheism applies Xi Jinping's guidance on the three systems to the building of an academic discipline.
quoteEn: The construction of the atheism discipline should likewise take the reality of contemporary China as its starting point for research and proceed from that reality.
quoteZh: 构建无神论学科也应该以当代中国实际为研究起点，从这个实际出发。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official body of ideas associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018. It is presented as the current stage of adapting Marxism to China.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan for the Party's drive to strengthen discipline, ideological education and organisation within its own ranks, prominent since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

glossary.zh: 学科体系、学术体系、话语体系
glossary.pinyin: xuékē tǐxì, xuéshù tǐxì, huàyǔ tǐxì
glossary.en: discipline system, academic system and discourse system
glossary.explanation: The 'three systems' that Xi Jinping's 2016 speech called for in building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. They cover the structure of disciplines, the body of knowledge and theory, and the concepts that express it.

glossary.zh: 哲学社会科学工作座谈会
glossary.en: Symposium on Philosophy and Social Sciences
glossary.explanation: A meeting held on 17 May 2016 at which Xi Jinping gave a speech setting out guidelines for philosophy and social science work in China. The Chinese philosophy and social science community treats the speech as a guiding document.
The atheist tradition rooted in Marx, Engels and Lenin and developed by the Chinese Communist Party. The article uses it as the central name for the discipline, alongside 'scientific atheism'.

t: The Marxist view of religion and the study of religion in the new era
zh: 马克思主义宗教观和新时代宗教学
paras: Marking the tenth anniversary in 2019 of the Research Office on the Marxist View of Religion at the CASS Institute of World Religions, Jia Runguo argues that religious studies in China has entered a new era in which a Marxist study of religion can be upheld and developed with Chinese characteristics. The author holds that Marxism must remain the guiding ideology of the field, and that the main problems in Chinese religious studies stem from departures from Marxist fundamentals. The piece, published in Science and Atheism, is part retrospective and part programme for the coming decade.

The article has four sections. The first restates the founding mission of the field. The second reviews the history of Marxist work on religion from Marx and Engels onwards. The third considers how to study foreign, especially Western liberal, religious studies. The fourth sets out how Marxist religious studies should relate to practice and governance.

Jia's central move is to reject the claim that Marxism has a view of religion but no religious studies. The author notes that Marx and Engels were born before Max Müller, began studying religion earlier, and wrote specialised works on it, such as Engels's essays on early Christianity. Jia traces a continuous Marxist tradition through Lenin, early Chinese communists and scholars such as Ren Jiyu. Jia therefore says that only research using scientific theory and methods counts as religious studies, and that research guided by theology should be excluded. The second move concerns the West. Jia says its religious anthropology, sociology and psychology are relatively scientific and worth critical absorption, while Western-centrism, cultural relativism, idealism and the bourgeois standpoint are to be rejected. Jia names Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism as an example of embellishing Christianity and capitalism.

Jia calls for Marxist religious studies to be built up in two parts. Theoretical work covers the nature, origins and history of religion and the laws of its emergence, development and disappearance. Empirical work covers the current religious situation at home and abroad, so as to support policy and religious governance. Jia criticises the theologisation and Westernisation of research, and the claimed suspension of belief and academic neutrality, and says these must be firmly abandoned. Jia also complains that the Marxist textbook Religious Studies, part of the Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project, has not been completed in ten years. Read the original if you want a clear statement of the hardline Marxist-atheist position on how religious studies should be organised in China, and of its view of Western scholarship.
quoteEn: The fundamental achievements of religious studies in China have been made under the guidance of Marxism, and its salient problems have been caused by departures from the basic principles of Marxism.
quoteZh: 我国宗教学研究的根本成就是在马克思主义指导下取得的，我国宗教学研究的突出问题是背离马克思主义基本原理造成的。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-Leninist set of positions on the nature, origins, social role and eventual fate of religion. In China it underlies official thinking on religious work and the study of religion.

The academic study of religion as a discipline. In the article, the term is contested between a Western tradition associated with Max Müller and a Marxist tradition that the author wants to establish as orthodox.
A term of criticism for research on religion that adopts the standpoint or methods of theology instead of scientific, materialist analysis.
The management of religious affairs by the Party and state, which the author says Marxist religious studies should support with research and policy proposals.

t: Keeping the combative edge of Marxist atheism
zh: 保持马克思主义无神论的斗争锋芒
source: Science and Atheism (《科学与无神论》)
paras: Zhu Weiqun, a former senior United Front official, argues that Marxist atheism in China must not be reduced to a purely philosophical doctrine. In a short piece first published in the journal Science and Atheism and posted in October 2021, Zhu contends that atheism has a political level as well as a philosophical one. Once religious questions are tied to the proletariat's own emancipation, Zhu holds, Marxist atheism necessarily carries a combative edge.

The article first sets out the two levels of atheism research and recalls how the Communist Party combined atheism with China's revolutionary and religious realities. It then takes up five disputed questions in turn: whether theism or Marxist atheism brings happiness to the Chinese people; whether Party members may hold religious beliefs; which of the two secures genuine freedom of religious belief; whether atheism should be actively propagated; and whether the freedom not to believe and to propagate atheism is protected by the constitution.

Zhu's central claim is that the Party's religious policy works because it rests on a scientific, materialist account of religion, not because it compromises with religion. Zhu maintains that the Party's unity of political programme and worldview distinguishes it from Western parties and underpins its discipline and its rule, so that allowing believers or believing members would bring down the "edifice" of the Party. Zhu warns that weakening atheist propaganda, a change in the balance of believers and non-believers, or a "de-Sinicised" and "extremist" religion linked to foreign forces would harm the Party's position. On the constitution, Zhu endorses Tian Xinming's reading that freedom of belief includes freedom not to believe, and adds a warning that propagating atheism could one day be made illegal.

Zhu calls on Marxist atheists to take up atheist work as a responsibility, to propagate it openly and not to set it against united front work, citing Zhou Enlai's 1950 remark that idealism and materialism differ and need not be concealed. Zhu insists that this goes together with the long-term policy of religious freedom and with uniting religious believers around the Party. Read the original if you want a concise statement, from a former senior official in religious and ethnic affairs, of how atheism is defended within the Party's religious policy debates.
quoteEn: Marxist atheism is open and aboveboard; there is no need at all to hide it away as though one had done something to be ashamed of.
quoteZh: 马克思主义无神论光明正大，完全不必藏着掖着，好像做了什么对不起人的事。

glossary.explanation: A principle written into China's constitution and Party policy. Zhu reads it as covering both the freedom to believe and the freedom not to believe.
The Party's long-standing strategy of building alliances with non-Party groups, including religious circles, under its leadership. It is handled by the United Front Work Department.

t: Atheist education and the transformation of ideas about medicine and health in the base areas during the War of Resistance
zh: 抗战时期根据地无神论教育与医疗卫生观念的变革
source: Science and Atheism (《科学与无神论》), posted on marxism.cass.cn 23 October 2021
paras: Li asks how the Chinese Communist Party carried out atheist education in the anti-Japanese base areas, how villagers came to abandon superstition for scientific medicine, and how ideas about health changed as a result. The article argues that the Party used Marxist theory to start what Li calls a silent revolution in border-region medicine. In Li's account, this produced a modern transformation of health concepts that served both the war effort and popular welfare.

The article opens with a survey of conditions in the base areas, mainly the Shaan-Gan-Ning and Jin-Cha-Ji border regions. Li cites very high illiteracy, epidemic disease, high infant mortality, and a severe shortage of doctors, with shamans (wushen) filling the gap. Li then covers three themes: the contest between doctors and shamans, the Party's prevention-first approach and mass hygiene campaigns, and four areas of changed thinking: regulation of medical qualifications, medical service, disease prevention and treatment, and maternal and child care.

Li first argues that shamans could not simply be suppressed, so the Party followed Engels's advice to educate patiently. It publicised cases of harm done by shamans, had shamans publicly confess and sign anti-shaman pledges, and put them under popular supervision. Li presents Mao Zedong's policy of combining Chinese and Western medicine as the way to rebuild medical forces. Second, hygiene campaigns followed the principle of "adapting to circumstances and guiding" (shitai shudao), with the theme of promoting medicine and opposing ignorance. They relied on hygiene competitions, songs, newspapers and free treatment, and Li treats testimony from cured villagers as especially persuasive. Li reports figures for outpatient treatment, midwife training and new-style childbirth to show change.

Li concludes that the Party, through dialectical and materialist thinking and a people-centred stance, achieved a modern transformation in the base areas' medical ideas. Li adds that "enemies in the masses' minds" persist, and that weak health provision and insufficient health education still allow new and old superstitions to arise. Li calls for better infrastructure, a more balanced supply of medical resources, better services, and regular health-knowledge education guided by the same principle of adapting to circumstances and guiding. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how anti-superstition and public-health work were linked in Yan'an-era base areas, as presented from within the Chinese Marxist tradition.
quoteEn: Lagging medical and health provision and insufficient health education are two important sources of both old and new \"superstition\" among the masses.
quoteZh: 医疗卫生建设滞后和卫生教育不足是群众新旧“迷信”产生的两个重要方面。

glossary.literal: suit the state of mind, unblock and guide
glossary.explanation: A principle of propaganda and education in which the content is matched to the audience's outlook and conditions. Listeners are encouraged to speak freely and are then led patiently toward what the Party regards as correct views.
Folk ritual healers who claimed to cure illness through spirits. The article treats them as fraudsters opposed to scientific medicine.
Mao Zedong's policy of uniting traditional Chinese practitioners and drugs with Western-style medicine, in order to expand medical capacity in the border regions.
Territories under Communist control and administration behind Japanese lines during the War of Resistance (1937–45), such as the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region around Yan'an.

t: The ban on Party members holding religious belief is not in contradiction with the Party's policy of freedom of religious belief
zh: 中共党员不准信仰宗教与党的宗教信仰自由政策并不矛盾
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theory, 2018 no. 2
paras: Writing in 2018, after the 19th Party Congress (2017) called for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, Zuo Peng takes up a debate over whether Communist Party members may hold religious belief. The author notes that some members still consult fortune-tellers or worship, and that some scholars claim that "Party members may believe" and "believers may join the Party", and that the ban contradicts the policy of freedom of religious belief. Zuo argues that there is no contradiction: the ban is a long-standing ideological principle, organisational principle and political discipline of the Party, and it is needed both to regulate inner-Party political life and to implement the religious policy fully.

The article has three sections. The first derives the ban from the dialectical-materialist worldview of Marxism and traces it through Party documents from Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai to the 1982 Central Committee document on religious questions, the 1991 Organization Department notice, and statements by Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping (2016). The second addresses citizens' constitutional freedom of belief, and the third asks who can implement the religious policy.

Zuo's central distinction is that freedom of religious belief includes freedom not to believe. In the author's reading, a person who swears the Party oath has accepted the requirement of atheism and thereby chooses the freedom not to believe. Party members are described as citizens with special political responsibilities who give up some freedoms ordinary citizens have. Zuo rejects the proposal to admit religious leaders and elites. The article argues that Lenin's remarks on priests joining the Social-Democratic Party require that they drop religious views, and that figures such as Fu Lianzhang completed their change of worldview before joining. Religious figures can instead be engaged through the united front. Finally, Zuo claims that only non-believing Party members can implement the policy fully, citing risks of favouritism among five religions, local officials promoting religious sites for economic gain, and the loss of atheist education. The article also rejects the claim that believers in power best secure religious freedom, pointing to historical examples from Europe and the United States.

Zuo concludes that the ban should be maintained and enforced, with ideological education for members who turn to religion and organisational measures if they persist. In minority regions, Party members may take part in traditional customs derived from religious rites, but must keep a clear ideological line from belief; the few who incite religious fanaticism should be disciplined. Read the original if you want a detailed statement of the official Party-theoretical case for atheism as a condition of membership, with its textual sources and its rebuttals of rival scholarly views.
quoteEn: Regarding the freedom of religious belief the Constitution grants citizens, ordinary citizens may choose to believe or not to believe, but Party members can only choose not to believe and cannot choose to believe.
quoteZh: 对于宪法赋予公民的宗教信仰自由，普通公民可以选择信仰，也可以选择不信仰，但党员只能选择不信仰，不能选择信仰

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the Party leadership since the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering discipline, anti-corruption and the regulation of inner-Party political life.
A constitutional right of Chinese citizens and a basic state policy. Official interpretation holds that it includes the freedom not to believe.
The Party's policy of building cooperation with non-Party groups, including religious figures, on a shared political basis. It is described in Party discourse as one of the "three magic weapons".

t: Upholding Marxist atheism as a major principle
zh: 坚持马克思主义无神论是大原则
paras: Wang Weiguang argues that upholding Marxist atheism is a major principle (da yuanze) for the Chinese Communist Party and for China as a socialist state. The article takes its starting point from Xi Jinping's statement at the National Conference on Religious Work in April 2016 that "upholding Marxist atheism is a major principle". Wang holds that this principle applies to legislation, administration and the judiciary, and to the economic, political, social, cultural and ecological fields alike.

The article has four sections. The first explains why the principle must be upheld, drawing on Marx's critique of religion. The second addresses Communist Party members as firm Marxist atheists. The third concerns the duty to propagate atheism among the masses, and the fourth sets out six points that Wang draws from Xi Jinping's statements on atheism since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Wang supports the argument with quotations from Marx, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, and with Party documents from 1982, 2004 and 2016.

Wang's central reasoning is that atheism is the starting point of Marxism, because the critique of religion leads into the critique of society and politics. In this reading, Marxist atheism is the most thorough materialism, and a person who does not uphold it is not a true Marxist. From this Wang derives a discipline for Party members: they may not believe in religion or take part in religious activities, because religion would weaken the Party's worldview, its ideals and its purity. Wang also warns that religious fervour threatens mainstream ideology and the Party's ruling position, and that atheism must remain dominant in the people's thinking. At the same time, Wang insists that propaganda should unite believers and non-believers politically, avoid hurting religious feelings, and focus on young people.

Wang concludes that Xi Jinping's statements on atheism are the latest result of adapting Marxist atheism to the Chinese context and a fundamental guide for the field. Wang calls for atheist propaganda to be reconciled with the policy of freedom of religious belief, for stronger atheist propaganda work, and for greater attention to the discipline and theoretical study of Marxist atheism. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party theorist set out, in 2017, the official case for atheism as Party discipline and ideological work, with a chronology of leaders' statements on the subject.
quoteEn: If one does not uphold Marxist atheism, one is not a thoroughgoing materialist and not a true Marxist.
quoteZh: 不坚持马克思主义无神论，就不是彻底的唯物论者，不是真正的马克思主义者。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official term for the atheist worldview grounded in dialectical and historical materialism. It is presented as part of Marxist theory and as the basis for the Party's stance on religion.
Xi Jinping's phrase at the April 2016 National Conference on Religious Work, used to stress that upholding Marxist atheism is a basic requirement across all areas of work.

glossary.en: policy of freedom of religious belief
glossary.explanation: The official policy guaranteeing citizens freedom of religious belief. Party documents state that it applies to ordinary citizens but not to Party members.

t: On the Marxist classical authors' idea of separating education from religion
zh: 论马克思主义经典作家的教育与宗教相分离思想
paras: Zhang asks how Marx, Engels and Lenin understood the separation of education from religion, and argues that it is a critical inheritance of early modern Western thought and an important component of the Marxist view of religion. In the article's account, the classical authors went beyond their Western predecessors by tying the principle to concrete social problems and to the basic theory of Marxism.

The article first traces the Western background: the Renaissance, the Reformation and the Enlightenment, which moved education from church monopoly towards state-run, secular provision. It then turns to the classical authors' practical critique of religious control of schooling, their theoretical construction of the principle, and the practical routes they proposed for realising it.

Zhang argues that Marx and Engels identified three harms of religious monopoly over education: it blocks human emancipation by helping ruling classes keep people ignorant, it shackles science (Engels's examples include Bruno and Servetus), and it lets religious morality displace social morality. Theoretically, the classical authors drew on dialectical and historical materialism to describe church–state relations. They also stressed that religion is a private matter, so that the state, and therefore public education, should be free of it. In practice, the author says, they proposed three measures: atheist propaganda and education, the separation of church and state with confiscation of church property and the end of state funding, and a secular national education system, citing Engels's account of English schools.

Zhang concludes that separating education from religion is a key part of the Marxist view of religion and a basic principle for handling the relationship between education and religion in a socialist country. It is presented as the product of combining theory with practice. Read the original if you want a source-based overview of Marx, Engels and Lenin's statements on schooling and religion, as presented in Chinese scholarship on religion and atheism.
quoteEn: The separation of education from religion is an important element of the relationship between state and religion.
quoteZh: 教育与宗教相分离是政教关系的一项重要内容。

t: Preliminary thoughts on building Marxist atheism as an academic discipline
zh: 马克思主义无神论学科建设刍议
paras: Zuo Peng asks how atheism, as a body of knowledge that negates and criticises theism, can become an independent academic discipline in China. The author argues that current classification rules do not allow this and proposes adding a second-level discipline, Marxist atheism, under the first-level discipline of Marxist theory. To make that case convincing, the article recommends building the field on the model of Fei Xiaotong's "five viscera and six bowels" formula for rebuilding sociology.

The article has three parts. The first sets out why independent disciplinary status is a precondition and where atheism should be placed. The second outlines a complete disciplinary system with four branches. The third describes the "departments" the discipline needs: learned societies, research institutes, academic departments, books and materials, and specialist journals. Zuo draws on the 2009 national classification standard, the 2011 degree catalogue, Ren Jiyu, Tian Xinming, Xi Wuyi and Fei Xiaotong's collected works.

Zuo notes that the 2009 standard lists atheism under religious studies, but the degree-granting catalogue does not list it, so atheism cannot recruit or train graduate students independently. Zuo describes religious studies as increasingly dominated by voices that stress religion's positive role, leaving atheism marginal. Placing atheism beside religious studies under philosophy would blur disciplinary boundaries, the author says. Under Marxist theory it would fit, since atheism is presented as the foundation of Marxism and since Party members' superstition and religious infiltration of universities call for atheist education. The four branches are principles of Marxist atheism, history of atheism, critique of theism (superstition and religious theology, the latter described as the hardest task), and atheist propaganda and education. Zuo says the field's institutions are thin, citing 115 directors in the China Atheism Society against 408 in the China Religious Studies Society. The author also reports few translations of atheist works and a single specialist journal, Science and Atheism.

Zuo concludes that the field is still at an early stage and its standard is bound to be low, but that the work must be started rather than merely discussed. The author calls for state support for projects and publications, for "borrowing a boat" by recruiting graduate students under neighbouring disciplines, and for more research centres and local societies. Read the original if you want a detailed view of how Chinese Marxist atheism scholars argue for institutionalising their field and how they see its place within Marxist theory and religious studies.
quoteEn: If the discipline of atheism is to develop, it must have fully independent disciplinary status, and the sign of that is entry into the Catalogue, so that it can legitimately award master's and doctoral degrees, recruit students and train them.
quoteZh: 无神论学科要发展，就必须拥有完全独立的学科地位，其标志就是能够进入《目录》，名正言顺地进行硕士、博士的学位授予、招生和培养。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义理论一级学科
glossary.explanation: A first-level discipline in China's degree catalogue, established in December 2005 to strengthen Marxism's guiding position in higher education. It has several second-level subdisciplines that support the ideological and political theory courses in universities.

glossary.zh: 学位授予和人才培养学科目录
glossary.pinyin: Xuéwèi shòuyǔ hé réncái péiyǎng xuékē mùlù
glossary.literal: Catalogue of disciplines for degree conferral and talent training
glossary.explanation: The catalogue issued by the Academic Degrees Committee of the State Council and the Ministry of Education, revised in 2011. Only disciplines listed in it can independently grant degrees, recruit and train graduate students.

glossary.literal: five organs and six hollow organs
glossary.explanation: A metaphor from the sociologist Fei Xiaotong, who used the body's organs to describe what a discipline needs to be established. The "five viscera" are society, institute, department, library centre and publishing outlet.

t: Keeping Marxist atheism dominant in the thinking of the people
zh: 始终保持马克思主义无神论在人民群众思想中的主导地位
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Zhu Xiaoming takes up a directive from the National Conference on Religious Work held that April: Party members must adhere to Marxist atheism and must not look for their values and beliefs in religion. The article asks how Marxist atheism can remain the dominant element of the mainstream ideology in the people's thinking. Zhu answers that atheism must be both upheld and actively propagated across the whole of society, not only within the Party.

The piece has two parts. The first argues that the theory of religion of socialism with Chinese characteristics is in essence Marxist atheism. The second sets out how atheism is to keep its leading position among the people, with three requirements: propagate it actively, do not let general Marxist education replace it, and carry it out persistently and widely. Zhu draws on Mao Zedong, Lenin's "On the Significance of Militant Materialism", and the religion scholar Ren Jiyu.

Zhu's central move is to distinguish audiences and policies. Atheism is a requirement for Party members, with Party cadres and young people as the main targets of propaganda. Toward religious believers and religious venues the Party practises "political cooperation and mutual respect in belief", and it does not conduct atheist propaganda among believers. Zhu therefore holds that freedom of religious belief and atheist education are two complementary basic principles of religious work. Zhu warns against treating policy toward the religious sphere as policy for society as a whole, and against letting central directives stay "locked in drawers".

Zhu also argues, citing Lenin, that general Marxist teaching cannot replace dedicated atheist education, which should use concrete everyday examples and be linked to science and advanced culture. Research on religion should be done from a non-believing, historical-materialist standpoint and should aim to "demystify" religion and counter religious extremism. Zhu concludes that atheist education is never finished, since new unknowns will keep producing supernatural fantasies, so it demands perseverance. Read the original if you want an official-line statement, from a leading atheism-society figure in 2016, of how Party policy separates atheist propaganda from the protection of religious freedom.
quoteEn: Atheist propaganda and education is never meant to set believers against non-believers, nor to make believers give up their faith, but to help more people learn to view religious phenomena correctly and choose their worldview rationally.
quoteZh: 无神论宣传教育绝不是制造信教与不信教群众的对立，绝不是要信教群众放弃自己的宗教信仰，而是要使更多的人学会正确看待宗教现象，理性选择自己的世界观

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path and theoretical system since reform and opening up. Here it qualifies the Party's theory of religion.
A high-level Party meeting that sets policy on religious affairs. The one held in April 2016 is the starting point of the article.
The official policy that citizens may believe or not believe in religion. The article pairs it with the Party's duty to carry out atheist education.

t: How we conceived and wrote "Foreign Religious Infiltration and the Soviet-East European Upheaval"
zh: 我们是如何思考和写作《境外宗教渗透与苏东剧变研究》的
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2016 no. 2
paras: This is a reflective account by Duan Dezhi, editor of the 2015 People's Publishing House volume on foreign religious infiltration and the Soviet and East European upheaval. Duan explains why the project was undertaken, what the book sets out to prove and how it was carried out. The book grew out of a major Ministry of Education research project on foreign religious infiltration and China's ideological security, begun in 2009 and completed in 2013. Duan's central claim is that infiltration by hostile external forces using religion was an important cause of the upheaval, though not the only one.

The essay has three parts.
