The first gives two reasons for making the upheaval a priority: it is the most representative case of religious infiltration of socialist states, and it is the factual basis on which theorists of the 'end of ideology' rely. The second sets out the book's three aims, and the third reports how each was pursued. Duan draws on Marx, Engels, Deng Xiaoping, Francis Bacon and the memoirs of Nikolai Ryzhkov, and on figures such as Gorbachev, Jaruzelski and Adam Schaff.

Duan treats the 'US–Vatican holy alliance' formed in 1982 as the central event of the upheaval. In this account it pursued a three-step plan: engineer change in Poland, extend it to seven other East European states, then dissolve the Soviet Union. Duan places this within Engels's 'theory of historical resultant forces', which also counts the rigid Soviet model and the right and 'left' errors of ruling parties as causes. The lessons drawn are that ruling parties accommodated infiltration and lacked an 'East–West' consciousness (awareness of the ideological adversary). Duan adds that religious work must avoid both right and 'left' errors, and aim to guide religion to adapt to socialist society. Against the 'end of ideology' thesis, Duan cites the later revival of communist parties in Russia and shifting views of Stalin. Duan also charges that the thesis rests on abstract logical centrism and narrow empiricism, which Bacon would have called 'idols of the theatre'.

Duan concludes that the upheaval is an episode that can be surpassed but not bypassed: international communism will go on, while its causes call for self-reflection by all communist parties. Duan presents the book's epistemological critique of the end-of-ideology thesis as its original contribution. Duan also reports favourable reception from reviewing experts. Read the original if you want a first-hand statement of how a Chinese scholar of religion links religious infiltration, ideological security and lessons from the Soviet collapse.
quoteEn: But flatly denying the influence of foreign religious infiltration on the Soviet and East European upheaval is equally contrary to historical fact, naive and absurd, and not worth following.
quoteZh: 但矢口否认境外宗教渗透对苏东剧变的影响也同样有违历史事实、幼稚可笑和不足为训。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Chinese Party-state discourse about protecting the dominant socialist ideology against perceived external and internal challenges.

The author's term for cooperation in the 1980s between the Reagan administration and Pope John Paul II against communist rule in Eastern Europe. The label and its causal weight are the author's own interpretation.

glossary.literal: theory of the end of ideology
glossary.explanation: A line of Western thought, from Daniel Bell and Raymond Aron to Francis Fukuyama, that Chinese Marxist scholars treat as an argument that socialism has been historically defeated.
Based on Engels's 1890 letter to Joseph Bloch, which says historical outcomes result from many intersecting individual wills. It is used here to treat the upheaval as the product of many forces.

t: Using scientific thought to eliminate belief in ghosts and spirits
zh: 用科学思想消除鬼神迷信
source: Science and Atheism (Kexue yu wushenlun), 2016 no. 1
paras: Writing in 2016, Jia Runguo argues that the ideological basis of violence by cult members and terrorists is anti-scientific belief in ghosts and spirits. Alongside legal and institutional measures against cults and terrorism, the author calls for sustained popularisation of scientific knowledge to drive out such belief. Since the social soil that produces it cannot be removed quickly, Jia holds that arming people's minds with a scientific worldview is the only route to immunity against extremist doctrines.

The article has five sections: exposing the anti-scientific essence of belief in the supernatural; criticising idealism and metaphysics; improving Marxist philosophy teaching; strengthening the popularisation of scientific atheism; and strengthening Party leadership over the study of religion. It draws on Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong, and ends with remarks on the institutional history of religious studies in China.

Jia defines supernatural force as spiritual force detached from matter, and traces the idea of the soul to early humans' lack of scientific knowledge about life and thought. Educated people and scientists also fall into superstition, the author says, because idealism and metaphysics supply the wrong method of thinking; Jia cites Engels on empiricists who scorn dialectics and end up in spiritualism. Philosophy teaching should therefore centre on refuting idealism, metaphysics and theism, with textbooks giving up to two-thirds of their space to criticism of erroneous ideas. Jia also rejects the view that atheist education is simple or conflicts with the Party's policy of religious freedom, and says implementation has been poor because the relevant documents sit with the united front and religious affairs bodies rather than with propaganda and education departments.

Jia proposes moving atheism requirements into propaganda and education documents, creating dedicated offices and staff in propaganda and education departments, and reinforcing Marxist guidance in religious studies. The author complains that scholars who combine study of religion with criticism of theology are becoming fewer, and cites Mao's 1960s remarks and the founding of the Institute of World Religions in 1964. Read the original if you want to see how a researcher in the state religious affairs system links atheist education, philosophy teaching and religious studies to counter-terrorism and anti-cult work.
quoteEn: To believe in forces arising from the motion of matter is science; to believe in forces detached from the motion of matter is superstition.
quoteZh: 相信物质运动的力是科学，相信脱离物质运动的力是迷信。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist-Leninist approach that presents atheism as grounded in science and philosophical materialism. In China it is promoted through publications, education and research, including the journal that carried this article.
The Party's official policy of protecting citizens' freedom to believe or not believe in religion. The author interprets it as also protecting the freedom to propagate atheism.

t: The value and significance of the young Marx's critique of religion
zh: 青年马克思宗教批判的价值意蕴
paras: Zhu Peili asks what the young Marx's critique of religion contributed to the formation of Marxist theory. The article argues that this critique was the starting point and precondition of Marx's wider social critique. In Zhu's account, it inherited and then surpassed earlier rational critiques, aimed at human emancipation, and still bears on modern fetishism of commodities.

The article has four parts. It first traces the origins of the critique: Marx's early religious and moral outlook, as seen in his school essays, the setting of Prussian absolutism allied with religion, and the influence of the Enlightenment and the Young Hegelians. It then assesses the theoretical value of the critique through Marx's debt to and break with Feuerbach. A third part treats human emancipation as its value aim, and a final part turns to its contemporary relevance.

Zhu's central move is a contrast with Feuerbach. Feuerbach saw religion as human self-alienation and proposed a "religion of love", but, on Zhu's reading, he treated people as abstract individuals and ignored the contradictions within secular society. Marx instead traced religion to an "inverted world" of oppression and exploitation, so that criticism of heaven turned into criticism of earth, of law and of politics. For Zhu this makes social critique the full completion of the critique of religion. Zhu then links the critique to emancipation: in the 1843 Introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, the proletariat is the force of human emancipation and philosophy its "head", with the proletariat its "heart".

Zhu concludes that the young Marx's critique gave later Marxist theory of human emancipation its starting point and a value reference. In the author's view it remains relevant because commodity fetishism functions as a secularised religious worship that produces spiritual emptiness and anxiety. Zhu holds that religious illusion can be removed only by changing the social relations that produce it, abolishing private ownership and the social division of labour and creating an "association of free individuals". Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language account of how the young Marx moved from Feuerbach's critique of religion to social critique, and how a Chinese scholar of atheism applies it to commodity fetishism.
quoteEn: The young Marx's critique of religion was the starting point of his social critique, and social critique was the full completion of his critique of religion.
quoteZh: 青年马克思的宗教批判是其社会批判的起点，社会批判是其宗教批判的彻底完成。

t: Scientific atheism and religious issues in the new situation
st: Report on the 2015 annual conference of the China Atheism Association
zh: 科学无神论与新形势下的宗教问题
zhSub: 中国无神论学会2015年学术年会综述
paras: This is a report on the 2015 annual conference of the China Atheism Association, held in Beijing on 5–6 December 2015 under the theme "Scientific atheism and religious issues in the new situation". It was co-organised by the Association, the CASS Research Center for Science and Atheism and the University of Science and Technology Beijing. More than 70 scholars from over 30 universities, research institutes and academic bodies in 12 provinces and cities took part.

The report arranges the papers under seven headings: the "Four Musts" for religious work set out at the 2015 Central United Front Work Conference; basic theory of scientific atheism; Marxist atheism; atheism and the study of religion; science and religion; propaganda and education in scientific atheism; and scientific atheism and curbing religious extremism. Speakers included Jia Runguo, Duan Dezhi, Du Jiwen, Xi Wuyi, Li Shen and Tian Xinming, along with many younger researchers and doctoral students.

On religious work, Jia Runguo presents the Four Musts as the guide to adapting religion to socialist society. Duan Dezhi reads the Soviet and East European upheavals partly through foreign religious infiltration, and several speakers warn against Western ideological penetration and religious extremism. On theory, Du Jiwen locates the strength of Chinese culture in humanism, and Li Shen insists that China's theistic traditions need criticism as much as its atheist ones. Tian Xinming, Zeng Chuanhui and Han Qi revisit Lenin, the young Marx and Engels's Anti-Dühring. Others argue that religious morality is in essence secular morality, and that scientific and cultural education should be strengthened. The Xinjiang papers criticise the stress on policing over ideological work and call for better management of religious affairs. They also propose "five-good" religious personnel and a lower profile for religious culture.

The report notes that attendance and paper quality rose compared with earlier conferences. Participants saw the mix of senior and younger scholars as a sign that scientific atheism is thriving as the Party strengthens ideological work. Some asked for more time for exchange and for an awards system to attract young scholars. Read the original if you want a detailed map of how Chinese atheism scholars and religious-affairs researchers framed religion, ideology and security in late 2015.
quoteEn: Only by upholding the Marxist view of religion and the basic Marxist guideline for religious work can foreign religious infiltration be effectively guarded against and resisted, and socialist ideological security and national security be safeguarded.
quoteZh: 唯有坚持马克思主义的宗教观、坚持马克思主义的宗教工作基本方针，才能有效地防范和抵制境外宗教渗透、维护社会主义意识形态安全和国家安全。

glossary.explanation: Four requirements for religious work set out at the Central United Front Work Conference in May 2015. They are to adhere to the direction of sinicization, to raise the level of rule of law in religious work, to view the social role of religion dialectically, and to value the role of religious figures.

The Marxist form of atheism, which claims to explain scientifically how religion arises, develops and declines. It is distinct from earlier atheist thought and is a recognised academic field in China.

glossary.zh: 积极引导宗教与社会主义社会相适应
glossary.pinyin: jījí yǐndǎo zōngjiào yǔ shèhuì zhǔyì shèhuì xiāng shìyìng
glossary.literal: actively guide religion to adapt to socialist society
glossary.explanation: A long-standing Party policy line on religion, which calls for religious communities to fit in with the socialist political and social order.
A high-level Party meeting on united front work, which covers relations with religious, ethnic and non-Party groups. The May 2015 conference issued new guidance on religious work.

t: Upholding and promoting atheism with a clear stand
zh: 旗帜鲜明地坚持和宣传无神论
paras: Writing in the Global Times in May 2016, shortly after the National Conference on Religious Work held in April, Zhu Weiqun asks how Marxist atheism can remain the dominant mainstream ideology among the people. Zhu argues that, because Marxism's worldview rests on dialectical and historical materialism, upholding socialism with Chinese characteristics necessarily means upholding and developing Marxist atheism. The article presents this as a major question that Party cadres, especially leaders and religious-affairs officials, need to think through.

This short commentary is organised under four headings. It treats atheism as part of mainstream ideology, as a precondition for sound religious work, as a matter of Party discipline for members, and as a feature that distinguishes the Party from most other parties. Zhu draws on Mao Zedong's Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan, his On New Democracy, and a passage from Engels, alongside observations on Chinese history and culture.

Zhu's central claim is that the Party cannot abandon atheism, stay neutral between theism and atheism, or let theism spread until it becomes the mainstream ideology. The reasons given are the ruling party's worldview, modernization, resistance to foreign religious infiltration, and the Party's mass base. Religion will long persist and believers are a positive force, Zhu says, so the theist–atheist divide is not a political opposition. Religious work, however, is atheists working with theists within the united front, and atheists should lead politically. Zhu describes China as historically a secular state with a secular culture, and warns against religious 'de-Sinicization' and 'extremization'. Zhu also reports that some Party members and scholars have argued that members may hold religious beliefs, or that believers may join the Party, and rejects both positions as illogical.

Zhu concludes that the rule that Party members may not hold religious beliefs is political discipline. In Zhu's account, lifting it would erode the unity of the Party's worldview, turn the Party into a loose body of religious factions, and make part of its religious work one believer addressing another. Zhu calls for atheist education, including for young people and in religious studies research and teaching, to be treated as a firm task. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-line case for atheism and the ban on religious belief among members, as put forward in 2016 by a senior figure in religious and ethnic affairs.
quoteEn: The significance and urgency of upholding and promoting atheism go far beyond the scope of religious work.
quoteZh: 坚持和宣传无神论，其意义和紧迫性已经远远超出宗教工作范围。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's theory and path of socialist development since the reform era. It is the framework in which the article places Marxist atheism.

The Party's strategy of building alliances with non-Party groups, including religious believers, under the Party's leadership. The article uses it to argue that atheists must lead theists politically.
A high-level Party meeting that sets policy on religion. The article refers to the one held in April 2016.

glossary.en: Party members may not hold religious beliefs
glossary.literal: Party members cannot believe in religion
glossary.explanation: A long-standing Party principle, treated as political discipline, that Communist Party members must not hold religious beliefs. The article defends it against proposals to relax it.

t: Frontier report on scientific atheism research in 2014
st: Keynote address at the 2015 annual conference of the China Atheism Association
zh: 2014年科学无神论研究前沿报告
zhSub: 在中国无神论学会2015年学术年会上的主旨发言
source: Keynote address at the 2015 annual conference of the China Atheism Association
paras: Xi Wuyi delivered this keynote address at the China Atheism Association's 2015 annual conference. It surveys research in scientific atheism during 2014 and is drawn from the corresponding chapter of the 2015 yearbook of disciplinary research. Xi presents it as basic work for building the discipline and as information for members' own research. The overall message is that scientific atheism is gaining ground in scholarship and is needed for Marxist religious studies and ideological security.

The address has two parts. The first reviews four books: the ten-volume Collected Works of Ren Jiyu, Du Jiwen's Collected Essays on Science and Atheism, the first series of Studies in the History of Chinese Atheism, and the Chinese translation of Richard Dawkins's The Blind Watchmaker. The second summarises journal and newspaper articles under six headings: theory, atheism and religion, resisting religious infiltration and curbing religious extremism, destructive cults, science and religion, and atheist propaganda and education. Xi also reports that about 60 per cent of the articles reviewed came from outside the journal Science and Atheism, against nearly 70 per cent from it in 2010–2013.

Across the surveyed work, Xi reports a common line. Marxist religious studies should keep to Mao Zedong's formula of 'studying religion and criticizing theology', as Ren Jiyu summarised it. Du Jiwen and Xi reject 'academic theology', and Xi calls it a challenge to that paradigm. Several authors treat Western, especially Christian, 'infiltration' of universities, the internet and the countryside as a threat to ideological security. Xi's own contributions argue that overseas religious right-wing forces use legal channels to spread values, and that universities should keep education separate from religion. Contributions on religious extremism and the cult 'Almighty God' call for a mix of measures: legal action, rural cultural development and stronger Party organization at the grassroots. Xi also notes disagreement. He calls the Studies in the History of Chinese Atheism claim that Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism are essentially atheist 'quite controversial'. On science and religion, Li Xingmin and Yu Qiming are reported as holding that scientists' personal faith is unrelated to their research.

Xi concludes that scientific atheism is one of the philosophical foundations of the socialist core value system and a long-standing policy of the Communist Party. Xi expects the discipline to play a distinctive part in strengthening ideological work and protecting national cultural security. Read the original if you want a detailed inventory of 2014 Chinese publications on atheism, religion and 'religious infiltration', and a view of how Party-aligned scholars framed these debates.
quoteEn: Scientific atheism is the bottom-most foundation stone of the edifice of Marxist theory, and its materialist worldview and positive outlook on life hold an important place in the socialist core value system.
quoteZh: 科学无神论是马克思主义理论大厦最底层的基石，其唯物主义世界观和积极的人生观更在社会主义核心价值体系中占有重要的地位。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist-based atheism taught and researched in China as part of Marxist religious theory. It is promoted through a dedicated discipline, a journal and research centres.

A formula derived from Mao Zedong's 1964 instruction to strengthen research on religion, as summarised by Ren Jiyu. Authors in the text treat it as the basic paradigm of Chinese Marxist religious studies.

A proposal to develop theology as a scholarly field within Chinese universities, including Chinese-language Christian theology. The authors surveyed oppose it as a challenge to Marxist religious studies.
A set of official values promoted since the early 2010s, beginning with prosperity and strength. The text treats them as an ideological basis for political identity across ethnic and religious lines.

A term in Chinese official and academic discourse for overseas religious activity, mainly Christian, that is seen as aimed at changing China's ideology or politics. It is a contested characterisation.

t: Seeing achievements, seeing the light: raising our confidence and courage
st: Address to the 2015 annual academic conference of the China Atheism Society
zh: 看到成绩看到光明提高我们的信心和勇气
zhSub: 在中国无神论学会2015年学术年会上的致辞
paras: This is the opening address given by Zhu Xiaoming, president of the China Atheism Society, to the society's 2015 annual academic conference, held in Beijing in December 2015. The conference was co-organised by the society, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) Research Centre for Science and Atheism and Beijing University of Science and Technology, under the theme "Scientific atheism and religious issues under the new situation". Zhu presents it both as an annual exchange and as an occasion to study central Party statements on religious work, ahead of a national religious work conference.

After welcoming participants, Zhu gives a numbered report on the society's work in 2015. Items include a March consultation with CASS leaders on religious policy, Zhu's remarks at a publication event for the collected works of Ren Jiyu, a seminar on atheists and traditional Chinese culture, a public lecture in Shandong, and training for Beijing university teachers and cadres on the Marxist view of religion. The report also covers the third Scientific Atheism Forum, a commissioned book project, a new science-exploration centre, the "Southern Research Centre" and a WeChat group. Zhu then lists scholars' publications and awards.

Zhu's central claim is that the Party leadership is receptive to the society's work. He reads the emphasis on Marxist atheism education in the Sixth Tibet Work Forum as a sign that the centre had "heard our voice". He cites Xi Jinping's call for religion to adapt to socialist society, Article 23 of the 2015 Party united front regulations (Party members may not hold religious beliefs) and the Party disciplinary regulations of October 2015. Zhu says these create favourable conditions for the field. He describes scientific atheism as temporarily at a low ebb but with "the fire still alive". He also says the society should keep watching the "new atheism movement" in China, whose organisers he describes as showing prejudice against Marxist atheism.

Zhu concludes that the society faces both opportunity and serious challenges. He names religious interference in social life and national education, a "religious fever" promoted in the name of culture, and the spread of cults and religious extremism. He calls on members to offer advice, recruit younger scholars and use the conference as a new starting point. He also announces plans for a 2016 commemoration of Ren Jiyu's centenary and the appointment of Gong Yun as head of the atheism research office and deputy secretary-general. Read the original if you want a detailed insider account of how organised atheism research in China operated and understood its political environment in 2015.
quoteEn: Although scientific atheism is for the moment at a low ebb and in some difficulty, the fire is still alive.
quoteZh: 尽管科学无神论暂时处于低潮，比较困难，但火种仍在。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-Leninist form of atheism promoted in China, presented as grounded in science and historical materialism. Its research and propaganda are organised through bodies such as the CASS atheism research office.
A national academic association of researchers of Marxist atheism, affiliated with CASS. It publishes the journal Science and Atheism.

t: The historical origins of Marxist atheism
zh: 马克思主义无神论的历史渊源
source: Marxist Forum (Marxism Luntan), vol. 11, Shandong People's Publishing House, December 2015
paras: Han Qi asks what the long history of Western atheism can teach present-day research and propaganda on Marxist atheism. The article starts from the claim that atheism is the starting point and cornerstone of Marxism, and that Marxist atheism is the highest form of atheist thought. Han argues that tracing its origins clarifies key points and helps China respond to the revival of religion, cults, pseudo-religion and religious extremism since reform and opening up.

The first part surveys Western atheism in five stages: the classical period, the Middle Ages, the Renaissance (16th–17th centuries), the Enlightenment, and the modern era (19th–20th centuries). It draws mainly on James Thrower's Western Atheism: A Short History and on a Chinese history of Western atheism. Thinkers discussed include Democritus, Epicurus, Lucretius, Hobbes, Spinoza, Diderot, d'Holbach, Hume, Kant, Feuerbach, Nietzsche, Darwin, Freud, Russell and Sartre. The second part draws seven lessons, and a short conclusion turns to China.

Han's core argument is that atheism was not one person's invention but the accumulated work of many thinkers. In this reading, by Marx's time the question of whether gods exist had largely been settled, and Marx inherited the verdict and applied it more thoroughly to society and history. Han stresses that atheism changes with the needs of each era, so research today should fit current conditions rather than copy the past. Han also holds that atheism should be studied within the wider field of non-belief, alongside pantheism, deism and agnosticism, which the article calls close relatives, and that scepticism has always accompanied it. Citing Michael Martin, Han suggests that many Chinese who regard themselves as agnostics may in fact be atheists without knowing it.

Han concludes that the naturalist tradition, the spirit of reason and science, and the era-specific character of atheism are key elements to grasp. In the article's view, developing atheist research and propaganda can answer today's 'religious fever' and curb pseudo-religion, cults and religious extremism. Han also points to the 'New Atheism' of Richard Dawkins and others, which has reached Chinese audiences, as a reason to keep following global developments. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS scholar uses a survey of Western atheism to justify the contemporary agenda of Marxist atheism in China.
quoteEn: Atheism is not the invention of any one person, but the crystallisation of the continually accumulating collective wisdom of countless people in history who held atheist ideas.
quoteZh: 无神论并非某一个人的发明，而是历史上无数带有无神论思想的人们集体智慧不断积累的结晶。

glossary.explanation: The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978. The article dates the revival of religion to the period since then.
The official Chinese term for groups the authorities classify as illegal or harmful sects, distinct from the recognised religions.
A term used in Chinese official discourse for violent or radical religious movements, which the article treats as a threat to national security.
The view that the existence of God cannot be known. The article treats it as close to, but distinct from, atheism.
The Enlightenment view that God created the world but stands outside nature and gives no revelation. The article counts it among atheism's 'close relatives'.

t: The scientific atheism of Anti-Dühring
zh: 《反杜林论》的科学无神论思想
source: Science and Atheism (Kexue yu wushenlun), 2015 no. 6
paras: Han Qi asks what Engels's Anti-Dühring, rarely read as a work on atheism, can contribute to scientific atheism today. The article argues that because the book rests on dialectical and historical materialism, it embodies a consistent atheism, and that its dialectics gives ordinary people an objective, rational stance toward the religious phenomena active in China since reform and opening up.

The article limits itself to the Philosophy section of Anti-Dühring, the first of Marxism's three component parts. After summarising the work's origins (written 1876–78 against Eugen Dühring's influence in German social democracy), it follows Engels's three-part critique of Dühring: his schema of the world, his philosophy of nature, and his doctrine of man. Han frames this with the present-day rise of religion, cults, pseudo-religious 'masters' and religious extremism.

Han's central move is to show that Dühring's errors are idealist and metaphysical, leaving room for a creator or 'first push'. Engels answers that the world's unity lies in its materiality, that motion is the mode of existence of matter, and that life is a mode of existence of protein bodies. The second move concerns truth and morality. Han reports Engels's view that human thought is sovereign only across endless generations, that no field of knowledge yields eternal truths, and that morality is always class morality tied to economic relations. Freedom, on this reading, is the recognition of necessity.

Han concludes that these positions exclude the idea of God or a creator and equip readers to see through cults and religious extremism. The author applies them to the claim that China's moral decline stems from a lack of religion, which Han rejects as contrary to history and to dialectics, since religious morality is no final truth or cure-all. Han calls for scientific atheism to use materialist dialectics in research and propaganda, tied to current religious phenomena and to close reading of the classics. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist atheism scholar reads Engels's Anti-Dühring in light of contemporary religious policy debates.
quoteEn: Scientific atheism needs precisely to use materialist dialectics to grasp the crux of these matters and to guide public opinion.
quoteZh: 科学无神论正要运用唯物辩证法思想来洞悉其中的关要，指导大众舆论。

glossary.explanation: A term for the Marxist-grounded study and promotion of atheism in China, treating religion as a social phenomenon to be analysed with materialist dialectics. It is associated with institutions such as the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and the journal Science and Atheism.
The Marxist method, developed by Marx and Engels from Hegel's dialectics on a materialist basis, that treats nature, society and thought as in constant motion and change.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978.

t: From Einstein's private bluntness to Hawking's public denial
st: An interpretation of Hawking's view of God
zh: 从爱因斯坦私下的直白到霍金的公开否定
zhSub: 解读霍金的“上帝观”
paras: Writing in December 2014 for the Science and Atheism section of the Academy of Marxism site, Yu Qiming asks how Stephen Hawking's attitude to God should be read. Yu argues that Hawking moved from an inner rejection of God, expressed cautiously in A Brief History of Time, to an open denial in The Grand Design (2010). For Yu, this shift, set beside Einstein's private remarks, shows science's growing social influence and leading scientists' growing sympathy for atheism.

The article opens with Einstein's handwritten German letter of 3 January 1954 to the philosopher Eric Gutkind, publicised when it was auctioned in London in 2008. In it Einstein called the word 'God' a product of human weakness and the Bible a collection of primitive, childish legends. Yu then sets out Hawking's 2010 statements and offers a biographical sketch: his illness, honours and popular science writing. The article also covers Hawking's boyhood interest in religion and parapsychology and the role of his first wife, Jane Wilde.

Yu's central move is to reject religious readings of Hawking. Believers have quoted the closing passage of A Brief History of Time, on knowing 'the mind of God', as proof of religious implications. Yu counters that Hawking meant the laws of nature, citing his remark that God should be a personification of natural law. Yu also cites Hawking's 1981 Vatican conference, where he privately welcomed that the Pope did not grasp that his no-boundary proposal left no moment of creation, and Carl Sagan's introduction to the book. Yu reads Hawking's complaint about philosophy's decline as showing a spontaneous materialist tendency.

Yu explains Hawking's earlier gentleness by his early scepticism towards the supernatural and by respect for Jane, a devout Christian. This is why he avoided calling himself an atheist and played down conflict between science and religion. Yu concludes that, once science and God conflict, a scientist pursuing the universe's origins can only side with science. Read the original if you want a Chinese atheist-propaganda reading of Hawking's religious views, with Einstein as a point of comparison.
quoteEn: From A Brief History of Time to The Grand Design, Hawking moved from denying God inwardly to denying God publicly, which shows that his view of God had become more fully settled.
quoteZh: 从《时间简史》到《伟大的设计》，霍金从内心否定上帝到公开否定上帝，表明他的上帝观更加成竹在胸了。

t: The religious ecology of contemporary China: Christianity and atheism
zh: 中国当代宗教生态景观•基督教•无神论
paras: This short commentary, posted in 2014, asks how China's increasingly plural religious landscape should be understood and answered, with particular attention to the growth of Christianity. Huang argues that this growth has an international background and that scientific atheism deserves a firmer place in mainstream ideology.

The piece has three parts. The first surveys contemporary religious life, giving the author's figures for believers (about 21 million Muslims, 5.5 million Catholics, and 16 million officially counted Protestants) and describing Buddhism, Islam, Tibetan Buddhism, folk belief and groups the author calls cults. The second discusses the international context of Christian expansion. The third turns to atheism in China today.

Huang contends that certain Western powers use religion and human rights as levers to pressure China, and that Western frameworks for church–state relations do not fit China. The author defends the Three-Self system as an expression of national sovereignty in religion. Huang reads rural conversion as largely utilitarian, driven by poverty, illness and conformity, and urban conversion as sometimes an expression of discontent or a protective strategy for dissidents. The author attributes this partly to a lack of appeal in mainstream ideology.

Huang calls scientific atheism the more valuable option and rejects the pragmatic view that religion is useful "social capital". The author proposes atheist education for young people as a cheap "vaccine", and for Party members and society as an ideological "firewall". Huang adds that atheism's prospects depend on economic and social policy, such as universal social security. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-affiliated atheist scholar framed Christianity and religious policy in 2014.
quoteEn: Creating conditions so that the public has ample opportunity to encounter atheism and scientific rationality is what it means to be truly responsible towards the people, and towards the nation and history.
quoteZh: 应当创造条件使社会大众有足够多的机会接触无神论、接触科学理性，才是对人民群众真正负责任的表现，才是对国家和民族、对历史真正负责任的表现。

glossary.explanation: The principles of self-governance, self-support and self-propagation for Protestant churches in China, associated with the officially recognised Three-Self Patriotic Movement founded in the 1950s.
The Marxist-influenced atheist position, tied to science and rationality, that is promoted in Chinese Party and academic circles, including through education.

t: The merits and faults of atheism research and propaganda in the former Soviet Union
zh: 前苏联无神论研究、宣传教育的历史功过
paras: Gong Xuezeng takes up a question that has long divided observers inside and outside the USSR: was Soviet atheist research and education a success or a failure? The author argues that the question should be answered from a standpoint of upholding socialism and with the method of historical materialism. On that basis, Gong concludes that the programme weakened religious influence and advanced secularisation, but suffered from serious and persistent defects.

The article is confined to atheism research and propaganda, not the wider Soviet religious policy. It begins with the guiding principles of Soviet atheist education, traced through to the Programme adopted at the 27th Congress of the CPSU (1986). It then gives a historical survey in two phases: from the October Revolution to the Great Patriotic War, and from the war's end to the mid-1980s. Gong goes on to identify three features of the system and ends with an assessment of its record and of Western interpretations.

In Gong's account, the first phase was marked by combative 'anti-religious propaganda' under the League of Militant Atheists, with excesses such as mockery and administrative closure of churches that were criticised at a 1926 conference. After 1954 CPSU Central Committee resolutions, the work revived. A 1964 institute and later reforms led the 1977 constitution to replace 'anti-religious propaganda' with a right to conduct atheist propaganda. Gong stresses that secularisation owed more to socialist transformation of economy, culture and science than to atheist education. The listed failings are uneven reach, formalism and oversimplification, a focus on counting lectures over results, and disagreement over whether such education was needed at all.

Gong rejects the Western religious view, associated with the Vatican, that Soviet atheism was forcible persecution that ended in religious revival. The author says this view reflects hostility to socialism and atheism, and mixes some true material with distorted, exaggerated or fabricated claims. Gong treats the USSR's atheism work as a closed historical subject, since Russia is no longer socialist, and urges that its lessons, especially its mistakes, serve as a warning for atheism research and education in China today. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-scholarly assessment of Soviet atheist policy and the lessons it drew for China.
quoteEn: The full development of the socialist cause will inevitably lead to a gradual weakening of religion's social influence.
quoteZh: 社会主义事业的充分发展，必然导致宗教社会影响的逐步削弱。

t: On the unity of atheism research, publicity and education with freedom of religious belief
zh: 试论无神论研究宣传教育与宗教信仰自由的统一
paras: Tian Xinming takes up a practical worry inside the Party: some cadres hesitate to research and promote atheism for fear of breaching the policy of freedom of religious belief, while others argue that atheist publicity destroys that freedom. Tian's answer is that the two are not in contradiction but form a unity. The article says this unity must be explained, and then achieved through conscious effort, so that the Central Committee's position becomes the voluntary practice of cadres and the public.

The article has three parts. The first sets out four shared foundations: the Constitution, Marxist theory, objective reality and the law-governed nature of religion, and the Party's commitment to the fundamental interests of the people. The second distinguishes three pairs of concepts: religion and religious ideology, religious ideology and theism, and atheism in general and Marxist atheism. The third discusses what each side must do, citing survey figures on superstition and religious belief among students and officials.

Tian argues that the Constitution protects both belief and non-belief, so atheist research and teaching are lawful rights. Religion, in this account, is more than an ideology. It also has economic and political dimensions, so criticising theism is not 'waging war on religion'. Marxist atheism, unlike the 'old' atheism of the French materialists, analyses religion historically and holds that it can only wither away naturally as social conditions change, never by administrative force. Tian then lists misreadings of the policy. These include treating a citizen's freedom as a licence for Party members to believe, confusing 'respect' with 'approval' and 'protection' with 'promotion', and neglecting atheist education for the non-religious majority and for young people.

Tian concludes that atheist work must follow Party religious policy, avoiding propaganda in religious venues and debates among believers, which could backfire. Equally, the policy must be read correctly so that Marxist atheism is strengthened. Tian calls for atheist education in school curricula, a ban on Party members holding religious belief, and curbs on officials who promote religion for 'political achievements'. Read the original if you want a detailed statement of how Party-aligned scholarship reconciles atheist propaganda with constitutional religious freedom.
quoteEn: Religion cannot be eliminated by artificial means; it can only die out naturally when the conditions of society and history are in place.
quoteZh: 宗教不能人为地消灭，只能在社会历史条件具备时自然消亡。

glossary.explanation: A right in Article 36 of the PRC Constitution, which protects both believing and not believing in religion. The Party's policy of upholding it is the starting point of the article.

t: An inquiry into the young Marx's shift from theism to atheism
zh: 试论青年马克思从有神论到无神论的思想转变
paras: Wang Zhen asks how and why the young Marx moved from belief in God to atheism. The article argues that Marx began as a theist, as his 1835 school essays show, and that his turn to atheism took shape around 1839 and is marked by his doctoral dissertation on Democritus and Epicurus, completed in March 1842. Wang further holds that the turn was incomplete until Marx developed the materialist conception of history in 1845–46.

The article has four parts. It first sets out the historical, social and family background of Marx's early faith: Trier's religious tradition, his rabbinical ancestry, and his baptism and confirmation. It then analyses two school essays, one on the union of believers with Christ and one on choosing a profession. A third part examines the dissertation-period atheism, and a fourth explains the shift through external and internal causes.

Wang reads the early essays as theist but already carrying seeds of doubt. God sets humanity a goal, ennobling oneself and mankind, but leaves people to find the means. Marx also looks for the human causes of union with Christ, and expresses confidence in human nature and in perfection. For the later period, Wang's central claim is that Marx converted the question of God's existence into a question about the idea of God. Drawing on Epicurus, Marx treats proofs of God's existence as tautologies that really prove self-consciousness. He sees gods as particular and local, in conflict with universal reason, and he sides with philosophy against religion. On this reading Marx was attacking the masses' idle suppositions about the gods, not the gods themselves.

For external causes Wang points to the Enlightenment and the Young Hegelians' philosophy of self-consciousness. Wang also cites his liberal school in Trier and his father's deism. The internal cause is Marx's prizing of self-consciousness as active subjectivity and as universal reason. Wang concludes that this orientation set the tone for Marx's later theory of religion. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of the young Marx's early writings on religion and the sources of his break with theism.
quoteEn: Why did Marx shift from theism to atheism? The key is, first, that he turned the earlier question of God's existence into reflection on the question of the idea of God; second, that in comparing religion and philosophy he took a stance favouring philosophy and distancing himself from religion.
quoteZh: 马克思为什么会发生有神论向无神论的转变？关键在于：第一，他把原先神的存在问题转向了关于神的观念问题的思考；第二，在宗教与哲学的对比中他采取了亲哲学、远宗教的立场。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory of history, which Marx and Engels worked out in the mid-1840s, that explains social change by material production and social relations.
A Hegelian-derived current developed by the Young Hegelians, which treats human self-consciousness as the highest standard of judgement, including of religion.
A group of German philosophers in the 1830s–40s who radicalised Hegel's thought and criticised religion and politics. Marx belonged to their circle in Berlin.

t: Scientific atheism and its social responsibility
zh: 科学无神论和它的社会责任
paras: Prepared for the annual meeting of the China Atheism Society held in Xinjiang, this text by Du Jiwen answers decades of criticism of atheism and scientific atheism. Du reports that some scholars and officials charge atheism with being a legacy of the Cultural Revolution and of 'ultra-leftism', with undermining social harmony, and with opposing religious freedom. Du declines to rebut these as political accusations and argues instead that atheism is a product of labour, human nature and civilisation, and that scientific atheism has a continuing social task.

The text is organised in four sections. It defines atheism and separates spontaneous from conscious atheism; it surveys Western, Marxist and Chinese forms; it distinguishes three senses of 'religion' and analyses the ideology and social character of Christianity, with a shorter note on Buddhism; and it sets out the present role of scientific atheism in China, including the meaning of freedom of religious belief.

Du holds that belief in gods concerns truth and error, not morality or politics, but that once belief is organised into doctrine and churches it acquires ideological and social functions. Reading the Old and New Testaments, Du argues that Christian doctrine contains exclusivity, expansion and closure, which Du links to religious wars, persecution and, in China, to missionary activity tied to imperialism. Du contends that religion has no essence or history of its own, only a social one, so it must be studied through its social base. For Marxism, Du adds, atheism is the basis of its view of religion and is built on historical materialism, scientific socialism and scientific spirit, and Du credits Lenin with an epistemological critique of religion that Du says is neglected.

Du concludes that freedom of religious belief includes the freedom not to believe and to hold atheism, so that Party policy, which protects belief while propagating atheism, involves no contradiction. Du calls on scholars and cadres who treat religion as an untouchable source of stability to reconsider, and argues that atheist work should rely on the people, improve material and cultural conditions and promote a science-based way of life. On this account scientific atheism is an organic part of the scientific socialist movement. Read the original if you want a candid statement of the case for atheist propaganda within Chinese debates on religion, including its sharply critical reading of Christianity.
quoteEn: Religion truly has no essence of its own and no history of its own; its essence and history lie entirely in its social character.
quoteZh: 宗教确实没有自身的本质，也没有自身的历史，它的本质和历史全在于它的社会性

t: Socialists are practical atheists
zh: 社会主义者是实践的无神论者
paras: Xi Wuyi takes up a phrase from Engels, "socialists are practical atheists", and argues that it is a living proposition for building a Marxist theory of religion today. Writing in the period of the Scientific Outlook on Development, Xi contends that Marx was a firm atheist, that scientific atheism is the philosophical basis of the historical-materialist view of religion, and that this atheism must be developed through socialist practice. The author criticises scholars who claim to study Marx's view of religion while avoiding atheism.

The article has three parts. The first traces how Marx and Engels reached historical materialism through the critique of religion, from Epicurus in Marx's dissertation to the 1844 Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and The German Ideology. The second sets out scientific atheism: the roots, nature and social function of religion, the critique of religion as ideology, and the link between atheism and communism. The third turns to Lenin, Soviet Russia and the Chinese Communist Party's present-day policy.

Xi's central move is to read Marx's critique of religion as inseparable from the critique of politics and economics. In this reading, religious alienation is rooted in the alienation of real life, so religion is abolished by changing the social system rather than by argument alone. From Lenin, Xi draws three points: separation of church and state with freedom of belief, the party's duty to uphold and propagate atheism, and the subordination of the struggle against religion to the proletariat's overall revolutionary task. Xi warns against crude anti-religious campaigns and rejects the argument, attributed to a professor at the National School of Administration, that Communist Party members may hold religious beliefs. The author also criticises the rise of American Christian neo-fundamentalism and "universal values" as religious ideology in foreign policy.

Xi concludes that in the primary stage of socialism religion will persist for a long time and should not be abolished by administrative force. The ruling party should unite believers and non-believers, guide religion to adapt to socialist society, and hold that Party members must be atheists. Xi relates this to a harmonious society, in which atheism and theism coexist, and to a people-oriented approach in which belief is a private matter but state decisions leave no place for gods. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of religion in 2014 argues for atheism as the foundation of Marxist religious theory and Party policy.
quoteEn: The form of religion changes as its social basis changes, and it will die out as the social reality that produces the need for religion dies out; there is no need to eliminate religion by coercive means.
quoteZh: 宗教的形态随着社会基础的变化而变化，也将随着产生宗教需要的社会现实的消亡而消亡,无需通过强制的手段消灭宗教。

glossary.explanation: An official Chinese Communist Party thesis that China is in a long early phase of socialism with a mainly public-ownership economy alongside several other forms of ownership.
A Party guiding concept associated with Hu Jintao, stressing people-oriented, comprehensive and sustainable development.
A Party goal promoted in the 2000s that stresses social cohesion and the balancing of different interests.
The term used in Chinese Marxism for atheism grounded in historical materialism, as opposed to earlier Enlightenment or purely philosophical atheism.

t: Marx's critique of religious teleology deserves attention
st: On J. B. Foster's study of Marx's doctoral dissertation
zh: 应当重视马克思对宗教目的论的批判
zhSub: 评J．B．福斯特对马克思“博士论文”的研究
paras: Writing in 2014, Chen Xueming presents and endorses the American Marxist theorist John Bellamy Foster's reading of Marx's doctoral dissertation, The Difference Between the Democritean and Epicurean Philosophy of Nature. The article asks how Marx's materialism arose. It reports Foster's answer that the materialism took shape in Marx's youth, mainly through a critique of religious teleology inspired by Epicurus. Chen takes this as a corrective to attempts to detach Marx from materialism.

The commentary opens with Foster's three-part account of materialism: ontological, epistemological and practical. Foster argues that Marx's practical materialism sits within a broader materialist view of nature and science. Chen then follows Foster's case in three steps: why Marx admired Epicurus, how Marx read Epicurus's break with Democritus, and why that break remained materialist. The piece closes with Chen's own assessment of the present-day relevance of the argument.

On the first step, Foster stresses that Marx valued Epicurus above all for opposing religious teleology and driving gods out of nature. Foster treats the dissertation as more than a Hegelian exercise: written in Marx's Young Hegelian period, it already aligns with Epicurean materialism and the Anglo-French Enlightenment. On the second step, Epicurus's "swerve" of the atom lets him go beyond Democritus's mechanism and determinism by allowing contingency and freedom. Foster holds that Marx saw this as a way past a weakness of ancient materialism, which reduced thought to passive sensation. Chen stresses that Foster's main point is the third step. Surpassing mechanism can lead either to idealism or to a materialist position. Foster says Marx gives three grounds for placing Epicurus in the second camp: Epicurus never denied necessity outright, never made atoms spiritual, and joined his anti-determinism to opposition to religious teleology. Marx also criticised Epicurus for abstract possibility, which Foster reads as a sign of Marx's firm commitment to materialism.

Chen concludes that Foster's work is of real contemporary significance. In his account, many people, including some who claim the Marxist label, doubt that Marx was a materialist or that his materialism opposed religious teleology. He charges them with trying to construct a Marx whose theory is compatible with religious teleology. He argues that Foster's study corrects both doubts. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language account of Foster's interpretation of Marx's dissertation and of how Chinese Marxist scholarship uses it in debates over Marx's materialism and religion.
quoteEn: They go to every length to \"manufacture\" a Marx who does not hold to materialism and whose theory is compatible with religious teleology.
quoteZh: 他们千方百计地在“制造”一个不信奉唯物主义、其理论与宗教目的论相容的马克思。

glossary.explanation: The view that nature and the world are directed by a divine purpose or design. Marx, following Epicurus, rejected this in his dissertation.

A term for the strand of Marx's materialism that stresses human practical, transformative activity in changing society. Foster, as Chen reports, says it should not be separated from ontological and epistemological materialism.
The circle of radical followers of Hegel in 1830s–40s Germany who used his philosophy to criticise religion and politics. Marx belonged to it when he wrote his dissertation.

t: What "view of religion" and what "religious studies"? With a discussion of "academic theology" (Part 2)
zh: 是什么“宗教观”，什么“宗教学”？兼论“学术神学”（下）
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), posted 2014
paras: This is the second half of a polemical rejoinder by Du Jiwen, a scholar of religion, to an article by an advocate of "academic theology" (xueshu shenxue) in China. Du asks why such a field should be built in contemporary China and whether it is really non-confessional. The article's answer is that the case for it rests on vague, unsupported claims and that, despite its academic label, it does the same work as church theology.

The piece has three parts. Sections five and six take up two questions: the reasons given for constructing academic theology, and its claimed status as theology "outside the church". A closing section, "Words beyond the article", turns to the opponent's proposals on how the Communist Party should treat religion. Du quotes the opponent at length and answers phrase by phrase, and sets out the background to the charge that Du had exaggerated matters (shangganshangxian) in an earlier essay.

On the first question, Du doubts the claimed national "crisis of belief" and a spiritual "vacuum" to be filled by Christianity. Du calls the language of "new spiritual life" and "spiritual aura" unclear and closer to shamanism than scholarship. Du also says the claim of Christianity's rapid growth ignores secularization and the rise of atheism in the West. On the second, Du reads "outside the church" as meaning outside China's officially recognised church bodies. The opponent's globalization talk of weakened sovereignty and of Chinese becoming "world citizens", Du argues, dilutes patriotism and echoes foreign efforts to spread Christianity in China. Du adds that academic theologians still hold Christian truth claims, so their work differs from church theology only in method.

Du also rejects the proposed "dual structure" in which Party members could hold a religious faith for the afterlife and a political faith in communism for this life. Du traces the labelling of Marxism as a "faith" to Bertrand Russell's contemptuous comparison and calls the idea nonsense from a Marxist standpoint. Du also objects to treating the theism–atheism dispute as a "false problem". Du affirms respect for religious freedom and welcomes a theology built by the Chinese churches. The objection is to an academic theology placed in state education and research institutions, which Du says breaches the legal separation of education from religion. Read the original if you want a sharply worded view from inside Chinese debates on Marxism, atheism and the place of theology in the university.
quoteEn: In short, the academic theology constructed by humanistic theologians is no different from "church theology", and of course carries the same mission of salvation.
quoteZh: 简言之，人文神学家建构的学术神学，与“教会神学”，没有任何差别，当然也负有同样的拯救使命。

glossary.explanation: A proposed field of non-confessional, university-based study of Christian thought, promoted by some Chinese scholars. Du argues it is in practice confessional theology under another name.

glossary.literal: raise to the level of principle and the party line
glossary.explanation: A phrase for inflating a minor issue into a grave political or ideological one. Du's opponent used it to accuse Du of this.
The opponent's term for theology done outside the official Chinese churches. Du takes it to mean outside the officially recognised two Christian bodies.

t: What kind of "view of religion" and what kind of "religious studies"? With a discussion of "academic theology" (Part 1)
zh: 是什么“宗教观”，什么“宗教学”？兼论“学术神学”（上）
paras: Du Jiwen replies to a 6 August 2013 article in the Chinese Ethnic Group News (Zhongguo minzu bao) that attacked views he gave in an interview in issue 5 of Marxist Studies. Du had argued that religious research had been turned into propaganda, that Mao Zedong's call to "criticise theology" had largely not been carried out, and that "constructing theology" had flourished instead. He answers the critic point by point and argues that the critic's "Marxist view of religion", "religious studies" and "academic theology" are in substance Christian theology presented under Marxist labels.

This is the first instalment of a polemical reply, and the text is marked as to be continued. After a personal opening that rejects the charge of speaking without having studied the subject, and an introduction tracing "academic theology" back to Plato, it takes up four topics in the order the critic raised them: the "Marxist view of religion", "religious studies", "criticising theology", and "academic theology". Du draws on the critic's own published wording, on Max Müller, on Russell, and on d'Holbach's Pocket Theology.

Du's central moves are textual. First, he analyses the critic's opening paragraph and argues that it replaces "guidance by Marxism" as a whole with guidance by a part, a "view of religion" that the critic has framed. Second, he argues that Müller's "science of religion" was itself Christian theology, and that the critic's wide and narrow senses of "religious studies" let the field absorb atheism and give theology a legitimate academic standing. Third, he contends that treating Mao's "criticise theology" as the same as "study religion" leads, through a chain of invalid inferences, to "promoting" and then "establishing" theology.

Du also sets out the critic's outline for a systematic "academic theology", with its doctrines of God, Christ, the Holy Spirit, salvation and the church. He argues that this is imported Western theology that avoids asking whether God exists, and calls it pseudo-scholarship. He calls for the legal separation of education and religion to be applied seriously and for a return to Marxism as the guiding framework, and presents his reply as an exercise of free speech. Read the original if you want a detailed example of the hostile debate in Chinese religious studies over theology, atheism and the guiding role of Marxism, and are prepared for its sharply personal tone.
quoteEn: It has turned into a thoroughly unscientific personal attack.
quoteZh: 变成了很不科学的人身攻击。

t: Religious extremism challenges the bottom line of human civilization
zh: 宗教极端主义挑战人类文明底线
paras: This is the text of a speech Xi Wuyi gave on 22 May 2014 at a seminar on resisting religious extremism and safeguarding ethnic unity. The seminar was jointly held by the Central Institute of Socialism-style ethnic cadre training and the China Ethnic News. Xi argues that religious extremism, although a political-science concept, is best analysed by scholars of religion. In Xi's account it is the product of extremist sects degenerating, and it forms the ideological support of violent terrorism.

The speech first describes violent terrorism as a threat to human rights and national security, citing the 2001 September 11 attacks and a series of incidents in China in 2013–2014. It then turns to the ideological roots of extremism, covering the historical Kharijites, contemporary religious fundamentalism and the global spread of Wahhabism.

Xi draws on Jin Yijiu's three-way typology of extremist forces: preaching, violent-terrorist and separatist. The preaching type is called the "spiritual pillar" of the other two, which Xi says call for hard power, while preaching calls for soft power. Xi links the rise of fundamentalism after the Cold War to neoliberal ideological hegemony and the decline of secular state ideologies, and attributes Wahhabism's spread to Saudi oil money. Xi describes it as displacing Sufi traditions in Xinjiang and elsewhere and lists the doctrines extremists promote, such as martyrdom, theocracy, hostility to non-believers and rejection of modern civilization.

Xi concludes that extremist preaching differs from ordinary missionary work because it targets believers of the parent religion itself. Patriotic religious figures therefore bear a special responsibility in resisting infiltration from abroad. Xi also calls for further study of the link between Wahhabism and violent terrorism. Read the original if you want an example of how an official-academic voice in China framed religious extremism, terrorism and Xinjiang in 2014.
quoteEn: The preaching of religious extremism is different from the missionary work of religion.
quoteZh: 宗教极端主义的布道宣教与宗教的传教事业不同。

t: Religious extremist ideas are the greatest danger poisoning the healthy growth of young people
zh: 宗教极端思想是毒害青少年健康成长的最大危险
paras: Writing in 2014, Erkenjan Tulahong, a senior Xinjiang Party official, argues that religious extremist ideas are the greatest danger to the healthy development of young people in Xinjiang. Citing Xi Jinping's remarks on Xinjiang work, the author presents resisting the infiltration of such ideas into schools as a long-term struggle with hostile forces at home and abroad over "what kind of people to train and how to train them". The author calls it a serious political matter bearing on lasting stability and the Party's position as the governing party.

The piece is organised under four headings: building a strong line of defence and consolidating education as a base for training people; heightening awareness of danger; deepening understanding and holding to a bottom-line mindset; and the confidence and persistence needed for a protracted fight. It moves from a characterisation of religious extremism, through its alleged effects on Xinjiang society and schools, to measures for the education system.

Tulahong describes religious extremism as political activity under a religious disguise. In the author's account, it promotes the politicisation of religion, the label of "infidel", the idea of "holy war" and the supremacy of religion, and it contradicts the peaceful teachings of Islam. The author says it feeds the "three forces" (separatism, terrorism and extremism), seeks to win young people away from the Party, and discourages study of modern science and culture. Some teachers and students are said to waver politically, and a very small number to take part in extremist activity. The author maintains that the struggle is neither an ethnic nor a religious question but one of defending national unity.

The author calls on schools to keep education separate from religion, as set out in the Constitution and education law. Tulahong also urges stronger teaching of Marxist religious theory, Party religious policy and scientific atheism, while explaining the positive values of Islam, so that students gain "immunity" to extremist ideas. The author asks for patience, a protracted effort and open denunciation of extremists, so that schools become a front against separatism and infiltration. Read the original if you want a primary example of how a senior Xinjiang official framed religion, education and security in 2014.
quoteEn: The principle of separating education from religion is the fundamental embodiment of putting the Party's educational policy into practice, and an objective requirement for training politically qualified future successors.
quoteZh: 教育与宗教相分离的原则，是贯彻落实党的教育方针的根本体现，是培养政治上合格未来接班人的客观要求。

glossary.explanation: Official term for separatism, terrorism and religious extremism, used in Chinese policy discourse on Xinjiang and Central Asian security since the late 1990s.
The Marxist-based doctrine, promoted in Party education, that religion is a historical phenomenon that will eventually disappear as society develops.
A Party phrase for planning by identifying the worst outcomes and the limits that must not be crossed.

t: Why the United States backs Islamic extremist forces
st: Chinese translation of Seymour Hersh's "The Redirection" (The New Yorker, 2007)
zh: 美国为何支持伊斯兰恐怖主义势力
paras: This is a Chinese translation, posted in 2014 with an editors' note, of Seymour M. Hersh's investigative report "The Redirection", published in The New Yorker in May 2007. Hersh reports that, as Iraq deteriorated, the Bush administration shifted its Middle East strategy to confront Shia Iran and its allies. In doing so, he says, it would be working with Sunni states and, as a side effect, supporting Sunni extremist groups sympathetic to al-Qaeda. The Chinese editors present the piece as a key to understanding later events, including Libya, Syria, Iraq in 2014 and Xinjiang, and as exposing the true nature of the United States.

The report draws on current and former US officials, intelligence and military advisers, Saudi and Lebanese figures and think-tank experts. It moves from Washington's policy debates and planning for action against Iran, through the role of Saudi Arabia and Prince Bandar, to Lebanon, Syria and an interview with Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah. It closes on the secrecy of the operations and Congress's limited oversight.

Hersh's central claim is that the strategy was driven largely by Vice President Dick Cheney and relied on Saudi money and covert channels that bypassed normal congressional funding. He describes Saudi and US support for Lebanese government allies and Sunni groups with al-Qaeda links as a buffer against Hezbollah, and support for Syrian opposition forces including the Muslim Brotherhood. Sources quoted warn that such money ends up with dangerous actors and that extremists, once released, cannot be controlled, as in the Afghan war of the 1980s. Hersh also reports Pentagon contingency planning against Iran, accusations that Iran fuelled the Iraqi insurgency, and a former official's view that this was meant to create a pretext for action. Nasrallah, whose claims Hersh says lack supporting evidence, predicts that the region will be partitioned along sectarian lines.

Hersh concludes that the policy is risky and badly overseen. He compares it with the Iran-Contra affair, in which Bandar and Elliott Abrams also figured, and cites officials who say Congress has not been fully informed. Senator Ron Wyden is quoted saying that trusting the administration is difficult. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of the 2007 shift in US Middle East strategy and its sectarian logic, or want to see the report the Chinese editors treat as background to later regional crises.
quoteEn: Seymour M. Hersh's 2007 report is of great benefit in helping us understand more deeply the situation in the Middle East and the world since 2007, and in recognising the true nature of the United States.
quoteZh: 西摩·M·赫什的2007年的这篇报道对我们深入认识2007年以来的中东及世界局势，认清美国的本质大有裨益。

t: The Sinicization of the Marxist view of religion and its contemporary value
zh: 马克思主义宗教观的中国化及其当代价值研究
paras: Shi Xiuxin asks how the Marxist view of religion has been adapted to Chinese conditions and what value it holds today. Writing in 2014, Shi argues that this view is an open theoretical system that keeps its vitality only by moving with the times and innovating. In Shi's account, it has been re-interpreted through China's revolution, construction and reform, and has become the theoretical basis for how the Communist Party understands religion and makes religious policy.

The article has four parts. The first traces how Marx and Engels formed their view of religion, and sets out its theoretical basis and its present significance. The second describes the Chinese adaptation of this view, covering theoretical innovation, basic policies and the Party's relations with religious figures. The third discusses problems it now faces, and a short conclusion follows. Shi draws on Chinese scholarship on Marxist religious theory and on Party documents and leaders' statements.

Shi first presents Marx's position as a sublation of the Young Hegelians and a move beyond Feuerbach. Marx accepted that humans make religion, but traced its root to alienation in the state and society rather than to abstract human essence. Historical materialism is therefore the basis of the theory. Shi then argues that the Party's formula of "actively guiding religion to adapt to socialist society" is the core of the Sinicized view. Shi lists the policies tied to it: freedom of religious belief, management of religious affairs according to law, resistance to infiltration by hostile foreign forces, and unity with patriotic religious believers. Shi also credits religion with integrative, moral and cultural functions that can serve a harmonious society.

Shi identifies three current challenges: Party members who hold religious beliefs, especially in ethnic minority areas; the complexity of religion and the rise of new religious movements; and the spiritual beliefs of the roughly one billion non-believers. Shi holds that Party members must remain committed atheists. Shi also holds that religious questions can be resolved gradually only through socialist economic, cultural and scientific development, while protecting freedom of belief. The article calls on scholars to build a Marxist religious theory with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of Marxist religious theory, writing in 2014, presents official religious policy as a continuation of Marx's thought.
quoteEn: The scientific thesis of \"actively guiding religion to adapt to socialist society\" is the core and foundation of the Sinicization of the Marxist view of religion. It is the Chinese Communists' inheritance and development of that view, and an innovation in the theory of the relationship between religion and socialist society today,
quoteZh: “积极引导宗教与社会主义相适应”这一科学论断，是马克思主义宗教观中国化的核心与根本，是中国共产党人对马克思主义宗教观的继承与发展，是当代宗教与社会主义社会关系理论上的创新，

glossary.zh: 积极引导宗教与社会主义社会相适应
glossary.pinyin: jījí yǐndǎo zōngjiào yǔ shèhuì zhǔyì shèhuì xiāngshìyìng
glossary.en: actively guiding religion to adapt to socialist society
glossary.explanation: A formula in Chinese Party policy on religion, associated with the 1990s. It asks religious groups and believers to obey state law and to serve national and ethnic interests.
The policy, written into the Chinese constitution, that citizens may or may not believe in religion. In the article it sits alongside state management of religious affairs according to law.
A goal in Party discourse of the Hu Jintao period, formalised in a 2006 Central Committee decision. It stresses easing social tensions and drawing on all positive social factors.
The Hegelian and Marxist idea of Aufhebung: a prior position is both overcome and partly retained in a higher one.

t: Your brain is addicted to religion: the science of belief revealed
zh: 你的大脑对宗教成瘾：揭秘关于信仰的科学
orig: Excerpt from We Are Our Brains, published on Salon.com
source: Excerpt from We Are Our Brains, via Salon.com; posted on marxism.cass.cn, 2014
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an excerpt from We Are Our Brains by the Dutch neuroscientist Dick F. Swaab, which first appeared on Salon.com. Swaab takes up a question he finds more interesting than whether God exists: why so many people believe. He answers that religiosity is shaped by genes, early brain programming and neurochemistry, and that religion gave humans evolutionary advantages.

The excerpt opens with figures on belief and conflict. It cites the number of religions, religious civil wars since 2000, and belief rates in the United States, China and the Netherlands. It then contrasts the low religiosity of leading scientists with the general population. The main body has two parts: six evolutionary advantages of religion, and a section on the "religious brain" drawing on brain scans and clinical findings.

Swaab argues that spirituality is about 50 per cent heritable, according to twin studies, and is linked to serotonin and to a variant of the VMAT2 gene discussed by Dean Hamer. Children, he says, absorb their parents' faith as they would a mother tongue. The six advantages are group bonding, traditional benefits of rules and taboos, comfort in hardship, answers to the unknown, relief from fear of death, and licence to attack other groups. Swaab notes that evidence for health benefits is mixed and that moderately religious people fear death most. He also reports that scans of meditating monks and Carmelite nuns show activation of particular brain regions and the dopamine reward system. He adds that such findings neither prove nor disprove God. Religious fanaticism, he says, is associated with several neurological and psychiatric conditions, and what counts as "normal" varies by culture.

Swaab concludes cautiously that globalisation and the decline of war may erode religion's advantages in group cohesion and aggression. He suggests this could eventually free people from outdated religious rules, whatever they believe or do not believe. The text is published in the Science and Atheism category of the site and presents a naturalistic, atheist view of religion. Read the original if you want a popular neuroscientific and evolutionary account of religion, or want to see what atheist science writing the site carries.
quoteEn: Religion is the reshaping of our spiritual feelings by local culture.
quoteZh: 宗教是本土文化对我们的精神感受的改造。

t: Strengthening the propaganda and education of scientific atheism among Party members and cadres
zh: 加强对党员干部科学无神论的宣传教育
paras: Writing in 2014, Zhu Xiaoming, head of the China Atheism Association, asks why scientific atheism, which the author says should hold a leading place in socialist ideology, has steadily declined. The article answers that five ideological obstacles hinder research and education on the subject, and that removing them is the first task.

The piece is a short commentary that takes the five obstacles in turn, drawing on Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme, Lenin's "On the Significance of Militant Materialism", Mao Zedong, Hu Jintao's 2003 instruction and the Party's 1982 Document No. 19 on religious work. It closes by linking the topic to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013).

Zhu's central move is to separate the citizen's private freedom of belief from the ruling party's ideological stance. Freedom of religious belief, the author argues, includes the freedom not to believe and to propagate atheism. Religion is a private matter for the state but not for a Marxist party, which must uphold materialism and atheism to keep its purity and advanced character. Zhu adds that general Marxist education cannot replace dedicated atheist education, that atheism is not shallow, and that promoting it does not conflict with religious policy provided it avoids hurting religious feelings. A patriotic united front with believers in political action, the author says, does not mean endorsing idealism.

Zhu urges united front and religious affairs cadres to work from the standpoint of Marxism and scientific atheism and with the whole of society in view, including non-believers. The article presents the Third Plenum's emphasis on socialist core values, cultural soft power and Marxism's leading ideological position as a new opportunity for atheist research. Read the original if you want to see how a leading atheist organisation reconciled Party atheism with the policy of religious freedom in 2014.
quoteEn: As individuals, people are free to choose their beliefs; as a society, guidance and management are needed.
quoteZh: 作为个人，信仰自由选择；作为社会，需要引导管理。

glossary.explanation: A basic Chinese policy and constitutional principle. The article reads it as covering both the freedom to believe and the freedom not to believe.
The Party's long-standing strategy of building political alliances with non-Party groups, here with patriotic religious believers, around common goals.

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: An official framework of values that the Party promotes as the ideological basis of society. The article argues that atheism's humanist and scientific spirit belongs within it.

t: Carrying on the past and opening up the future: striving to create a new situation for the cause of scientific atheism
st: Work report of the Third Council of the China Atheism Association
zh: 继往开来，努力开创科学无神论事业的新局面
zhSub: 中国无神论学会第三届理事会工作报告
source: Posted on marxism.cass.cn, 19 March 2014; Science and Atheism category
paras: This is a work report delivered by Xi Wuyi on behalf of the Third Council of the China Atheism Association to the Fourth Members' Congress, covering the council's term from November 2005 to August 2013. It also mourns the deaths of the association's president Ren Jiyu and vice-president Guo Zhengyi. Xi argues that scientific atheism has made real institutional progress with Party backing, but remains an endangered discipline facing foreign religious infiltration, shortages of staff and funds, and a need for deliberate strategic building.

The report has three parts. The first reviews the history of the cause since 1978: a series of Party instructions and documents from 2003 to 2013, two "windows of opportunity" (the late 1990s and winter 2009 to spring 2010), and the work of the association, the journal Science and Atheism, and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) research centre and office. The second analyses current threats and tasks. The third sets out the responsibilities of scientific atheism workers.

Xi's central claim is that scientific atheism belongs to the Party's ideological work and to the "core socialist value system".
