The report describes overseas religious forces, above all the American Christian right, as pursuing "legitimate infiltration" through cultural exchange, scholarship and campus evangelism, which Xi calls cultural colonization. In this account, Christian theology entering universities challenges the legal separation of education and religion. Xi therefore supports the position that Communist Party members cannot hold religious belief, while also stating that belief is a private matter and that religious believers are not to be treated with hostility. The report criticises scholars who promote "cultural theology" and who, in Xi's words, try to remove atheism from the Marxist view of religion.

Xi concludes that scientific atheism needs a proper disciplinary system. The report proposes a national "scientific atheism discipline innovation project" led by CASS, dedicated research bodies in universities and Party schools, master's and doctoral programmes, and targeted funding and source materials. It calls training younger scholars the most urgent task, noting that the current researchers are ageing and few. Read the original if you want a first-hand account, from within the atheism research community, of how scientific atheism was institutionalised in China and how its advocates framed religion, ideology and national security around 2013.
quoteEn: In contemporary Chinese academia, scientific atheism has not yet formed an independent disciplinary system.
quoteZh: 在当代中国学术界，科学无神论还没有形成独立的学科体系。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-based form of atheism promoted in China as a worldview and an academic discipline. The report treats it as the philosophical foundation of Party ideology and as a field in need of institutional support.

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: An official formulation of the main values of Chinese socialism, promoted by the Party in the 2000s. The report places scientific atheism at its philosophical base.
A principle written into China's constitution and education law, barring religion from the state education system. The report cites it against campus evangelism.

t: Why we must uphold atheism
zh: 我们为什么要坚持无神论
paras: This text is a edited transcript of a speech given by Zhu Weiqun, director of the Ethnic and Religious Affairs Committee of the national CPPCC, on 18 August 2013 at the Fourth Congress of the Chinese Atheism Society; it was revised by Zhu and published in 2014. Zhu observes that the ruling Party's dialectical materialist worldview has recently been met with neglect and mockery, and that atheism as a discipline is nearly endangered. He answers the question in the title by giving three reasons why atheism must be upheld, followed by practical requirements.

The speech first sets out the three reasons: atheism is the foundation of the Party's worldview, it is a deep-rooted tradition in Chinese culture, and it is needed to counter a growing range of anti-scientific phenomena. It then turns to what upholding atheism requires: Party self-discipline and education, mass education and propaganda, higher standards among atheist scholars, and a link to the united front with religious circles. Zhu illustrates the last point with the campaign against self-immolations in Tibetan areas.

Zhu argues that atheism is the starting point of historical and dialectical materialism, written into the Party constitution, and that removing it would bring down the Party's theoretical edifice and change its nature. He contends that China has historically been a secular state and culture, so that religion there has been less fanatical, and that claims that only theism supplies morality or that China needs religious "catch-up lessons" are myths. In his account, superstition among officials (consulting feng shui masters, worshipping spirits while embezzling) and the rise of cults and "masters" have a common root in belief in supernatural forces, which past campaigns have rarely addressed at the level of worldview.

Zhu calls for atheism education in Party training, in schools and textbooks, and on campuses, where he wants proselytising stopped, citing the Constitution and the Education Law. He also calls for atheist scholars to answer "scientific theism" with broader scientific and religious knowledge. He stresses that atheist propaganda should not set believers against non-believers or demand that they abandon their faith, and that the aim is political unity and mutual respect in belief. He describes cooperation with Buddhist figures against self-immolation as a model. Read the original if you want a senior official's own account of Party policy on atheism, religion and the united front in the early 2010s.
quoteEn: If the Party cannot hold fast to its own worldview, it will not be able to hold fast to its own cause.
quoteZh: 党如果不能坚持住自己的世界观，就不可能坚持住自己的事业。

glossary.explanation: The Party's policy of building alliances with non-Party groups, including religious circles, around shared political goals. Zhu uses it to describe cooperation with religious believers and clergy alongside atheist education.

The philosophical foundation of Marxism as taught in China, holding that matter is primary and develops dialectically. Together with historical materialism, it is stated as the Party's worldview in its constitution.
A national academic society for the study and promotion of atheism, in whose Fourth Congress the speech was delivered.

glossary.literal: National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference
glossary.explanation: The Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, a national advisory body that brings together Party and non-Party figures and is part of the united front system.

t: Studying religious policy and doing religious work well
zh: 学习宗教政策 做好宗教工作
paras: Zhu Weiqun presents an overview of the Communist Party's religious policy, apparently drawn from a talk or lecture (the text does not state the occasion). Posted in March 2014, it argues that the Party's approach to religion has proved correct in the course of reform and opening up, but that new circumstances demand that theory, policy and practice be kept up to date. Zhu describes the work ahead as arduous, complex and long-term.

The text begins with a survey of China's main religions (Buddhism, Daoism, Islam, Catholicism and Protestantism) and gives the author's figures for clergy and believers. It then sets out three historical features that Zhu treats as present-day advantages: state authority standing above religion, tolerance among religions, and a population that is mostly non-religious and focused on this life. The longer middle section examines the four-part basic guideline on religious work, and the final sections deal with disorderly religious growth and with foreign infiltration.

Zhu argues that the Party's contribution lies in a complete set of policies for a ruling party, and that three of the four clauses of the guideline were the Party's own creation. These clauses are the freedom of religious belief, the management of religious affairs according to law, the principle of independence and self-administration, and the guiding of religion to adapt to socialist society. Freedom of belief, in Zhu's account, rests on the Marxist view that religion will disappear only when its roots do, so administrative force cannot abolish it; it includes freedom not to believe, and Zhu rejects the claim that only believers in power can guarantee it. Zhu also calls for tackling excessive religious growth, citing local officials who build temples for profit. In Zhu's view, atheist education and legal management are compatible with freedom of belief. Zhu rejects treating religion simply as culture, or as a core or 'universal' value. Zhu describes foreign infiltration, naming Vatican interference, extremist forces, the Dalai Lama clique and Western use of Protestantism, as the hardest task, and stresses limits: the aim is not to oppose religion in general.

Zhu concludes that religious work needs firm management, support for religious bodies' own efforts to adapt to socialism, and clear policy limits so that more people can be united against infiltration. Zhu says restricting illegal preaching does not mean requiring believers to give up their faith, or refusing to employ foreign teachers who hold religious beliefs. Read the original if you want an authoritative account of how a senior Party figure explained China's religious policy in 2014, including its history, its legal framework and its handling of foreign influence.
quoteEn: We implement and uphold the policy of freedom of religious belief because it accords with the laws governing the development of religious phenomena and with the fundamental interests of the people and the state.
quoteZh: 我们实行和坚持宗教信仰自由政策，是因为这一政策符合宗教现象发展规律，符合人民和国家的根本利益

glossary.explanation: The policy, enshrined in China's constitution, that citizens may believe, not believe, or change their religion. The Party presents it as compatible with atheist education and state management of religious affairs.

The principle that Chinese religious bodies and affairs should be run by Chinese believers without control by foreign forces. It grew out of the anti-imperialist religious movements of the early 1950s.

glossary.zh: 宗教与社会主义社会相适应
glossary.pinyin: zōngjiào yǔ shèhuì zhǔyì shèhuì xiāng shìyìng
glossary.explanation: The Party's guideline that religions should adjust themselves to socialist society and obey its laws, and contribute positively to it. It forms the fourth clause of the basic guideline on religious work.

glossary.en: management of religious affairs according to law
glossary.explanation: The principle that religious activities, venues and organisations are regulated by law, notably the 2004 Regulations on Religious Affairs, while personal belief remains free.

t: Science and Atheism, 2013, no. 3 (issue 83): table of contents
zh: 《科学与无神论》2013年第3期（总第83期）
paras: This is not an article but the table of contents of issue no. 3 (cumulative no. 83) of the journal Science and Atheism, published in 2013. It lists thirteen items and a back-cover feature, with no abstracts or argument, so the issue's themes can only be read from the titles.

The first group of items concerns scientific atheism in higher education and student belief. Li Shen writes against vulgarising the 'two-sided' (two-point) approach. He Husheng discusses the main content of Marxist scientific atheism education in universities. Other items include a survey of students' interest in star signs (Li Zhiying), an analysis of the present state, causes and countermeasures of students' religious belief (Ma Yutang and Zhang Jiuxian), and a call to strengthen scientific atheism to resist religious proselytising in campus culture (Yang Junfeng).

A second group deals with superstition, science and religion. Ma Jinfei offers an explanation of superstitious behaviour based on control-strategy theory, and Zuo Peng treats the merging and separation of science and religion. Sun Qian asks how the universe relates to God. Yun Peiji's piece cautions against believing in the Duke of Zhou's dream interpretation.

The remaining items are historical and social. They include Zhao Guangqing on Emperor Guangwu and prophetic apocrypha, Zhang Yingshan's translation of part two of a history of materialism, Huang Chao on the religious-ideological roots of the American anti-Chinese movement, and Chen Qingping on a social early-warning model against cult-group activity. The back cover carries a feature on the image of non-religious people: atheists, sceptics and secularists. Read the original if you want a quick view of the topics the journal covered in 2013, such as scientific atheism, campus religion and superstition.
quoteEn: On the main content of Marxist scientific atheism education in universities
quoteZh: 论高校马克思主义科学无神论教育的主要内容

t: Science and Atheism, 2013, no. 3 (issue 83): table of contents
zh: 《科学与无神论》2013年第3期（总第83期）
paras: This is the table of contents of issue no. 3 (cumulative no. 83) of the journal Science and Atheism, published in 2013. It is not an article and contains no argument, only the titles and authors of thirteen pieces and a back-cover feature.

The listed items cluster around several themes. Several deal with atheism education and religion among university students, including Li Zhiying's survey of students and astrology, a study by Ma Yutang and Zhang Jiuxian on students' religious belief, and He Husheng's piece on the main content of Marxist scientific atheism education in universities. Yang Junfeng's title concerns strengthening scientific atheism and resisting proselytising in campus culture.

Other titles address the relation between science and religion (Zuo Peng; Sun Qian on the universe and God), superstition and its explanation (Ma Jinfei, applying control-strategy theory; Yun Peiji on the Duke of Zhou's dream interpretation), and history, including Zhao Guangqing on Emperor Guangwu and prophetic texts, Huang Chao on the religious-ideological roots of the American anti-Chinese movement, and a translated instalment of a history of materialism by Zhang Yingshan. The first item is Li Shen's piece on not vulgarising the "two-sided approach", and Chen Qingping proposes a social early-warning model against cult activity. The back cover is titled "The image of the non-religious: atheists, sceptics and secularists".

Because only titles are given, the contents and positions of the individual pieces cannot be described. Read the original if you want a quick overview of the topics a Chinese scientific-atheism journal covered in mid-2013, or need the authors and titles for tracing individual articles.
quoteEn: He Husheng: On the main content of Marxist scientific atheism education in universities
quoteZh: 何虎生 论高校马克思主义科学无神论教育的主要内容

t: The formation of Chinese anti-religious theory: an analysis of the anti-religion discourse of the 1920s
zh: 中国反宗教理论的成型：1920年代非宗教话语分析
paras: Yang Weihua asks when Chinese anti-religious theory took definitive shape and what that theory consisted of. The article argues that the 1920s were the formative period: later anti-religious discourse in China, including that of the People's Republic, added no new theoretical elements. In Yang's account, political discourse dominated the decade, above all the claim that religion is a tool of imperialist aggression, so that the critique was in effect "a critique wrapped in politics".

The study is a textual analysis of discourse produced during the organised non-religion and anti-Christian movements, which began around the 1922 World Student Christian Federation conference at Tsinghua. It has three parts. The first sets out the value orientations behind the critique, the second examines which social groups used the discourse and how they differed, and the third traces the sources, influence and evaluation of these ideas. Evidence comes mainly from declarations, periodicals, Communist Party documents and speeches by figures such as Li Dazhao, Cai Yuanpei, Qu Qiubai and Liao Zhongkai.

Yang identifies four orientations: religion as a tool of national oppression (imperialism), as a tool of class oppression, as superstition opposed to science and reason, and as a destroyer of mind and body that obstructs individual liberation. Groups used them unevenly. Students and the Socialist Youth League were the main force. The Communist Party deployed all four, the Nationalists mostly opposed Christianity on anti-imperialist political grounds, and the intellectuals in the middle leaned on science and individual freedom. On sources, Yang says the "opium" and "narcotic" theories and class analysis came from Marx and Lenin, and the scientific rationalism came from the Enlightenment and the New Culture Movement. The imperialist-tool theory, by contrast, was a local product of rising nationalism and of triumphalist missionary slogans, with no equivalent in Russia or the West.

Yang credits the movement with deepening awareness of imperialism and of "cultural aggression", and with prompting some Christians to reform. The author also finds the critique reasonable in part, given the era's national crisis. Yang adds that it was slogan-like and emotional, rarely engaged with religion itself, and tended to reject everything connected with Christianity. The author regards academic objections as beside the point, since reality demanded a politically oriented critique. Read the original if you study the intellectual history of Chinese atheism, the anti-Christian movement, or the roots of later Chinese views of religion.
quoteEn: So to a certain extent, it was a critique wrapped in politics.
quoteZh: 所以从某种程度上而言，它是一种政治包裹中的批判。

t: Religion cannot support the values of modern society
zh: 宗教支撑不起现代社会价值
paras: Writing in 2014, Shen Guiping takes up a question raised by social problems in fast-growing China: counterfeiting, corruption, social indifference, ethnic-religious disputes and violent terrorism. Because these have produced moral crisis and loss of belief, some people look to religion for comfort and for value support. Shen answers firmly that religion cannot resolve the problems of modernization or rescue society from crisis.

This short commentary first sets out the social functions of religion and its two-sided character. It then looks at the Western experience of Enlightenment and secularisation, turns to the place of religion in contemporary China, and ends with the relation between rule of law and core values.

Shen argues that religion can stabilise society but can also divide ethnic groups, dull the public mind and obstruct reform. Citing Max Weber's "disenchantment of the world", Shen holds that Western modernization meant leaving religious control behind, leaving faith in the private sphere while faith in law became the public consensus. In China, Shen invokes the historical-materialist view that people create religion and social development determines religious development. Shen also cites Ren Jiyu to stress that religion rests on blind belief rather than reason. Rule of law, Shen says, rests on shared core values: in China, socialist core values of fairness, justice, equality and inclusiveness.

Shen concludes that society may acknowledge the guiding role of religious values for some citizens, but should not promote religion as the foundation of civilisation or as a core value. Building industrial strategy on religious culture or social values on religious ethics, Shen warns, would heighten tension between religions. The ruling Party must therefore remain clear-headed, resolute and forceful in handling religion's social role. Read the original if you want a concise statement of an official-academic position on religion and core values in China in the early 2010s.
quoteEn: In the modernization of contemporary Chinese society, religion likewise does not serve as a value foundation or play an important guiding or dominant role.
quoteZh: 宗教在当代中国社会现代化发展中同样不具有价值支撑、重要引领或者主导性作用。

glossary.explanation: An official set of values promoted by the Chinese Party-state as the shared ideological basis of society. Shen describes them here as fairness, justice, equality and inclusiveness.
Chinese rendering of Max Weber's Entzauberung der Welt, the process by which rational explanation displaces religious and magical worldviews in modern society.

t: How to view religious issues and what to do about them
st: An interview with Wang Zuo'an, director of the State Administration for Religious Affairs
zh: 宗教问题怎么看怎么办
paras: This is a question-and-answer interview, posted in January 2014, with Wang Zuo'an, who is introduced as director of the State Administration for Religious Affairs. The reporter asks why religion draws growing attention in China and how it should be understood. Wang answers that rising numbers of believers, complications in the religious sphere and religion's wider social influence require correct handling, and that they also raise a deeper question about Chinese people's beliefs.

The interview works through three questions Wang says must be settled: how to see the growth in believers, how to see religion's social role, and how to see the mass of believers. It then turns to the policy of freedom of religious belief and to the lawful administration of religious affairs. Wang gives figures, comparisons with other countries and practical examples of administration and services.

Wang says the commonly cited figure of "over 100 million" believers is a mix of statistics and estimates, and that the real number is probably higher. He attributes the growth to recovery after the Cultural Revolution, foreign influence and, above all, deep social change, stratification and uncertainty. He judges the situation "basically orderly" and "basically stable", comparing it favourably with the former Soviet Union and with Europe and America. Religion, he argues, will exist for a long time and may grow, so believer numbers can be neither forced down nor promoted. Citing the Marxist view of religion, he describes its social role as dual, and says believers are part of "the masses" whose basic political and economic interests match those of non-believers. Impatient attempts to "liberate" them from religion would be counterproductive. Freedom of belief rests on three adherences: freedom to believe or not, separation of religion and state, and unity of rights and duties.

Wang concludes that religious affairs should be managed by law: by bringing them within the legal system, setting clear rules under the Regulations on Religious Affairs, tackling difficult cases such as infiltration, and providing services. He gives examples such as social security for clergy and infrastructure for places of worship. He also stresses protecting lawful religious rights against forced demolition and against temples being commercialised or contracted out. Read the original if you want an official statement of how China's religious affairs chief explained policy on believers, religious freedom and legal administration around 2014.
quoteEn: Believers are also part of the masses; we should treat them as we treat the masses, without discrimination and without prejudice.
quoteZh: 信教群众也是群众，我们怎么对待群众，就应该怎么对待他们，不能有歧视，不能有偏见。

glossary.explanation: In Wang's usage, state power is kept apart from religious organisations. The state protects normal religious activity and manages affairs by law, while religion may not interfere in administration, justice or education.
The State Council regulations governing religious bodies, venues, clergy and activities in China. Wang says detailed rules should be built on them.
The government body responsible for administering religious affairs in China, headed by Wang at the time of the interview.
A standard Party term for ordinary religious followers, treated as part of the people whom the Party seeks to unite and rely on.

t: On the Marxist study of religion in China
zh: 关于我国宗教学的马克思主义研究
source: Originally in International Confucian Studies (Guoji Ruxue Yanjiu), vol. 15; reposted on marxism.cass.cn in 2013
paras: Du Jiwen asks what a Marxist study of religion in China should look like and how it began. The article answers through the work of Ren Jiyu, founding director of the Institute of World Religions, and argues that Marxist religious studies must rest on solid knowledge, historical-materialist analysis, scientific atheism and intellectual independence. Du presents it as a personal view, written to mark Ren's 90th birthday.

The essay has five parts. It starts from Mao Zedong's directive proposing the Institute and then examines Ren's Buddhist studies, which Mao held up as a model. It goes on to the Institute's work in collecting materials, training scholars and building disciplines through history, theory and reference works. Du then discusses scientific atheism and the journal Science and Atheism, and ends on independence in research. A note says the piece was first given as a 2006 conference talk and was later printed in a shortened form. This version restores the cut passages.

Du's first main move reads Mao's directive as a call for knowledge of religion and for Marxist analysis, not for crude denunciation. Ren's method is described as treating religion as a product of social existence and the economic base. It also credits the active role of consciousness, and offers "critique" as reasoned, historicist evaluation in the sense of sublation, not the mass denunciation of the Cultural Revolution. Du cites the Religious Dictionary (1981), the History of Chinese Buddhism and the multi-volume world religious histories as outcomes. The author reports that Japanese and Taiwanese scholars and publishers recognised their scholarly value. Du's second move defends atheism as inseparable from serious religious research. Du defines Marxist atheism as a philosophical and scientific critique of the worldview of theology and of belief in spirits, and as training in correct thinking. Religious belief remains a citizen's right, but Du says China lacks science, not spirits.

Du concludes that the Institute is a research body, neither a religious organisation nor an administrative office. Its work should accord politically with patriotic religious groups and government departments while being academically original. Du argues that independence needs material support, and criticises policies of "income generation" and "pushing research into the market" as damaging to scholarship. The essay treats patriotism as the bottom line of Marxist research and closes with a polemic against a Chinese commentator who urged the US president to bring political change to China. Read the original if you want an insider's account of the Institute of World Religions, Ren Jiyu's methods, and the case for scientific atheism within Chinese Marxist religious studies.
quoteEn: Atheism is not simply denying gods or not believing in them; it should also involve learning and teaching correct methods of thinking and a correct outlook on life and values, linked to the overall progress of science and society.
quoteZh: 无神论并不是简单地否认神，不信神，而且应该学习和教人以正确的思维方法，正确的人生观和价值观，与科学和社会的整体进步衔接起来。

glossary.explanation: A research institute of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, founded in the 1960s following a proposal by Mao Zedong. Ren Jiyu was its first director.
The Hegelian and Marxist notion (Aufhebung) of overcoming something while preserving its valuable elements. Du uses it to describe what Marxist critique of religion should mean.
Atheism presented as grounded in science and philosophy and as part of Marxist research. Du treats it as an independent academic field.

t: Be vigilant against the cultural infiltration of the international Christian right
zh: 警惕国际基督教右翼势力的文化渗透
paras: Writing in 2013, Xi Wuyi asks how foreign religious forces threaten China's security and what response is needed. The author argues that the global expansion strategy of American Christian neoconservatism has become a tool of US hegemony, that China is its key target, and that its aim is to change China's ideology and political system. Xi concludes that China must pay particular attention to the "legal infiltration" of the overseas Christian right and must build up the discipline of scientific atheism.

The article defines religious infiltration in three parts: hostile forces using religion to subvert the state; foreign religious bodies seeking to control Chinese religious groups or set up bases; and right-wing religious forces working through "cultural exchange" and "academic research". It is organised in five sections: the global strategy of Christian neoconservatism; its intentions towards China; the resulting threat to national security; legal infiltration in universities and scholarship; and the case for scientific atheism. Evidence includes the 1998 International Religious Freedom Act, US State Department reports, a 2006 White House meeting with house-church figures, campus evangelism, internet missionary work and Templeton-funded lectures.

Xi contends that after the Cold War "religious freedom" was made the cornerstone of a human-rights discourse that serves US national interests, citing the 1998 Act as a form of "faith-based diplomacy". In Xi's reading, the Western aim is to "peacefully evolve" China through support for house churches, campus fellowships and online evangelism, which the author calls cultural colonisation. The most subtle channel, Xi argues, is academic: foundations such as the Templeton Foundation fund talks and books claiming that modern science depends on Christianity, which Xi says have reached leading Chinese universities and been echoed by Chinese scholars. Xi counters with Engels on medieval theology, the Galileo case and the Enlightenment critique of religion.

Xi argues that scholarship in China has tilted towards "carefully protecting" religion, that scientific atheism has almost no voice, and that some authorities try to separate atheism from Marxism. The author calls for a systematic scientific atheism discipline, linked to historical and dialectical materialism, the core socialist value system and Party religious policy, as the theoretical weapon against foreign religious infiltration. Xi adds that ideological work should be gentle and persuasive. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of atheism framed foreign Christianity as a security and ideological issue in 2013.
quoteEn: Foreign forces' promotion of Christianity in China is in essence a form of cultural colonisation and ideological infiltration.
quoteZh: 境外势力推动基督教在我国传播，实质上是一种文化殖民和意识形态渗透。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist-materialist approach to the study and propagation of atheism, treated in Chinese scholarship as part of Marxist religious theory. Xi seeks to develop it as an academic discipline.
Protestant congregations meeting outside the state-sanctioned Three-Self Patriotic Movement churches; the article calls them illegal gatherings.

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: An official formulation of the guiding values of socialism with Chinese characteristics, promoted from the mid-2000s.

t: Strengthening the discipline of scientific atheism to resist "cultural proselytizing" on campus
zh: 加强科学无神论学科建设，抵御校园文化传教
paras: Writing in 2013, Yang Junfeng asks how scientific atheism can respond to what the article calls "cultural proselytizing" in universities and research institutions. Yang argues that religious theism is spreading into education and research with funding from religious bodies and overseas forces. In this account, scientific atheism's voice has almost vanished from academia and schooling, so that "theism has speakers, atheism has none", as in the 1990s. The article's answer is that the discipline of scientific atheism itself must be strengthened.

The article has two parts. The first argues that atheism is by nature a body of thought that keeps pace with the times. The second sets out four proposals for building the discipline. Yang draws on Engels's Anti-Dühring and Marx's Capital for the roots of religion. The article also looks back at the 1990s "qigong fever" and the Falun Gong affair, citing Ren Jiyu's criticism of pseudo-science.

Yang's central claim is that atheism has no content of its own beyond negating and criticising theism. It must therefore change whenever theism changes. The article traces atheism from ancient naive atheism through early modern militant atheism to Marxist atheism. Yang says only the last explains the real roots of religion, and that superstition keeps returning in new disguises, such as "national learning fever" today. The proposals are: (1) answer modern Western theology directly and academically, through "internal critique" rather than slogans, on five issues: the origin of faith, religion and culture, religion and morality, religion and science, and specific doctrines such as "intelligent design" and the "religious market" theory; (2) publicise the policy of separating education from religion and strengthen atheist education in schools; (3) give atheism a positive content, offering answers on life's meaning and moral foundations as well as criticism; (4) update basic theory, since the two standard histories of atheism, from 1992 and 1993, are dated and the field's only journal is outside the core-journal indexes.

Yang concludes that atheism's strength depends on whether it can respond squarely to the theism of its day, as Epicurus, Fan Zhen, Hume and Russell did. Yang also calls for atheism to propose its own solutions to social problems such as food-safety scandals and corruption. Some scholars, the article says, blame atheist education for a loss of belief. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic atheist's own account of the 2013 debate over religion in universities, and of the programme proposed for rebuilding scientific atheism.
quoteEn: There must be not only "demolition" but also "construction".
quoteZh: 不仅要有“破”，而且要有“立”。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist form of atheism taught and researched in China. It treats religion as a product of definite natural, social, cognitive and psychological conditions and aims to criticise theism on that basis.
A term used by the author and others for religious outreach carried out through academic seminars, translated theology, courses and lectures. It is not official policy vocabulary.

t: Why Communist Party members cannot hold religious belief
zh: 共产党员为什么不能信仰宗教
paras: Writing in 2013, Li Shen defends the principle that Communist Party members should not believe in religion. The article's single ground for the principle is that gods do not exist. Li argues that a Communist who wants to make revolution and secure human happiness cannot coherently seek help from a non-existent deity or embrace a religion built on belief in one.

The piece has three numbered sections. The first traces the history of divine figures, from animal gods to composite creatures, deified heroes and kings, and finally the purely spiritual gods of the civilised era. The second looks at how new gods have always displaced old ones, at the eighteenth-century European break that denied the existence of gods altogether, and at the claim that atheists cannot disprove God. The third turns to the origin of religious doctrine and to present-day calls for Party members to be religious.

Li's central claim is that human beings, finding that each kind of god failed to deliver the promised happiness, learned that they can rely only on themselves. Responding to the argument that atheists cannot prove a negative, Li says the burden lies with those who assert the existence of a god, and that the history of changing ideas of the divine shows gods to be non-existent. Li also points to Anselm and Thomas Aquinas: a proof of God's existence is needed only because some doubt it, and Tillich is cited as saying that arguing for God's existence is itself a profanation. All "divine will", Li holds, is in fact human will, that of shamans, theologians and clergy, and religions that were once progressive turn backward because they present their ideas as eternal truth.

Li rejects the view that religion improves morality, drives science or widens the Party's base of support. Li notes that the people urging Party members to believe are mainly Party members themselves, some of them scholars or senior cadres, who take part in religious activities or have become believers, and calls for special attention to this. Such talk, Li concludes, is either ill-intentioned or confused, and must be resolutely resisted. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the atheist argument against Party members holding religious belief, as it was put in China in 2013.
quoteEn: Gods do not exist. A Communist who wants to make revolution and secure happiness for humankind: how could such a person turn for help to a god who does not exist, or believe in a religion whose intellectual foundation is the existence of gods?
quoteZh: 神是不存在的。一个共产党员，要革命，要为人类谋幸福，又怎么能够去求助那个并不存在的神祇，去信仰那个以神的存在为思想基础的宗教呢!

t: China's humanist tradition and the spirit of atheism
zh: 中国的人本主义传统和无神论精神
paras: Du Jiwen asks what distinguishes the Chinese religious and moral tradition from the monotheist West, and answers that China has long been "human-centred" rather than "god-centred". Where Western humanism is tied to the Renaissance, Du argues that Chinese humanism was already forming in ancient civilisation. It rests on two principles: in the relation of heaven and humans, "the human is the root"; in the relation of ruler and people, "the people are most precious". Du calls this the key to understanding China's whole history and present.

The article, published on this site in 2013 under the category of science and atheism, has three parts. It first describes the humanist features of traditional Chinese religion (Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist). It then traces the move from humanism to atheism, from Buddhism's adaptation in China through the late Qing and the May Fourth movement. Finally it examines Confucian answers to the origins of morality, before turning to the present-day state.

Du's core argument has three moves. First, in China the sacred is made by humans, anyone can become a sage or immortal, and gods are created and discarded by people. On this basis Du claims China had no religious hatred, persecution or wars, and that polytheism and atheism coexisted. Second, Du holds that morality in the tradition is secular. Buddhism succeeded because it fitted this ethos, whereas Christianity's exclusive monotheism kept it from taking root; efforts at "saving the nation through religion" failed, while science and democracy changed China. Third, Du reads Confucian sources (Guanzi, the Liji, Mencius, Xunzi) as explaining morality by living conditions, distribution, social system and human nature, never by gods.

Du concludes that the new China inherits this tradition: the state is founded and its constitution made according to the people's will, with power belonging to the people. In Du's account, believers and non-believers have equal rights and duties, belief is a private matter, but there is no place for gods in state decision-making. Read the original if you want a Chinese atheist scholar's account of how traditional Chinese culture is used to ground secular politics and religious policy.
quoteEn: Whether to believe in a religion should be entirely a private matter, equally protected and respected; but in state decision-making there is no place for God or gods.
quoteZh: 信不信教，应该完全成为个人的私事，得到平等地保护和尊重；但在国家决策上，没有上帝和神灵的位置。

glossary.pinyin: rén wéi běn, mín wéi guì
glossary.literal: humans as the root, the people as most precious
glossary.explanation: Du's shorthand for Chinese humanism. The second half echoes Mencius's idea that the people rank above the ruler.

t: Scientific atheism and its social responsibilities (Part 2)
zh: 科学无神论及其社会职责（下）
paras: This is the second half of a two-part article by Du Jiwen. It asks what "religion" actually consists of and what scientific atheism should do about it today. Du argues that theism is the core of every religion, but that a religion's historical character and social function come from the ideology and organisation attached to that core, not from belief itself. On that basis Du presents scientific atheism as compatible with freedom of religious belief and as a lasting task.

Part 3 separates three senses of "religion": religious ideas, religious practices, and organised, ideologised religion. It then uses historical cases (Zoroastrianism, Buddhism in India and Central Asia, the decline and expansion of Christianity) and a close reading of the Bible and of Buddhist scriptures. Part 4 turns to the historical role of atheism in the West, to current religious and political conditions in China, to the history of religion in China, and to the Chinese Communist Party's stance.

Du contends that only the third sense has a social character and that it obeys historical laws, so religions have a "historicity" and "changeability" rather than permanence or ethnic essence. Du reads the Old and New Testaments as adding doctrines to belief in God: original sin and redemption, absolute exclusivity and expansionism, and internal closure. Du says these supply the basis for religious wars, persecution and missionary drives, and that the New Testament's "love" amounts to a duty to convert. Buddhism is described as milder but also exclusive in places. Du holds that Western atheism targeted Christianity, while Christianity changed its service from divine authority to capital.

On China, Du claims that religious persecution and religious wars are absent from its history, and that religion became a serious problem only with Christian expansion after the Opium War. Du warns that some Party members and officials treat religion as untouchable and atheism as an offence, and says central policy on atheistic research and education has not changed. Du calls freedom of belief inclusive of the freedom to hold atheism. Scientific atheism should protect the core of belief, weaken exclusive ideology, raise citizens' independence, and help improve people's material and cultural lives. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese scholar of religion argues for the compatibility of Party atheism and religious freedom, with detailed critical readings of Christian and Buddhist texts.
quoteEn: Only when people are economically self-sufficient can they be independent in personality; only when they are independent in personality can they effectively free themselves from the bonds of religion.
quoteZh: 只有经济上自给了，才有人格上的独立；只有人格上独立了，才能有效地摆脱宗教的束缚。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-materialist form of atheism promoted in Chinese academic and Party discourse. It combines criticism of theism with scientific and educational work on the social roots of belief.
A citizen's right, written into the Chinese Constitution, to believe or not to believe in a religion. Du stresses that it includes the freedom to hold atheism.

t: Scientific atheism and its social responsibilities (Part 1)
zh: 科学无神论及其社会职责（上）
paras: Du Jiwen responds to the poor reputation that atheism, and scientific atheism in particular, has acquired in recent decades. Prompted by the Chinese atheism annual conference held in Xinjiang, Du notes that the attacks come not from religious circles but from some scholars and officials. Critics charge atheism with being a legacy of the Cultural Revolution's "ultra-leftism", with damaging social harmony and with opposing the policy of freedom of religious belief. Du declines to rebut these as political accusations and instead argues that atheism is a legitimate body of knowledge, grounded in labour and human nature, and an integral part of Marxism. This is the first part of a two-part article.

The first part has two sections. The first defines atheism and distinguishes spontaneous from conscious atheism. The second surveys types of atheism: Western forms, Marxist atheism and its Leninist development, and the Chinese tradition. The discussion moves from the Renaissance and Enlightenment to the Young Hegelians and Feuerbach, then to Marx, Engels and Lenin, and finally to the Chinese terms for atheism, from ancient debates to Zhang Taiyan, Chen Duxiu and Hu Shi.

Du argues that labour and sexual reproduction show that humans are atheists by instinct, so religion is a burden added later. Conscious atheism arose to criticise theism and has developed alongside religion, and Du cites the Encyclopaedia Britannica's description of atheism as a product of civilisation and thought. For Du, theism and atheism concern truth and error, not morality or politics, but once theism is organised in churches it acquires social and ideological functions. Marxist atheism, which Du ranks as the highest form of scientific atheism, has three features: the materialist conception of history, the practice of the scientific socialist movement, and a consistent scientific spirit. Du holds that no Marxist view of religion exists apart from the whole of Marxism and criticises scholars who detach it from atheism. Du also contends that Lenin's epistemological critique of religion has been neglected. In China, Du says, atheism had no name of its own because the tradition mixed polytheism with non-belief and recognised no creator god.

The part published here ends with the argument that Chinese usage of "atheism" descends from the May Fourth tradition, which rejected both monotheistic and popular superstitious belief. Du's stated aim is to show that atheism is a scholarly and scientific position, not a political liability. The social responsibilities of scientific atheism promised in the title presumably follow in the second part. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese scholar of religion defends atheism against critics inside the Chinese academy and in debates over Marxist views of religion.
quoteEn: We can say that there is no Marxist view of religion or atheism outside the whole of Marxism; whoever speaks idly of one apart from that whole is cutting Marxism apart.
quoteZh: 我们可以说，没有离开马克思主义整体之外的什么马克思主义宗教观和无神论，谁若离开马克思主义整体奢谈之外的马克思主义宗教观和无神论，谁就在割裂马克思主义

glossary.explanation: A term for atheism grounded in scientific methods and findings. In Chinese Marxist scholarship it often designates Marxist atheism as the most developed form.
The body of Marxist theory on the origin, nature and social role of religion. Chinese scholars debate whether atheism is its core or only one component.

t: An investigation of the Templeton Foundation's religious orientation and its funding
zh: 邓普顿基金会的宗教倾向及其资助情况调查
paras: Writing in 2013, Huang Yanhong takes up a question the author says Chinese scholars have rarely examined: what is the John Templeton Foundation, which has become a frequent presence in Chinese academia, and what orientation lies behind its funding? The article argues that the foundation has a clear religious, specifically Christian, tendency. In the author's reading, it presents itself as neutral between science and religion while using science and established scientists to defend religion.

The article is built in three parts. The first covers the foundation's history, its founder John Templeton (1912–2008), an investor and devout Christian, and the Templeton Prize, including the 2012 award to the Dalai Lama. The second analyses the foundation's funding areas and two China-related projects. The third reports criticism from Western scientists, drawing on the foundation's own website and university sites for its material.

Huang's central move is to read the funding portfolio itself. The author argues that the "Science in Dialogue" and "Human Sciences" categories are mostly about religion, and that projects are tilted toward it, so the answers to the foundation's "Big Questions" are one-sided. Two China projects are examined as evidence. The first is "Science, Philosophy and Faith: A Programme for Chinese Scholars" (2005, US$2 million, Calvin College). Huang says its design, with study visits to church-run universities, 10,000 books and lecture series, aims to Christianize Chinese intellectuals. The second is the 2009–2013 "Chinese Spirituality and Society Program" (Purdue University, nearly US$2 million). Huang says its required research themes, such as religion and entrepreneurship and religious markets, are favourable to religion and survey the distribution and influence of religion on the mainland.

Huang then cites Western critics, including Sean Carroll, Richard Dawkins and a 2011 article in Evolutionary Psychology that raised five doubts about the foundation's integrity. The author concludes that the natural sciences can correct themselves, but the humanities and social sciences are more exposed, and that the foundation's growing footprint there in China deserves serious attention. Read the original if you want an early Chinese critical account of Templeton's funding in China, with specific project details and the Western criticisms the author draws on.
quoteEn: It supports pro-religious research and training projects, and funds conferences such as "Science and Religion in Dialogue" and the publication of related collected papers, and has already had considerable influence in China.
quoteZh: 它支持亲宗教的研究和培训项目，资助《科学与宗教的对话》等会议的召开和相关论文集的出版，等等，已经在中国造成了不小的影响。

t: Religious studies needs to be set right, and the critique of theology needs to be made up
st: An interview with Du Jiwen, former director of the Institute of World Religions, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences
zh: “研究宗教”亟须拨乱反正 “批判神学”必须开展补课
zhSub: 访中国社会科学院世界宗教研究所原所长杜继文
paras: This is an interview, conducted by a reporter from the journal Science and Atheism in 2013, with Du Jiwen (born 1930), second director of the Institute of World Religions at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and editor-in-chief of the journal. It marks the 50th anniversary of Mao Zedong's 1963 instruction to set up the institute. Du argues that religious studies in China has grown enormously but has drifted from Marxist guidance, and that Mao's call to "criticise theology" was neglected, with serious consequences.

The interview moves from the institute's early work (dictionaries, histories of the three major religions, training of graduate students) to present problems. Du discusses the blurring of religious research and religious propaganda, popular claims that religion promotes goodness and harmony, and the difference between legal religions and underground churches or cults. He then turns to the phrase "the Marxist view of religion", and to the "Sinophone Christian theology movement" and its overseas links.

Du's core claims are three. First, he holds that market incentives have turned some religious scholarship into advocacy, and that "Western religious studies" is in essence Christian theology. Second, he criticises official-style formulations of "the Marxist view of religion" as conceptually loose, and argues that they risk turning academic questions into matters of principle and reading historical materialism as saying that religion is "good" because society is. Third, he describes the Sinophone theology movement, begun in Hong Kong in the 1990s and linked to Nordic conferences and North American funders, as an effort to replace "Christianity adapted to China" with "China adopting Christianity". In his account it is a continuation of Western cultural missionary strategy and, increasingly, a social and political movement.

Du concludes that the knowledge of religion now being supplied is distorted and needs to be set right, and that theological preaching in universities and research institutes should be criticised and kept apart from education, as the principle of separating education from religion requires. He distinguishes this from criticism of church theology, which he treats as a private matter protected by law. He sees the rescue of atheism as an "endangered discipline" as a promising step. Read the original if you want a detailed, polemical insider account of 2013 debates in Chinese religious studies, the atheist critique of theology, and the Sinophone Christian theology movement.
quoteEn: Theology as an ideology has the particular function of penetrating to the very marrow of a culture.
quoteZh: 神学作为一种意识形态，最突出地功能是能够深入到文化的骨髓。

t: Only firm belief in scientific materialism can sustain scientific atheism
zh: 只有坚信科学唯物论，才能坚持科学无神论
paras: Writing in 2013, Yang Mingwei argues that scientific atheism cannot be upheld unless Marxism's scientific materialism is first firmly held. Yang identifies as the most worrying phenomenon in Chinese intellectual and social life a shaken theoretical foundation and a loss of belief, rooted in doubts about the scientific character of Marxism and the prospects of the communist cause. In Yang's account this drift shows up as a slide toward idealism, religious theology and theism.

The piece is built around two requirements: holding the correct standpoint and reading the situation correctly. The first part draws on the constitution, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to affirm dialectical and historical materialism as the basis of the Party's guiding thought. The second part surveys the international scene after the global financial crisis, citing a series of Western economists, journalists and politicians, as well as communist parties and the Cuban setting.

Yang contends that voluntarism and idealism now affect decision-making, comparing present-day rushes for rapid results to the Great Leap Forward. Yang also describes a situation in which theism is preached while atheism goes unspoken, with some Party members and officials turning to spirits and religious superstition. Citing Lenin's philosophical notebooks, Yang holds that abandoning materialism leads to 'priestcraft', since idealism and clericalism are treated as one. On the second requirement, Yang argues that Marxism has historically developed in opposition to religious theology. Yang reads Fukuyama's later remarks, and the comments of Nouriel Roubini, Stephen Resnick, Richard Wolff, Jean-Claude Delaunay, Georg Magnus and others, as evidence of a Marxist revival abroad. The crisis, in this reading, reflects the failure of a system resting on idealist philosophy and religious theology.

Yang concludes that two developments should settle the matter: the achievements of the Chinese path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the worldwide return to Marx. Together these, Yang says, give no reason to waver in belief or in the guiding role of scientific materialism and scientific atheism. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-affiliated researcher linked the defence of atheism to ideological discipline and to Western commentary on Marx after 2008.
quoteEn: Therefore, fundamentally speaking, to uphold scientific atheism one must first uphold Marxism's scientific materialism.
quoteZh: 因此，从根本上讲，要坚持科学无神论，必须首先坚持马克思主义的科学唯物论。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path and system of socialism since the reform era, associated with Deng Xiaoping's formulation in 1982.
The Marxist-materialist atheism promoted in Party education, which treats religion as a product of social conditions and opposes theism and superstition.
The author's term for dialectical and historical materialism, the philosophical basis of Marxism as taught in China.
The 1958–60 mass campaign for rapid industrial and agricultural growth, later officially criticised for voluntarism and excessive haste.

t: An analysis of the factors behind superstition among some officials
zh: 部分官员迷信的影响因素透析
paras: Writing in 2013, Cheng Ping asks why some Chinese officials turn to superstition and what can be done about it. Citing recent press cases, including a decommissioned aircraft placed in front of a county Party committee compound in Hebei, the renaming of a lake in Jiangsu and a "sword against evil" at a court in Changchun, Cheng argues that such acts reflect weak ideological cultivation, spiritual emptiness and lost belief, and that they damage Party and social conduct and feed corruption.

The article is a short commentary in two parts. The first identifies three main causes, ordered from historical-cultural background to present circumstances to personal interest. The second proposes two remedies: ideological and moral development, and institutional development.

On causes, Cheng points to the lingering influence of traditional folk practices such as divination and feng shui, which some local officials revive or package as local culture while pursuing GDP growth. Cheng also cites a crisis of belief and the heavy psychological pressure on officials. Unfair promotion practices, in which \"running and gifting\" brings advancement, leave officials anxious and powerless. Finally, Cheng argues that fear of losing vested interests drives superstition, above all among corrupt officials who seek supernatural protection from punishment, so that corruption is the root of such belief.

Cheng concludes that solutions require rebuilding both minds and institutions. Discipline and education are to be combined, with firm punishment of corruption and of officials who use superstition in their work. Cheng also calls for reform of cadre selection and for confining power within institutional limits, as set out in the 18th Party Congress report (2012). Once corrupt officials are certain to be caught and punished, Cheng holds, superstition will lose its basis. Read the original if you want an official-discourse view that links officials' superstition to corruption and promotion practices.
quoteEn: Corruption and superstition are bound by a necessary causal relationship; corruption is the root of officials' superstition.
quoteZh: 贪污腐败和迷信有着必然的因果关系，贪污腐败是官员迷信的根源。

glossary.zh: 把权力关进制度的笼子
glossary.pinyin: bǎ quánlì guān jìn zhìdù de lóngzi
glossary.literal: lock power in the cage of institutions
glossary.explanation: A slogan from the Party's anti-corruption campaign after the 18th Party Congress (2012), calling for institutional checks on the exercise of power.
The Communist Party of China's national congress of November 2012, which began Xi Jinping's leadership and stressed anti-corruption and institutional supervision of power.

t: Superstitious behaviour: an explanation based on control strategy theory
zh: 迷信行为——基于控制策略理论的解释
paras: Why do superstitious practices persist, and even take new forms, in an age of rapid scientific and technological change? Ma Jinfei takes up this question from a psychological angle, using control strategy theory. The article argues that superstition is a way of regaining a sense of control in uncertain, stressful situations, and that rising scientific literacy will eventually eradicate it.

The article opens with Chinese survey data on university students, including figures on belief in ghosts and fate, wearing lucky charms, divination and online fortune-telling. It then sets out control strategy theory, first proposed by Rothbaum and colleagues in 1982 and developed by Heckhausen and Schulz. Ma applies the theory under four headings: situational triggers, cognitive factors, emotional factors and adaptive function. The evidence is drawn almost entirely from Western psychology, such as studies of athletes, gamblers, sailors, investors and soldiers, Keinan's exam-stress experiment and Langer's work on the illusion of control. Ma also cites their own earlier master's thesis on risk and control illusion.

The theory distinguishes primary control, which acts directly on the environment, from secondary control, which changes the person's own cognition. Superstition is classed as a secondary illusory control strategy, resting on beliefs in luck or fate that have no causal link to outcomes. In Ma's account, people turn to it when preparation reaches its limits, as with exam questions or an opponent's play. Even people who doubt its effectiveness may still use it to gain a feeling of control. Ma presents this feeling as a way to ease anxiety and to counter learned helplessness. Citing Neil and Keinan, the article adds that superstition can work as a psychological placebo and a self-fulfilling prophecy, raising optimism and performance.

Ma concludes that humans in every era face the unknown, so superstition survives as a way of regaining control and inner calm, and attracts people whenever their sense of control weakens. The article calls for science education and continued ideological and political education, especially for university students, to make people doubt that superstitious strategies work. Education would stop superstition from being used as a primary control strategy, which Ma regards as having no adaptive value. Read the original if you want a short, psychology-based account of superstition from a Chinese science-and-atheism perspective, with a bibliography of English-language studies on the topic.
quoteEn: Whatever people's existing attitude to superstition, when their sense of control weakens, superstitious strategies come to hold a universal appeal.
quoteZh: 无论人们现有的对迷信的态度如何，当人们的控制感削弱，迷信策略就会产生普遍的吸引力。

t: On the main content of Marxist scientific atheism education in institutions of higher learning
zh: 论高等学校马克思主义科学无神论教育的主要内容
paras: Writing in 2013, He Husheng asks what Marxist scientific atheism education in Chinese universities should actually teach. He treats such education as an important part of Party building and ideological and political education on campus. In He's account it bears on Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, on the Party's advanced and pure character, and on training qualified builders and reliable successors for socialism. His answer is a framework of "five points": a basic point, a key point, a core point, a focal point and a point of arrival.

The article opens by defining scientific atheism as atheism founded on dialectical and historical materialism. It then devotes one section to each point. The basic point is education in dialectical and historical materialism. The key point is education in upholding science and opposing superstition. The core point is education in the Marxist view of religion. The focal point is education in the socialist core value system, and the point of arrival is education for the free and all-round development of the human being. A short closing section ties the five together.

In He's reading, the core is the Marxist view of religion, taught through three strands. The first is the basic theory of religion's origins, nature and eventual disappearance, which He says rules out any attempt to abolish religion by administrative force. The second is the Party's and state's religious policy: freedom of religious belief, administration of religious affairs according to law, and independent self-management of religion. The third is the rule that Party members, including student Party members, may not hold religious belief. Alongside this, He says students must distinguish religion from "evil cults" and from folk custom, and must learn to oppose feudal superstition and pseudo-science while respecting customs. The socialist core value system is presented as the platform for this teaching. He's final point is that overcoming the intellectual bondage of theism, raising scientific and cultural quality and developing the productive forces serve the free and all-round development of the person, which he calls the starting point and destination of scientific atheism.

He concludes that the five points are interconnected and inseparable, and that together they should produce students with a scientific worldview, outlook on life and values. He wants students to respect freedom of religious belief while drawing a clear line against theism as a worldview. The aim is for them to become qualified builders and reliable successors of socialism. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese academics frame the curriculum of atheism education, Party-member restrictions on belief, and religious policy in universities around 2013.
quoteEn: Students should be educated and guided to hold firmly to this common ideal, to combine realising their life's value with that ideal, to ground that value in real hard struggle and the soil of the common ideal, and to establish scientific atheism firmly, rather than place their life's pursuits in the illusory world of theism.
quoteZh: 要教育和引导大学生坚定这一共同理想，把实现人生价值与坚定共同理想很好地结合起来，切实把人生价值建立在现实的艰苦奋斗和共同理想的土壤中，牢固树立科学无神论，不应把人生追求置于有神论的虚幻世界里。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义科学无神论
glossary.explanation: Atheism grounded in dialectical and historical materialism, which explains religion as a product of social conditions and human alienation. In Chinese Party-academic usage it is a field of study and an element of ideological education.

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: A formulation first put forward at the Sixth Plenum of the 16th Central Committee (2006). It comprises Marxist guiding ideology, the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the national and reform spirit, and the socialist concept of honour and disgrace.
The official term for groups the state bans as illegal organisations. The article argues they are not religion, but use religious, qigong or other names to deceive and control members.
A right guaranteed by the Chinese constitution and described in Party policy. The article pairs it with the rule that Communist Party members may not hold religious belief.

t: Propagating scientific atheism with confidence
st: Reply to a reader's letter on why atheist education should be strengthened
zh: 理直气壮地宣传科学无神论
paras: This text is a reply to a reader's letter. The reader, Shen Zhang of Beijing's Haidian District, writes that witchcraft, superstition and pseudo-science are resurging while work on scientific atheism is weakening. The reader asks an expert to explain why it should be strengthened. The Party journal invited Ren Jiyu, honorary director of the National Library and head of the China Atheism Society, to answer. Ren argues that scientific atheism must be propagated openly and with conviction, and that this does not conflict with religious freedom.

The reply is organised around questions printed as headings. They cover the difference between 'naive' and scientific atheism, the Marxist view of religion, whether atheist propaganda contradicts Party religious policy, what makes an ideology rational, and how political respect for belief relates to ideological commitment to atheism. Ren draws on Engels, Lenin, the history of Western atheism from the Renaissance onwards, and the Party's own record.

Ren distinguishes pre-modern 'naive atheism', which criticised particular ghost-and-god notions but could not deny them at root, from scientific atheism, which rests on the scientific revolution from Copernicus onwards and also explains how belief in gods arises. Science is therefore atheism's 'natural ally', and Marxism took this tradition to a new level. Drawing on the Marxist view that religion has social roots, Ren holds that religious organisations and religious ideas should not be confused. Religious problems are to be solved by changing social relations, not by ideological struggle alone. Ren says atheism is acquired through education, so propaganda is needed. Quoting Engels, Ren says demanding that everyone become an atheist would be 'serving the gods'. Atheist work is aimed mainly at the Party's own base, not at believers, and past ultra-'Left' errors must be corrected.

Ren concludes that political respect for citizens' freedom of religion and ideological insistence on scientific atheism form a unity of opposites, not a metaphysical contradiction. Freedom to believe without freedom to propagate atheism would be a loss of freedom. Attacking believers in atheism's name would violate their rights and damage unity. For the Party, religious belief is not a private matter, since its worldview is dialectical and historical materialism. Ren also describes plurality of belief as normal in a healthy society. Read the original if you want a short statement of how a leading Chinese atheist scholar reconciled atheist propaganda with the constitutional protection of religious belief in 2013.
quoteEn: Upholding and respecting citizens' right to freedom of religious belief in politics, and adhering to and propagating scientific atheism in ideology, form a unity of opposites, not a metaphysical contradiction.
quoteZh: 在政治上维护和尊重宗教信仰自由的公民权利，与思想上坚持和宣传科学无神论，是对立的统一，而不是形而上学的矛盾

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese Marxist writing for atheism grounded in modern natural science and historical materialism. It is contrasted with earlier, unsystematic forms of unbelief and is promoted in Party education.
The label for pre-scientific-revolution atheist thought. In this account it criticised particular beliefs in ghosts and gods but could not deny their existence at root.

t: A review of surveys on the religious beliefs of university students in Beijing
zh: 北京大学生宗教信仰调查研究综述
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), posted on marxism.cass.cn 2013-04-01
paras: This literature review, published in 2013 in the Science and Atheism category, surveys published empirical studies of religious belief among university students in Beijing. Huang sorts the findings into five areas and then argues that the field has three shortcomings, the main one being the lack of a scientific-atheist perspective.

The review covers survey and fieldwork studies from the late 1990s to about 2011. They include projects funded by the Beijing education authorities, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, the Ministry of Education and the Communist Youth League, and work by teams at Beijing Normal University and Renmin University. It also covers several master's and doctoral theses. Huang excludes literature reviews and purely textual analyses. The five areas are the basic situation of belief, routes into religion and reasons for belief, religious ideas and activities, the effects of belief, and policy recommendations.

On the basic situation, Huang reports that the surveys put the share of believing students at roughly 9 to 22 per cent, with a rising trend, and Christians at about 3 to 5 per cent. Believers are more often female and in lower years, and they differ by family background and field of study. Most students are said to meet religion through books, classes and friends and to convert at university. Reported motives are mixed, and the studies disagree on how far family influence matters. Student Christians are said to prefer fellowship groups and house gatherings, often led by foreigners. Several studies cited by Huang describe this as foreign religious infiltration, and they stress its effects on students' values.

Huang identifies three weaknesses. No survey proceeds from a scientific-atheist standpoint, a discipline Huang calls endangered. Some studies lack objectivity because they apply Western theories such as the religious-market theory and rely on believers' own accounts. Others show too little grasp of religion or sociological method, for example in probing doctrines such as sin or the funding of house churches. Huang calls for respecting students' beliefs while guiding them towards the socialist core value system, developing scientific-atheist research and education, keeping education separate from religion, and resisting overseas religious infiltration of universities. Read the original if you want a map of the Chinese survey literature on student religion, with its main figures and sources, and a view of how Party-aligned scholars of atheism assess it.
quoteEn: However, these studies still have some shortcomings or gaps that need to be considered in further research.
quoteZh: 但是，目前这些研究还存在一些不足或缺失，在进一步的研究时需要考虑。

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: An official framework of ideological values promoted in China's education and propaganda work. The author says students' religious beliefs should be guided to fit it.
Christian gatherings held outside the officially registered Three-Self churches. The studies reviewed observe student believers in both settings.

t: Some reflections on Marxist religious-outlook education in universities
zh: 高校开展马克思主义宗教观教育的若干思考
paras: He Husheng and Liu Fujun ask how Chinese universities should teach students a Marxist view of religion. Writing in 2013, they argue that hostile foreign forces are using religion, campus proselytising and the student body as a channel for 'Westernization' and division. In their account, education in the Marxist view of religion is therefore an urgent strategic task, tied to training qualified builders and reliable successors for socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article is organised in three parts. The first covers basic Marxist theory on religion: its nature, its long-term development and its social functions. The second covers the Party's basic policies on religious work, and the third covers education in Marxist scientific atheism. Each part is framed as content that universities should deliver, mainly through ideological and political theory courses and Party and Youth League organisations.

The authors hold that religion has a multiple nature: it is a theistic, idealist worldview, a mass belief and a part of culture. They hold that it will persist for a long time under socialism but will eventually disappear, and that it has both positive and negative social effects. On policy, they list freedom of religious belief, management of religious affairs according to law, independence and self-administration of religion, guiding religion to adapt to socialist society, separation of education from religion, the patriotic united front, and Party leadership. They stress that Communist Party members must be atheists and that religious activity and preaching on campuses are barred. They add that students should learn to distinguish religion from superstition and from folk belief.

The authors conclude that universities should combine dialectical and historical materialism, the promotion of science against superstition, and ideals-and-convictions education. They want this to reduce the influence of religious idealism on students, defend Marxism's guiding position in ideology and resist infiltration from abroad. They also say that students should respect believers and that Marxist atheism does not mean political opposition to religious people. Read the original if you want to see how official Chinese discourse in the Hu Jintao era set out religious policy as a curriculum for higher education.
quoteEn: When we speak of the long-term nature of religion, we do not mean that religion will exist forever; the aim is to overcome short-sightedness on the religious question and to understand correctly, and actively seek, the paths by which religion will die out.
quoteZh: 我们讲宗教的长期性，不是说宗教永远存在，而是为了克服宗教问题上的短视症，正确认识和积极寻找宗教消亡的途径。

glossary.zh: 宗教与社会主义社会相适应
glossary.pinyin: zōngjiào yǔ shèhuì zhǔyì shèhuì xiāng shìyìng
glossary.en: guiding religion to adapt to socialist society
glossary.explanation: A core principle of Party religious policy, written into the 2004 basic guideline on religious work. It asks believers to support the Party and the socialist system and obey the law, and does not ask them to give up belief.
The principle that Chinese religious bodies and affairs are run by Chinese believers and not controlled by foreign forces. It is rooted in the historical link between missionary work and imperialism.

The Party's framework for cooperating with non-Party groups, including religious figures, on the basis of patriotism and support for socialism. The Party describes the relationship as political cooperation with mutual respect in matters of belief.
The Marxist-materialist form of atheism that Party ideology promotes through education. It is presented as grounded in science and as part of the Marxist worldview.

In this article, the legal principle that religion must not interfere in the state's education system, so no religious activity is allowed in universities. The article cites the Constitution, the Education Law and the Regulations on Religious Affairs.

t: Capitalist religion and historical materialism
zh: 资本主义宗教与历史唯物主义
paras: Why did a group of Central European Jewish intellectuals, once influenced by Max Weber, move to Marx's critique of fetishism? Zhang examines this revival of fetishism critique in the twentieth century through Ernst Bloch, Georg Lukács and Walter Benjamin. Zhang argues that reflection on the "Jewish question" carried them beyond Weber's thesis of disenchantment to the view that capitalism has itself become a religion, and that this view prepared their turn to Marx.

The article has two main parts and a conclusion. The first part takes Bloch as its example. It traces how his Jewish messianism and his reading of Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism led him to a theory of capitalist religion, which Benjamin's fragment "Capitalism as Religion" then developed. The second part turns to Lukács's History and Class Consciousness and its account of the secret of this religion. The conclusion compares the three thinkers' views of how capitalist religion might be overcome.

Zhang's central claim is that these thinkers reconstructed Marx's critique in two directions. First, Bloch and Benjamin describe capitalist religion as self-contradictory: its idol is both a concrete human creation (Mammon, the golden calf) and an empty abstraction. It is a practical cult without doctrine that nonetheless breeds sectarian faiths. It is also non-redemptive, because it multiplies guilt and debt while presenting itself as progress. Second, Lukács explains these features through commodity fetishism. Abstract labour is the sole social category, and it rules through rationalization, the contemplative stance and reified consciousness. Zhang reads this as "abstract domination", which separates form from content and part from totality, so that capitalism moves from one catastrophe to the next.

In the conclusion Zhang sets out a split over historical materialism. Lukács proposes a non-religious historical materialism: proletarian class consciousness would achieve the sublation of religion through philosophy and social revolution alone. He criticises Bloch's proposed alliance with religion. Bloch and Benjamin hold to an alliance between historical materialism and theology, illustrated by Benjamin's image of the hidden dwarf and the puppet. Zhang concludes that in a seemingly secularised world, the question of how to sublate religion positively remains open. Read the original if you study Western Marxism, Weber's influence on Lukács and Bloch, or the debate over Marxism and religion.
quoteEn: In this sense we can say quite clearly that capitalism itself has become a religion, and that in the religion of capitalism capital has become the new god.
quoteZh: 在这个意义上，我们可以很明确地说，资本主义本身成为了一种宗教，在资本主义宗教里，资本成为了新的上帝。

glossary.explanation: The tradition of Marxist thought associated with Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci and the Frankfurt School. It emphasises philosophy, culture and consciousness, and Chinese scholarship treats it as a distinct field.
Marx's term, in Capital, for the way social relations between people appear as relations between things. The article treats it as a quasi-religious structure of domination.
The Chinese rendering of Hegel's Aufhebung, meaning to overcome something while retaining part of it. The article uses it for the overcoming of religion.
Max Weber's term for the loss of magical and religious meaning in the modern, rationalised world.
The article's name for the secret of capitalist religion: abstract labour and value rule over people through the commodity form.

t: On the dual measure of Marx's critique of religion
zh: 论马克思宗教批判的双重尺度
paras: Shang Yu takes issue with the traditional view that Marx's system is cut off from, or simply opposed to, religious consciousness, and that the spirit of the Gospel weakens the movement for human emancipation. The author calls this view an unhistorical, abstract assertion. The article argues instead that Marx's critique of religion works on two measures: an ultimate-value measure, on which the realm of freedom and the messianic idea are covertly linked, and an economic-science measure, on which Marx exposes religion's illusory, inverted and conservative character.

The article has three sections. The first traces the history of salvation thinking from Christian eschatology and Augustine through the Enlightenment, Kant, Hegel and Feuerbach, to Marx's labour-based conception of emancipation.
