glossary.explanation: The December 1978 meeting that marked the start of reform and opening up and shifted Party work towards economic modernisation.

t: Communist Party members cannot hold religious beliefs
zh: 共产党员不能信仰宗教
paras: Writing in 2012, Zhu Weiqun responds to what the article describes as a growing number of Party members who take part in religious activities or become believers, and to calls inside and outside the Party to "lift the ban" on members holding religious beliefs. Zhu argues that the Party's principle that Communists cannot believe in religion has been consistent and unshaken, and that it follows from the Party's dialectical-materialist worldview. The author insists that all Party organisations and members must uphold it without wavering.

The article has four parts. It first traces the principle through Marx, Lenin and Mao Zedong, and through Party documents from 1982, 1990, 2002, 2006 and 2010. It then explains why a Party of materialists nonetheless practises a policy of freedom of religious belief, and sets out the harm Zhu expects if members were allowed to believe. It closes with proposals for education and discipline.

Zhu's central move is to distinguish citizens from Party members. Freedom of religious belief, the author says, is a right of citizens; a person who joins the Party voluntarily accepts the materialist worldview and thereby chooses not to hold a religion. A member who later turns to religion has, in Zhu's words, ended the process of joining the Party in thought, and the Party may deal with that organisationally without "discriminating against religion". Second, Zhu argues that admitting believers would split the Party ideologically and organisationally, weaken its work against separatism in Tibet and Xinjiang, and turn officials into advocates of particular religions. The author cites local officials who promote temples and Buddha statues as examples of the problem.

Zhu calls for stronger education in the Marxist view of religion and in atheism, in Party schools, universities and research bodies. The author proposes patient persuasion of members who join religious activities, and discipline for officials who use their power to foster religious fervour. Particular attention is urged for religious-affairs cadres, young members, retired members and members from ethnic minorities, with some flexibility allowed over customs derived from religion. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement from a senior United Front official of the Party's position on members and religion at the start of the 2010s.
quoteEn: When a citizen voluntarily joins the Communist Party of China, it means he unconditionally accepts the Marxist dialectical-materialist worldview, and that, on the strength of the citizen's right to freedom of religious belief, he has voluntarily chosen not to believe in any religion.
quoteZh: 当一个公民志愿加入中国共产党的时候，就意味着他无条件地接受马克思主义的辩证唯物主义世界观，也就意味着他根据公民所享有的宗教信仰自由权利自愿选择了不信仰任何宗教。

glossary.explanation: A constitutional right of Chinese citizens and a long-standing Party policy. The article argues it applies to citizens but not to Party members.
The denial of gods. The article presents it as the required position of Communists and as a subject for public propaganda and education.

t: Upholding the separation of education and religion, and advancing education and the discipline of atheism: a review of the 2011 annual conference of the China Atheism Association
zh: 坚持教育与宗教相分离原则，促进教育发展与无神论学科建设 ——中国无神论学会2011年学术年会综述
paras: This is a report on the 2011 annual conference of the China Atheism Association, held on 29–31 October 2011 in Jinhua, Zhejiang. The association, the CASS Research Center for Science and Atheism and the School of Teacher Education at Zhejiang Normal University co-organised it. About 50 scholars attended, under the theme "educational development and the building of the atheism discipline". The report presents the meeting as a response to the spread of religion into public life and into university campuses.

The report is arranged in four thematic sections, each summarising individual speakers. They cover the separation of education and religion, with historical and policy papers; the theoretical construction of scientific atheism; surveys of religious belief among university students, including online Christian communication; and foreign religious infiltration, together with related topics. The speakers came from CASS, Renmin University, Beijing Normal University, Shanghai Normal University, Nanjing University and other institutions. Further papers dealt with the psychology of atheism and with religious neuroscience.

Xi Wuyi and others reviewed how Christian mission schools were secularised in modern China and argued that the separation principle must be upheld unwaveringly. They called Marxist atheism the basic safeguard against infiltration and campus proselytising. Du Jiwen set out a discipline plan of one general theory, two histories (Chinese and Western atheism) and a dictionary. He listed obstacles, including foreign-funded theology and trends that treat religion as a remedy for moral decline. Tian Xinming and Zhang Xinying held that atheist education is compatible with the policy of religious freedom, and Jia Runguo defended the Marxist view of religion against the reading of it as a mere "opium" doctrine. Surveys of students at several universities reported self-declared believers at roughly 5.8 to 18.55 per cent, though one author estimated true believers at about 4 per cent. Huang Chao described a US "new religious extraterritoriality" in religious infiltration of China. Xu Lin claimed that some Party committees ignored official policy on student belief.

The report records calls for stronger Marxist and scientific-atheism education, stricter management of religious activity on campus and online, and more work on the discipline's textbooks and histories. Participants also urged scholars to confront pseudo-science and superstition. Several speakers tied the agenda to defending socialist core values and the Party's governing position. Read the original if you want a detailed view of how Chinese atheism scholars in 2011 framed religion, campus education and foreign influence, and of the policy proposals they put forward.
quoteEn: Building the atheism discipline is a need of the situation, a call of the times, and should also be a long-term strategic plan.
quoteZh: 无神论的学科建设，是形势的需要，是时代的呼声，也应该是长期的战略布局。

glossary.explanation: A principle in Chinese law and policy that public education should not carry religious teaching or proselytising. Speakers at the conference presented it as long-standing state policy.

The Marxist-materialist form of atheism promoted in China's academic and educational institutions. It is distinguished from religious studies and presented as the worldview basis of Marxist religious theory.
The Party and state policy of protecting citizens' freedom to believe or not believe in religion. Speakers discussed how it relates to atheist propaganda and to Party members' own obligations.

t: A brief commentary on the US International Religious Freedom Act of 1998
zh: 简评美国《1998年国际宗教自由法案》
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论)
paras: Writing in 2012 in the category 'Science and Atheism', Xi Wuyi examines the US International Religious Freedom Act of 1998 and argues that it marks a post-Cold War strategic shift: a superpower legislating a regular review of religion worldwide. Xi describes this 'faith-based diplomacy' as the latest version of earlier missionary diplomacy and of 'human rights diplomacy'. The article takes China's 'xiejiao' problem, which it says the US reports have long scrutinised, as the main case.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the American Christian neo-conservative global strategy, summarises the content of the Act (an ambassador-at-large, an annual report, a commission, presidential action against designated 'countries of particular concern') and argues that US definitions of religious freedom follow national interest. The second part reviews how Chinese law defines xiejiao and discusses how to translate the term into English. The third turns to Protestant 'destructive cults' in China, drawing on statistics and field reports.

Xi argues that the Act is a tool by which evangelical and neo-conservative forces use state power to spread a Christian-based 'universal values' agenda and to legitimise interference in other states. As evidence of selectivity, Xi cites Iraq's removal from the 2004 watch list despite the violence there. Xi rejects the US claim that China has no public criteria, pointing to the 1997 Criminal Law, the 1999 NPC Standing Committee decision and the judicial interpretation. Xi holds that xiejiao is a modern legal concept, not equivalent to the Western 'cult', and proposes translating it as 'destructive cults'.

Xi concludes that, as Falun Gong declines and becomes more political, Christian-type groups, which the article says make up over 85 per cent of the banned organisations, will become a factor in social stability. Xi attributes their growth to foreign funding and to the rapid spread of Christianity in China, citing studies putting Protestants at about 39–40 million. Xi urges a cross-cultural scholarly framework based on the Western concept of destructive cults, so that Chinese research can enter international discourse. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's official-line critique of US religious-freedom diplomacy, or the debate over translating xiejiao and the field-report evidence on Protestant groups in China.
quoteEn: The 'international freedom of religious belief' that the US government vigorously promotes takes US national interest as its standard.
quoteZh: 美国政府大力促进的“国际宗教信仰自由”，是以美国国家利益为标准的。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese legal and political term for banned organisations said to use religion, qigong or superstition to deceive and control followers. It is commonly rendered 'evil cult' or 'heterodox religion'; the article proposes 'destructive cults'.
The rendering Xi proposes for xiejiao, borrowed from Western sociology of religion's term 'cult' (膜拜团体) with the qualifier 'destructive'.
US law that created an ambassador-at-large and an annual State Department report on religious freedom worldwide. It also provides for designating 'countries of particular concern'.
The article's term for US foreign policy that makes religious freedom central. Xi presents it as a successor to missionary diplomacy and human rights diplomacy.

t: The Sinicization of Marxist atheism (Part I)
zh: 马克思主义无神论的中国化历程（上）
paras: How did Marxist atheism, a doctrine formed in nineteenth-century Europe, take root in China? In this first part of a two-part article, Xi argues that Chinese Communists, proceeding from China's own social conditions, have steadily added new content to Marxist atheism while adapting Marxism to Chinese realities. Xi presents scientific atheism as the starting point and cornerstone of the Marxist worldview.

The article opens with a comparison of China's religious culture and the Europe of Marx and Engels. It then follows the Chinese Communist Party's handling of religion through three periods: the New Democratic revolution, the early years of socialist construction after 1949, and the start of reform and opening up in 1978. Xi draws on Party documents, speeches by Mao Zedong and the 1982 central directive on religious policy. The account stops with the policies of the early 1980s, and the second part is still to come.

Xi identifies three features of Chinese belief culture: pluralism in which humanism, polytheism and atheist thought coexist; state power that always dominates religious authority; and a worldly, utilitarian outlook centred on venerating Heaven and ancestors. From these Xi derives two basic principles for a Chinese Marxist atheism. The first is the separation of religion from politics together with freedom of religious belief, which keeps belief apart from political questions. The second is persuasion in ideological education, coupled with theoretical criticism of theology where it competes for the young. Xi then reads the Party's practice through these principles. Examples are Mao's view that peasants must discard the idols themselves, the 1950 directive on Christianity and Catholicism, the 1958 religious reforms in minority regions, and the 1982 document. That document says Party members must be atheists, that propaganda should be gentle, and that the shared political and economic interests of believers and non-believers outweigh differences of belief.

Xi concludes that Marxist atheism in China has combined firm worldview opposition to theism with religious freedom for citizens and a united front with patriotic believers. In Xi's account this approach serves the goal of building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of scientific atheism presents the historical development of Party religious policy, and which Party documents and Mao texts support that account.
quoteEn: The idea of religious theism is mistaken and opposed to science and materialism, but it is a question of ideas, which cannot be resolved by administrative means and can only be addressed by persuasion and education.
quoteZh: 宗教有神论的观念是错误的，是与科学和唯物论相对立的，但它属于思想问题，不能动用行政手段解决，只能采取说服教育的方法

glossary.explanation: The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched under Deng Xiaoping, formally from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee in December 1978.
Mao Zedong's term for the stage of the Chinese revolution, roughly 1919–1949, led by the proletariat against imperialism and feudalism, before the move to socialism.
A principle in Party policy that religion should not take part in politics, law or education. In the article's account belief remains a private matter for citizens.
A Party strategy of building political alliances with non-Party groups. Here it covers cooperation with religious believers on shared political goals despite differing worldviews.

t: Religion and international relations in the age of globalization
zh: 全球化时代的宗教与国际关系
paras: Xu Yihua asks what the worldwide religious resurgence since the 1970s, and especially since 9/11, has done to the study of international relations and to practice in the field. The article argues that religion has returned from what it calls the 'Westphalian exile' to the centre of international affairs. Xu holds that the effect is only 'semi-subversive': it unsettles older assumptions without overturning them.

The article has three parts. The first sets out five respects in which the resurgence challenges received views: secularization theory, the Westphalian system, the geography of world religion, the political role of religion, and the internet. The second surveys approaches to studying religion and international relations, drawing on Western scholars such as Scott Thomas, Ron Hassner and Jack Snyder. The third turns to the consequences for China.

On the first part, Xu argues that secularization theory is contested rather than refuted, and that transnational religion has not displaced the nation-state, since religion is still not a 'hard currency' alongside politics, military and economics. Xu reads Western human-rights and religious-freedom advocacy, including the 'responsibility to protect', as a pretext for intervention against non-Western states. Xu also doubts that online religion amounts to a 'second Reformation'. On method, the article reports Hassner's 'broad', 'deep' and 'thick' routes and Snyder's four attitudes among IR scholars, and concludes that mainstream IR still prefers to absorb religion into existing paradigms.

For China, Xu lists pressures: foreign religious exchange in a 'post-missionary era', online religion outrunning regulation, the 'evangelization' of US foreign policy, and extremism, separatism and terrorism combined with religious NGOs able to assist 'colour revolutions'. Xu also sees opportunities: religion as soft power, public diplomacy and national image, with traditional ideals of harmony offering a model of religious coexistence. The article calls for closer links between religious studies and IR in China, where the two fields have so far run on 'separate tracks'. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's survey of Western literature on religion and IR, together with an official-adjacent view of its security and soft-power implications for China.
quoteEn: Without taking religion seriously, one cannot understand international relations.
quoteZh: 不重视宗教就无法理解国际关系

glossary.explanation: The European order of sovereign states associated with the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which ended the Thirty Years' War. IR theory often treats it as removing religion from interstate politics.

An international norm, first proposed by the ICISS, holding that the international community may act when a state fails to protect its civilians from mass atrocities. The article presents it critically, as a vehicle for Western intervention.

The term used in Chinese official and scholarly discourse for the popular uprisings that changed governments in several post-Soviet states in the 2000s. It is generally used to describe externally encouraged regime change.
Xu's term for the period since reform and opening up, in which foreign missionaries are barred from China. Religious exchange continues through other channels.

t: Some problems in the relationship between natural science and religion
zh: 自然科学与宗教关系的若干问题
paras: Yu Qiming takes up the debate on the relationship between science and religion, which the author says has drawn growing attention at home and abroad. The article objects that many recent discussions are too loose and tend to evade the essential difference between the two. In the author's account, such discussions play down the way scientific advance has forced religion to change its doctrines, and instead promote complementarity or fusion. They also advance claims such as "religion is the mother of science". Yu's thesis is that science and religion arise from a common practical source but are essentially opposed, and that religion has not guided or enabled modern science.

The article first distinguishes broad and narrow senses of the relationship: science and religion as institutions, as practices and as systems of ideas. It then concentrates on the narrow sense, the relation between scientific knowledge and religious consciousness. It takes up the complaint that science and religion are alike because both rest on faith. It then turns to scientists with religious beliefs, using Galileo and Newton as cases. Finally it considers whether modern science arose in Europe because of Christianity, by way of the "Needham question". Engels, Einstein, Marx and Joseph Needham are among the authorities cited.

Yu argues first that science and religion emerged together from the labour and survival practice of early humans. They later diverged, and Yu holds that they are opposed in kind: scientific knowledge can be tested in practice, whereas religious belief in supernatural powers cannot. Second, the author rejects the claim that science also depends on transcendent faith. In Yu's view, trust in the lawfulness and intelligibility of the world is a conception of nature built up from practice, and scientific imagination and idealised thought experiments remain grounded in experience. Third, Yu holds that scientists achieve most when religious dogma interferes least, as in Galileo's case, and that Newton's turn to God for the planets' tangential motion marked the end of his creative work. Yu also argues that modern science drew on the Greek traditions of natural philosophy and formal logic and on socio-economic conditions, not on Christianity. In this account, the "rational element" in Christian theology came late and derived from Aristotle.

Yu concludes that the cooperation of religious bodies with education and learning has only helped spread science in an incidental and limited way. Missionaries such as Matteo Ricci, in the author's reading, used science as bait for conversion. The article also credits Chinese inventions with contributing to European science, while holding that ancient China lacked the traditions of formal logic and causal experimentation. It therefore rejects any claim that China must adopt Christianity to develop science. Read the original if you want a Marxist, atheist reading of the science–religion debate, with detailed historical cases from Galileo, Newton and the Needham question.
quoteEn: The practical foundation of science is the fundamental guarantee that it has no need of transcendent, extra-experiential faith.
quoteZh: 科学的实践基础是它不需要超经验信仰的根本保证。

t: Freedom of belief and the "other", law and the state: interpreting China's policy on freedom of religious belief
zh: 信仰自由与“他者”、法以及国家——解读我国的宗教信仰自由政策
paras: Writing in 2012, Chi Xiqin asks how China's policy on freedom of religious belief should be understood. The author argues that freedom cannot be defined abstractly and has meaning only within relationships. Chi therefore reads the policy through religion's relations to three things: the "other", law and the state. The article concludes that religion, as a socio-cultural system built on belief in a transcendent realm, should be guided by the policy to serve public and national interests and to act as a socially "most useful hypothesis".

The article begins from the Marxist principle that belief is a private matter and from the policy's treatment of religious freedom as a basic human right enjoyed equally by all citizens. It is organised in three sections. The first covers religion and the "other", split into the materialist "other" (science and atheism) and the religious "other" (other faiths). The second covers religion and law, and the third covers religion and the state. Chi draws on Sartre, Locke, Aristotle, Tillich and official documents, including the 1982 central document on religious questions in the socialist period.

In the first section Chi holds that citizens are free to believe or not to believe, and to choose among religions. The author denies that atheist propaganda contradicts religious freedom: science and religion are presented as separate "languages" with different functions, so relations should be "politically united and cooperative, mutually respectful in belief". The second section argues that law makes freedom concrete and protects it, while obliging believers not to harm health, social order or ethnic unity. Law is also said to open space for religion in charity and disaster relief. The third section makes the state the absolute precondition of freedom. Religious activity must serve national and public interests, be patriotic and uphold the socialist system, and church and state are separated. Under the principle of independence and self-management, Chi cites Article 36 of the Constitution and calls for resisting infiltration by hostile foreign forces that use religion.

Chi concludes that the policy guides religion towards adapting to socialist society and unites believers and non-believers around common fundamental interests. In Chi's account, religion's positive functions (psychological adjustment, cultural exchange) have corresponding negative ones, so the task is to promote the former and avoid the latter. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned exposition of how Chinese scholars justified the religious policy in 2012, including its stress on law, patriotism and independence from foreign religious bodies.
quoteEn: Religion, as a socio-cultural system centred on belief in the transcendent, should, under the guidance of China's religious policy and proceeding from public and national interests, play its positive role as society's "most useful hypothesis".
quoteZh: 宗教作为以超世信仰为核心的社会文化体系，应在我国宗教政策的引导下，从公共利益和国家利益出发，发挥其作为社会之“最有用的假设意义”这一积极作用。

glossary.explanation: A constitutional principle and the core of the Chinese Party-state's religious policy. It protects citizens' right to believe or not to believe, within limits set by law and state interests.

The principle that Chinese religious bodies run their own affairs without foreign control, often summarised as self-governance, self-support and self-propagation. It is rooted in Article 36 of the Constitution.

t: On education in the Marxist view of religion for university students
zh: 论高校大学生的马克思主义宗教观教育
paras: He Yanfeng and Feng Xue take up the question of how Chinese universities should teach students the Marxist view of religion. Writing in the early 2010s, they start from the premise that religion will persist for a long time in China's socialist society. Their thesis is that education in the Marxist view of religion is a core part of ideological and political education for the young people who are to carry on the socialist cause, and that it is currently weak and needs strengthening.

The article has three parts. The first sets out why the task is urgent. The second diagnoses three problems in university ideological and political theory courses. The third proposes three remedies: richer course content, better teaching methods and a better-qualified teaching staff. The authors support their case with survey figures cited from other scholars and from their own earlier work.

On urgency, the authors say students are drawn to religion by its philosophy, its ethics and its rites, and by growing competitive and psychological pressure. They also claim that foreign forces, led by the United States, use the internet and multimedia to infiltrate students through religion. They cite a Heilongjiang survey in which 19.6 per cent of students said they believed in religion and 65 per cent were half-convinced, and an overall estimate of 3–4 to about 20 per cent. On the problems, they find that religion occupies only a few minutes in the courses, that lecture-style indoctrination loses students' interest, and that some teachers lack knowledge of Marxist religious theory and Party religious policy. The remedies include adding material to specific courses, such as religion's origin, nature, function and eventual disappearance in the principles course, and the sinicisation of the Marxist view of religion in the Mao Zedong Thought and socialism with Chinese characteristics course. The authors also call for films, multimedia and interactive teaching that engages emotion as well as reason.

The authors conclude that teachers must sincerely believe in and understand Marxism, grasp religion's content, features, functions and long-term nature, and be able to explain its positive and negative cultural value. In their view, teachers should also use Marxist atheism to help students resist idealism and what the authors call heterodox doctrines. Only then, they argue, can students internalise the Marxist view of religion and form a Marxist belief. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese university ideological-education researchers framed religion among students around 2012, including the survey figures they cite and their course-by-course proposals.
quoteEn: "Educators must first be educated" is the precondition of Marxist religious education.
quoteZh: 教育者先受教育”这是马克思主义的宗教教育的前提

glossary.explanation: The Marxist account of religion's origins, nature, social functions and eventual disappearance. In Chinese official usage it is paired with Party religious policy and taught in university political courses.
Compulsory courses on Marxism, Chinese Communist Party theory, morality and law, and current affairs that all Chinese university students take.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era. The article treats Chinese religious theory as one component of it.
A traditional teaching approach in ideological education in which teachers deliver content one-way to students. The authors criticise it as ineffective.

t: On freedom of religious belief and university students' choice of belief
zh: 论宗教信仰自由与高校学生信仰选择
paras: Writing in 2012, Zhao Dong asks how freedom of religious belief, as guaranteed in China, should be understood and how university students should approach the choice of a belief. The article's answer is that religious freedom is a legally protected citizen's right and a private matter, but that students should be guided towards a Marxist worldview and a Marxist belief, and should respect the rules that separate education from religion.

The article has two parts. The first sets out basic categories: it defines religion and religious belief, explains their origins and essence, and then interprets religious freedom through China's laws and Party policy. The second part turns to young students and offers four recommendations for making a belief choice. The discussion draws on Marx, Lenin and Mao Zedong, and on constitutional and legal provisions from 1949 to the 1990s.

Zhao presents religion as a social phenomenon arising from natural and social forces, with social, cognitive and psychological roots. In Zhao's account, its essence is a distorted and illusory reflection of the alienated social relations of class society, and the author cites Marx and Lenin's well-known characterisations of it. Zhao then lists the legal basis of religious freedom, including Article 36 of the 1982 Constitution and Document No. 19 (1982), and argues that belief is a private matter and a question of the spiritual world. This holds only if it does not harm the state, society or others, and Zhao says Communist Party members, by the Party's nature, can only be atheists. For students, Zhao stresses the Education Law's separation of education from religion and the rule that no organisation or individual may conduct religious activities in schools.

Zhao proposes four steps: study the basic theory of scientific socialism and communism systematically; establish a scientific worldview and outlook on life, together with the socialist core value system; learn the policies and regulations on religion in universities; and take part in social practice, so that a belief in Marxism is genuine rather than nominal. Doubts about communism are attributed to superficial study of Marxism. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese university ideological education around 2012 combined legal explanation of religious freedom with Marxist atheist guidance for students.
quoteEn: Only by actively throwing oneself into social practice can one make the correct choice of belief through practice.
quoteZh: 只有积极投身社会实践，在实践中才能作出正确的信仰选择。

glossary.explanation: A citizen's right guaranteed by Article 36 of China's Constitution, covering the freedom to believe or not to believe and to choose among religions. State protection applies to 'normal' religious activities.

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: A Party formulation, prominent from the mid-2000s, setting out the core ideological values to be promoted in society and education. It centres on Marxism as the guiding ideology.

t: Higher education should guide students to resist religious infiltration correctly
zh: 高校教育要引导学生正确抵御宗教渗透
paras: Writing in 2012, Tian Yufen takes up how Chinese universities should educate and guide students to resist what the article calls religious infiltration. Tian argues that universities train the builders and successors of the socialist cause and are a prime target for ideological subversion by hostile forces abroad. The article therefore treats the topic as a central task for the study of religious theory and for keeping a socialist orientation in higher education.

The article has four parts. It first defines religious infiltration and sets out why resisting it matters. It then lists the basic features of infiltration, distinguishes it from normal religious activity, and ends with a set of countermeasures for universities. Tian draws on a 1995 collection of documents on religious work, a 2000 book by Wang Zuo'an and Hu Jintao's speech at the 90th anniversary of the Party's founding (2011).

Tian defines infiltration as reactionary political activity under a religious cover, or missionary activity aimed at controlling Chinese religious bodies and establishing unlawful bases, and not as friendly religious exchange. In the article's account, hostile Western forces use religion to pursue "Westernization" and "division" of China, and the author cites the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union as a warning. Tian lists six features: political malignity, cultural aggression, international scope, varied methods, hidden organisation and severe destructiveness. Normal religious activity, in this view, differs from infiltration in purpose, agents, methods and social effect, since it is open and lawful while infiltration is concealed and aims to subvert the socialist system.

Tian proposes a long-term mechanism with five elements: university leaders must set up an anti-infiltration organisational network. Students should be taught the Marxist view of religion and atheism, and ideological and political education should build the core socialist value system. The university should strengthen its teams of political-work staff and counsellors and put students first, including help with employment. It should also tighten supervision, which means cooperating with public security, policing campus networks and monitoring foreign teachers, international students, students from Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, and believers. Read the original if you want to see how a 2012 Chinese academic text frames religion as a security and ideological issue on campus and what practical measures it recommends.
quoteEn: Religious infiltration is the process by which hostile forces, using religion as cover and freedom of belief as a pretext, replace Marxist ideology with non-Marxist ideology, achieving "peaceful evolution" first of all in the ideological sphere.
quoteZh: 宗教渗透就是敌对势力以宗教为掩护，以信教自由为借口，用非马克思主义意识形态取代马克思主义意识形态的过程，首先在意识形态实现和平演变。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese official discourse for foreign religious activity viewed as aimed at political subversion or unlawful control of religious affairs. Official documents distinguish it from ordinary religious exchange.
A phrase in official Chinese rhetoric for alleged Western strategies to change China's political system and split the country.

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: A set of official ideological principles formulated in the mid-2000s, led by Marxism and including socialism with Chinese characteristics and patriotism.

t: The "opium cornerstone theory" is a distorted summary of Lenin's view of religion
zh: “鸦片基石论”是对列宁宗教观的歪曲概括
paras: Jia Runguo takes issue with a label that, in the author's account, has gained influence in recent years: the "opium cornerstone theory". It reduces Lenin's view of religion to one sentence, that "religion is the opium of the people" is the cornerstone of the Marxist worldview on religion. Jia argues that this is a distorted, decontextualised summary of Marxism-Leninism on religion.

The short piece, posted in 2012, first sets out what Marx meant and how Lenin developed it, citing Marx's introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right and Lenin's "Socialism and Religion" and "The Attitude of the Workers' Party to Religion". It then reviews the Chinese Communist Party's attitude, including Zhou Enlai's 1950 remarks and the Central Committee's 1982 Document No. 19. It ends by listing the errors of the "opium" and "struggle against religion" labels.

Jia contends that Lenin used Marx's phrase to insist that the Party keep a firm materialist and atheist worldview, and tied it to Russian revolutionary conditions. Lifting the sentence out of its context turns it into a rigid dogma. Jia reports that Zhou Enlai treated the slogan as belonging to the revolutionary period, to be played down once the Party held power. The label also severs Party religious policy from Marxist theory and presents part of Lenin's writing as his whole view. Jia says Lenin's essays enrich Marx's and Engels's view and do not form an independent one.

Jia concludes that those who use the label to claim that Marxist religious theory is outdated, and who want to "develop" it with fashionable Western theories, are working metaphysically and against historical materialism. Jia presents the Party's religious policy as a continuing enrichment of Marxism-Leninism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese Marxist case against reading Lenin's "opium" remark as his whole theory of religion.
quoteEn: Lenin's several essays on religion do not form an independent view of religion detached from that of Marx and Engels; rather, they enrich and develop it.
quoteZh: 列宁论述宗教问题的几篇文章，并不构成一个离开马克思和恩格斯的宗教观的独立的宗教观，反而是对马克思和恩格斯宗教观的丰富和发展。

t: New patterns of American religious infiltration of China and their ideological evolution
zh: 美国对华宗教渗透新模式及其意识形态演变
paras: Writing in 2012, Huang argues that after the Cold War the United States developed a new pattern of religious infiltration of China, shaped by what the author calls a "new Cold War ideology". In Huang's account, this ideology combines a revived theocratic politics with older geopolitical thinking. Its basic aim, the article contends, is a "new religious extraterritoriality", symbolised by the 1998 International Religious Freedom Act.

The article has three parts. The first describes the new pattern through four features: new goals, new strategies, new carriers and a new organisational system. The second traces the ideological evolution behind it, through theocratic, geopolitical and new Cold War strands, drawing on the history of Sino-American relations from the nineteenth century, including the Exclusion Act of 1882. The third turns to China's response. Huang relies on Huntington, William Engdahl, Kenneth Scott Latourette and Chinese religious studies scholars.

Huang reads the 1998 Act as an attempt to recreate, in the form of US domestic law, the extraterritorial privileges that foreign missionaries held under the unequal treaties. The article says the strategy has shifted towards "politicising religion". It cites Christian rights-defence activism, work among Chinese students and scholars in North America, and organisations such as ChinaAid, which Huang says set up a national house-church body that China's Ministry of Civil Affairs banned in 2008. Huang finds the roots of this approach in a theocratic politics whose universalism gives way to US interests, citing the contrast between the "open door" and the Exclusion Act. The article sees continuity between old and new forms of hostility: "yellow peril" thinking becomes the "China threat", and anti-communist evangelism becomes the new Cold War outlook. It treats religion as a tool of international monopoly capitalism or hostile external forces, which Huang calls the "ultimate subject" of infiltration.

Huang concludes that China should neither err to the left nor to the right, and should let religion be religion, as Zhou Enlai put it. The article proposes three measures: maintaining a new type of state–religion relationship based on separation and harmony; upholding independent, self-run churches free of foreign domination, with no "state within a state"; and building a long-term crisis-response mechanism for sudden religious incidents. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of religion in 2012 framed foreign missionary activity as political and ideological infiltration, or if you are studying official Chinese views of US religious-freedom policy.
quoteEn: So-called religious infiltration is in essence a form of "political infiltration".
quoteZh: 所谓宗教渗透，其实质是一种“政治渗透”。

glossary.explanation: Refers to privileges that foreign missionaries and Chinese converts held under nineteenth-century unequal treaties, placing them partly outside Chinese jurisdiction. The author applies it to the US International Religious Freedom Act as a "new" form.

A principle proposed by patriotic Christian and Catholic figures in the 1950s and backed by the Party and government. It holds that Chinese religious bodies must be free of foreign control, and the Constitution says religious bodies are not subject to foreign domination.

t: A new model of US religious infiltration of China and its ideological evolution
zh: 美国对华宗教渗透新模式及其意识形态演变
paras: Writing in 2012, Huang Chao asks how US religious policy towards China changed after the Cold War and what ideology lies behind it. The article argues that a "new Cold War ideology", which it says combines a revived theocratic politics with older geopolitical thinking, has produced a new model of religious infiltration. In Huang's account, the model aims at a "new religious extraterritoriality", embodied in the 1998 International Religious Freedom Act.

The article has three parts. The first describes the new model through its goals, strategies, human and technical vehicles, and organisational system. The second traces the ideological evolution through three strands: theocratic, geopolitical and new Cold War ideology. The third sets out the author's proposals for a Chinese response, under the heading of harmony between government and religion.

Huang compares the Act with the extraterritorial privileges that missionaries held under the unequal treaties abolished in 1943, and contends that the Act aims to create a "state within a state" in China. The article describes a strategy of "politicising religion", pursued through Christian "rights defence" campaigns, work among Chinese scholars and students in the US, and organisations such as ChinaAid. It presents this as part of a US "new human rights strategy". Drawing on Michael Hunt, Samuel Huntington and William Engdahl, Huang traces a continuity from the nineteenth-century Toleration Clauses and the Chinese Exclusion Act through the "clash of civilizations" thesis to the "China threat" thesis. The author calls the US attitude contradictory, because religious universalism is upheld only where it serves American interests, and treats infiltration as essentially political, with foreign religion as an instrument of hostile forces.

Huang proposes three responses. China should uphold a new type of government–religion relationship, based on the separation of state and religion and aimed at harmony between them. It should keep the principle of independent, self-run churches and reject any foreign law above the Constitution. And it should build a lasting mechanism for handling sudden religious incidents, since the author warns of non-violent regime change through "swarming" tactics. Huang presents China's approach of managing religious affairs by law as a model that could also help ease international religious and political crises. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese religious-studies scholar framed US religious diplomacy and the "China model" of state–religion relations in 2012, with extensive citations of Huntington, Engdahl and missionary sources.
quoteEn: No religion enjoys privileges beyond the laws and regulations of our country (or of any sovereign state with its integrity intact), and no other country's law can stand above the Constitution of the People's Republic of China.
quoteZh: 任何宗教都不享有可以超出我国（任何主权完整国家）法律、法规的特权，任何其他国家的法律都不可能成为中华人民共和国宪法的上位法。

glossary.explanation: Refers to the privileges that foreign missionaries and converts held in China under the unequal treaties, which exempted them from Chinese jurisdiction. The author uses "new religious extraterritoriality" for what he sees as a modern equivalent in US law.
The author's term for church bodies that would operate outside the control of the Chinese government.
An official formulation for China's state–religion relationship. It rests on the separation of state and religion but aims at positive interaction between them.

A principle set out in the 1950s by patriotic Christian and Catholic figures in China. It holds that religious bodies should be governed, financed and propagated by Chinese believers without foreign control.

t: China Atheism Society 2010 annual meeting and symposium on the theory and practice of scientific atheism held in Urumqi
zh: “中国无神论学会2010年年会暨科学无神论的理论与实践研讨会”在乌鲁木齐召开
paras: This is a very short conference notice reporting that the China Atheism Society's 2010 annual meeting, combined with a symposium on the theory and practice of scientific atheism, took place in Urumqi on 26–27 June 2010. The text gives no argument of its own and only records the event and its themes.

The meeting was co-organised by the China Atheism Society, the Research Centre for Science and Atheism of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, the Xinjiang Academy of Social Sciences, and the School of Law and Economics at Xinjiang Normal University. According to the notice, more than 60 experts and scholars from across the country attended, and with observing scholars the total exceeded one hundred.

Participants discussed a range of topics under the heading of the theory and practice of scientific atheism. The notice lists scientific atheism and society, the theoretical system and disciplinary development of scientific atheism, propaganda and education on atheism, and atheism education among ethnic minorities. It describes the discussions as broad and in-depth but reports no individual papers, positions or disagreements.

The notice reaches no conclusions and announces no follow-up. It mainly documents the topics and institutional sponsors of a scientific-atheism gathering held in Xinjiang. Read the original if you need a brief record of the date, organisers, attendance and agenda of this 2010 meeting.
quoteEn: The symposium centred on the theory and practice of scientific atheism, and held broad and in-depth discussions on several topics, including scientific atheism and society, the theoretical system and disciplinary development of scientific atheism, atheist propaganda and education, and atheist education among ethnic minorities.
quoteZh: 研讨会围绕着科学无神论的理论与实践，就科学无神论与社会、科学无神论的理论体系和学科建设、无神论的宣传教育以及少数民族无神论教育等多个专题展开了广泛深入的研讨。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist-influenced approach to atheism that presents the rejection of religious belief as grounded in science and materialism. In China it is promoted as an academic field and as a subject of public education.

t: Eliminating religious extremism should begin with textbooks
zh: 消除宗教极端主义应从教科书开始
paras: This short commentary, published in 2012 under the Science and Atheism category and with no named author, asks how religious extremism can be uprooted. It argues that military action alone is insufficient and that the soil in which extremism grows, namely textbooks and schooling built on prejudice and intolerance, must also be addressed.

The piece begins with a study released by the US government, as reported by People's Daily Online on 10 November. According to that report, Pakistani textbooks portray religious minorities as inferior or second-class citizens, and most teachers regard non-Muslims as enemies of Islam. The author links this to a curriculum drawn up under the Zia ul-Haq military government in the 1980s, then mentions two bombings in Atyrau, Kazakhstan, by a group called the "Caliph's Soldiers". The commentary closes with the 2009 Texas curriculum dispute and the German practice of teaching religious ethics.

The author contends that textbooks are a "specimen" of national culture and a "template" for the outlook of young people, so extreme ideas absorbed through them can easily be distorted and exploited. Yet the author does not conclude that religion should be removed from textbooks. Religion permeates language, history, ethics and art in every country, and schools also shape morals and ideas. Textbooks should therefore present religious knowledge objectively and rationally, opposing both the vilification of other faiths and the promotion of a single faith or sect.

The author suggests three routes: describing religion through historical development, comparing the similarities and differences of faiths, and showing their value through art courses. Germany's secondary-school religious ethics classes are offered as a model. The author concludes that cultural interests outlast national or ethnic conflicts, and that sowing hatred yields revenge while sowing goodwill yields understanding. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language argument, from 2012, on how religion should be handled in school textbooks as a way to counter extremism.
quoteEn: Religion may be exploited by extremist organisations through radical textbooks, but it can also serve world harmony through peaceful and rational ones.
quoteZh: 宗教既可能在偏激的教科书中为极端组织所利用，也能够在平和理性的教科书中服务于世界和谐。

t: On the constitutional principles governing religious belief
zh: 论宗教信仰的宪法准则
paras: Writing in 2012 (the article carries no named author), the text asks how the Chinese constitution frames the state's stance towards religion and believers. It argues that Article 36 of the constitution, on freedom of religious belief, sets out a compact set of principles for handling religion. These are religious freedom, the separation of state and religion, independence and self-management of religion, and administration of religious affairs according to law.

The article opens by quoting Article 36 in full and noting that, by its figures, over 100 million Chinese citizens follow a religion and that several religions coexist in the country. It then devotes one section to each of the four principles. Each section links constitutional wording to the wider themes of citizens' rights, state sovereignty, foreign policy and social stability.

On religious freedom, the author presents it as a basic human right, in line with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and as including the freedom not to believe. The author divides belief into an inner side (conviction and feeling, a purely personal matter) and an outer side (organisation, institutions, conduct), which belongs to social life and must stay within the law. Separation of state and religion is described as the precondition and guarantee of religious freedom: no state religion, no state subsidy or religious tax, and no religious interference in justice, administration or education. The author justifies independence and self-management by the history of imperialist control over some religions in China. It holds that all major religions except Daoism came from abroad, and that Western hostile forces and separatists use religion to promote Westernization and division. Legal administration is presented as complementing, not opposing, freedom of belief.

The author concludes that no religion holds privileges above the constitution and that religious freedom and separation of state and religion cannot be pretexts for escaping state administration. The article calls for protecting normal religious activity, resisting foreign infiltration, and cracking down on crime and superstition done under a religious cover. It also rules out any use of religion to oppose the leadership of the Communist Party and the socialist system or to undermine national unity. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Chinese legal scholarship in 2012 explained the constitutional basis of religious policy.
quoteEn: Separation of state and religion is the precondition of freedom of religious belief, and also its guarantee.
quoteZh: 政教分离是宗教信仰自由的前提，也是宗教自由的保障。

glossary.explanation: A principle of Chinese religious policy that religious bodies run their own affairs without control by foreign organisations. It is tied to Article 36's clause that religious bodies and affairs are not subject to foreign domination.
The principle that the state neither backs nor bans any religion and that religious bodies do not interfere in state functions. In the article it is tied to the Chinese constitutional framework.

glossary.en: administration of religious affairs according to law
glossary.explanation: The policy of regulating religious organisations and activities through laws and regulations. The article presents it as part of governing the country according to law.

t: Reflections on the adaptation of the Marxist view of religion to the Chinese context
zh: 对马克思主义宗教观中国化的几点思考
paras: The article asks how the Marxist view of religion, formed in nineteenth-century Western Europe and developed in Russia, has been adapted to China, and what that adaptation requires. Its answer is that the Party's Sinicised view of religion inherits the basic principles of historical materialism while revising specific classical judgements to fit China's conditions. The author does not appear to be named in the source; the piece was posted in 2012 under the heading Science and Atheism.

The text has three parts. It first sets out the Marxist view of religion in the narrow sense (Marx and Engels) and in the broad sense (which also covers Lenin and the Chinese Communist Party). It summarises Marx and Engels on the nature, roots, social role and eventual disappearance of religion, and Lenin's additions on the roots of religion under capitalism and on Party policy. It then lists nine innovations and six features of the Chinese view, and closes with three basic requirements for adaptation.

The core argument is that the Chinese view departs from the classical one in several ways. The article says it treats religion as a social, historical and cultural phenomenon and as a matter of belief among the people, rather than only as an ideology or "opium". It describes religion in China as long-term, mass-based and complex, with both positive and negative functions. Policy rests on freedom of religious belief, management of religious affairs according to law, independent and self-run religious bodies, a united front with patriotic religious figures, and guiding religion to adapt to socialist society. The author names six features: ideological character, scientific character, wholeness, practicality, openness and national character. Adaptation, the author argues, requires holding to the basic principles of historical materialism, starting from China's concrete national conditions, and enriching the theory further. Some classical formulations, such as "religion is the opium of the people", "religion as spiritual booze" and "struggle against religion", must be reconsidered and not copied mechanically.

The author concludes that the Marxist view of religion as developed by the Party is an important source and component of the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It is presented as the fundamental guide for handling religious questions under socialism, for national unity, social stability and a harmonious society. The author expects it to keep developing under Party leadership and claims that it has wider significance for other socialist countries. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Chinese Marxist theory justifies its move beyond the classical "opium" thesis in religious policy.
quoteEn: Without China's concrete national conditions, and cut off from China's specific social and historical circumstances, there can be no talk of adapting the Marxist view of religion to China.
quoteZh: 离开了中国具体国情，脱离开中国的具体社会历史条件，马克思主义宗教观中国化便无从谈起。

glossary.explanation: The policy that citizens may believe or not believe in a religion. It is a core principle of the Party's religious policy, subject to the requirement that religious activity be lawful.
The Party's strategy of building alliances with non-Party groups, including religious figures, around shared political goals.

glossary.zh: 宗教与社会主义社会相适应
glossary.pinyin: zōngjiào yǔ shèhuì zhǔyì shèhuì xiāngshìyìng
glossary.explanation: Official formula, from the 1990s, for guiding religion to coexist with socialism. It asks believers to support the leadership of the Party and the socialist system, not to give up their faith.
A goal of the Hu Jintao era, promoted from the mid-2000s, which stressed social cohesion and the easing of social tensions.

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义理论体系
glossary.pinyin: Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì lǐlùn tǐxì
glossary.explanation: The Party's official name for its path since reform and opening up. The theoretical system comprises the main lines of Party thought from Mao Zedong Thought through the Scientific Outlook on Development.

t: Atheism as the crystallisation of human civilisation and thought
zh: 无神论是人类社会文明和思考的结晶
paras: This article, published in 2012 with no author named, treats atheism as a product of human social civilisation and thought. It defines atheism in the West as the denial of a single God and his theology, and in China as the denial of all ghosts, spirits and supernatural forces. The author argues that atheism and theism will coexist for a long time, and that atheism's philosophical task is to criticise the illusions of religious theology, establish a scientific outlook on life and values, and promote social development.

The piece is organised in three historical sections. The first surveys atheism in Chinese philosophy, from Xunzi, Han Fei, Wang Chong and Fan Zhen through Liu Zongyuan, Zhang Zai and Wang Fuzhi to the May Fourth movement, Zhang Taiyan, Chen Duxiu, Hu Shi and Li Dazhao. The second traces Western atheism from the ancient Greeks and Epicurus, through medieval persecution, pantheism, mechanical materialism, deism and French Enlightenment 'militant atheism', to Feuerbach, Darwin, Russell, Sartre and the 'new atheism' of Richard Dawkins. The third turns to Marxist scientific atheism.

The core argument is that Marxist atheism is the 'higher form' of scientific atheism. The author reads Marx and Engels as moving beyond Feuerbach: religion is an inverted worldview arising from an inverted world of exploitation, so criticism of religion alone cannot overcome religious alienation, which requires changing the social system and economic base. Lenin is credited with sharpening the philosophical critique of religious thinking. For China, the author identifies two principles: full freedom of religious belief, with religion barred from threatening national security, ethnic unity or the socialist system; and no administrative means against theistic ideas, which are to be handled by persuasion and social change, while 'studying religion and criticising theology' applies in culture and education.

The author sets out three values of Marxist atheism in contemporary China. It is the worldview starting point of the socialist core values system, and attempts to remove atheism from Marxism and socialist ideology are called dangerous. It is a healthy way of life that contributes to building a harmonious society. And, pursued thoroughly, it leads to a rational social system, so that its education and propaganda should be built into socialism with Chinese characteristics, with Communists uniting believers and non-believers to remove the social roots of religion. Read the original if you want a broad, Party-aligned overview of atheism in Chinese and Western thought and of how a Chinese Marxist scholar justified its place in official ideology around 2012.
quoteEn: The philosophical mission of atheism is to criticise the illusions of religious theology, establish a scientific outlook on life and values, and promote the development of human society.
quoteZh: 无神论的哲学使命是批判宗教神学的虚幻、树立科学的人生观和价值观、推动人类社会的发展。

glossary.explanation: An official set of values promoted by the Chinese Party-state, formally articulated in 2012. The article uses the related earlier phrase 'socialist core value system'.
A goal promoted by the Party leadership from the mid-2000s, stressing social cohesion and balanced development.
The official name for the Chinese Party-state's path of socialist development since reform and opening up.

t: On the significance of propagating scientific atheism in the strategy of rejuvenating the country through science and education
zh: 论科教兴国战略中科学无神论宣传的意义
paras: The article asks why propaganda and education in scientific atheism should be part of China's strategy of rejuvenating the country through science and education. Its thesis is that the two are internally connected: the strategy cannot be carried out effectively unless scientific atheism is also vigorously promoted. The author, writing in the context of Deng Xiaoping Theory and the goal of a moderately prosperous society, treats the strategy as a basic national policy for developing the productive forces.

The text has three parts. The first defines scientific atheism and traces its history, from the scattered and commonsense atheism of antiquity to the modern atheism built on natural science, including French militant atheism of the eighteenth century and its Marxist form. The second sets out the substance of the science-and-education strategy as part of Deng Xiaoping Theory, citing Deng's statements from 1977 to 1992, including the thesis that science and technology are the primary productive force. The third gives three reasons why atheist propaganda is intrinsic to the strategy.

The author argues that Marxism is the most thoroughgoing atheism because it explains the roots, conditions and eventual disappearance of religious theism, and that atheism is also a premise of Marxism itself. On this basis the author claims, first, that modern science arose with the rise of atheist thought, so scientific atheism is a precondition of technological development. Second, the strategy depends on workers and researchers with a spirit of innovation and openness, which the author says can only rest on a scientific atheist worldview. Third, scientific atheism is science's natural ally, so advances in science and education will in turn erode superstition and theism and spread atheist convictions in society.

The author concludes that the strategy and scientific atheism are inherently linked, and calls for effective, energetic propaganda and education in scientific atheism alongside implementation of the strategy. The piece is a short, programmatic statement that shows how atheism work was justified within the development policy framework of its period. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Marxist writers around 2012 tied scientific atheism to Deng Xiaoping Theory and to science, education and talent policy.
quoteEn: Scientific atheism is the natural ally of science, and the development of science can supply atheism with theoretical and empirical support.
quoteZh: 科学无神论是科学的天然盟友，科学的发展能够为无神论提供理论与实证的支持。

glossary.en: rejuvenating the country through science and education
glossary.literal: revitalise the nation through science and education
glossary.explanation: A national strategy adopted in the mid-1990s that gives priority to science, technology and education in economic and social development. The article presents it as part of Deng Xiaoping Theory.
In the Marxist tradition, atheism grounded in natural science and in dialectical and historical materialism, which seeks to explain the social origins of religion rather than merely deny belief.
The body of ideas associated with Deng Xiaoping on reform, opening up and socialist modernization, which the Communist Party counts as part of its guiding ideology.

glossary.zh: 科学技术是第一生产力
glossary.en: science and technology are the primary productive force
glossary.literal: science and technology are the first productive force
glossary.explanation: A thesis Deng Xiaoping put forward in 1988, which became a key justification for giving priority to science and education.
A long-standing Party goal of general, moderate material well-being, used as a benchmark for national development.

t: The development of "new theism" since reform and opening up, and related laws and policies
zh: 改革开放以来新有神论的发展与相关法律和政策
paras: Writing around 2011–2012 from the standpoint of scientific atheism, the article asks how organised, non-religious-label forms of belief in spirits and deities spread in mainland China after reform and opening up, and how law and policy responded. The author, who is not named, groups qigong, "extraordinary powers" and Falun Gong under the heading "new theism" and argues that the legal and policy framework still has gaps. The author also holds that scientific atheism remains under-researched and under-promoted.

The article first notes that earlier scholarship has dealt with qigong, extraordinary powers and Falun Gong mostly from the angle of controlling "evil cults", and that few studies treat them together as new theism. It then gives a short history of the three phenomena from the 1980s to the 1990s. A second part surveys the Constitution (1982), the Education Law, Labour Law and Criminal Law of the 1990s, Party Document No. 19 (1982), Document No. 6 (1991), the 1997 white paper, the 1999 decision on banning cult organisations, and the 2004 and 2007–2011 notices on atheist education. The third part offers four reflections.

In the author's account, the "qigong fever" of the late 1980s and early 1990s produced thousands of groups with self-invented doctrines and religious-style organisation. Claims of "extraordinary powers", first reported in 1979, were researched as science even though they presuppose spirits. Falun Gong, founded by Li Hongzhi in 1992, is described as an eclectic mix of Buddhist, Daoist and qigong elements with theistic content, and the author notes that these phenomena faded quickly only after its 1999 ban. Reviewing the laws, the author concludes that most provisions aim to guarantee religious freedom, while the 1999 decision was a direct response to cults, and that the Party's documents show a continuing commitment to Marxist atheism.

The author calls for clearer legal definitions of religion, religious activity and religious organisation, and for rules covering groups that spread theism without a religious label or that act outside the law under a legal religious name. Home churches are cited as a case outgrowing the 1997 white paper's exemption from registration. The author also urges serious research and public education in scientific atheism, arguing it addresses the public sphere rather than religious bodies, and says new theism was linked to overseas new religious movements. Finally, the author calls for building the core socialist value system rather than relying on religion for a harmonious society. Read the original if you want an official-leaning Chinese scholarly view of how qigong, Falun Gong and atheist education were handled in law and policy up to 2011.
quoteEn: To build a harmonious society, we cannot rely on developing religion, but must rely on building the core socialist value system.
quoteZh: 我们要建设和谐社会，不能依靠发展宗教，而是要依靠社会主义核心价值体系的建设。

glossary.explanation: The author's label for organised belief in spirits or deities that arose after reform and opening up outside officially recognised religions, including qigong groups, "extraordinary powers" and Falun Gong.
A Marxist-based approach that promotes atheism through science education and research in the public sphere rather than through political campaigns against religion.
The official Chinese term for groups the state deems illegal and harmful that claim a religious guise. Falun Gong was designated as such in 1999.
A traditional practice of breathing, movement and meditation for health. In the 1980s–90s it became a mass movement, and some groups took on religious features.

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: A term from the Party's 2006 ideological programme, setting out the guiding values of socialist culture and ideology.
A goal promoted by the Party leadership of Hu Jintao from the mid-2000s, stressing social stability and balanced development.

t: Marx and evolutionary theory: rethinking the relationship between Marx's and Darwin's doctrines
zh: 马克思与进化论——对马克思与达尔文学说关系的重新思考
paras: The article takes up a long-standing question: how did Marx actually regard Darwin's theory of evolution? It notes that some scholars have called Marx a "socialist Darwinist", that others see Marxism and Darwinism as differing in form but similar in substance, and that many Marxists simply pair the two thinkers. Using Marx's own letters and texts, the author argues that Marx affirmed Darwin in limited respects but criticised him more extensively, and that the two doctrines differ fundamentally on human beings.

The piece is built in three parts plus a conclusion. The first part gathers Marx's positive comments on Darwin from 1859 to 1867 and Engels's graveside speech. The second sets out Marx's doubts, drawing on his 1862 and 1869 letters and his 1866 preference for the French naturalist Pierre Trémaux. The third compares Darwin's The Descent of Man (1871) with Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and The German Ideology on human nature and development. The two views cited as misreadings come from a 1979 article by L. S. Feuer and a 1983 article by P. van den Berghe, both known to the author through Chinese translations.

The author argues that Marx valued Darwin chiefly for dealing a blow to religious theology and teleology and for supplying a natural-historical confirmation of historical materialism, which, the author stresses, was already formed before 1859. Marx faulted Darwin for misusing Malthus and for projecting English competitive society onto nature, and rejected the idea that a struggle for existence governs human history. For Marx, humans differ from animals through conscious practical activity, and human sociability is a product of social, economic and political conditions. Darwin, in the author's reading, treats human nature as a slow biological inheritance shaped by natural selection. On this basis the author says Darwin's view leans towards conservatism, while Marx's supports revolution because human nature can change quickly when the economic base changes.

The author concludes that Marx refused to apply natural selection and the struggle for existence universally to human society and held that natural laws cannot simply be transferred to it. Marx's stress on human agency is described as the philosophical foundation of his theory of social revolution. Read the original if you want a short, letter-based account of how Marx's remarks on Darwin have been read in Chinese Marxist scholarship, and of the case for separating the two thinkers.
quoteEn: Marx opposed the universal validity of natural selection and the struggle for existence in Darwin's theory of evolution within the sphere of human society; he held that human existence is special and that natural laws cannot be transplanted directly into human society.
quoteZh: 马克思反对达尔文进化论中自然选择与生存斗争在人类社会领域的普遍有效性，他认为，人的存在具有特殊性，不能将自然法则直接搬用到人类社会中。

t: The theory of "cultural proselytising"
zh: 文化传教说
paras: This short editorial-style commentary, published in the Science and Atheism section and posted in January 2012, asks readers to pay attention to "cultural proselytising". The author argues that foreign missionary activity in China now works through culture and economic inducement, and that its aim is political and economic advantage rather than faith alone.

The text defines the term as proselytising by cultural means and proselytising directed at cultural elites. It then moves from the general nature of religious propagation, through the history of Buddhism, Islam and Christianity in China, to the unequal treaties after the Opium War and the present day. It closes with a wartime literacy-textbook lesson.

The author holds that spreading one's religion is unobjectionable from the believer's standpoint, but that for those targeted it means changing beliefs and so brings conflict. Religious divisions, the author says, add a further line of cleavage in contemporary local wars, though material interests are their root cause. Before the Opium War, the entry of religions into China is described as legitimate and voluntary. After it, the author says, missionary clauses were written into treaties imposed by gunboats, so that China was made to surrender its souls along with its territory. Today, in the author's account, missionaries aim at influential intellectuals, the "brains and backbone" of China, to serve their own interests. The author points to a US government commission monitoring proselytising and questions whether Chinese intellectuals who assist understand the role they play.

The author concludes that Chinese people should be on guard against efforts to place so-called "universal values" above national and ethnic interests. Certain intellectuals, the author suggests, should revisit the lesson "We are Chinese; we love our motherland." Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese atheist-propaganda outlet framed religion, foreign influence and "universal values" in 2012.
quoteEn: We are Chinese; we love our own motherland.
quoteZh: 我们是中国人，我们爱自己的祖国。

t: "Doomsday" in the United States: what does it signify?
zh: “世界末日”在美国——它表象的是什么?
paras: Prompted by the failed prediction that Jesus would return on 21 May 2011, this commentary asks what the American "doomsday" phenomenon says about US society. The author argues that it should not be dismissed as foolish entertainment. In the article's account, belief in the end of the world rests on deep religious and cultural foundations in the West and is tied to social polarisation, weak scientific education and politics.

The piece opens with Harold Camping of Family Radio, whose 1994 date and later 2011 dates for Judgment Day all passed without event. Camping then moved the date to 21 October 2011. The author then turns to the ancient Chinese story of the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall, as told in the Liezi, and sets out the four attitudes in it. The last third presents Gallup and Pew Research Center figures on religious belief, evolution and expectations of Christ's return, with a table of survey results.

The author argues that doomsday belief in the West fuels a climate of fear that shapes national character and political decisions, including the treatment of other nations, beliefs and values as threats to security. In this reading, such fear lets interested groups profit and contributes to world instability. The author holds that today's believers fall into two groups, those with ulterior motives and those left behind by scientific civilisation, and that both are social problems. The cited surveys show 41 per cent of Americans expecting Jesus to return before 2050, with higher rates among white evangelicals, people without college experience and Southerners. The author links this to the finding that only 39 per cent accept evolution, and to the pushing of intelligent design into textbooks.

The author concludes that the answer to natural disasters and doomsday fears is to put \"revitalising the country through science and education\" into practice, rather than religious explanations. In the author's view, wars and conflicts are man-made products of social structure and the interests of particular states and groups, and in the end the peoples concerned must wake up and speak for themselves. The author describes US society as sharply polarised in culture as well as economics, with a dominant minority also ruling in religion and ideology while cultural elites stay silent. The Liezi story is offered as a model of persuading people out of baseless dread. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese science-and-atheism writing of 2012 interpreted American religiosity, with the survey data it cites.
quoteEn: In fact, in today's age of scientific civilisation there are roughly two kinds of groups who believe in the end of the world. One is those with ulterior motives, the other is those forgotten by scientific civilisation. Both are social problems.
quoteZh: 实际上，在科学文明的今天，信仰世界末日的群体大约有两种。一是别有用意者，一是被科学文明遗忘者。二者都是社会问题。

glossary.en: revitalising the country through science and education
glossary.literal: science and education to rejuvenate the nation
glossary.explanation: A national development strategy announced by Jiang Zemin's leadership in 1995, which gives priority to science, technology and education in China's modernisation.

glossary.en: the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall
glossary.literal: the man of Qi worries about the sky
glossary.explanation: A Chinese idiom from the Daoist text Liezi, for groundless anxiety. The story is used in the article as a contrast to Western doomsday belief.

t: "The end of the world" in America: what does it represent?
zh: “世界末日”在美国——它表象的是什么?
paras: This commentary, published in the Science and Atheism section and written in 2011–12, takes the failed prediction that Christ would return on 21 May 2011 as a window onto American society. The author argues that the episode is not mere entertainment for the gullible. In the article's reading, it reflects deep religious and cultural roots, a polarised social structure, and a politics that profits from fear.

The article opens with Harold Camping of the Christian broadcaster Family Radio. His earlier prediction of an end in September 1994 failed, and he then moved the date to 21 May 2011 and, after that failed, to 21 October 2011. It then turns to the Chinese story of the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall, quoting the Liezi at length. It closes with survey figures from Gallup and the Pew Research Center on American belief in the Second Coming, evolution and religion.

The author makes three main moves. First, belief in the end of the world is a basic doctrine of monotheism, and the author says centuries of such prophecies have left a psychology of fear that shapes national character. In the author's view, this fear carries over into US politics, where "cultural conflict" and weapons of mass destruction make other nations and beliefs look like threats to security. Second, the author holds that today's believers are of two kinds, people with ulterior motives and people left behind by scientific civilisation, and calls both a social problem. The Pew data are cited as evidence: 41% of Americans expect Christ's return by 2050, rising to 58% among white evangelicals and 59% among those without college experience, against 19% of college graduates. Third, the author links this to a society polarised economically, culturally and ideologically, in which a ruling minority dominates religion and ideology while cultural elites stay silent.

The author concludes that natural disasters should be met with science and education, citing the slogan "rejuvenating the country through science and education", and not with religious readings. Conflict and war are described as man-made and tied to the political and economic demands of certain states and interest groups. The author says this is a question of social structure and system, which in the end only each country's own people can resolve. Read the original if you want a Chinese atheist-oriented reading of American religiosity, with Pew and Gallup figures and the Liezi parable of the man of Qi.
quoteEn: But this is the advantage of religion: no fact can prove that God does not exist, and the devout will go on believing as before.
quoteZh: 但宗教的好处就在这里：无论什么事实都不能证明上帝不存在，虔诚的人们依旧会坚持地信仰下去

glossary.en: rejuvenating the country through science and education
glossary.literal: revitalise the country through science and education
glossary.explanation: A national development strategy announced in 1995 that makes science, technology and education the basis of economic and social development. The article presents it as the proper response to disasters and end-of-world fears.

t: Some reflections on anti-cult work in universities
zh: 对高校反邪教工作的几点思考
