paras: This article, written around 2012 and published without a named author, asks how Chinese universities should respond to the spread of "cults" (xiejiao) on campus. It argues that cult infiltration of higher education has taken on new features, that universities have a particular responsibility to resist it, and that a set of practical measures can make campus anti-cult work effective. Falun Gong is the main example throughout.

The text has three parts. The first describes the new situation: infiltration of students and of university teachers, and the cults' growing use of high technology. The second sets out why anti-cult work matters, looking at the causes of cult growth, current trends among cults, the social standing of universities and their social functions. The third proposes five approaches: theoretical research, strengthening anti-cult organisations, classroom teaching, innovative themed activities and psychological intervention.

On the diagnosis, the author contends that cults deliberately target students, who are described as immature, curious about the supernatural and short of social experience. Cults also target teachers, whose standing can lend a "scientific" gloss to cult doctrine. The article claims that cults borrow scientific vocabulary, use the internet and satellites, and have moved from open to underground proselytising, while their followers disrupt teaching and sometimes turn to self-harm or violence. On the remedy, the author argues that universities hold the research capacity, the teaching platform and the student base to counter this. The proposals include surveys of students' beliefs and their ability to recognise cults, and comparative study of foreign experience. They also include teaching that ties anti-cult content to each discipline (for example, perpetual motion machines in mechanics, or the difference between religion and cult in philosophy) and programmes to counter psychological suggestion and to help affected staff and students.

The author concludes that the struggle against cults is sharp, complex and long-term. Universities should raise the banner of science, spread scientific knowledge, break down modern superstition and strengthen political awareness among staff and students, with the aim of building a civilised campus. The article is a short policy-oriented piece from the early 2010s, useful as an example of how anti-cult work was framed in Chinese higher education. Read the original if you want to see the specific measures, such as the "Two Courses" teaching and themed campus activities, that an official-minded Chinese academic proposed for universities at the time.
quoteEn: The struggle against cults is sharp, complex and long-term.
quoteZh: 反邪教的斗争是尖锐的、复杂的、长期的。

glossary.explanation: In official Chinese usage, a legal and political category for organisations judged to deceive and control members and to endanger society, with Falun Gong the best-known example. It is wider and more pejorative than the Western term "cult"; the article's characterisations follow this official usage.
The compulsory university courses in Marxist theory and in ideological and political education, taught to all students. The article treats them as a main channel for anti-cult education.

t: A brief discussion of Ren Jiyu's thought on scientific atheism
zh: 简论任继愈的科学无神论思想
paras: The article introduces the scientific atheism of Ren Jiyu, whom it presents as the founder of Marxist religious studies in China. Its author argues that Ren combined Marxist research on religion with publicity for the Party's religious policy and with sustained criticism of superstition. Noting that pseudo-science and superstition remain active while atheist advocacy is weak ("theism has its speakers, atheism has none"), the author holds that Ren's ideas still matter for Marxist education and for public morals.

The text has three parts. The first sets out what scientific atheism means, tracing atheism from early Greek and Chinese thought to the modern natural sciences and then to Marxism. The second covers Ren's view of religion, its long persistence under socialism, and his handling of religious freedom. The third turns to his campaign against what he called the "new theism", which includes pseudo-science, "special powers" and fortune-telling presented as traditional culture.

On the first point, the article reports Ren as holding that modern atheism, grounded in natural science, differs from ancient atheism because it explains why belief in spirits arises. Marxism is the most thorough form, since it identifies religion's social roots and the laws of its rise and decline. Ren is said to compare scientific atheism to elementary mathematics, which a Marxist worldview needs as its foundation. On religion, the article relays Ren's view that it is ultimately harmful to the people, a "spiritual anaesthetic" that peasant uprisings could not turn to their advantage. Because religion will fade only when alien natural and social forces are overcome, atheist education is the only means of struggle, and it must go together with legal protection of the freedom to believe or not to believe. The Party, Ren argues, must keep its own worldview independent. On the new theism, he sorted its forms into four kinds and criticised its distortion of "practice as the criterion of truth", urging that its demonstrations be replicated and exposed.

The author concludes that scientific atheism is part of advanced culture and of building socialist spiritual civilization. Ren's call to escape ignorance as well as poverty ("脱愚") is offered as a continuing task. The author also cites Party members who practise religion and scholars who propose a more tolerant policy towards them, and treats Ren's position as a warning against both. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of Ren Jiyu's views on atheism, religion policy and pseudo-science, drawn mostly from his collected essays.
quoteEn: No one is born an atheist; becoming an atheist is the result of education acquired later in life.
quoteZh: 任何人都不是天生的无神论者，成为无神论者是后天教育的结果。

glossary.explanation: A term for atheism grounded in modern natural science and, in the Marxist version, in dialectical and historical materialism. It is promoted in China through bodies such as the China Atheism Society and the journal Science and Atheism.
Ren Jiyu's label for pseudo-scientific and quasi-religious practices that claim scientific or cultural authority, such as "special powers", qigong "external qi" and Zhouyi divination.
A Party policy concept for the cultural, ideological and moral side of socialist development, paired with material civilization.

t: Similarities and differences between terrorism and cults
zh: 恐怖主义与邪教的异同
orig: Cultic Studies Review, vol. 2 no. 1, 2003 (Chinese: 《膜拜问题研究与评论》)
source: marxism.cass.cn, Science and Atheism section, posted 9 January 2012
paras: This is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by Christopher M. Centner, a senior analyst at the US Defense Intelligence Agency, first published in 2003. Centner asks how terrorist organisations and cults overlap and where they differ, using al-Qaeda as the main case. He argues that al-Qaeda is a representative terrorist organisation with some cult-like traits, but that it differs from most cults in important structural ways.

The Chinese editors added a note that the text was published after the killing of Osama bin Laden (announced 2011) to help the public recognise and guard against terrorist and cult groups. The article starts from Western definitions of each type of group. It then covers recruitment of al-Qaeda members, training and control, the figure of bin Laden, and suicide attacks. It ends with lessons for Western policy and seven warning signs of violent religious movements.

Centner's central distinction is one of orientation. Terrorist groups look outward, towards what they do to non-members and towards political change. Cults look inward, towards control of members, self-preservation and growth. He cites Aum Shinrikyo as a cult that used terrorism and Peru's Shining Path as a terrorist group with a cult-like leader. Al-Qaeda resembles apocalyptic cults in its recruitment of alienated young people, its use of deception, its isolation of members and its view of a cosmic struggle between good and evil. Unlike cults, Centner argues, it depends on broad popular and financial support, and its followers do not deify bin Laden. He describes suicide attacks as glorified by social and religious norms, so that coercion by a cult leader is unnecessary.

Centner concludes that a movement like al-Qaeda would survive its leader's death, because it draws on mainstream currents in contemporary Islamic thought. He describes a struggle inside Islam over how to govern Muslim societies that may last generations. He proposes that outside powers promote trade and ties with moderate regimes, fund schools, and help revise textbooks to cut hatred and glorification of war. He also proposes that academics warn governments of violent trends using seven indicators, including grievance rooted in past injustice, politics seen as cosmic conflict, violence justified by divine will, paramilitary training, and a violent, visionary leader. Read the original if you study how US security analysts compared terrorism and cults, or want the seven warning signs in full.
quoteEn: Terrorist organisations are a kind of suicide cult, but there are differences.
quoteZh: 恐怖组织是一种自杀式的邪教，但又有区别。

t: "Seizing China's head and back": on cultural proselytising and religion in universities
zh: “抓住中国的脑袋和脊背”
paras: Writing in December 2011, the author, who publishes under the pen name "Wenhua Chuanjiao" (literally "cultural proselytising"), responds to a report in the journal Science and Atheism (2011, no. 2). The report covered a Beijing Normal University symposium on how to respond to the spread of religion in universities. The author argues that Christian theology, "cultural Christians" and the "religious market theory" are forms of cultural proselytising. In the author's reading, they continue a long Western Christian effort to influence China through education and ideas, and that effort now reaches into Chinese universities.

The commentary is built in three steps. It first distinguishes teaching general knowledge about religion from spreading theology. It then criticises the "religious market" idea and opposition to state regulation of religion. The longest section reviews historical statements by missionaries and Western figures, which the author takes from Luo Guanzong's book Never Forget the Past, a Guide for the Future (2003). It closes with the present: foreign theologians hired to teach the Bible, and a university press publishing creationist books.

The author holds that universities in a socialist country should teach religion as an object of objective study, not train missionaries. Theology, whether inside or outside the church, is in the author's view theism opposed to atheism. "Cultural Christians" are said to be more persuasive than clergy because they dress theology in new concepts. The "market" theory, the author argues, trivialises believers' faith and amounts to a pretext for unregulated religious expansion. The historical quotations carry the main weight: the 1887 Society for the Diffusion of Christian and General Knowledge's William Williamson aimed to "disarm" the Chinese, and Timothy Richard sought control of public opinion and higher education in order to "seize China's head and back". In 1949 John Leighton Stuart and John Mott described the Bible as having a political value against Marxism and atheism. The author reads these as evidence that missionary work was political.

The author concludes that infiltration of universities is not a new problem and has intensified since reform and opening up, and now takes the new form of invited "professors". The author suggests that some universities may be abandoning the Four Cardinal Principles, and praises Beijing Normal University's leaders for taking a clear stand. The author also calls for specialised research and for vigilance, since Western church bodies are said to study infiltration strategy. The author also says Christian scripture is part of human cultural heritage and that not all missionaries were hostile. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese atheist-oriented commentator in 2011 framed religion in universities as a question of ideological security, with the historical missionary quotations the author relies on.
quoteEn: Strictly speaking, popularising knowledge about religion and spreading theology or training "professional missionaries" are two different things.
quoteZh: 严格说来，普及宗教知识与传播神学、培养“职业传教士”是两码事。

glossary.explanation: A term used in the Science and Atheism report and by the author for the spread of religious ideas through academic, scholarly or cultural channels instead of direct preaching.
A sociology-of-religion approach that treats religion as a market. The author understands it as a call to open China to religion and to resist state regulation.
Chinese scholars who engage with Christianity as an academic or cultural subject, and who may or may not be church members. The author treats them as covert propagators of theism.
Deng Xiaoping's 1979 formula: upholding the socialist path, the people's democratic dictatorship, Communist Party leadership, and Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world that began in China in 1978.

t: Who is the "designer"? Reflections on reading Hawking's The Grand Design
zh: “设计”出自谁之手?——霍金《大设计》读后感
paras: This is a reader's review, posted in 2011 under the category Science and Atheism, of Stephen Hawking and Leonard Mlodinow's The Grand Design (Chinese edition translated by Wu Zhongchao, Hunan Science and Technology Press, 2011). The reviewer takes up the "riddle of existence": why there is something rather than nothing, and who created or "designed" the universe. The review argues that Hawking answers from a purely naturalist standpoint, using science to remove God from the last domain he occupied.

The review is organised in four parts. The first sets out why Hawking raises the question, tracing human answers from myth through Greek rationalism, medieval theology and Newtonian mechanism to Laplace, Nietzsche and Russell. The second explains how the book reads the existence of the universe and life, and why its title is read as a metaphor. The third considers the book's implications for worldview and culture, and the last gives an overall assessment.

On the book's reasoning, the author highlights Hawking's historical account of how natural law came to be understood. Hawking sees two detours back toward theology, Aristotelian teleology and its medieval uptake by Aquinas, and the attempt by Descartes and Newton to make God the lawgiver. Two milestones led away from theology: the Ionian view of a non-human-centred cosmos, and Laplace's scientific determinism. The author then reports Hawking's case for M-theory: it follows determinism, uses model-dependent realism, and builds on tested theories, so that many universes arise from physical law without divine intervention. The author reads "grand design" as a negative metaphor for a unified theory of natural laws, not a supernatural designer.

The author concludes that the book removes God from the origin of the universe, spreads a scientific worldview and supports scientific rationality and atheism. The review sets this against the growth since the 1960s and 1970s of New Age movements, mysticism and postmodernism, and against the American "intelligent design" disputes, which it calls a version of creationism. It calls for a new Enlightenment and praises the book as a rare popular work on scientific worldview. Read the original if you want a Chinese atheist-science-popularisation reading of Hawking, or an example of how the science–religion debate was framed in Chinese discussion in 2011.
quoteEn: Hawking's understanding of the meaning of the existence of the universe, all things and life is purely naturalist, with no supernatural factor whatsoever.
quoteZh: 霍金对宇宙、万物、生命存在意义的理解是纯粹的自然主义的，没有任何超自然因素。

t: Promoting the scientific spirit to raise the quality of China's citizens
zh: 弘扬科学精神，提高我国国民素质
paras: The article, published without a named author in the Science and Atheism section of the Academy of Marxism site in 2011, asks how China can raise the overall quality of its citizens (guomin suzhi) to meet the needs of modernization. It argues that the scientific spirit is seriously lacking among Chinese citizens because of the influence of traditional culture, and that this deficit fundamentally limits improvement in national quality. Promoting the scientific spirit and reforming traditional culture is therefore presented as essential to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

The text is organised in four parts. It first contrasts the rational tradition inherited from ancient Greek philosophy and modern Western natural science with Chinese culture, which it describes as shaped by practical, morally centred reason. It then considers the scientific spirit in relation to citizens' ideological and moral quality, their scientific and cultural level, and their sense of themselves as agents (subjectivity). Examples include Copernicus, Bruno, Galileo, Marx, Einstein and Chinese scientists such as Qian Xuesen.

The author's central claims run as follows. Traditional Chinese culture, grounded in feudal patriarchal autocracy and agrarian production, is said to have matured prematurely and left habits of vague thinking and superstition. The author adds that rapid social transformation encourages impatience and a search for quick results. Education is a second target: exam-oriented schooling transmits finished conclusions and neglects scientific attitude. Following the Self-Strengthening Movement, the article argues, China imported scientific techniques while rejecting their underlying logic and philosophy, a split it illustrates with Lu Xun's line about new skills and old thinking. Third, drawing on historical materialism, the author holds that a scientific spirit of independent thought, scepticism and respect for facts builds the subjectivity that socialist democracy needs, citing Lenin's remark that illiterates stand outside politics.

The author concludes that the scientific spirit is a basic quality of modern people in a scientific age, and that promoting it matters especially for a China undergoing reform and opening up and rapid social change. Raising citizens' quality is also linked to the Scientific Outlook on Development's people-centred approach and to Marxism's idea of the all-round development of the individual. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2011 Chinese Marxist text connects science, education reform, anti-superstition work and popular subjectivity to national modernization.
quoteEn: The absence of the scientific spirit in China's traditional culture has had a profound effect on the quality of Chinese citizens, and raising that quality must begin with promoting the scientific spirit and reforming traditional culture.
quoteZh: 我国传统文化中科学精神缺失对我国国民素质的影响极为深远，提高我国国民素质必须要从弘扬科学精神，改造中国传统文化做起。

glossary.explanation: A guiding policy concept associated with Hu Jintao's leadership, stressing people-centred, comprehensive and sustainable development.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A long-standing official goal of restoring China's strength and international standing, widely used in Party discourse.
The policy of economic reform and engagement with the world launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.
A late-nineteenth-century Qing effort to adopt Western military and industrial technology while keeping the Confucian political and cultural order.
An education approach centred on preparing students for examinations, often contrasted in China with 'quality education' (suzhi jiaoyu).

t: Spirit worship in ancient China
zh: 中国古代的神灵崇拜
paras: This article, published in the Science and Atheism section, surveys the forms of spirit worship in traditional Chinese culture. It opens from the premise that ideas of gods and spirits are an illusory and distorted reflection of nature and society in the human mind. The author argues that tracing the sources and development of this culture can raise understanding and help establish a scientific view of culture.

The survey moves through three broad areas: nature worship (heaven, earth, sun, moon, stars, thunder, wind, rain, water, fire, mountains and stones), the worship of animals and plants, and the worship of spirits proper. The last section sorts popular belief into creator gods, guardian and household gods, ghosts, nature spirits, deified persons (divine figures, immortals, sages, shamans), and sacred objects and souls. Examples come from the Han majority and from many ethnic groups, drawing on classical texts such as the Classic of Mountains and Seas.

The author's core claim is that all such worship rests on animism and theism, which suit human ignorance and naivety, and that it ultimately serves survival. Bear-hunting peoples, for example, honour the bear as an ancestor while hunting it, which the author reads as a conflict between awe of nature and material need. The article also traces how worship of historical figures such as Yue Fei, Qu Yuan and Guan Yu drifts into superstition, and criticises discrimination against women in shamanic and hunting taboos. It treats shamanism as the most deceptive form because it is closest to everyday life. Some modern practices, including folk medicine using animal bones and near-death-experience research, are described as pseudo-science that carries on old worship.

The author concludes that spirit worship is a rich but mystical part of traditional culture whose continued survival, even in an era that promotes atheism, shows how persistent such beliefs are. The article offers no programme beyond clarifying origins in order to support a scientific outlook. Read the original if you want a broad catalogue of Chinese popular deities, ghosts and nature cults, and an example of how Chinese atheist scholarship in 2011 framed religious folk belief.
quoteEn: The idea of gods and spirits is an illusory and distorted reflection of nature and society in people's minds.
quoteZh: 神灵观念是自然和社会在人们头脑中的虚幻和歪曲的反映。

t: The rise of religious belief in the countryside in the new period: causes and effects
zh: 新时期农村宗教信仰的兴起、原因和影响
paras: This article, published on the site in 2011 with no author named, asks why religious belief has grown so quickly in rural China since reform and opening up, and what that growth means for the construction of a new socialist countryside. It argues that the rise has deep social and historical roots and that its effects are mixed. Overall, the article holds, the benefits outweigh the harms, provided the government guides and regulates religion properly.

The article first describes the trend as it sees it: more believers, more religious venues and larger gatherings. It notes a shift from folk belief towards Christianity, Buddhism and Daoism existing side by side, and a believer population moving from the 'three mores' (elderly women, the sick, the uneducated) to the 'three increases' (men, young people, intellectuals). Part one sets out four causes; part two lists three positive and three negative effects. It draws on other Chinese scholars' studies, including a survey of Christians in a coastal town, and on Habermas's notion of the public sphere.

On causes, the author points to anomie and social strain during modernization, in which many peasants cannot keep pace and seek spiritual consolation, while migration leaves the elderly, women and children behind. The author also cites the shrinking rural public sphere after the dissolution of the people's communes, state neglect of rural culture under an economy-centred policy, and peasants' growing desire to participate in public life. On effects, the author credits religion with building trust, enriching rural culture and training participation skills. The author warns of commercialisation, including officials and religious leaders profiting from temples and believers, of insular cliques that resist village authority, and of exclusivist attitudes that strain relations with non-believers.

The author concludes that officials should reflect on their own conduct and respond rationally. They should neither ignore the surge nor treat it as a menace to be suppressed, but manage it according to law and guide religion to adapt to socialist society. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese scholar writing in 2011 explained rural religious revival in sociological terms and what policy stance the article recommends.
quoteEn: In sum, faced with the surging rise of religious belief in the countryside, government departments should reflect deeply on their own conduct and respond with rational policies.
quoteZh: 总之，面对农村汹涌澎湃的宗教信仰的兴起，政府管理部门应该深深反思自身的行为，采取理性政策来对待。

glossary.explanation: A rural development programme announced in the mid-2000s, aiming to improve rural production, living conditions, governance and culture.
The collective rural organisations of the Mao era, combining production and local administration, dissolved in the early 1980s.

t: Folk religion and the Marxist view of religion
zh: 民间宗教与马克思主义宗教观
paras: Writing in 2011, the author takes up a gap in Marxist religious studies in China. Since reform and opening up, popular belief has revived quickly, and cross-Strait exchange has made cults such as Mazu better known. Yet the Marxist classics say little about folk religion. The article argues that folk religion nonetheless deserves a place within the Marxist view of religion, and that researchers have wrongly treated it as a theoretical no-go area.

The piece has three parts. The first treats folk religion as 'non-orthodox' religion, drawing on the historian Ma Xisha's work and on Marx and Engels's writings on the Reformation, peasant wars and early Christianity. The second looks at the social functions of folk religion in rural China, using examples of local deities, ancestor worship and the temple of Sun Yat-sen's home village. The third argues for a place in the Marxist view of religion.

The author makes two main moves. First, following Ma Xisha, the author holds that folk and orthodox religion differ mainly in political status, not in religious nature. Citing Marx's early comment on Prussian censorship, the author reasons that in class society the state decides which religion counts as orthodox. Engels's remarks on superstition and on medieval heresy lead the author to say that such beliefs could serve rulers as tools for dulling the masses, or could clothe the masses' interests for 'revolutionary' ends. Second, using Marx's image of isolated smallholders, the author shows local gods marking land claims, uniting villages, and serving as rallying points in grain-tax revolts. Ancestor cults express kinship, and village temples can also be closed and exclusive, as at Cuiheng, where the Sun family was kept out of the temple.

The author concludes that the classics mostly dealt with one type, the suppressed secret sects, whereas the commoner type is lawful and routine and appears secretive only because officials and literati rarely recorded it. Some scholars now use 'local religion' to mark this ordinary form. The author invokes Marx's call to explain superstition through history, and says folk religion should be studied as part of the Marxist view of religion. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language argument from 2011 for treating folk belief as a legitimate object of Marxist religious theory, with village-level examples.
quoteEn: Folk religion should have its place within the Marxist view of religion.
quoteZh: “民间宗教”在马克思主义宗教观中应有其地位。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese scholarly category covering popular, non-institutional beliefs and sects outside the officially recognised religions. In narrower usage it refers to secret sects suppressed by the state.
A term some scholars use for the ordinary, lawful, locally rooted form of folk belief, to distinguish it from secret sects.

t: Marxism and religion
st: A Chinese digest of Michael Löwy's "Marxism and Religion: Opium of the People?"
zh: 马克思主义和宗教
paras: This is a Chinese-language digest of an article by the French scholar Michael Löwy, "Marxism and Religion: Opium of the People?", which appeared in The New Socialist (no. 51, 2009). Löwy, a member of France's Revolutionary Communist League, is the author of The War of Gods: Religion and Politics in Latin America. He challenges the habit of reducing the Marxist view of religion to the slogan "religion is the opium of the people". He argues that the Marxist tradition holds a richer and more dialectical position.

The digest follows Löwy's survey in roughly chronological order. It starts with the origins of the "opium" phrase among German writers, then turns to the young Marx's 1844 text and the more sociological approach of The German Ideology. It next covers Marx's remarks on Protestantism and capitalism, and Engels's studies of early Christianity and of peasant and Puritan movements. Löwy then looks at Lenin, Rosa Luxemburg, Ernst Bloch, the Frankfurt School and Lucien Goldmann. It ends by pointing to Latin American liberation theology.

Löwy's central claim is that the classics grasped religion's double character. In his reading, religion both legitimates the existing order and can voice protest or revolt. He notes that Marx's 1844 formula already treats religious suffering as both an expression of real suffering and a protest against it. He credits Engels with analysing religion through class struggle and with admiring rebel currents such as the Anabaptists, while faulting him for sometimes reducing religion to a class "disguise". Löwy presents Luxemburg as defending Christianity's social tradition against conservative clergy. He presents Bloch as the first Marxist to rebuild the framework, treating heretical religion as a vehicle of utopian hope. Goldmann, in his account, compared religious and Marxist faith as parallel "wagers". Löwy adds that the classical discussions give almost no attention to how religious doctrine and practice affect women.

Löwy concludes that, although the 19th-century view of religion as a bastion of reaction still fits many churches, fundamentalist groups and new sects, it is not the whole picture. He holds that understanding liberation theology in Latin America, and to a lesser extent elsewhere, requires integrating Bloch's and Goldmann's insights into the utopian potential of the Judaeo-Christian tradition. Read the original if you want a compact overview of how Marxist thinkers from Marx to Bloch have treated religion's ambivalence, or want to see how this material was introduced to Chinese readers in the science-and-atheism field.
quoteEn: Marxist research on religion in the strict sense came later, especially in The German Ideology (1846), where Marx began to study religion as a social and historical reality.
quoteZh: 严格意义上的马克思主义宗教研究是后来的事情，尤其是在《德意志意识形态》中(1846年)，马克思开始把宗教作为一种社会的和历史的现实来研究。

t: Separation of religion and politics, or their unity? The Nationalist Government's policy considerations on Tibet's political and religious relations
zh: 政教分离，抑或政教合一？——国民政府对西藏政治和宗教关系的政策考量*
paras: This article, posted in 2011 without a named author, examines how the Nationalist Government (Nanjing, 1927–1949) approached Tibet's system of unity of religion and politics. It notes that scholarship has studied the system itself but not its twentieth-century evolution or the Nationalist attempts to reshape it on the principle of separating religion from politics. The article argues that the government wished to introduce that separation as part of political integration with the interior, but lacked the strength to do so. Tibetan authorities, for their part, resisted any change.

The article first defines the two principles and traces the Tibetan system from the Sakya period to its formal Gelug shape in 1751. It then proceeds chronologically in four sections. These cover the late Qing and early Republic and the policy statements of 1929–1932, the Huang Musong mission to Lhasa (1934) and the later Wu Zhongxin mission, and the post-1945 "high degree of autonomy" schemes and the 1946 Constitution. A concluding section assesses why the effort failed. The evidence is mainly archival: Mongolian and Tibetan Affairs Commission documents, government directives and Tibetan responses.

The author's central claim is that the government's real aim stayed constant while its stated policy shifted with its capacity. In 1929 the Commission planned a six-year programme to separate administrative and religious powers, but Chiang Kai-shek's 1934 remarks favoured "soft" conciliation over force. Official texts then repeatedly promised to preserve the Dalai and Panchen Lamas' religious and political authority, while omitting any endorsement of the system itself. The 1945 draft autonomy plan and the post-war programme reaffirmed separation, and the Commission wavered on whether the constitution's "Tibetan autonomy system" meant the existing theocracy. The author reads these shifts as a consistent aim under unfavourable conditions. Tibetan authorities invoked a "patron–priest" relationship, feared Soviet-style outcomes as in Outer Mongolia, and treated change as a threat to elite privilege.

The author concludes that separation was a historical necessity of building a modern nation-state, but the Nationalist Government could not extend effective control to Tibet. Tibetan society, in the author's account, lacked internal forces for self-reform under serfdom, so separation historically followed strong central intervention. Only the People's Republic, from the suppression of the 1959 rebellion to the founding of the Tibet Autonomous Region in 1965, is said to have ended the system. Read the original if you want a documented account of Nationalist-era policy debates on Tibet's religious and political order, bearing in mind that it is framed in terms of integration and central authority.
quoteEn: Whether unity or separation of religion and politics prevailed depended essentially on the degree to which the central government intervened with real strength.
quoteZh: 是实行政教合一，还是实行政教分离，基本取决于中央政府的实力介入程度。

glossary.explanation: A system in which religious and political authority are combined. In Tibet it refers to the order centred on the Dalai Lama, formalised under the Gelug school in 1751.
A relationship in which a lay patron supports a religious teacher. Tibetan authorities used it to describe ties with the central government as purely religious, denying political subordination.
The Nationalist Government's central body for Mongolian and Tibetan affairs, which drafted policy for the region.
A traditional imperial approach to frontier peoples that relies on soft control and inducements rather than direct rule. Chiang Kai-shek used it for his 1934 policy of "soft" restraint.
A policy announced by the Nationalists in 1945 for Tibet and Outer Mongolia. The article says it later shrank into ordinary local autonomy.

t: Seminar on the Marxist view of religion (2011) held in Beijing
zh: 马克思主义宗教观研讨会(2011)在京召开
paras: This is a report on the academic seminar "Marxist View of Religion (2011)", held in Beijing on 2–3 July 2011 to mark the 90th anniversary of the Communist Party of China. It was co-organised by the Institute of World Religions at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and the Religious Research Centre of the State Administration for Religious Affairs. The report says participants affirmed Marxism as the guiding thought for religious studies and stressed adapting the Marxist view of religion to Chinese conditions.

The report lists attendees from the Institute (including its director Zhuo Xinping), the United Front Work Department and the State Administration for Religious Affairs. It names about twenty papers. They cover Capital's place in the Marxist view of religion, Marx's early views, Lenin's scientific atheism, and religious policy in the Party's history, including Daoism, Xinjiang, Tibet, Laos and the Italian Communist Party. The seminar followed the 2010 creation of a research office on the Marxist view of religion, set up in response to the call to make the Academy a "strong base of Marxism".

Jia Runguo traces the Party's religious policy after the Cultural Revolution through successive leaderships. He sees Document No. 19 of 1982 as the foundation of a socialist theory of religion with Chinese characteristics. He sees the Jiang Zemin era as adding the basic policy of "actively guiding religion to adapt to socialist society". He treats the Hu Jintao era's aim of "harmonious religious relations" as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. Min Xianliang similarly presents the Party's religious theory as part of the Marxism with Chinese characteristics. Huang Kui offers a political-economy reading. He argues that religion is rooted in private ownership and class division, and that class analysis is not outdated. He urges renewed atheist education. He says united front work should be limited to religious elites. He describes freedom of religious belief as in essence a "bourgeois right", and he rejects absolute separation of church and state.

The report concludes that the Party's 90-year experience in handling religious questions is of theoretical and practical importance for current work. The main point of contention it reports was how to study the Marxist view of religion under present conditions. Participants debated moving from stress on struggle and "criticism" of religion towards "active guidance" and the building of a harmonious society, in light of the 17th Party Congress (2007). Read the original if you want a record of how Chinese religious-studies scholars and officials framed Party religious policy in 2011, including the full paper titles.
quoteEn: Freedom of religious belief is in essence a kind of bourgeois right.
quoteZh: 宗教信仰自由，本质上是一种资产阶级法权。

glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context
glossary.explanation: The official formula for combining Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete conditions. The report applies it to the Party's view of religion.
The policy guaranteeing citizens' religious belief, set out in Party documents and the constitution. The report records both official affirmation and a scholar's critique of the concept.
The Party's strategy of building alliances with non-Party groups, including religious figures, handled by the United Front Work Department.
Hu Jintao-era goal of easing social tensions. It is applied here to relations among religions and between believers and non-believers.

t: Opposing cults is an act of civilisation, and the intellectual world must take responsibility
st: Marking the tenth anniversary of the China Anti-Cult Association
zh: 反邪教是文明之举，思想界需要担当责任 ——纪念中国反邪教协会成立十周年
paras: Marking the tenth anniversary of the China Anti-Cult Association (founded 2000), this 2011 commentary reviews more than a decade of the campaign against cults, symbolised by the ban on Falun Gong. The author argues that opposing cults is an act of civilisation, rooted in Chinese history and culture. It also holds that preventing cults serves political stability, economic development, national security and a harmonious society. The article calls on the intellectual world to attend to the ideas and public opinion that allow cults to grow, and to accept social responsibility for doing so.

The text is organised in five sections. It first traces cults to shamanic (wu) culture and to imperial-era rulers' dealings with magicians, from the Qin and Han dynasties to the Three Kingdoms. It then turns to the 'spiritualism' (lingxue) movement of the late 1910s and the May Fourth critics who opposed it. A third section covers the 'human body science' and 'supernormal powers' wave, the deified qigong boom and Falun Gong from 1979 onwards. The last two sections discuss the post-Falun Gong period and the duty of thinkers.

The author's central claim is that banning Falun Gong removed neither the social roots of cults nor their intellectual justification. In the article's account, the main new form uses a Christian label, with 'underground churches' as a seedbed. Three reasons are given: Protestantism's decentralised character, its foreign character and what the author calls US support under the 1998 International Religious Freedom Act, and a 'Sinophone Christian theology movement' that is said to dominate academic discourse on religion. The author also criticises scholars who attribute cults to the suppression of legitimate religion or who want religion to supply moral education, and adds that academia has barely responded. The author prefers 'ideals' to 'faith', arguing that faith leads to blind obedience.

The author concludes that prevention is better than reactive crackdowns, and that the key is the direction of public opinion. The author urges popularising scientific knowledge and the scientific spirit, systematic building of scientific atheism as a discipline, and a stronger legal footing for the judiciary. The author holds up the late academician Zhuang Fenggan, Ren Jiyu, Yu Guangyuan, Gong Yuzhi, Ye Shengtao and Zhou Jianren as models of thinkers who spoke out. The author is confident that China will not become a religious country. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese scientific-atheist writer in 2011 framed cults, folk belief and Christianity together, and how the article uses history to argue for a role for intellectuals.
quoteEn: Our thinkers should take up the social responsibility of popularising scientific knowledge and the scientific spirit and breaking down belief in ghosts and spirits, so that no form of theism of spirits parades through the streets and scientific reason sheds the light of contemporary civilisation.
quoteZh: 我们的思想者，应当承担起普及科学知识和科学精神，破除鬼神迷信的社会责任来，让任何形式的鬼神论不得招摇过市，让科学理性发出当代文明之光。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese legal and political category, opposed to 'orthodox religion' (zhengjiao). The author says that in contemporary China it is a legal concept, distinct from the legally protected religions.
A qigong-based movement founded by Li Hongzhi in the early 1990s. The Chinese government banned it in July 1999 and designated it a cult.
Claimed paranormal abilities, such as reading characters with the ear, that were promoted from 1979 under the label 'human body science'. The author treats them as pseudoscience.
A Marxist-materialist approach and academic field that critiques religion and belief in spirits, and promotes a scientific worldview.
Christian congregations outside the state-registered churches. The author treats them as a breeding ground for cults.

t: Upholding Marxism and upholding scientific atheism
zh: 坚持马克思主义与坚持科学无神论
paras: Writing in 2011, the author asks whether it is legitimate and reasonable, in the primary stage of socialism and amid diverse and shifting currents of thought, to propagate scientific atheism and criticise theism. The article treats this as a prior question for any research on scientific atheism. It links the worry to a perceived imbalance in scholarship, where theism has many advocates and atheism few. The author's answer is that upholding scientific atheism is inherent in upholding Marxism, and that Marxism in turn must guide atheist research and propaganda.

The text has three parts. The first argues that scientific atheism follows from Marxist philosophy and from the Marxist view of religion. The second takes up those who accept atheism but object to criticising theism. The third sets out how research and propaganda should be guided by Marxism and by the Party's basic principles and policies on religious work. It rests heavily on Engels, Lenin, Hu Jintao's speeches and Party documents.

The author reads Engels's account of the basic question of philosophy, and passages by Engels and Lenin on idealism and "priestcraft", as showing that atheism is bound up with dialectical and historical materialism. In the author's account, scientific atheism is the core of the Marxist view of religion, since religion's essence, its development and its eventual disappearance are all explained through the idea of gods. On criticism, the author argues that scientific atheism cannot take gods as its object, because they do not exist. Its object is ideas of gods, and in a deeper sense theism itself, so an atheism barred from criticising theism would lose its object. The author also holds that social harmony rests on shared economic, political and ideological foundations, not on shared belief or unbelief, so atheism does not conflict with the Party's call for harmonious coexistence among believers and non-believers.

The author concludes that atheist research must rest on dialectical and historical materialism, draw on useful earlier scholarship, and help build a Marxist study of religion that avoids treating Marxism as a slogan. It must also follow Party religious policy. Two limits are stressed: atheist propaganda should not be given undue priority, since Engels and Lenin opposed "declaring war on religion", and it must be reconciled with respect for citizens' freedom to believe. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar in 2011 justified scientific atheism within Party religious policy, using extensive citations of the classics.
quoteEn: The particular nature of the object and basic conclusion of scientific atheism means that upholding it cannot but involve opposing theism, and researching and propagating it cannot but involve analysing and criticising theism.
quoteZh: 科学无神论研究对象和基本结论的特殊性决定了坚持科学无神论就不能不反对有神论，研究和宣传科学无神论就不能不剖析和批评有神论。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist form of atheism, grounded in dialectical and historical materialism and studied as a discipline in Chinese academia. It is distinguished from earlier or non-Marxist atheisms.
The official Party characterisation of China's present developmental stage, adopted in 1987, which is expected to last a long time.

glossary.en: the Party's basic principles and policies on religious work
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guidelines on religion, including freedom of religious belief, management of religious affairs according to law, independent self-run religious bodies, and guiding religion to adapt to socialist society.

t: The social cost of religious belief: the cases of Gannan and Linxia prefectures in Gansu
zh: 宗教信仰的社会代价 ——以甘肃甘南和临夏两州为例
paras: Writing in 2011, Liu Xiaoxiong asks how religion affects economic and social development in minority regions where belief is nearly universal. The article accepts that religion has had positive effects on people's spiritual life. It argues, however, that where religion has not developed reasonably or adapted to society, it becomes one important cause of regional backwardness. Liu's thesis is that believers in Gannan (Tibetan) and Linxia (Hui) prefectures in Gansu pay a heavy social cost for their faith.

The study rests on the two autonomous prefectures, where Tibetan and Hui residents are described as almost entirely religious. Liu notes that five of Gannan's eight counties and cities, and all of Linxia's except Linxia city, are national-level poverty counties. Liu grants that geography, climate, transport and history also matter. The article draws on provincial statistics for Gansu's religious venues, clergy and believers, plus a Chinese study of religion and economics and the economist Robert Barro. It is organised into five sections: consumption of resources, occupation of land, consumption of time and energy, constraints on thinking, and a conclusion.

Liu's central claim is that religious activity diverts wealth from productive to non-productive use. Building and maintaining temples, mosques and tomb shrines, supporting clergy who do not take part in production, and funding rituals are all described as burdens met by donations from local people. Liu cites official figures of 6,771 approved religious venues and over 20,000 clergy in Gansu, and contrasts splendid temples with run-down believers' homes. The article adds that religious sites take up farmland and complicate planning, that worship and ritual absorb time otherwise available for work, and that doctrines favouring renunciation and the afterlife sap the drive to pursue wealth. Liu also attributes disturbances such as those of 2008 and 2009 to reactionary elements among the clergy, incited by hostile forces at home and abroad.

Liu concludes that the restraining effect of religion runs through every aspect of life in these communities, and that excessive religious burdens are one cause, though not the only one, of poverty. Under the Scientific Outlook on Development, the author calls on the state, the government, religious circles and society to guide religion so as to minimise its negative effects and help it adapt to China's society and a harmonious, sustainable social development. Read the original if you want an example of how 2011 Chinese scholarship on atheism and sociology framed religion in minority regions as an economic and social burden.
quoteEn: Although there are many reasons for poverty and backwardness in religious regions, an inappropriate religious burden is one of the causes of the low living standards and lagging social development of the people in these parishes.
quoteZh: 虽然信教地区贫困落后的原因有很多，但不适当的宗教负担却是教区人民生活水平低下和社会发展滞后的原因之一。

glossary.explanation: A guiding policy concept associated with Hu Jintao and written into the Party constitution in 2007. It stresses coordinated, balanced and sustainable development.

t: The atheism of Marx's philosophy seen through the logic of its development
zh: 从马克思哲学的展开逻辑看其无神论特质
paras: The article asks in what sense thoroughgoing atheism is an inherent feature of Marx's philosophy, and answers by tracing how that philosophy unfolded. The author argues that going beyond a religious view of history was a precondition for founding historical materialism. Marx's consistent aim, the scientific study of social development in order to achieve real human freedom and emancipation, is said to have been realised in three stages, so that the formation of Marx's philosophy is the unfolding of his atheism.

The article follows Marx's texts in chronological order. It begins with the doctoral dissertation on Democritus and Epicurus, the Rheinische Zeitung period, the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, On the Jewish Question, the Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right: Introduction, and the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. It then turns to The German Ideology, and finally to The Poverty of Philosophy, the Grundrisse and Capital. Engels's early remarks on religion are also drawn in. The text closes with practical implications for contemporary China.

The author's central claim is a shift from criticising religion to analysing the social conditions that produce it. In the early works Marx calls for the liberation of individual subjectivity, but the author says this remained at the level of value-based ought. Marx then concluded that religion is a symptom of worldly limits, not their cause, so that criticism of heaven becomes criticism of earth. In The German Ideology, in the author's reading, Marx and Engels reject the Young Hegelians' purely ideological critique and ground history in material production, treating communism as a real movement, not an ideal. The author holds that the mature critique of political economy completes this path. Capital is shown to be a social relation and not a thing, and the discovery of surplus value exposes the reproduction of capitalist relations of production. Human emancipation then depends on rationalising social relations through the proletariat overthrowing capitalism.

The author concludes that no link in this logic places human liberation in any supernatural power, and cites Raymond Aron's remark that atheism is essentially tied to Marx's Marxism. Three lessons for present-day China are drawn. Liberation relies on human agency, not on saviours. It requires grounding in practice, attention to the laws of social development, and solutions to people's real problems. It also needs fairness and justice and rationalised social relations, with a people-centred approach in harmonious development, so that religion loses its soil. Read the original if you want a close reading of Marx's early to mature texts as a genealogy of atheism, or an example of how Chinese scholars framed this theme around 2011.
quoteEn: The process by which Marx's philosophy formed and developed is the process by which his thoroughgoing atheism unfolded.
quoteZh: 马克思哲学的形成和发展过程，就是其无神论思想的彻底展开过程

glossary.literal: taking the people as the foundation
glossary.explanation: A principle associated with the Scientific Outlook on Development promoted in the 2000s, stressing that development should serve people's needs and well-being.
A term linked to the official goal of building a harmonious society, promoted from the mid-2000s, which stresses balance among social groups, regions and the economy and environment.

t: The atheism of Marx's philosophy seen through the logic of its development
zh: 从马克思哲学的展开逻辑看其无神论特质
paras: The article, written in 2011 and carried in the site's Science and Atheism category, asks how the thoroughgoing atheism of Marx's philosophy should be understood. Its thesis is that atheism is intrinsic to Marx's philosophy and that going beyond a religious view of history was a precondition for founding historical materialism. The author argues that the formation of Marx's philosophy is itself the unfolding of this atheism, and that tracing the logic of that unfolding is the key to grasping its atheistic character.

The article follows Marx's work in three stages. The first covers the early writings: the doctoral dissertation on Democritus and Epicurus, the Rheinische Zeitung period, On the Jewish Question, the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, and the 1844 Manuscripts. The second is the practical turn and the historical-genesis approach set out in The German Ideology. The third runs through The Poverty of Philosophy and the 1857–58 manuscripts to Capital. Throughout, the author sets Marx against Bruno Bauer, the Young Hegelians and Proudhon, and against classical political economy.

The author contends that the aim of human liberation stays constant while its realisation changes. Marx begins with a value-based call for individual freedom, and the author notes that this stayed at the level of what ought to be. He then moves, from criticism of religion, to criticism of politics and law, to analysis of material production. The author reads The German Ideology as rejecting the Young Hegelians' war on religious phrases, because it left the real world untouched. The author reads the later economic works as locating the roots of religion and exploitation in the reproduction of capitalist relations of production. On this reading, capital is a social relation, not a thing, and surplus value explains proletarian poverty. Religion therefore disappears of itself once its worldly basis is removed.

The author concludes that no link in this development rests human liberation on a supernatural force. The article endorses a Western scholar's remark that atheism is essentially bound up with Marx's Marxism. It draws three lessons for present-day Chinese social development. Liberation depends on human subjectivity, not on saviours. It requires grounding in practice and in the laws of social development, with comprehensive and sustainable development that solves people's practical problems. It also requires fairness and rationalised social relations in the name of putting people first, so that theism loses its soil. Read the original if you want a stage-by-stage account of how Chinese scholars link Marx's critique of religion to his critique of political economy.
quoteEn: The formation and development of Marx's philosophy is the process of the thoroughgoing unfolding of his atheist thought.
quoteZh: 马克思哲学的形成和发展过程，就是其无神论思想的彻底展开过程

t: A brief commentary on America's "faith-based diplomacy" and China's cultural security
zh: 简评美国的“信仰外交”与我国文化安全
paras: Writing in 2011 from a scientific-atheism standpoint, the author asks how the post-Cold War revival of religion in international politics bears on China's national and cultural security. The article argues that religion's social role has been deliberately inflated, and that certain states and interest groups use theism as a tool for political and economic gain. In the author's reading, the United States' "faith-based diplomacy" is a hegemonic instrument and a threat to China, which calls for a response from scientific atheism.

The piece has two parts. The first traces a line from missionary diplomacy through human-rights diplomacy to faith-based diplomacy, centred on the US International Religious Freedom Act of 1998 and the annual reports it requires. The second turns to the religious factors the author sees as affecting China's security, and to the state of China's own academic and ideological response. It draws on US government statements, press figures on the Iraq war and the work of other Chinese scholars.

The author contends that Washington ties "religious freedom" to democracy and national security, and applies it selectively according to US interests. As evidence, the author cites Iraq's removal from the list of "countries of particular concern" despite civilian casualties and violence, and rising suicide attacks after "counter-terrorism" campaigns. Domestically, the author names three religious threats: Tibetan and Xinjiang separatism, which the article links to religious extremism and to the 2008 Lhasa and 2009 Urumqi violence, and the expansion strategy of the American Christian new right. The author calls the last a "soft knife" that enters China through culture, education and academic exchange, funding of house churches and "cultural theology". Scientific atheism, in this account, has almost no voice against it.

The author calls for China to secure discursive power, build academic strength in scientific atheism and hold its ideological ground. Scientific atheism, the author says, is an important part of the socialist core value system, and removing it from the Marxist view of religion and socialist ideology would be dangerous. The author also holds that both US parties pursue the same strategic direction. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scientific-atheism scholar framed religion, US foreign policy and cultural security around 2011.
quoteEn: Religious infiltration has become the main content of foreign cultural infiltration.
quoteZh: 宗教渗透已经成为国外文化渗透的主要内容。

t: Difficulties facing scientific atheism today and experts' proposals
zh: 当前科学无神论面临的难题和专家建议
paras: Writing in 2011, the authors report the views of a number of Chinese experts and scholars on why scientific atheism, in their account a core part of Marxist ideology, is in difficulty in Chinese society. The article's thesis is that atheist education has been neglected while theism, religious activity and 'new superstitions' spread, and that this must be reversed through a clearer Marxist view of religion and more active propaganda.

The piece has three parts. The first describes the present predicament, including the growth of religious belief among students and Party members and officials. The second sets out problems that must be clarified before atheist propaganda can proceed. The third lists the experts' recommendations. The authors present these views as the shared concern of scholars and do not name individual speakers.

In the first part, the experts see a drift from atheism being a 'prominent field' to a 'marginal' one, with growing belief among cadres, whom they characterise by four patterns, and among students. They trace causes to an educational gap, Western ideological influence, and uneven local support for religion over atheism. In the second part they argue three points: atheism is the foundation of Marxism and is compatible with the policy of freedom of religious belief; it supports a harmonious society, whose basis is shared fundamental interests rather than shared belief; and religion cannot supply ultimate concern, which communist morality and traditional Chinese virtues can. They hold that Party members who adopt religion lose their vanguard character.

The recommendations include strengthening Marxism's guiding position in ideology, applying the Marxist view of religion while avoiding 'two one-sided approaches', and making atheist work practical and mass-oriented. This means closer attention to the spiritual lives of cadres and students, stricter Party discipline on belief, and criticism aimed at the social roots of religion rather than believers. The authors add that propagandists need both a fighter's resolve and a scholar's rigour. Read the original if you want a documented example of how Party-affiliated scholars framed atheism, religion and Party membership in 2011.")
quoteEn: When speaking of freedom of belief, one cannot speak only of freedom of religious belief; one must also speak of the freedom not to believe in religion.
quoteZh: 讲信仰自由不能光讲宗教信仰自由，也要讲不信仰宗教的自由。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-Leninist atheist position, presented in Chinese Party discourse as grounded in historical materialism and as the basis of the Marxist view of religion.
The official policy that citizens may believe or not believe in religion. The article stresses that it includes the freedom not to believe.
A policy goal promoted under Hu Jintao in the 2000s, stressing social cohesion and the management of social contradictions.

t: Difficulties facing scientific atheism today and experts' proposals
zh: 当前科学无神论面临的难题和专家建议
paras: Writing in 2011, the authors report the views of Chinese scholars and experts on a perceived crisis in the promotion of scientific atheism. In their account, theism and superstition are spreading while atheism is rarely discussed, including among Party members. The article presents the experts' consensus that atheist education must be strengthened as part of upholding Marxism and the Party's ideological foundation.

The text has three parts. The first describes the present predicament: the rise of religious belief and 'new superstitions', growing religious belief among students and Party cadres, and the arguments used to oppose atheist propaganda. The second sets out several questions that must be clarified. The third gathers the experts' recommendations for education and propaganda.

The authors report that atheism is held to be the ideological basis of the Marxist worldview, and that Marxism is fundamentally incompatible with theism. On this view, promoting atheism does not conflict with the policy of freedom of religious belief, which also includes the freedom not to believe. It is likewise said to support a harmonious society, whose basis is the shared fundamental interests of all groups under the socialist system and not a shared religion. The experts also reject the claim that religion supplies 'ultimate concern' or higher morality. They argue that communist morality and traditional Chinese virtues meet spiritual needs better, and that a Party member who adopts religion loses the Party's vanguard character.

The recommendations include consolidating Marxism's guiding position in ideology and applying the Marxist view of religion. They also call for avoiding two one-sided errors: abandoning atheist propaganda for the sake of religious freedom, and denying religious freedom for the sake of propaganda. Other proposals are to focus on the root causes of religion, to work through the real concerns of cadres and students, to tighten Party discipline on belief, and to combine a combative spirit with scholarly rigour. Read the original if you want to see how Party-affiliated scholars framed the case for atheist education and Party members' non-belief around 2011.
quoteEn: When we speak of freedom of belief, we cannot speak only of freedom of religious belief; we must also speak of the freedom not to believe in religion.
quoteZh: 讲信仰自由不能光讲宗教信仰自由，也要讲不信仰宗教的自由。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-Leninist atheist position, presented in Chinese Party discourse as grounded in historical materialism and as the basis of the Party's view of religion.
The constitutional and Party policy protecting citizens' right to hold or not hold religious beliefs. The article stresses that it includes the freedom not to believe.
A policy goal promoted under Hu Jintao in the 2000s, stressing social stability and the handling of social contradictions.

t: If there are no ghosts in the world, how can there be a "ghost culture"?
zh: 世间没有鬼，何来鬼文化？
paras: Writing in 2011, Chen Zujia, a senior People's Daily reporter, objects to official promotion of "ghost culture". The trigger is a report that a deputy director of a department in the Ministry of Culture publicly backed gathering China's ghost-themed culture in Chongqing as a brand, and that Chongqing planned to spend 700 million yuan restoring the Fengdu "ghost city". Chen argues that without ghosts there can be no ghost culture, and that promoting it contradicts atheism.

The commentary places the issue within the current "national studies fever" (guoxue re), in which Chen sees folk beliefs such as feng shui and the I Ching spreading under the label of traditional culture. It then moves through the origins of belief in ghosts, literary examples (Lu Xun's Xianglin's Wife, the Peony Pavilion tradition, Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio), and ancient Chinese sceptics, before turning to present-day conditions.

Chen contends that belief in ghosts and gods arose from very low productive forces, when people feared disasters they could not explain, and that rulers in slave and feudal societies used it to control minds. In Chen's reading, such belief brought ordinary people no benefit, as Xianglin's Wife shows, and is a "spiritual heroin" that poisons people and hinders social development. Chen cites ancient anti-ghost writing, including Confucius's reticence about spirits, Fan Zhen's essay on the extinction of the spirit, and a tale in which a ghost loses a debate with a sceptic.

Chen accepts that ghost belief existed historically and that some artists used ghost images against feudal despotism, and allows a few experts to study it from a materialist, historical standpoint. But Chen opposes large public investment in it, notes officials who believe in feng shui rather than Marxism, and calls for reasonable and lawful means to eliminate ghost-and-spirit doctrines. Chen asks whether this runs counter to the Scientific Outlook on Development and amounts to turning back history. Read the original if you want an example of a 2011 atheist critique of the revival of traditional folk belief and of official cultural policy.
quoteEn: But what good fortune can these doctrines of ghosts and spirits bring to the people?
quoteZh: 但是，这些鬼神之说又能给民众带来什么幸运呢？

glossary.explanation: A popular revival of interest in traditional Chinese learning and culture from the 2000s, seen in television lectures, Confucius Institutes and private academies.
A guiding concept of the Hu Jintao era, written into the Party constitution in 2007, stressing people-centred, coordinated and sustainable development.

t: If there are no ghosts in the world, where does "ghost culture" come from?
zh: 世间没有鬼，何来鬼文化？
paras: Writing in 2011, Chen Zujia, a senior People's Daily reporter, objects to the promotion of "ghost culture" as part of traditional Chinese culture. The trigger is a report that a deputy director-general in the Ministry of Culture publicly endorsed it, and that Chongqing planned to spend 700 million yuan restoring the Fengdu "Ghost City". Chen's answer is that ghosts do not exist, so "ghost culture" is a form of superstition that should not be promoted.

The commentary sets the case against the background of the then-current "national learning fever" (guoxue re), in which Chen sees feng shui, divination and ghost lore spreading under the label of tradition. It briefly traces the origins of belief in ghosts and gods, then cites Lu Xun's Xianglin's Wife, ghost operas, Confucius, Pu Songling's Liaozhai and the early atheists Fan Zhen and Ruan Zhan.

Chen argues that ghost and god beliefs arose when productive forces were very low, and were products of despotic slave and feudal systems that rulers used to control people's minds. In his view these beliefs brought ordinary people no benefit, and he calls them "spiritual heroin" that poisons people and holds back social development. He grants that they existed historically and that some artists used ghost figures against feudal despotism, and he accepts that a few specialists may study them in a historical, materialist way.

Chen calls for reasonable and lawful means to eliminate belief in ghosts and gods. He points to officials who he says trust feng shui rather than Marxism, to temples built where science museums are needed, and to a policy of rejuvenating the country through science and education and the Scientific Outlook on Development. Read the original if you want an example of how a state-media atheist voice in 2011 criticised official promotion of folk religion as heritage.
quoteEn: Although the doctrine of ghosts and gods once objectively existed, it is after all a spiritual heroin that poisons humankind and obstructs social development.
quoteZh: 尽管神鬼之说曾经是客观的存在，但它毕竟是毒害人类、阻碍社会发展的精神海洛因。

glossary.explanation: A popular revival of interest in classical Chinese culture and thought, visible in the 2000s in television lecture series and Confucius Institutes.
A guiding concept of the Hu Jintao era, written into the Party constitution in 2007, stressing people-centred, coordinated and sustainable development.

glossary.en: rejuvenating the country through science and education
glossary.explanation: A national strategy announced in 1995 that makes science, technology and education the basis of national development.

t: Scientific atheism and Marxism: marking the tenth anniversary of the journal Science and Atheism
zh: 科学无神论与马克思主义——纪念《科学与无神论》杂志创刊十周年
paras: Writing in 2011 to mark the journal Science and Atheism's tenth anniversary, Yu Qiming asks why scientific atheism, an important component of Marxism, has been left with 'nobody to talk about it'. Yu names two causes: worry that atheist education would harm freedom of religious belief, which the author sets aside as already answered elsewhere, and the view that Marxist education makes separate work on scientific atheism unnecessary. The article argues that the second view is mistaken and that the two must be combined.

The piece is short and runs in three steps. It first sketches how atheism evolved and what epistemological basis it has. It then defines 'scientific atheism' and separates it from earlier forms. Finally it explains why general study of Marxist principles cannot replace atheist education, drawing on Engels, Lenin and a 1999 Central Committee document, before ending with praise for the journal's work and its turn towards an academic publication.

Yu says atheism passed through three forms: ancient naive atheism, modern atheism and Marxist atheism, tied respectively to spontaneous, metaphysical and dialectical materialism. French eighteenth-century and Feuerbachian atheism used scientific findings, but did not fully explain the origin, development, essence and social role of religious theism. Yu holds that only Marxist atheism meets three criteria: it uses current science, explains religious phenomena thoroughly, and rests on dialectical and historical materialism. The link between Marxist philosophy and atheism is refusing to believe in powers that practice cannot test.

Marxist principles, Yu argues, supply only the worldview basis of scientific atheism and cannot cover or replace it. As evidence the author cites students who had taken Marxism courses yet still believed in planchette divination, astrology, pseudo-qigong or Falun Gong. Religious theism also keeps changing its forms, for example by turning towards the secular and the moral, and by moving into philosophy of science. Yu therefore calls for vivid atheist education tied to everyday life, and for drawing on the best atheist writings, as Lenin urged. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar in 2011 justified scientific atheism as a distinct field of Marxist education.
quoteEn: Therefore education in scientific atheism cannot be skipped.
quoteZh: 因此科学无神论的教育是不能跨越的。

t: Scientific atheism and Marxism
st: In commemoration of the tenth anniversary of the journal Science and Atheism
zh: 科学无神论与马克思主义——纪念《科学与无神论》杂志创刊十周年
zhSub: 纪念《科学与无神论》杂志创刊十周年
paras: Writing in 2011 to mark the journal Science and Atheism's tenth anniversary, Yu asks why scientific atheism, an important part of Marxism, has been neglected to the point that "nobody talks about it". Yu names two causes: worry that atheist education may affect freedom of religious belief, which the author sets aside as already well argued, and the view that Marxist education makes separate work on scientific atheism unnecessary. The article rejects the second view, arguing that Marxist theory and scientific atheism education must be combined but cannot substitute for each other.

The piece has three parts. It first sketches the evolution of atheism through ancient naive, modern, and Marxist forms, each tied to a type of materialism. It then defines what counts as "scientific" atheism. Finally it considers why general study of Marxist principles cannot replace atheism education, drawing on Engels, Lenin and a 1999 Central Committee document on ideological and political work. A short closing section praises the journal's work and its shift towards an academic publication.

Yu holds that eighteenth-century French militant atheism and Feuerbach's humanist atheism used science to show there are no gods, but could not explain the origin, development, disappearance, essence and social role of religious theism, because their worldview was not fully materialist. Scientific atheism, in Yu's definition, must use contemporary scientific findings, explain religious phenomena thoroughly, and rest on dialectical and historical materialism; only Marxist atheism qualifies. Its link to Marxist philosophy is the refusal to believe in powers that practice cannot test.

Yu argues that Marxist principles supply only the worldview basis of scientific atheism and do not cover it. As evidence, Yu cites university students who had taken Marxism courses yet still believed in spirit-writing, astrology, pseudo-qigong or Falun Gong. Religious theism also keeps changing form, for example towards secularised and moralised versions, and entering philosophy of science. Citing Lenin, Yu calls for lively, concrete atheist education connected to everyday life, including popular science and the use of good atheist writings, past and present. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of atheism argued in 2011 for a separate place for scientific atheism within Marxist ideological education.
quoteEn: It seems that education in Marxist principles cannot replace education in scientific atheism; the two should be closely combined and mutually reinforcing.
quoteZh: 看来，马克思主义原理的教育不能代替科学无神论的教育，二者应紧密结合、相互促进。

t: Reflections on the question of the "relationship between religion and culture"
zh: 关于“宗教与文化关系”问题的思考
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论) category, marxism.cass.cn, 2011
paras: Zhu Xiaoming takes up a question that, in the author's account, has drawn growing attention in recent years: how should the claim that "religion is culture" be understood, and how should a ruling Communist Party handle it? Writing in 2011, Zhu argues that the claim is true as far as it goes but captures only one attribute of religion, not its essence. The Party, the article holds, should support religious believers' and scholars' cultural readings of religion while declining to talk about religion in general terms as culture.

The article has three parts. It first surveys views on the relationship: the remarks of Zhao Puchu, Qian Xuesen, Mao Zedong and Fan Wenlan, then four strands of current Chinese scholarship. These range from enthusiastic endorsement of "religion is culture" to warnings against it. It then describes what kind of culture religion is, citing scholars on its features and on its material, institutional and spiritual layers. The last part sets out how the ruling Party should respond.

Zhu draws on scholars' analysis to identify distinctive traits of religious culture: alienation, exclusivity, organisation, expansiveness and comprehensiveness. Zhu also stresses its "dual nature" under socialism. It can offer psychological adjustment, moral restraint and cultural identity, but it can also encourage conservatism, fanaticism and obstruct scientific learning. Zhu says it can be exploited by hostile foreign forces. Zhu then argues that the Party must keep to Marxist views of religion, which the article sums up as three "views", three "principles" and three "laws". The central principle is that religion's essence cannot be explained by culture or other spiritual factors, only by social development. Religion is also a social entity with organising and mobilising power, so it cannot be separated from politics.

Zhu concludes that the Party should encourage theological and scholarly work that draws out the positive elements in religious traditions and helps religions adapt to socialist society. It must not reduce religion to culture. The article warns against missionary activity, theological propaganda or foreign strategic containment carried out "in the name of culture", and it calls for unity between believers and non-believers as part of building a harmonious society. Read the original if you want an account, from within the Party's religious-work establishment, of how Marxist religious theory is used to limit the "religion is culture" thesis.
quoteEn: The ruling party should not talk about religion as culture in loose, general terms.
quoteZh: 执政党不宜泛谈宗教是文化。

glossary.explanation: A goal promoted by the Party leadership in the mid-2000s, stressing social cohesion and the easing of social tensions. The article ties religious work to this aim, including unity between believers and non-believers.

The Party's official theoretical framework for understanding religion, based on historical materialism. The article treats it as the guiding basis of Party religious policy, not just one research approach among many.

glossary.zh: 宗教与社会主义社会相适应
glossary.pinyin: zōngjiào yǔ shèhuìzhǔyì shèhuì xiāng shìyìng
glossary.explanation: A long-standing Party policy line that religions in China should adjust themselves to socialist society. The article presents cultural interpretations of religion as one way of finding common ground for this adaptation.

t: Reflections and proposals on strengthening atheism research, propaganda and education
zh: 关于加强无神论研究宣传教育的思考和建议
paras: This is the text of a speech given by Jia Runguo, a deputy director of the Religion Research Centre of the State Administration for Religious Affairs, at a symposium on atheism research, propaganda and education. The symposium was convened by the general office of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences on 15 February 2009.
