Jia argues that the Party's two basic points on religion, freedom of religious belief and sustained atheist education, are meant to go together. In Jia's view the second has been neglected over thirty years.

The speech opens with the record since the early 1980s. Jia cites the 1982 Central Committee Document No. 19 and statements by Deng Xiaoping and Jiang Zemin, and notes that Hu Jintao's remarks on atheism were not made public. It then asks which bodies are responsible and moves to proposals on philosophy teaching, research institutions and the publication of atheist works.

Jia says that belief in religion has become freer and more widespread while atheist work has shrunk. According to Jia, no research institution for atheism exists, and only one journal, Science and Atheism, is run on a part-time basis. Responsibility has been divided among the religious affairs bureau, the Party's propaganda department and the education ministry, and none of them gives atheism priority. Jia argues that philosophy teaching must refute idealism, metaphysics and theism as well as set out materialism, dialectics and atheism, and that Marxist philosophers need to study religious theism. Drawing on the Marxist view of religion, Jia treats natural, social and epistemological roots of religion. Jia holds that private ownership remains the deepest social root, and that this explains why religion thrives in technologically advanced Western countries and why secularisation theory failed. Jia also rejects the claim that atheism has no audience, since most people hold ambiguous beliefs and turn to faith in a crisis.

Jia proposes dedicated Marxist research bodies, for example a research office on materialism and atheism within the Academy's Institute of Marxism or a Marxist-view-of-religion office in the Institute of World Religions. Jia also proposes translating Enlightenment and modern atheist works with attractive packaging, state funding for the work, and expert studies of present-day forms of theism. Jia treats the last as the most practical task to start with. Read the original if you want a first-hand statement, from an official researcher in 2009, of the case for reviving state-backed atheist education in China and of the institutional arrangements proposed.
quoteEn: However deep theism goes, atheism goes just as deep, or even deeper.
quoteZh: 有神论有多深，无神论就有多深，甚至比它还深。

glossary.explanation: The policy, set out in the Chinese constitution and in Document No. 19 of 1982, that citizens may choose whether to hold a religious faith. Jia treats it as one of the Party's two basic points on religion.
A 1982 Central Committee document on religious work that restored the policy of religious freedom after the Cultural Revolution. It also called for science education and atheist propaganda.

t: Reflections and proposals on strengthening atheism research, propaganda and education
zh: 关于加强无神论研究宣传教育的思考和建议
paras: This is the text of a speech by Jia Runguo, deputy director of the Religion Research Centre of the State Administration for Religious Affairs. Jia delivered it on 15 February 2009 at a symposium on atheism research, propaganda and education, organised by the General Office of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. The speech was posted online in 2011. Jia argues that the Party's two basic points on religion, freedom of religious belief and atheist propaganda and education, are out of balance, because the second has been neglected over the past thirty years.

Jia starts from the Marxist view of religion, citing Marx, Engels, Lenin and later Party leaders, and from Document No. 19 of 1982. Jia then describes how the tasks have been divided among departments: the religious affairs bureau manages affairs, the propaganda department promotes the scientific outlook and the education ministry trains specialists. Jia reports that bodies and people studying or promoting theism are numerous, while no institution studies atheism and only one journal, Science and Atheism, is devoted to it. The remaining sections address philosophy teaching, the roots of religion, institutional arrangements and methods of dissemination.

Jia's central claim is that, in the division of labour, atheism research and propaganda has fallen between departments and gradually come to nothing. The remedy lies first in philosophy education: textbooks should not only set out materialism and dialectics but also refute idealism, metaphysics and theism, including Christian and Buddhist forms, so that students can discriminate and resist. Jia restates the Marxist account of religion's natural, social and cognitive roots, and holds that private ownership is the deepest root of modern religion. On that basis Jia criticises secularisation theory for overlooking this root and contends that atheism is as demanding a subject as theism and cannot be treated as simple.

Jia proposes specialised institutions, such as a research office on Marxist materialism and atheism within the Academy's Institute of Marxism or a Marxist view of religion office in the Institute of World Religions. Jia also calls for large-scale translation and attractive repackaging of Enlightenment and atheist works, state funding to counter foreign-funded theist publishing, and expert study of how theism currently spreads. Jia also urges wider scientific and psychological education. Read the original if you want a candid, insider account from 2009 of how a state religious-affairs researcher framed the neglect of atheist education and what institutional remedies were proposed.
quoteEn: However deep theism runs, atheism runs as deep, or even deeper.
quoteZh: 有神论有多深,无神论就有多深,甚至比它还深。

glossary.explanation: The official policy that citizens may hold or not hold a religious faith. Party documents treat it as one of two basic points of Marxist policy on religion, alongside atheist education.
Party-led efforts to spread a materialist, non-theistic worldview, especially among young people. In Chinese usage 宣传 (propaganda) is a neutral term for public dissemination.
A 1982 Central Committee document on religious work, issued after the Cultural Revolution. It restored the policy of religious freedom and also called for scientific and atheist education.
The Marxist-Leninist account of religion's nature, origins and decline, tied to social conditions such as class society and private ownership. It is the framework for official policy on religion.

t: Promoting religious harmony and serving scientific development
st: A review of religious work during the 11th Five-Year Plan period
zh: 促进宗教和谐 服务科学发展
paras: Published in 2011, this unsigned official-style review assesses religious work during the 11th Five-Year Plan period (2006–2010). It argues that, guided by the Scientific Outlook on Development, religious work promoted harmony in religious relations and made a positive contribution to economic development and a harmonious society.

The article is organised in five parts: deepening understanding of religious questions; raising the standard of administering religious affairs according to law; strengthening patriotic religious organisations; encouraging the religious community to play a more active role; and developing religious exchanges abroad. It closes with lessons from the period and tasks for the 12th Five-Year Plan.

The article claims that the Party leadership under Hu Jintao deepened its understanding of religion. It cites the 17th Party Congress (2007), which reaffirmed the basic policy on religious work: freedom of religious belief, administration of religious affairs according to law, independence and self-management, and guiding religion to adapt to socialist society. On the legal side, it reports that the Regulations on Religious Affairs were implemented through supporting rules from the State Administration for Religious Affairs, and that 17 provinces, regions and municipalities made or revised local rules. It also states that clergy were brought into the social security system. It describes patriotic religious bodies as bridges between the Party and believers, and lists their doctrinal and organisational work. It gives examples of the religious community's role in disaster relief, major events and charity, and of its engagement in international dialogue, including exchanges with Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan. It also says Chinese delegations rebutted Western criticism of China's religious freedom in human rights dialogues.

The article concludes that effective religious work requires adherence to the Scientific Outlook on Development, a firm Marxist view of religion, service to the overall interests of the Party and state, full implementation of the basic policy and the Regulations, and an innovative response to new problems. For the 12th Five-Year Plan it calls for continued reliance on Deng Xiaoping Theory and the Three Represents, for mobilising religious figures and believers, and for promoting harmony in religious relations. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese discourse summarised religious policy and its achievements in 2011.
quoteEn: Doing good work among believers is the fundamental task of religious work.
quoteZh: 做好信教群众工作是宗教工作的根本任务。

glossary.explanation: Guiding concept associated with Hu Jintao, written into the Party constitution in 2007. It stresses comprehensive, balanced and sustainable development with people at the centre.
State Council regulations on religious affairs, issued in 2004 and effective from 2005. They set out rules for religious organisations, venues, clergy and property.

Theory associated with Jiang Zemin, introduced around 2000. It holds that the Party represents advanced productive forces, advanced culture and the interests of the overwhelming majority of the people.
Policy goal promoted under Hu Jintao from 2004–2006, aiming to ease social tensions and balance interests in socialist construction.
China's national development plan for 2006–2010. Five-year plans set economic and social targets for each period.

t: Promoting religious harmony and serving scientific development
st: Religious work during the Eleventh Five-Year Plan period
zh: 促进宗教和谐 服务科学发展
paras: Published in 2011, this official-style review takes stock of religious work in China during the Eleventh Five-Year Plan period (2006–2010). It argues that, guided by the Scientific Outlook on Development, the Party's religious work promoted harmonious relations among religions, mobilised religious figures and believers, and so contributed to development and a harmonious society. The author is not named.

The article is organised in five sections: deepening understanding of religious questions; raising the level of law-based administration of religious affairs; strengthening patriotic religious bodies; encouraging religious circles to play a more active role; and developing religious exchanges abroad. It then draws lessons from the period and sets out requirements for the Twelfth Five-Year Plan period. Evidence is mostly descriptive: regulations issued, campaigns run, disaster-relief efforts and overseas events.

The central claim is that the Party's basic policy on religion, in four elements, was the guiding framework: freedom of religious belief, administering religious affairs according to law, adherence to independence and self-management of religion, and actively guiding religion to adapt to socialist society. The author reports that the Regulations on Religious Affairs produced supporting rules from the State Administration for Religious Affairs, local regulations in 17 provinces, and a developing legal system. The article says religious clergy were brought into social security. It also reports religious bodies' efforts to draw out doctrinal content suited to the times, the "harmonious temples, monasteries, mosques and churches" campaign, and training of younger patriotic clergy. Religious circles are credited with disaster relief, support for the Beijing Olympics and the Shanghai World Expo, and charity. The author further describes exchanges with Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan and engagement in human-rights dialogues, where the author says Western criticism of China's religious freedom was refuted.

The author concludes that religious work must keep to the Scientific Outlook on Development, a firm Marxist view of religion and service to the overall interests of the Party and state. It must also grasp the basic laws of religion and respond to new problems innovatively. For the Twelfth Five-Year Plan period, the article calls for continued guidance by Deng Xiaoping Theory and the Three Represents, better policy and stronger management, and the mobilisation of religious figures and believers. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official sources in 2011 presented religious policy and its rationale.
quoteEn: Working well with believing masses is the fundamental task of religious work.
quoteZh: 做好信教群众工作是宗教工作的根本任务。

glossary.explanation: Hu Jintao's guiding concept, written into the Party constitution in 2007, stressing people-centred, comprehensive and sustainable development.
A social goal promoted under Hu Jintao from the mid-2000s, emphasising balanced relations among social groups and interests.
Jiang Zemin's theory, holding that the Party represents advanced productive forces, advanced culture and the fundamental interests of the majority.

glossary.en: the Party's basic policy on religion
glossary.explanation: The four-part formulation of religious policy affirmed at the 17th Party Congress (2007): religious freedom, law-based management, independence and self-management, and adaptation to socialist society.
State Council regulations on religious affairs, issued in 2004, which set the legal framework for administering religious bodies, sites and clergy.

t: Intelligent Design theory: the latest version of creationism
zh: 创世论的最近版本
paras: Cai Zhong examines the American Intelligent Design (ID) movement, which the article presents as the newest form of creationism. ID holds that complex, information-rich biological structures cannot arise from natural forces and require a supernatural intelligence. Cai argues that the movement uses the neutral word 'design' to avoid terms such as 'God' and 'creation' and so get past legal barriers to religious teaching in schools. The article also argues that its rise is tied to relativism in recent philosophy of science.

The article has two main parts and a short conclusion. The first part traces the movement's origins with the law professor Phillip Johnson in the 1990s. It then covers its 'wedge' strategy, its funding through the Discovery Institute's Center for the Renewal of Science and Culture, and its legal struggles, from early anti-evolution statutes through the 1987 Edwards v. Aguillard ruling to the 2005 Kitzmiller v. Dover case. The second part reflects on the movement's intellectual background.

Drawing on Barbara Forrest, Cai describes the wedge strategy as a three-step plan: research, shaping public opinion, then cultural confrontation. The article reports Forrest's literature searches, which found no ID research papers in biology journals, and concludes that the strategy failed in the scientific sphere. It also reports that the movement pressed on with lobbying, publishing and educational campaigns, until Judge Jones's 2005 ruling that teaching ID in public-school science classes was unconstitutional. In the second part Cai argues that Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions and later social constructivism, including David Bloor's symmetry principle, gave creationists an opening. In this reading, science and creation 'science' became rival, incommensurable paradigms and the dispute became a contest for cultural authority.

Cai concludes that methodological naturalism cannot build a firm wall between science and religion. Postmodern relativism, in Cai's view, swings to the opposite absurdity, and both discuss science and religion in the abstract, detached from scientific practice. The article proposes comparing the actual practice of evolutionary biology with that of creation science, so as to identify creationism's non-scientific character and draw a real line between science and religion. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosopher's account of the ID movement, the Dover trial and the link between constructivist science studies and creationism.
quoteEn: We hold that methodological naturalism cannot erect a solid wall between science and religion, while postmodern relativism goes to the other, absurd extreme.
quoteZh: 我们认为方法论自然主义无法在科学与宗教之间立起一堵坚实的墙，而后现代相对主义却走向了另一荒谬的极端

t: The latest version of creationism: Intelligent Design theory
zh: 创世论的最近版本
paras: Cai Zhong examines Intelligent Design (ID) theory, which the article calls the late-twentieth-century version of creationism. It asks how the ID movement tried to enter American science education and why it arose. The author argues that ID is a religiously motivated political and cultural project, not a scientific theory. They also argue that it drew on the relativism of late philosophy of science.

The article opens with the 2002 resolution of the American Association for the Advancement of Science against teaching ID as science. Part one traces the movement's origins with the law professor Phillip Johnson and the Discovery Institute's Center for the Renewal of Science and Culture. It then covers the "wedge" strategy, its funding, and the legal contests from the 1925 Tennessee law to Edwards v. Aguillard (1987) and the Kitzmiller v. Dover trial (2005). Part two reflects on the movement's intellectual background, and a short conclusion follows.

Cai first presents the wedge strategy as a three-stage plan: research programmes, opinion-shaping, and cultural confrontation, including removing legal barriers to classroom teaching. Citing Barbara Forrest's database searches, the article reports that no peer-reviewed biological work supporting ID could be found, so the research stage failed. Judge Jones's 2005 ruling then ended the attempt to enter public schools. In the second part, Cai links ID to the collapse of logical empiricism's demarcation project after Kuhn, and to the social constructivism of David Bloor's symmetry principle. In this reading, creationists can present science and creationism as incommensurable paradigms with equal standing, and Johnson frames the dispute as a clash of stories and worldviews.

Cai concludes that the court defeat does not end the conflict between creationism and evolution. Methodological naturalism cannot build a firm wall between science and religion, and postmodern relativism lurches to the opposite extreme. Both discuss science and religion abstractly, apart from scientific practice. Cai proposes comparing the actual practice of evolutionary biology with that of creation science to identify the latter's non-scientific character and draw a real boundary. Read the original if you study the ID movement, the American legal history of the evolution dispute, or the way Chinese philosophers of science criticise social constructivism.
quoteEn: Social constructivism has a strongly relativist colouring; it directly gave creationism an opportunity to appear in the name of science and forms the theoretical basis of creation science.
quoteZh: 社会建构主义带有强烈的相对主义色彩，它直接为创世论以科学的名义出现提供了一个契机，并构成了创世科学的理论基础。

t: The social cost of religious belief: the cases of Gannan and Linxia prefectures in Gansu
zh: 宗教信仰的社会代价——以甘肃甘南和临夏两州为例
paras: Writing in 2011, Liu Xiaoxiong asks how religion affects economic and social development in minority regions where belief is intense. The article acknowledges religion's positive historical role, especially for people's spiritual lives. Its thesis, however, is that where religion has not developed reasonably or adapted to society, it becomes an important cause of backwardness. Liu focuses on the Tibetan Gannan and Hui Linxia autonomous prefectures in Gansu, where the author says nearly the whole population believes.

The article first notes that five of Gannan's eight county-level units, and all but one of Linxia's, are national-level poor counties. It concedes that geography, climate, transport and history also contribute. It then sets out five channels of what it calls religion's inhibiting effect: consumption of people, materials and money; occupation of land; consumption of time and energy; and constraint on thinking, followed by a conclusion. Liu draws on provincial statistics on religious venues, clergy and believers, and on one cited economic argument by Robert Barro.

Liu's core reasoning is economic. Building and maintaining venues, supporting clergy who do not take part in production, and funding rituals and festivals all rely on donations from local believers. Liu calls this non-productive, parasitic consumption that moves wealth out of production and blocks accumulation and expanded reproduction. The author points to magnificent temples beside shabby homes as evidence. Religious sites are also said to take good land and to disrupt planning, and daily worship is said to take time from productive work. Liu adds that religious teaching disparages the pursuit of wealth and so saps believers' drive. The article also says some clergy, encouraged by foreign anti-China forces, have caused unrest, and cites the 2008 and 2009 incidents.

Liu concludes that inappropriate religious burdens are one cause, among several, of low living standards and lagging development in believing regions. The author calls on the state, government, religious circles and society to guide religion under the Scientific Outlook on Development. The aim is to minimise its negative effects and help it adapt to Chinese society and contribute to a harmonious society. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese sociologist in 2011 framed the economic burden of religion in minority regions, or if you study official-era discourse on religion and poverty.
quoteEn: Religious consumption is a form of non-productive consumption with a strongly parasitic character, relying mainly on almsgiving by believers.
quoteZh: 宗教消费是一种非生产性消费，具有很强的寄生性，主要依赖于信徒布施。

glossary.explanation: A guiding concept of the Hu Jintao era, written into the Party constitution in 2007. It stresses people-centred, comprehensive and sustainable development.
A policy goal promoted from the early 2000s under Hu Jintao. It stresses social stability and balanced development and the easing of social tensions.

t: The social cost of religious belief: the cases of Gannan and Linxia prefectures in Gansu
zh: 宗教信仰的社会代价——以甘肃甘南和临夏两州为例
paras: Writing in 2011, Liu Xiaoxiong asks how religion affects economic and social development in ethnic-minority areas where belief is intense. The article acknowledges that religion has had positive effects on society and on people's spiritual lives. Its thesis, however, is that where religion has not developed reasonably or adapted to society, it becomes an important cause of regional backwardness and imposes a heavy 'social cost' on believers.

The study is built on two autonomous prefectures in Gansu: Gannan (mainly Tibetan, Buddhist) and Linxia (mainly Hui, Muslim), where Liu says almost the entire population is religious. Liu notes that five of Gannan's eight county-level units, and all but one in Linxia, are national-level poverty counties. Liu grants that geography, climate, transport and history also contribute, but argues that heavy investment of hope and resources in religion deepens the poverty. The analysis rests on provincial statistics on religious venues, clergy and believers, plus the author's observations.

Liu sets out four channels of inhibition. First, religion consumes people, materials and money: lavish construction and upkeep of temples, mosques and shrines, support for over 20,000 clergy who do not take part in production, and ritual activity, all funded by donations. Liu calls this non-productive, 'parasitic' consumption that hinders productive accumulation and expanded reproduction, citing the contrast between magnificent religious buildings and dilapidated believers' homes. Second, religious sites occupy farmland and building space and cause planning disputes. Third, devotional practice absorbs time and energy. Fourth, Liu claims that religion's inherent aversion to the pursuit of profit breeds contentment with the present or hope for the afterlife, and so weakens enterprise.

Liu concludes that these constraints reach every part of religious communities' social life and that improper religious burdens are one cause of low living standards, though not the only one. Liu also links some clergy to the unrest of 14 March 2008 and 5 July 2009, attributing it to hostile forces at home and abroad. Under the Scientific Outlook on Development, Liu calls on the state, government, religious circles and society to guide religion so as to minimise its negative effects and fit it to a harmonious, sustainable society. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese sociologist in 2011 framed religion's economic costs in Tibetan and Hui areas, and the official language used to do so.
quoteEn: Religious consumption seriously hinders productive accumulation, hinders the expansion of reproduction, and even hinders the development of the productive forces.
quoteZh: 宗教性消费严重地妨碍了生产性积累，妨碍了再生产的扩大，乃至妨碍了生产力的发展。

glossary.explanation: A guiding concept of Party policy associated with Hu Jintao, put forward in the early 2000s, stressing balanced, people-centred and sustainable development.

t: A brief discussion of the basic spirit of Hobbes's religious theology
zh: 略论霍布斯宗教神学的基本精神
paras: The article asks what role religion and theology play in the thought of Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), the English materialist philosopher and political thinker. It points out that roughly half of Leviathan (Parts III and IV) deals with religion, with more than 700 direct citations of the Bible. The author's thesis is that Hobbes built a distinctive system of religious thought in which he exposed the falsity of religious belief and tried to overturn its theoretical foundations, while also offering valuable arguments on the unity of religion and politics and on the rational construction of social order.

The article is organised in four sections after a short introduction. It treats in turn Hobbes's critique of the essence of theology; the philosophy he built in opposition to theology; the "isomorphic unity" of religion and politics; and the role of reason in constructing social order. It draws mainly on Leviathan in the Chinese Commercial Press translation, on a Chinese anthology of Western philosophical texts, and on two Chinese journal articles. The setting is the English bourgeois revolution, the restoration, and the advance of the natural sciences.

The author argues that Hobbes, starting from materialist principles, treated belief in God, angels and spirits as the product of ignorance of natural causes, cultivated by rulers for their own purposes. He reinterpreted the Bible rationally, defined spirit as a thin, invisible body, and transferred the authority to judge miracles from the Church to the sovereign. His slogan that philosophy excludes theology is read as the basic principle of his atheism. The author also argues that Hobbes saw religion and politics as both founded on fear and obedience to power, so that religion is necessarily political. His contractual account of the state, in which government and royal power come from human transfer rather than divine grant, is said to strip the state of its religious cloak. His account of reason, equal in all people and leading them from the state of nature through natural law to contract, is presented as an expression of the same project.

The author concludes that Hobbes's critique greatly liberated thought and secularised political theory, giving later thinkers an important foundation. The author also lists limits: his mechanical materialism, his generalised view of human nature as selfish, his fragmented epistemology, his lack of dialectics, and a continuing use of theological arguments. The author also warns against blind faith in reason, since social order is tied to tradition, custom and culture. The author notes the dispute over whether Hobbes defended Christianity or covertly undermined it. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language overview of how Hobbes's religious thought is assessed from a materialist and atheist standpoint.
quoteEn: Hobbes applied rationalist principles to give religious theology a wholly new interpretation and launched a merciless critique of Christianity, which under the social conditions of the time undoubtedly played a great role in liberating thought.
quoteZh: 霍布斯运用理性主义原则对宗教神学进行了全新的解释，对基督教展开了无情的批判，这在当时的社会条件下，无疑起到了巨大的思想解放作用

t: A brief discussion of the basic spirit of Hobbes's religious theology
zh: 略论霍布斯宗教神学的基本精神
paras: The article asks what Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) was doing in the religious sections of Leviathan, roughly half of which, the author notes, deals with religion and cites the Bible more than 700 times. Its thesis is that Hobbes built his own religious-theological system with two sides: a materialist and atheist critique that exposes the falsity of religious belief, and a set of reasoned, valuable arguments linking theology to politics, social order and philosophy. The author presents him as a materialist thinker who nonetheless remained bound by his era.

The text has four numbered sections. The first treats Hobbes's exposure and criticism of the nature of religious theology. The second deals with the philosophy he built on opposition to theology, including its weaknesses. The third examines the structural unity of religion and politics. The fourth discusses how theology bears on the rational construction of social order. It places Hobbes against the English bourgeois revolution, the restoration of the monarchy and the advance of natural science, and closes with an overall assessment.

On religion, the author argues that Hobbes, starting from materialist principles, treated belief in God, angels and souls as the product of ignorance of natural causes and of rulers' cultivation of religion. He attacked the Roman Curia and reinterpreted spirit as a rarefied bodily substance. He also moved the authority to judge miracles from the Church to the sovereign. The author holds that Hobbes's formula 'philosophy excludes theology' is the clearest mark of his atheism. The author also faults his philosophy for mechanistic materialism, a simplified view of human nature and a lack of dialectics. In politics, Hobbes saw both religion and the state as grounded in fear and obedience to power, and derived government from contract rather than divine will. Even so, the author says, he still used theological arguments, and scholars disagree about whether he was defending or undermining Christianity. His account of reason as the basis of the state, through the state of nature, natural law and contract, is said to have removed divine authority from social order.

The author concludes that Hobbes liberated thought from Christian theology, secularised political theory and launched a new philosophical revolution, laying a foundation for later thinkers. The author adds that his reliance on reason has limits, since social order is also tied to tradition, custom and culture. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language overview of Hobbes's critique of religion and its place in his politics, written from a Marxist-materialist standpoint.
quoteEn: The proposition that 'philosophy excludes theology' is the most distinct mark and basic principle of Hobbes's atheist system.
quoteZh: “哲学排除神学”这一命题是霍布斯无神论体系最鲜明的标志与基本原则。

t: Reflections on firmly establishing the Marxist view of religion
zh: 关于牢固树立马克思主义宗教观的思考
paras: This text is the edited script of a lecture by Jia Runguo, delivered in May 2010 at the State Administration for Religious Affairs and again in June 2010 at a Marxist view of religion symposium at the CASS Institute of World Religions. Jia responds to Hu Jintao's call, made at the Fourth Plenum of the 17th Central Committee (2009), to "firmly establish the Marxist view of religion". Jia argues that two questions must be settled first: how to regard the Marxist view of religion, and how to understand and grasp it.

Jia opens by tracing how, since the 1980s, liberalisation, the collapse of the Soviet bloc and later neoliberalism, social democracy and historical nihilism are said to have weakened the guiding position of Marxism. In this climate, idealist views of religion were popular while research and teaching on the Marxist view were neglected. Part one takes on three objections, and part two sets out three principles of understanding, with extended quotations from Marx, Engels, Lenin and Party leaders from Deng Xiaoping to Hu Jintao.

Jia labels the three objections the "outdated" view, the "school" view and the "different" view. The "outdated" view holds that a revolutionary party's doctrine no longer suits a ruling party. The "school" view treats Marxism as one school among many, which Jia says amounts to pluralising the guiding ideology. The "different" view separates Chinese Party theory from Marxism-Leninism, for example by reducing Lenin to an "opium theory" and a "struggle theory". In reply, Jia says the real dividing line in religious studies is theism versus atheism, and that Party members must be atheists and atheist propaganda must continue. Jia adds, citing Lenin, that such propaganda must serve the Party's basic task and must not become its priority, and that religious freedom protects believers and non-believers alike. Jia also distinguishes a broad sense of Marxist view of religion (Marx to Hu Jintao as one continuous system) from a narrow one.

Jia concludes that the view to be established is the broad, unified system: materialism and atheism, a dialectical and historical-materialist attitude that unites believers and non-believers, and continuity combined with keeping pace with the times. Jia calls for atheism to be treated as a third basic philosophical pair, alongside materialism versus idealism and dialectics versus metaphysics, and for the Party's basic policy on religious work to be carried out in full. Read the original if you want a detailed account, from a Chinese official researcher writing in 2010, of how Party theorists defend the Marxist line on religion and atheist propaganda against rival interpretations.
quoteEn: The Marxist view of religion is a thoroughgoing scientific atheist view of religion, whose philosophical foundation is dialectical materialism and historical materialism.
quoteZh: 马克思主义宗教观是彻底的科学无神论宗教观，其哲学基础是辩证唯物主义和历史唯物主义。

glossary.explanation: The body of Marxist theory on the nature, origins and social role of religion, and the Party's attitude towards it. In Chinese Party usage it also covers the religious policies built on that theory.
The constitutional and Party policy that citizens may believe or not believe in religion. The author pairs it with the Party's continued promotion of atheism.

t: Reflections on firmly establishing the Marxist view of religion
zh: 关于牢固树立马克思主义宗教观的思考
paras: This text is the published version of a lecture by Jia Runguo, a researcher at the State Administration for Religious Affairs. It was first given on 14 May 2010 at the Administration's first "Religious Work Forum" and then, revised, at a Marxist view of religion symposium held on 5–6 June 2010 at the CASS Institute of World Religions. Jia responds to Hu Jintao's call, at the Fourth Plenum of the 17th Central Committee (2009), to "firmly establish the Marxist view of religion". Jia argues that this requires settling two questions: how to regard the Marxist view of religion, and how to understand and grasp it.

Jia begins with the background: liberalisation in the 1980s, the collapse of the Soviet bloc, and the spread of neoliberalism, social democracy and historical nihilism, which Jia says have shaken Marxism's guiding position while idealist views of religion gained popularity. The first part rebuts three views Jia thinks obstruct the task: the "outdated" thesis, the "school" thesis and the "difference" thesis. The second part sets out three principles for understanding the Marxist view of religion.

Jia's central claim is that the Marxist view of religion is a single, complete system of scientific atheism running from Marx and Engels through Lenin to Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. Treating it as outdated, as one school among many, or as divided into mutually opposed stages is, in Jia's reading, a way of removing its guiding status. Jia adds a "third pair" of basic philosophical questions, theism versus atheism, to materialism versus idealism and dialectics versus metaphysics. Jia holds that the Party must uphold and propagate atheism while the state guarantees freedom of religious belief. Citing Lenin's "The Attitude of the Workers' Party to Religion", Jia adds that atheist propaganda must be subordinate to the Party's basic task and must not be given first place.

Jia concludes that the view to be established is the broad one, combining the classical texts with the Party's policies and innovations since reform and opening up, not only the post-1978 statements. Jia also urges that atheism be taught systematically, including in philosophy textbooks, because theism is spreading. Jia also calls for protecting believers' legal rights and drawing them into socialist construction. Read the original if you want an official-academic statement of how Chinese religious-policy researchers in 2010 justified atheist propaganda alongside religious freedom, with extensive quotation from Lenin, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao.
quoteEn: Introducing pluralism of guiding thought into the religious field is in essence a way of using theistic views of religion, or incompletely atheist ones, to offset and even replace the Marxist scientific-atheist view of religion, which is thoroughly materialist.
quoteZh: 在宗教领域搞指导思想多元化，实质是用有神论宗教观或不彻底的无神论宗教观抵消乃至取代马克思主义彻底唯物主义的科学无神论宗教观。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official body of theory on the nature, origins and social role of religion, drawn from Marx, Engels and Lenin and later Chinese leaders. It underpins Chinese religious policy.
The Marxist form of atheism, which grounds the rejection of belief in supernatural powers in dialectical and historical materialism and in an account of religion's social roots.
The constitutional policy under which citizens may or may not believe in religion. Party members are nonetheless required to be atheists.

t: The religious market: open to whom?
zh: 宗教市场，对谁开放?
paras: This unsigned critical commentary, posted in 2011, asks what lies behind the adoption in China of the "religious market" theory (also called religious economies or rational-choice theory) associated with the American sociologist Rodney Stark. The article argues that the theory, which is used to study Christian "house churches", is not ideologically neutral. In the article's view, the call to "open the religious market" serves the interests of Western, mainly American, Christian influence, and China should reject it.

The article first outlines Stark and Roger Finke's theory, in which religious growth depends on free competition among religious "firms", and traces its introduction to China. It follows the Chinese translation of The Act of Faith (2004) and the annual summer seminars on the social-scientific study of religion that were organised at Renmin University of China. It then turns to Yang Fenggang's "three-colour market" model of red, black and grey religious markets. Its second half reviews Cold War religious politics, American religious-freedom policy, and Yang's own statements about Christianity and the market economy.

The author makes three main moves. First, the article presents house churches as a product of international politics. It cites Nixon, the alliance of Pope John Paul II and Reagan against communism in Poland, Albright's 1997 State Department document and the 1998 International Religious Freedom Act, and concludes that American attention to religion abroad is strategic rather than a matter of human rights. Second, it rejects Yang's claim that "the more plural religion is, the more harmonious society is", citing Philip Jenkins on Christian–Muslim conflict and pointing to India. It argues that an open market would not be equal, because global Christianity is dominant. Third, it says the American model is the product of American conditions, invokes the "cultural exception" and cultural diversity, and reads Stark's theory as reviving Weber's Protestant-ethic thesis as a value judgement. It also quotes a Chinese scholar's suggestion that Chinese scholars use the theory to criticise religious regulation indirectly.

The article concludes that China protects freedom of religious belief by law, that the five major religions coexist harmoniously, and that critics ignore the government's efforts while exaggerating "persecution". It also notes that European governments regulate religion without similar condemnation. It ends by echoing Putin's reply to Bush on democracy: if a religion is to be imposed on China and its market opened to it, "we do not want such a market". Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese critic in 2011 read the religious market theory and the house-church debate in terms of geopolitics and cultural security.
quoteEn: "The more plural religion is, the more harmonious society is" is in fact a specious, false proposition.
quoteZh: “宗教越多元，社会越和谐”其实是个似是而非的伪命题。

glossary.explanation: A sociological approach developed by Rodney Stark, Roger Finke and others from the 1980s. It treats religious choice and organisations in terms of supply, demand and competition, and was introduced to Chinese scholars in the 2000s.
Protestant congregations in China that meet outside the officially registered, state-recognised church organisations. Their status is politically sensitive.
Yang Fenggang's model dividing China's religious sphere into a red market (officially recognised), a black market (groups the state classes as "evil cults") and a grey market (ambiguous status).
A right guaranteed by China's constitution, which official discourse says is protected within a system of state religious administration and five recognised religions.
A principle, associated with France in trade negotiations, that cultural goods should be exempt from free-trade rules in order to protect national culture.

t: New features of religious activity in frontier ethnic regions and their impact on rural Party organisations and grassroots government
st: The case of Wuding County, Yunnan Province
zh: 边疆民族地区宗教活动新特征及其对农村基层党组织与基层政权建设的影响——以云南省武定县为例
paras: Writing in 2011, Xiao Sa asks how the spread of Christianity in poor frontier ethnic areas affects rural Party branches and grassroots government, taking Wuding County in Yunnan as a case. The article argues that religious organisations there hold superior resources and appeal. In some places, the author says, this leaves Party and government organs hollowed out, so that strengthening them is central to building a harmonious society in such regions.

The article opens with a profile of Wuding: a mountainous, poor, multi-ethnic county where, by the author's figures, 8.9 per cent of the population are religious believers and there are 227 religious venues. It then recounts the history of Protestant missions since 1905 and the emergence of unorthodox groups such as the "Small Group Religion". The second part analyses the impact on Party and government work, and the third describes Party-building measures taken by the county, under the guidance of the Scientific Outlook on Development.

Xiao's core argument has two strands. First, poverty and low education encourage the "localisation" and "abnormalisation" of religion: mission teaching, script creation and church schools, medical aid and public-works mobilisation, and foreign-funded church buildings. The author says these give churches the best broadcast equipment, the only public space and the strongest mobilising power, drawing young people away from scientific culture and the core socialist values. Xiao calls this a structural distortion and a challenge to the government's hold on popular support. Second, citing Marx, Engels and Lenin against "declaring war" on religion, the author proposes that the answer lies in development and in rebuilding Party organisations rather than in confrontation.

Xiao reports the county's measures: allowances for elderly rural Party members, activity rooms with flags and distance-education equipment, new village-group branches, increased branch funding, and the "three assets, dual management" and "three dual" systems. The author credits these with restoring branch cohesion, pride among members and better relations between cadres and villagers, and notes two national and provincial advanced-branch awards and rising peasant incomes. Read the original if you want a detailed local case study, from 2011, of how Party-building was used to answer church influence in a Yunnan border county.
quoteEn: In parts of Wuding County the church enjoys an advantage in people, money and material resources, so that the organisation with the greatest power to mobilise locally is neither the grassroots government nor the grassroots Party organisation, but the church.
quoteZh: 在武定县的部分地区，教会拥有人财物三方面的资源优势，使得在当地最有号召力的组织不是基层政府，也不是基层党组织，而是教会。

glossary.explanation: A guiding concept associated with Hu Jintao, written into the Party constitution in 2007. It stresses people-centred, comprehensive and sustainable development.
A policy goal promoted from the mid-2000s under Hu Jintao, emphasising social stability, balanced development and reduced social tensions.

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: An official value framework, formalised in the mid-2000s, that the Party presents as the ideological basis for education and cultural work.

t: New features of religious activity in border ethnic regions and their impact on rural Party organisations and grassroots government: the case of Wuding County, Yunnan
zh: 边疆民族地区宗教活动新特征及其对农村基层党组织与基层政权建设的影响——以云南省武定县为例
paras: Writing in 2011, during the Party's campaign to study and apply the Scientific Outlook on Development, Xiao Sa asks how the spread of Christianity in poor border ethnic areas affects rural Party branches and grassroots government. The article argues that where churches hold more people, money and cultural resources than village authorities, the Party's grassroots organisations are weakened. Xiao concludes that the remedy is to build up those organisations, not to confront religion.

The case is Wuding County, in the Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture of Yunnan. Xiao describes it as a mountainous, poor, multi-ethnic county where, by the article's figures, 52 per cent of the population are minorities and 8.9 per cent are religious believers. The article first sets out the history of Protestant missions there from 1905, then analyses the effects of religious change on Party and state organs, and finally describes the county's Party-building measures.

Xiao's central claim is that Christianity in Wuding has been localised and in places made "abnormal", producing groups such as the "Small Group Religion" that oppose Party policy and are open to infiltration by cults. Even ordinary church activity is said to challenge the grassroots. Churches run schools, medical aid and public-works labour where state services are thin, and they supply the main cultural space and equipment for young people. Xiao adds that overseas funding of church building shifts popular allegiance. The result, in Xiao's words, is a "structural distortion" and in some places hollowed-out village organisations, Fugong County being the most striking example.

Citing Engels, Lenin and Marx, Xiao rejects a campaign against religion and calls for development as the core response. Wuding's measures include allowances for elderly rural Party members, new Party activity rooms with flags and distance-education equipment, more branches, guaranteed funds, and the "three funds, dual management" and "three dualities" systems. Xiao reports that these have revived branch cohesion, improved cadre–mass relations and raised rural incomes. Read the original if you want a local case study of how a Party scholar in 2011 framed church influence as a problem of grassroots governance and presented Party-building as the response.
quoteEn: In parts of Wuding County, the church enjoys advantages in people, money and material resources, so that the organisation with the greatest local appeal is neither the grassroots government nor the grassroots Party organisation, but the church.
quoteZh: 在武定县的部分地区，教会拥有人财物三方面的资源优势，使得在当地最有号召力的组织不是基层政府，也不是基层党组织，而是教会。

glossary.explanation: A guiding concept associated with Hu Jintao, written into the Party constitution in 2007. It stresses people-centred, coordinated and sustainable development.
A system in which village funds, assets and resources are managed on the village's behalf by the township. Xiao presents it as a way of regulating rural finances.

t: A critique of Li Hongzhi's "view of science"
zh: 李洪志“科学观”评析
paras: This 2011 piece, published in the "Science and Atheism" column (co-sponsored by the China Anti-Cult Association), takes up the claim of Falun Gong's founder Li Hongzhi that "Falun Dafa" is a "supernormal science" and a "broad and profound science". The author, identified in the text as a researcher at the China Research Institute for Science Popularization, argues that this is not science in the modern sense but a mixture of supernatural tales and pseudo-scientific assertion.

The article begins by quoting Li's Zhuan Falun and related materials, in which Buddha-law is said to explain particles, the human body and the whole cosmos. It then offers three lines of critique: Li's self-aggrandisement and mystification, his double-sided treatment of modern science, and the \"evidence\" his followers cite, chiefly a natural nuclear reactor in Gabon and the Egyptian pyramids. It closes with a history of pyramidology, from Charles Piazzi Smyth to Erich von Däniken.

In the author's reading, Li uses two \"cards\". First, he exploits the real limits of science to declare modern science unscientific, which frees him to invent \"facts\" without proof, such as soul-travel into molten steel or a cyclically destroyed Earth. The author distinguishes this from the genuine limits of science, which lie in incomplete knowledge and practice and call for continued inquiry. Second, he relies on distorted or fabricated evidence. The Oklo reactor, the author says, was explained by Western scientists as a natural fission process, not a prehistoric human-built plant. The pyramids are dated to the Old Kingdom and are explained by human labour and ordinary design ideas, so the claimed mysteries, such as pi and the solar distance, are shown to be groundless.

The author concludes that Li's judgements on the pyramids and \"prehistoric civilisation\" have no basis in archaeology or science and are deceptive. Li's method is compared to what Lu Xun described in 1918: mixing ghost stories into science to muddy the distinction. Pyramid mysteries, the author adds, survive only because some people want to find religious inspiration or assert individuality. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese science-popularisation circles rebutted Falun Gong's scientific claims, and of the evidence they chose to contest.

quoteZh: 李洪志的这个“超常科学”、“博大精深的科学”，我们可以从以下几个方面来评析：

glossary.explanation: A qigong-based spiritual movement founded by Li Hongzhi in the early 1990s and banned in China in 1999, where it is officially labelled an "evil cult".
A Chinese state-linked organisation that campaigns against groups the authorities classify as cults, including Falun Gong.
